<meta>This page is a formal dedication following the title page. The editor, Venantius Mutius, addresses his friend and colleague Alexander de Bartolacis, framing the publication as a collaborative effort to improve medical education.</meta>

## Venantius Mutius of Camerino <note>A humanist scholar and editor active in the late 15th century.</note> sends many 
## greetings to Alexander de Bartolacis of Monteulmi <note>Now the town of Pollenza in Italy.</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a dragon or serpent-like creature entwined with stylized floral and foliage motifs.</image-desc>

I have recently undertaken, Alexander—best of friends and the honor and glory of your homeland—led by a concern for the common benefit of young students of medicine, the correction of two short works. They are most beautiful indeed, and extremely necessary to know; one of them is titled **On Pulses** and the other **On Urines**. When I wished to submit this correction of mine to the judgment of someone learned and skilled, you occurred to me as worthy of this evaluation. For I have long known the sharpness of your intellect, as well as your supreme diligence and expertise, both in all other matters and especially in this <term>art of healing</term> <note>Original: "medendi arte," referring to the practice of medicine.</note>. Added to this is our mutual love and goodwill, which has brought it about that I would rather undergo your examination than that of anyone else. For I know well that you, as becomes a true friend, are a stranger to all pretense and flattery, especially in this matter which, if correctly completed, I have no doubt will be both most useful and most welcome to student youths. Therefore, I ask you to read through these two short works and carefully weigh my <term>corrections</term> <note>Original: "castigationes," a term used by Renaissance humanists for the process of "cleansing" a text of errors introduced by previous medieval scribes.</note>; furthermore, correct them as you see fit, so that we may more boldly hand them over to the printers to be transcribed. Farewell.

<meta>This page begins the main text of the work by Gilles of Corbeil (Master Egidius), a 12th-century physician to the King of France. # On things to be considered in the judgment of urine 2

### The poems on the judgments of urines, published by the most excellent Lord Master Gilles, with his own commentary, here begin happily.

<image-desc>A large square woodcut initial 'I' featuring a physician or scholar wearing a flat cap and academic robes. He is seated and holding up a clear uroscopy flask (matula) toward the light to examine its contents. The letter 'I' forms the left vertical border of the scene.</image-desc>

This book of new instruction, composed with studious artistry, is drawn and brought forth from the sciences of the ancient authors. Within it, the secrets of <term>physical science</term> <note>Meaning "medicine" or "natural philosophy" in this context.</note> are revealed, and the hidden judgments of urines are contained. Indeed, because it lifts up and ennobles the mind of the reader, we have written it at the 

<margin>Definition of the art.</margin>
urgency of our friends. The traditions of the judgments of urines and the instructions are described metrically in this work. For a metrical speech, running with succinct brevity and bound by defined terms, is tied to certainty; therefore, it confirms the memory and strengthens the teaching. Truly, prose speech, escaping by its own freedom, disturbs the memory and gives birth to confusion in the ignorant. Hence, those who ought to be judged by certain reason at the time of recollection, and sealed with its character, rather desire the compendium of metrical brevity over the expense of prolix prose. Perhaps, therefore, a critic might accuse us of uncomposed verses and incongruity of meter. But let him consider that the law and reason for medical words is the cause; because the customary terms for urine in metrical speech can hardly be tamed even with great effort, and can scarcely be corrected to be constrained by the laws of meter. However, let those who are "wanderers" <note>Original: "planetici," referring to wandering, uneducated practitioners.</note> flee from this work, as they are imbued with the dregs of others; and let those who are strangers to the <term>teachings of Musandinus</term> <note>Refers to Petrus Musandinus, the teacher of Gilles of Corbeil at the famous medical school of Salerno.</note> stay away. To our companions of domestic faith, however, for whose sake we undertook this work, we offer this new instruction. ¶ This book is divided into two parts: namely, the first and the second. ¶ In the first part, it deals with the judgment of urines according to the knowledge of colors and substances. ¶ In the second, it deals with the judgments of urines according to the distinction of their contents <note>Original: "contentorum," referring to the sediment or particles visible in the urine.</note>.

### ¶ He provides the derivation of the name "urine."

> It is called **urina**, because it is **one** <note>Original: "una," creating a wordplay with "urina."</note> with the kidneys (**renibus**).
> Or from the Greek **uzith**, which is said to mean "demonstration."
> Or because it bites, dries, and **burns** <note>Original: "urit," another etymological pun.</note> that which it touches.
> As clear humor filters itself as **whey** from milk,
> So the liquid of urine comes from the mass of blood.
> Urine is the thin liquid whey of the blood,
> And of the humors, which the <term>governing art</term> <note>The "virtus regitiva," or the body's natural faculty for managing biological processes.</note> of the second digestion prepares.
> It is the prince of the work while the "sieving" of things occurs,
> While the pure part is separated from the impure.

<margin>Exposition.</margin>
¶ It is called urine. ¶ **A brief exposition.** In this book, the author, intending to hand down the teaching on urines, places the derivation of the name at the beginning. Therefore, urine, according to the meaning of those three verses, is derived in three ways. ¶ The first derivation is this: Urine is called as if it were "one with the kidneys," because it is formally generated in the kidneys, although it takes its beginning and substance in the <term>liver</term> <note>Original: "epate" (hepar).</note>. It takes its form in the 

<column-break/>

kidneys according to appearance, or because it more faithfully signifies the condition of the internal matters and other members. Therefore, this opinion is entirely true. ¶ **Or from "uzith."** ¶ The second derivation is placed in this verse, the meaning of which is this: Urine is named from *uzith* in Greek <note>This is a medieval false etymology; there is no such Greek word for "demonstration," though it was a common trope in medieval medical texts.</note>, which is "demonstration" in Latin, because through the urine itself the dispositions of the human body are demonstrated—such as health, sickness, and neutrality; fullness and emptiness, or the middle state, and similar things. ¶ **Or because that which it touches.** ¶ Here the third derivation of urine is placed, which is as follows: Urine is named from *uro, uris* [to burn], because it has the power of burning and drying. And therefore it is said to be effective against pustules, etc., as is expressly written in the commentary. ¶ **As whey from milk.** ¶ Here he places a certain similarity between whey and urine, so that the teaching on the essence of urine itself may be clearer. Namely, just as whey is separated from milk by the pressing out of the thick parts, so the liquid of urine is filtered from the mass of blood. ¶ **Urine is of the blood.** ¶ In this place, he provides the definition of urine, which is a definition taken from the *Urines* of <term>Isaac</term> <note>Isaac Israeli (c. 832–932), a highly influential Jewish physician and philosopher whose work on uroscopy was a standard textbook.</note>. Urine is the straining of the blood, etc.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **One with the kidneys:** because it is formally generated and discerned in the kidneys, although it first receives its substance and color in the liver according to its condition; however, it assumes its final form in the kidneys according to its appearance. Or it is said because it more faithfully announces the condition of things and of other members. Whence urine is called from *uzith* in Greek, which is the "demonstration of the interior members." Hence, when we seek certainty about the interior parts, we then consult the judgment of the urine. It is also named from "burning" (*urendo*), because it has a drying power. Hence it is effective against <term>creeping sores</term> <note>Original: "serpiginem," a general term for spreading skin diseases like ringworm or herpes.</note>, and against pustules, and against ulceration of the penis. Also, when the gall of a hawk is strained through a cloth, it removes spots; and when drunk, it benefits those with <term>spleen disorders</term> <note>Original: "spleneticis."</note>. ¶ **As whey from milk.** ¶ Here a similarity is noted between whey and urine, so that a more evident teaching may be completed concerning the essence of the similarity of urine. Just as whey is strained from milk by the pressing of the thick parts, so urine filters from the mass of blood. Whence <term>Theophilus</term> <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century Byzantine medical writer.</note> says: "Some have called it similar to whey." ¶ **Urine is of the blood.** What urine is, is thus defined in this place. ¶ The definition assigned here resonates well with the definition provided by Theophilus and Isaac in the *Book of Urines*, which is as follows: "Urine is the straining of the blood and other humors, born from the actions of nature." It is not truly whey, but a whey-like substance filtered from the blood. ¶ **Of the humors which the governing art prepares in the second [digestion].** That is, the governing power—namely, of the second digestion. **And it is the prince of the work while the sieving of things occurs.** That is, the sequestration; which sequestration occurs in the liver. For <term>phlegmatic matter</term>, generated in the first movement of boiling, is sent to the lungs to be converted into phlegm. <term>Choleric matter</term> [yellow bile] is transmitted to the gallbladder. <term>Melancholy</term> [black bile] is diverted to the spleen. <term>Sanguine matter</term> [blood] is refined and purified in the liver. But the watery substance—that is, the urine—is carried with the blood to the kidneys and sweats through the <term>urinary pores</term> <note>Original: "poros euritides," an old term for the passages leading to the bladder.</note> into the bladder.

### ¶ Things to be considered in the judgment of urine.

> The **quality**, **what**, or **in what way**; **how much**, **how often**, **where**, and **when**.
> **Age**, **nature**, **sex**, **labor**, **anger**, **diet**,
> **Medical care**, **hunger**, **motion**, **bathing**, **food**, **anointing**, **drink**—
> All these must be noted by the practitioner with certain reason,
> If you desire to be held as a learned judge of urine.
> Since four from the first [list] especially dominate,
> A more powerful judgment of the sentence ought to be taken from them.
> **Integrity**, **failure**, **vice**; whether it has **less** or **more**,
> And let the **middle status** be certain from this examination.

¶ **A brief exposition.** ¶ **Quality, what.** ¶ Here Gilles [Egidius] sets down the conditions for urines.

<sig>a 2</sig> <meta>catchword: Exposition.</meta>

It concludes by listing the clinical factors (such as age, diet, and emotional state) that a physician must consider when examining a patient's sample.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the instructional portion of Gilles of Corbeil's uroscopy treatise. <header>On Colors</header>

...which are required for the true judgment of urines, as is clearly declared in the commentary below. ¶ **Four from the first.** Here he shows which conditions the physician ought especially to consider. And he says: that the physician ought first and principally to attend to the first four conditions: namely, to color, substance, quantity, <note>The OCR repeats "quantitatem" (quantity), but the standard medical Four are Color, Substance, Quantity, and Contents.</note> and to the contents; for from these four conditions, since they are the substantial parts of urine, the best opinion for judging is taken. ¶ **Integrity.** Here he shows the utility gained from the judgment of urines, saying: that through the judgment of urine, the physician recognizes the health of a person, their sickness and "neutrality" <note>A middle state between health and illness.</note>, the strength or weakness of their <term>vital virtue</term> <note>The underlying life-force that governs bodily functions.</note>, emptiness or fullness, and a moderate habit of body; and this is the utility gained from the judgment of urine.
<margin>Pigment.</margin>
¶ **Lomentum.** <note>original: "Lomentum"; likely referring to a type of pigment or wash used to describe urine color.</note> ¶ **Of what kind.** He declares for himself the form of the description or speculation in another, or the intention of the title. For in this place he declares and shows which things are to be considered in the judgment of urine. For consideration must be had of the **color**, the **substance**, the **quantity**, and the **contents**. And these are the natural or substantial and intrinsic considerations which are weighed from the urine itself. There are also certain accidental or extrinsic qualities which are drawn from the properties of the patient, such as from age, <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, and others which follow. ¶ **Of what kind.** This refers to the quality, that is, the **color**. ¶ **What.** This refers to the **substance**. Therefore, the substance is diversified into thinness, thickness, and mediocrity [the middle state]. Thinness is divided into total thinness, and into moderate or slight thinness; thickness is divided into total thickness and mild thickness. ¶ **How in this.** This regards the difference of the **contents** [sediment]. ¶ **How much.** This pertains to the **quantity**. For quantity is divided into a multitude, a middle amount, and a small amount. ¶ **How often.** This pertains to the number of times it is poured out or inspected: namely, whether the urine was passed once or several times. For we are greatly instructed by the frequency or rarity of the urination, and we are more fully certified by the frequency of inspection. ¶ **Where.** This refers to the **place of collection**, which ought to be collected in a clear glass vessel made in the shape of a bladder <note>This vessel is called a "matula."</note>, so that through the quality of the vessel all parts of the urine may faithfully show themselves to the sight. ¶ **Where.** This also refers to the **place of inspection**, because it ought to be inspected in a place that is neither too radiant nor too dark. And if a ray of light is opposite, the hand should be placed in the way, so that the discernment of the contents is better made, lest the visual spirit be scattered by the radiance. ¶ **Where.** It can also be understood as the **position of the contents**: namely, whether the contents hold the top place in the urine, or the middle, or the bottom. ¶ **When.** This refers to the **time of passing**, which is in the morning hour, after digestion is completed. For then it is more faithful, and is a certain messenger of the internal members. ¶ Or "when" refers to the **time of inspection**: for it is to be inspected immediately, and if the opportunity is there, it is to be inspected a second or third time after it has settled and the vessel has been stopped up. For many times one urines thin [urine], and afterward it thickens, and conversely, many times it is thin and remains thin, as is read in Theophilus <note>Referring to Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century medical writer.</note>. ¶ **Age.** Because it ought to be one way in a child, another in an old person, and another in a youth, according to the intensity or lessening of heat. ¶ **Nature.** That is, as to the **complexion**: for in a choleric person it ought to be orange and thin; orange from heat, thin from dryness. In a phlegmatic person, it ought to be colorless and somewhat thick. In a melancholic person, it ought to be colorless and thin. In a sanguine person, colored and moderately thick. ¶ **Sex.** To distinguish between male and female. ¶ **Labor.** This pertains to the exercise of the body. For from labor, as the body is heated, the urine becomes colored; by "labor" its contrary is also understood, namely, rest. ¶ **Anger.** That is, fury of the mind; for anger pertains to the perturbation of the mind, by which the urine is changed. ¶ **Diet.** As to the administration of the six <term>non-natural things</term> <note>External factors like air, diet, and sleep that affect health.</note>, by all of which the urine is varied. ¶ **Care.** As to worry and sadness. ¶ **Hunger.** As to the lack of drink and food during fasting. ¶ **Motion.** As to the quantity of exercise,

<column-break/>

for in some exercise the body is moved more and in others less. ¶ **Bathing.** As to the difference of baths. For from a sulfurous or sea-water bath the urine is colored, and from a fresh-water bath it is discolored. ¶ **Food.** This changes the urine in quality and quantity. A great quantity of food discolors and makes the urine "crude" [undigested] by suffocating the natural heat. A small amount of food renders it intense by inducing dryness, from the "filing" of which the color is sharpened. As for quality: whether it be hot, cold, or dry; and also whether in substance it be subtle, gross, or middling. ¶ **Ointment.** As to salves; for instance, if one is anointed with laurel oil the urine becomes intense, or with "marciaton" [a specific ointment], or oil of henbane, by which the heat is lessened or increased. ¶ **Drink.** By its own quantity, quality, substance, and color it changes the urine. In quantity, if one has drunk much or little; in quality, if it was very hot or cold, and the like; in substance, if it was styptic [astringent] or diuretic and subtle—for by a subtle and diuretic drink the urine is multiplied, while by a styptic and gross one it is diminished. In color: as if it were red or white wine; for this kind of drink tints the urine and renders it blood-colored. Cooked: for a decoction of rhubarb or saffron renders it saffron-colored. ¶ **They ought by artistry.** That is, by a considerate and discreet physician. ¶ **Four from the first.** That is, four things considered, which we called "substantial." ¶ **Integrity.** Here he declares what utility is had from the judgment of urines. ¶ **Integrity.** As to health. ¶ **Lapse.** As to sickness or neutrality. ¶ **Vice.** As to the imperfection of bodily operations. ¶ **Virtue.** As to perfection. ¶ **Less.** As to diminishment [of fluids/humors]. ¶ **More.** As to repletion [fullness]. ¶ **Status.** As to the middle state. ¶ **From this examination.** That is, from the judgment of urine.

---

### On the colors of urine, and first regarding black.

---

-> Twenty colors can vary the urine, <-
-> Which you can weigh from the forms written below. <-
-> A blacker appearance of urine dissolves the troublesome <-
-> Quartan fever; it portends death; and it burns. <-
-> If a black humor residing at the bottom sinks itself, <-
-> The bilge of the womb is purged by a great flow. <-
-> In a fever, black, burning, scanty, and oily urine brings death, <-
-> When age and fault are removed from the matter. <-

---

¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **Twenty colors, etc.** After the author has taught us in general the conditions that are to be attended to in the judgment of urines and what they are, here he proceeds to one condition: namely, to the quality, showing how many colors of urine there are, which are twenty. But what they are will be declared below. ¶ **A blacker appearance of urine.** Here he proceeds to the colors of urine, and first regarding the color black. The meaning of these two verses is this: Black urine in color signifies three things. One: the solution and liberation from a <term>quartan fever</term> <note>A fever that returns every four days, often associated with malaria and "black bile."</note>, and especially if it is great in quantity. Another is that it signifies the mortification [death] of natural heat, and then it is black with a certain surrounding blackness, and then a "livid" [bluish-black] color precedes it. The third is that it signifies ultimate "adustion" [burning of humors], and such blackness is like polished horn, and then a green color precedes it. ¶ **If a black humor sinks to the bottom.** Here he puts another rule about the black color, and it pertains only to women, which is this: Whenever black urine appears to you with black sediment, it signifies the purgation of the menses, because the black and melancholic humor is poured out into the urine and turns it black. And it is to be noted: that such urine, through its settling [portends] death, etc. <note>original: "per residentiam mortem"</note> it is thickened at the top and the bottom. ¶ **In a fever it brings death, etc.** Another rule is put forward about black color. Whenever in an acute fever black urine appears in color, small in quantity, and foul-smelling...

<summary>This page details the specific factors a physician must observe when examining urine (uroscopy), including the 20 external factors that can change its appearance. It also begins the specific study of urine colors, starting with the grave significance of black urine, which can indicate either recovery from a long fever, impending death, or menstruation in women.</summary>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the specific diagnostic analysis of urine qualities, shifting focus from general principles to the classification of twenty distinct colors and the grave significance of black urine in various medical contexts.</meta>

# Urine

...foul in odor, and oily in substance: then you can undoubtedly judge death. However, this is provided that an ailment of the kidneys and loins is ruled out; for if there were a defect in the kidneys or in the bladder, the urine would be less suspicious <note>Meaning the abnormal urine would be a sign of a local organ problem rather than a systemic sign of approaching death.</note>. Therefore, such urine can appear from a suffering in the kidneys or in the bladder.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
**Commentary.** ¶ **Twice ten urines.** <note>original: "Bis deni vrinam"</note> In this chapter, the number of urine colors is distinguished. There are twenty in total. The description or distinction of colors is manifold. One distinction of color is made according to **qualities**; another according to the **nature of digestion** and <term>concoction</term> <note>The "cooking" or processing of food and humors by the body's natural heat</note>; and a third according to the **properties of the humors**. ¶ According to qualities, the distinction of colors is made as follows: some are intense, some are middling, and some are "remiss" <note>Pale or weak</note>. All those from "sub-citrine" and below are judged remiss. But all those from "reddish" and above are judged intense. Middling colors are citrine and sub-citrine, reddish and sub-reddish in a certain <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of humors in an individual</note>. ¶ According to the nature of digestion, this distinction of colors is made: some signify "mortification" <note>Death of tissue or the body</note>, such as black, green, and livid <note>Lead-colored or bluish-grey</note>. Others signify indigestion, such as white, milky, <term>glaucus</term> <note>A grey-blue or sea-green color</note>, and <term>caropos</term> <note>A color like that of a sea-eagle’s eye; a pale, glassy grey</note>. Others signify the beginning of digestion, but not perfectly, such as sub-pale and sub-citrine close to paleness. Others signify perfect digestion, such as citrine, reddish, and sub-reddish. Others signify an excess of digestion, such as sub-red, red, sub-rubicund, and rubicund. Others signify <term>adustion</term> <note>A "scorching" or overheating of the humors</note>, such as <term>onopos</term> <note>Wine-colored</note> and <term>kianos</term> <note>Deep blue</note>. Others signify extreme over-scorching and death, such as green and black. ¶ If it is objected that we began with black and ended with the same: ¶ We respond that the black color that arises from mortification (which happens because of coldness and the extinction of natural heat) is one thing; the blackness that arises from the highest and final scorching is another. Thus, the diversity of effects must be distinguished according to the diversity of causes.

¶ The distinction according to the humors is evident. For certain colors signify <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile</note>, some signify blood, others <term>melancholy</term> <note>Black bile</note>, and others <term>phlegm</term>. But to signify the humors, a combination of colors and substances must be made. ¶ The author treats black color in the first and last place, so that a progression may be made from colors signifying mortification (or the intensity of cold) to colors signifying scorching, passing through colors signifying a middle state. Thus, he reasonably proceeds from one extreme to the other. ¶ **Twice ten.** That is, twenty; what these colors are must be determined below. ¶ **Which.** That is, the colors. ¶ **From the written forms.** That is, the rules. ¶ **Blackness of urine, etc.** **Resolves the quartan.** <note>original: "Quartane soluit"</note> In this chapter, he treats black color for the reason aforementioned. Black color in urine can signify three things: either coldness (that is, mortification), and then the urine should be black with a certain surrounding darkness due to the extinction of natural heat, preceded by a livid color. Or it signifies complete and final scorching, and then it should be bright, like black polished horn; just as it appears on the faces of Ethiopians, in whom, because of scorching, a certain brightness is drawn to the face from the scorching and oiliness of the blood drawn there. <note>This reflects medieval physiological theories attempting to explain skin color through the "burning" of internal fluids.</note> Greenness preceding it is also a manifest sign that the succeeding blackness arises from the scorching of blood. Black color in urine signifies—especially in a **quartan fever** <note>A fever that spikes every fourth day, traditionally linked to black bile</note>—the resolution of the quartan and the purging of the melancholic humor, if the quantity is large. For melancholic matter is black and earthy, and by its mixing, it blackens the urine. I said "if the quantity is large" because the urine ought to be increased by a great purging. Therefore, if it appears in a small amount, it is suspicious. The text is plain. ¶ **Resolves.** That is, it signifies it is being resolved. ¶ **Portends death.** That is, it signifies mortification from intense cold, with lividness preceding. ¶ **Scorches the thing.** That is, it signifies scorching, with green preceding. ¶ **If black at the bottom.** Another rule for black color is given, and it is specifically for women and does not apply to other subjects. For black urine with black sediment appearing at the bottom signifies the purging of the menses from the eruption of black and

<column-break/>

melancholic humor. Hence the whole surface of the urine is sprinkled with a certain blackness; but such urine is thickened at the top by the settling and thinned at the bottom. ¶ **The womb purges.** That is, it signifies being purged. ¶ **Bilge.** <note>original: "Sentina"</note> That is, a pool or receptacle. For just as all superfluities run down to the bilge of a ship, so the superfluities of a woman's body are diverted to the womb as if to a certain bilge. ¶ **In fever it brings.** He posits another rule for black color. Black urine in color, small in quantity, foul-smelling, and oily—with nothing being wrong with the bladder—undoubtedly signifies death, once a defect of the kidneys and loins is ruled out. And I said this because such urine can appear from a defect of the kidneys or loins, and then it will be less suspicious. We take this rule from <note>Theosi.; likely Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century medical writer.</note> in the chapter on foul-smelling urine at the end of his work. For he says there: "Urine in an acute fever that is black, foul, and fatty—with nothing wrong with the bladder—signifies death." And he adds: "Urine having a heavy odor signifies mortification and putrefaction." In an acute fever, blackness brings death: that is, it signifies mortification. Black from mortification; foul from corruption; fatty (oily) from the melting of fat and substantial moisture.

### ¶ On black urine: which has a black cloud.

> Much on the critical day: when a black and hanging cloud
> More largely obscures, and disturbs the floating sediment.
> With ears oppressed and the peace of sleep disturbed
> It signifies a future bloody flow from the nostril.
> But if signs of death or health concur
> By judgment, it condemns the sick man to death or sets him free.

<margin>Expos.</margin>
**Exposition.** ¶ **Much on the day.** Here the author posits another rule for black urine; and he does not only mean that urine which is black throughout, but also that which has a black cloud. This is therefore the rule: Whenever you see urine black or blackish in color, large in quantity, with a high black <term>hypostasis</term> <note>Sediment that sinks to the bottom</note> or a floating one appearing on a **critical day** <note>A day when a disease's outcome is decided</note>, occurring during a burning fever with sleeplessness and deafness of the ears, then know that a future crisis is coming through a flow of blood from the nostrils, leading to health or death. To health if good signs accompany it; to death if bad signs accompany it. The reasons for these are given in the commentary; let these suffice for now.

<margin>Comment.</margin>
**Commentary.** ¶ **Much on the day.** He posits another rule for black or blackish urine. By black or blackish urine, we do not only mean that which is black through and through, but also that which has a black cloud, or a black or blackish <term>eneozima</term> <note>A cloud-like suspension in the middle or top of the urine</note>, from which the surface of the urine is blackened. This is the rule: Black or blackish urine, appearing in large quantity, and with a black, high, and floating hypostasis, holding the form of an eneozima, arriving on a critical day during a burning fever with sleeplessness and deafness, signifies a future crisis by a flow of blood from the nostrils toward health, if praiseworthy signs concur; but toward death if they are unpraiseworthy. ¶ **Much on the day.** By the fact that there was much urine on the critical day, it signifies that nature is moving on the day appointed for the crisis to purge the matter, and was strong enough to purge the matter through the urine; and therefore it was plenty. ¶ The eneozima was hanging in the middle; by this is signified the movement and disposition of the matter. That it is an eneozima indicates its lightness. That it is black signifies an excess of heat converting the matter into a certain scorching. But the scorching is shown not to be too violent when the eneozima is floating and high. For if the scorching were violent and final, it would consume the moisture and resolve nothing, and would take everything into windiness <note>gas or vapors</note>; which consumption would make the hypostasis sink rather than be high. ¶ Thus, much turbulent urine arriving on the seventh day signifies a resolution, etc.—a brief resolution. But a little signifies death on the seventh day.

->Gilles on Urines.<-

<meta>This page continues the specific diagnostic analysis of urine colors, focusing on the grave significance of black and livid (lead-colored) urine, citing authorities like Hippocrates, Galen, and Isaac Israeli to explain how these colors indicate various physical crises and the state of the body's humors.</meta>

### On Colors

In this case, since insomnia <note>original: "vigilie"</note> and deafness occur, it demonstrates that the material is ignited: and the sharp substance, resolved into smoke, ascends to the head; it induces the restlessness of insomnia and an impediment to hearing. And since this material is sharp and penetrating, it breaks the small veins of the nostrils: and breaking through them, it works to provoke a flow of blood from the nose by moving and reopening the passages. This same material, by its dryness and its sharpness, induces insanity by desiccating the brain. This same material also, exiting through the pores, pricks and stings the nerves in its passage and causes shivering; reaching even to the skin, it softens it and induces sweat. Hence it is that Isaac says in his *Book of Urines*: "Black or sub-black urines having <term>eneozimata</term> <note>Floating particles or sediment suspended in the middle or upper part of the urine</note> high up signify that a <term>crisis</term> <note>The turning point of a disease</note> will occur with shivering and sweat." Copious and black urine with sweat and insomnia, followed by black and floating <term>hypostasis</term> <note>Sediment that settles at the bottom</note>, signifies a bloody flow from the nostrils. The same, with favorable signs, portends the resolution of the disease. Hence Theophilus says in his *Book of Urines*: "Black urines having suspended sediment high up signify a future crisis with shivering, sweat, and insanity, and a flow of blood from the nostrils." Hence it is that Hippocrates says in the fourth part of his *Aphorisms*: "From a <term>causone</term> <note>A heat-intensive, burning fever</note>, if a shivering fit occurs, a resolution follows." That is, a shivering fit coming upon the patient resolves the sickness. Regarding black urine, Hippocrates says in the *Epidemics*: "It is impossible for those sick people in whose urines blackness dominates to be healed, except in those whom the urine passes during a crisis." The same says in the same work: "If the menses are withheld in women, they are healed when black urines occur." Also Galen, commenting on Hippocrates's *Epidemics*, says: "Sometimes a sick person at the beginning of a disease produces black urine with troublesome and terrible signs, and yet is healed, if it happens that their strength is constant and their breathing is easy." Likewise, sometimes at the beginning of a disease, black urine comes with a fear of complications and remains until the ninth day. But afterward, the arrival of black urine with white sediment, as the body's strength exerts itself, signifies the <term>concoction</term> <note>The "cooking" or processing of the disease by the body's natural heat</note> of the disease and the health of the sick person at that time. This is certain according to Hippocrates in the second part of the *Aphorisms*, where he says: "The prognostications of acute diseases are not entirely certain, neither of health nor of death." But you should know for certain, as Galen says, that the significance is not favorable if it is accompanied by distress of breath, sweat only on the head, alienation of the mind, and loss of appetite; then know that the ruin of nature is manifest and the body of the sick person is in peril. ¶ Note what Theophilus says on urines: that if the urine in a burning fever has a black cloud, it signifies a transformation into a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every fourth day</note>. Through the blackness, it signifies the "burning" of the material; through the cloud, windiness is declared; and also that the burning is not so great that some moisture does not remain, which, resolved into windiness, raises the sediment into a cloud. Therefore, the material of the burning fever, expelled from the vessels to the sources, putrefies in them and induces a quartan fever. The literal meaning is plain from these explanations.

### With what substance black color occurs.

> You keep fitting alliances of mixture with the thick,
> The blackness of the liquid flees the union of the thin.
> It would take away the thinness, for it would not cling as a color.
> It obtains outcomes and makes for violent events.
> Closed passages do not prepare an unobstructed flow.

**Explanation.** ¶ **Fitting.** In this chapter, the author demonstrates concerning the black color, with what substance it is naturally suited to be joined. The meaning of these five verses is briefly as follows: Black color is naturally mixed with a thick substance, but it is never mixed with a thin one. And the reason is: because where there is blackness, there is a darkening and obscu-

<column-break/>

rity: which happens from the disturbance and thickening of the parts. I see that it is rightly associated with a thick substance, but not with a thin one: because thinness happens from the rarity <note>The opposite of density; a looseness of the components</note> of the parts. And blackness, as was said, arises from the disturbance of the parts; those things are opposites. And therefore they do not endure each other. And this is to be understood naturally: since accidentally, black color is sometimes joined with a thin substance; for example: thick black urine passing through obstructed places is narrowed; then, by reason of the obstruction of the place, it is stripped of its thickness, and thus it remains thin. And this is what the author intends.

**Commentary.** ¶ **Fitting alliances.** In this chapter it is demonstrated to which substance black color is naturally wedded. And it says that it is impossible for black color to be joined with a thin substance. And Isaac testifies to this same thing in the *Book of Urines*, from whose fountain we have drawn this doctrine. For where there is blackness, there is shadow and obscurity which happens to arise from the disturbance of parts; therefore, where there is shadow, there cannot be thinness, which happens from the rarity of parts. Hence it is that blackness cannot be naturally joined with a thin substance. I said "naturally" because sometimes it receives a joining with a thin substance by accident, such as because of an <term>emphraxis</term> <note>An obstruction or blockage</note> of the urine: as when naturally black urine passes through places where there is an obstruction; because in the place of the obstruction, the thickness of the urine remains, it is stripped of its thick substance and assumes a certain thinness. Likewise, black urine signifies the burning of the blood and the consumption of its natural moisture from the intensity of fiery heat, or from the intensity of natural heat, or from congealing due to excessive cold, or because of <term>melancholic humors</term> <note>Black bile, associated with cold and dryness</note> expelled during a crisis; by all of which the substance of the urine is thickened. From the intensity of the blood because of excessive boiling; from congealing because of excessive cold; and from the purging of melancholic material during a crisis because of the earthiness of the substance mixed with the urine. And therefore black color cannot exist with a thin substance.

### On the livid color.

<margin>Cornelius <note>Possibly a reference to a specific commentator or medical authority</note></margin>

> If it should be livid, or a partial lividness,
> It will be either total, livid throughout the whole limb,
> Or it shows the humor of the limb is being mortified.
> Or appearing livid above, suited to various causes,
> It emits births; medicine; and the falling sickness.
> Ascites; synochus; rupture of a vein; catarrh;
> The lapse of strangury; the passion of the womb; the flow
> Of the loins; a vice of the lung; joint pain.
> Consumptive phthisis; the extinguishing power of heat.
> Let these be the causes of lividness for you, which you collect by signs.

**Livid if it should be. Explanation.** Above, the author determined concerning the black color; here he determines concerning the livid <note>A lead-gray, bluish-purple, or bruised color</note>, which is the path and beginning toward <term>mortification</term> <note>The death of a body part or the whole body</note> and the extinction of natural heat. And therefore livid color does not differ from black except according to the lessening of the mortification. Hence the meaning of those two verses is briefly this. ¶ **Livid color.** That is, lead-colored: it is either according to the whole substance of the urine, or according to a part, namely in the upper part of the urine. If it is according to the whole substance of the urine: then either it makes a residence <note>Sediment</note>, and then it is thickened below and thinned and cleared above; and then know that such urine, being livid throughout and making such a residence, signifies the mortification of the humors. Or it makes no residence, and then it signifies not only that mortification is within the humors, but in the limbs.

### On the judgment of urine

<note>The text here refers to lividity</note> rooted in the members: and this is what he intends. ¶ **Or livid above.** Here he determines the meaning of a livid color appearing in the upper part of the urine, saying: that whenever a livid color appears to you in the upper part of the urine, it signifies various and diverse illnesses, such as minor <term>semitertian fever</term> <note>original: "emitriteum"; a type of malaria-like fever with a specific cycle of peaks</note>, the medium type, epilepsy, and others, as is declared in the commentary. 
<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Pigment.** ¶ **If it should be livid.** After the color black, the author treats the livid color, because it signifies the preparation, beginning, and final stage of <term>mortification</term> <note>The death of tissue or "gangrene" of the humors</note>; it does not differ from black except in the lessening of its malice. However, the livid color in urine is sometimes "total," occupying the whole urine; at other times it is "particular," affecting only the upper part. Total lividity signifies either the mortification of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> and not the organ, or it signifies the mortification of both the humor and the organ, or the organ and not the humor. If it signifies the mortification of the humor and not the organ, then the urine ought to thicken at the bottom through <term>sediment</term> <note>original: "residentiam"</note> and retain its lividity, while the upper part becomes clear, receding from the livid state. If both the humors and the organ <note>original: "membrum"</note> are affected, no sediment can clear the stain of lividity from the urine, by which it is signaled that the vice of mortification is not only fixed in the humors but is rooted in the limbs. These things being known, the literal meaning is plain. ¶ **Or livid above.** The author previously spoke of total lividity; now he adds a section on particular lividity. ¶ **Apply to various.** That is, distinguish it for various and diverse passions. ¶ **Minor semitertian fever.** It should be noted that particular lividity can arise from many causes: because sometimes it is from mortification due to the extinction of natural heat, as in semitertian fevers; or from a disturbance of the humors, such as in a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, and then the urine ought to be scanty, with certain humors appearing as long-stretched resolutions with a certain impurity of essence. This happens because earthy and watery elements are mixed together, from which the livid color follows. At other times, a livid color arises from a suffering of the <term>respiratory organs</term> <note>original: "spiritualium"; the heart and lungs</note>, as in pleurisy, pneumonia, <term>empyema</term> <note>A collection of pus in the chest cavity</note>, and <term>phthisis</term> <note>Tuberculosis or wasting of the lungs</note>. For when the respiratory organs suffer, the nourishing membranes—namely the stomach and the liver—suffer with them. They transmit their spirit and natural heat to aid those organs. Thus, being impoverished of spirit and natural heat, they grow cold; then, from the weakness of heat and the impurity of the second digestion, since the urine is its surplus, it contracts a certain lividity. Or otherwise, in pleurisy or pneumonia, there is a great collection of superfluous matter oppressive to the respiratory organs; sometimes natural heat even strives to transform the moisture into foul vapors, and something powdery and contagious from the bad matter is derived through the vein to the liver and infects the blood and corrupts the spirit. Hence the urine, with the infection of the spirits and blood, becomes livid in its upper part. ¶ **And if you ask why it becomes livid in the upper part rather than the lower:** ¶ **It must be answered thus:** namely, that the fumes and vapors emitted with the urine, since they are light aerial bodies, have an upward motion; and where they dwell most, there they show their infection. Lividity sometimes occurs in epilepsy with a certain leaden color in the <term>circle</term> <note>The topmost rim of the urine in the glass</note>, which signifies an infection of the respiratory organs from a passion of the <term>animate members</term> <note>The brain and nervous system</note>. In <term>synochus</term> <note>A continuous fever</note> the urine also becomes livid because of the corruption of the blood; for when the blood is corrupted, the spirits are greatly infected. It also becomes livid in <term>ascites</term> <note>A type of dropsy</note> because of the corruption of the second digestion and the impurity of the humors; in the rupture of the <term>chyle vein</term> <note>Likely the vena cava or mesenteric vessels</note>; and in every effusion of blood, the urine is livid because of the disturbance of the humors. In <term>strangury</term> <note>Painful or restricted urination</note>, and in catarrh, and in arthritis, the urine is not without lividity, which happens from the infection of the spirits passing through the suffering places and from the humors, which happen to be disturbed and corrupted...

<column-break/>

...the urine takes on a stain of lividity; that is, they receive it. And in a suffering of the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "matrice"</note> it is livid for the same cause: especially since the womb is a hollow and the sink of all superfluities, and this is what he says. ¶ **Minor semitertian fever.** There are three species of semitertian fever about which it is spoken sufficiently elsewhere. ¶ **The falling sickness.** Which is called by another name, epilepsy. ¶ **Ascites.** That is, the third species of <term>hydropsy</term> <note>Dropsy or edema</note>; and it is named from *aschi*, which is a "wineskin," because in this disease the belly, when struck, resounds in the manner of a half-full wineskin. ¶ **Synochus.** It is a continuous fever from putrefied blood within the veins. ¶ **Rupture of a vein.** Such as the chyle vein or another vein. ¶ **Catarrh.** A flow of humors descending from the head. ¶ **Stranguries.** When there is a blockage of the bladder, either from collected humor or from an <term>aposteme</term> <note>An abscess or swelling</note>. ¶ **Passion of the womb.** As if the womb suffers from emptiness, or from some displacement, or distension in the upper part, or from leaning toward the right or left side or the vertebrae. ¶ **And above, and the belly.** ¶ **The ribs.** Pertaining to pleurisy. ¶ **Of the lung.** From a vice of the lung the urine is livid for three causes: namely, from the dripping of <term>rheum</term> <note>Mucous discharge</note>, whence the circuit is rheumatic and granular; and from pain around the respiratory organs if it suffers from fullness, and then heaviness is felt and weight around the respiratory organs, and pain of the left side. ¶ **By vice:** It is leaden and swollen, as in arthritis due to dripping humors, and in <term>semitertian fevers</term> <note>original: "emitriteis"; a fever with a cycle of peaks every day and every other day</note> because of the duality of the matter. ¶ **By disturbance of humors:** as in continuous fevers. ¶ **By abscess of the spiritual parts:** as in pleurisy with empyema, it turns leaden from <term>adustion</term> <note>The "burning" or scorching of humors by excessive heat</note>. ### Specification of ailments associated with a leaden color.

¶ A leaden, oily urine, passed in tiny amounts, barely at all, portends death.
¶ Frequent, scanty, leaden urine shows <term>strangury</term> <note>painful, drop-by-drop urination</note>.
¶ Leaden urine with separate and tiny grains
¶ Constantly speaks of an ailment of the <term>spiritual members</term> <note>the organs of the chest, like the heart and lungs</note>.
¶ Atomic leadenness proves an ailment of the joints.
¶ It is also a faithful messenger of a <term>rheumatic</term> <note>referring to the "flow" of harmful humors</note> evil.
¶ If the womb has pressed against the vertebrae or the diaphragm,
¶ A leaden color infects the surface of the urine.

<margin>Exposition.</margin> ¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **Tiny amounts.** Above, the author said that a leaden color appearing in the upper part of the urine has to signify various and diverse causes. Here he specifies them by other joined conditions, and according to this, he sets down rules, the first of which is this: Whenever you see urine leaden in color, passed with difficulty, tiny in quantity, and oily or greasy, you can then judge death without a doubt. ¶ And note that leadenness happens, as was said, by reason of mortification; it is passed with difficulty by reason of the desiccation of the passages and ways; in tiny amounts by reason of the consumption of the members; and it is oily by reason of the liquefaction of fat. Such urine, therefore, signifies death. ¶ **Strangury.** Another rule. Urine that is leaden, scanty, and passed frequently signifies strangury; the reasons are declared in the commentary. ¶ **Leaden with grains.** Another rule. Urine that is leaden, appearing with tiny and separate grains, frequently signifies an ailment in the spiritual members. ¶ **Leadenness.** Another rule. Leaden urine with atomic resolutions <note>finely divided particles</note> signifies an ailment in the joints. ¶ **It is also.** He says that this same urine with atomic resolutions faithfully signifies a flux of humors from a rheum. ¶ **Vertebra.** Another rule. Leaden urine on the surface of the urine signifies the compression of the womb against one of the vertebrae, or the compression of the diaphragm; and this is what he says regarding the leaden color.

<margin>Commentary.</margin> ¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Tiny amounts.** Here the specifications are set down through the aforementioned causes, showing how they must be determined from other circumstances. For leadenness, whether particular or universal, does not determine the ailment except by a collection made of other actions or occasions; but when joined with others, it is more truthful. ¶ **Tiny amounts.** From the consumption of the members, which is a sign of the vehemence of heat consuming the members and devouring the mass of humors. Hence, when the moisture and juiciness are consumed and little remains, and it overflows to the liver, the urine cannot be multiplied. ¶ **Barely micturated.** From the desiccation of the passages and a lack of urine. ¶ **Leaden.** From approaching or mediating mortification. ¶ **Oily.** That is, greasy from the melting of fat; such urine, he says, signifies death. The aforementioned urine, if it is leaden with scantiness and frequency, signifies strangury. Strangury is the pouring out of urine drop by drop from a blockage of the neck of the bladder, or from its sharpness. It is leaden in strangury because the <term>spirits</term> pass through the place of the blockage, and therefore it draws the infection of leadenness

<column-break/>

from the corrupt humors. ¶ **It is scanty** because of <term>emphraxis</term> <note>an obstruction or blockage</note>, the blockage of thick and viscous humors; hence the bladder cannot sufficiently empty itself of urine at one time. However, frequency of pouring out makes up for the lack of quantity, and therefore it becomes scanty urine passed frequently. ¶ **With grains.** That is, staying in the <term>ring</term> <note>the top layer or "corona" of the urine in the glass</note> and remaining in the settled urine. For if they vanished immediately, then they would arise from another cause rather than a rheumatic one. ¶ **Tiny.** That is, small in quantity. ¶ **Spiritual evil.** Namely, an ailment of the spiritual members and the chest. ¶ **Atomic.** That is, full of atomic resolutions: white, round, and tiny. But why they are white, round, and tiny will be more easily explained in the chapter on white and tiny things. ¶ **Articular evil.** That is, ailments of the joints. ¶ **Vertebra.** That is, ailments of the womb when it tilts more than usual toward one of the vertebrae; hence compression occurs from the pressure of the vertebra. And thus pain is caused by the womb, and from the pain, a provocation of rheums of superfluous matter, from which the urine turns leaden. Likewise, if the womb, by its own displacement, should press upward against the diaphragm, the urine also turns leaden.

### On the white color with thin substance.

<margin>White.</margin> Thin urine joined to a white color
Signifies the spleen, dropsy, <term>surfeit</term> <note>original: "crapulam"; illness from over-eating or drinking</note>, kidney disease, frenzy,
Arthritis, black bile, <term>pedicon</term> <note>an unclear technical term, possibly related to foot ailments or a specific parasitic infection</note>, and <term>scotoma</term> <note>dizziness or dimmed vision</note>.
It notes coldness of the liver; and with the burning of fever, death.
In the elderly, a fragile strength; or in a child, a defect.
In those injured, the shoulders or the neck; or <term>lipothymia</term> <note>fainting or swooning</note>.
It declares quartan fever and <term>amphimerina</term> <note>a daily recurring fever</note>.
In a woman, it marks various complaints of the womb.
It signifies hemorrhoids and <term>condylomas</term> <note>warts or growths</note>.
Unless an error brings a false judgment upon me,
Such urine can be called crude and undigested.
White urine, when no <term>crisis</term> <note>the turning point of a disease</note> has preceded, portends
A continuous frenzy; and death approaches for the frenetic.

# In the Judgment of Urine

...is. For whiteness is the daughter of coldness, as <term>Haly Abbas</term> <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician whose works were central to medieval European medicine</note> says in the *Tegni*: it is thin and radiant because of the excessive dryness of <term>melancholy</term> <note>the "black bile" humor, associated with coldness and dryness</note>, from which the urine becomes subtler and thinner in the upper regions due to the refined spirits. It is also thin and radiant because the melancholic superfluity, descending to the dwelling of the spleen, overflows and constricts the urinary passages; when these are constricted, the urine is filtered and made thinner.

**¶ Dropsy.** That is, <term>leucophlegmatia</term>, namely <term>hyposarca</term> or <term>anasarca</term> <note>historical terms for different types of swelling or fluid retention</note>. This appears at the beginning of the illness, but if it appears for a long time, it declares a disease of the spleen. If the spleen is affected, there will be a certain lividity in the upper part; this lividity and darkness happen because of the impurity of the humors. For when the <term>natural heat</term> <note>the vital energy believed to power digestion and metabolism</note> is weak, it cannot fully cleanse and purify the blood. I said "in the beginning" because when the illness is long-standing and the matter has multiplied over time, the urine appears white and thick.

**¶ Overindulgence.** <note>original: *crapula*; referring to the physical effects of gluttony or heavy drinking</note> When other circumstances are set aside, natural heat is suffocated by a heap of excessive food. Thus, it cannot prevail in its duty of digestion, just as the light in a lamp is overwhelmed and extinguished by too much oil, or a weak fire is put out by a great heap of wood. From overindulgence, urine should also be produced in great quantity, for from many foods there must be a great redundancy of juices flowing to the <term>liver</term> <note>original: *epar*</note>, which suppresses the natural heat. According to <term>Theophilus</term> <note>a 7th-century authority on uroscopy</note>, such urine signifies that excessive food and drink preceded it, especially if it is very thin and light, because it penetrates the system quickly.

**¶ Nephritis.** That is, a suffering of the kidneys caused by a confirmed <term>calculus</term> <note>a kidney stone</note> there. This is preceded by thick and white urine with certain sandy sediments. And if, after such urine, there appears thin and white urine without a purging of the melancholic humor or the thick phlegm through <term>diuretic</term> potions, it signifies nephritis from a stone confirmed in the kidneys. Such a case is very bad, for a stone already hardened is worse than one yet to form or be diminished. This agrees with <term>Hippocrates</term> in the book of *Aphorisms*, where he says: all clear and white urines are bad, especially when they appear in those with <term>phrenitis</term> <note>delirium or brain fever</note>. Urine is white in phrenitis because the entire action of the natural heat is occupied with the place containing the matter of the disease; thus the place of the "second digestion" is left crude, and the urine is whitened. It is thin because the loins and kidneys are compressed and constricted; the thinner urine is strained by the heat and stripped of its substance, and thus it appears thin and white.

**¶ Phrenitis.** It is specifically identified thus: if in an acute fever, preceded by red or reddish urine, without any sign of digestion or "cooking" of the matter, and without any critical determination—either through sweat, a nosebleed, a bowel movement, or any other critical resolution—if thin and white urine appears afterward, it signifies the seizure of the matter to the upper parts. This matter, thinned by the action of heat, exhales or ascends to the membranes of the brain. The urine becomes white because the nutritional and respiratory organs, suffering in sympathy with the "animate members" <note>the brain and nervous system</note> as they are more noble, delegate their spirit and natural heat to assist them. Thus, deprived of spirit and heat, they grow cold. In the absence of heat, the urine appears discolored in them, for the matter which used to color the urine by its presence causes this disposition by its absence as it is snatched upward.

**¶ And it must be noted:** that if phrenitis arises from a subsequent nosebleed or much sweating of the head, and the urine remains thin and white, it signifies death. Hence Theophilus, in the chapter on white and thin urine, adds: "If the urine is such and the fever remains, the patient so disposed shall die."

**¶ Diabetes.** Specifically, thin and white urine signifies this if it is produced in great quantity and passed frequently, and with <term>fleshy resolutions</term> <note>small bits of tissue or sediment appearing like shredded meat</note>. It is white because the watery parts of the "second digestion" flee incessantly from the liver through the capillary veins to the kidneys, due to the loss of balance of heat and dryness. Thus, the "attractive power" flourishes in them, and they desire to be refreshed by the drawn-in moisture. The urine cannot then remain in the liver for a continuous

<column-break/>

passage long enough to receive full heat, but is derived to the kidneys while crude and undigested. In the kidneys, however, the urine cannot be colored, especially since it does not linger there, or lingers only briefly. Instead, through the urinary pores which are thinned and relaxed by heat, it is immediately poured into the bladder. Thus it is urinated often and in great quantity. Diabetes is an immoderate discharge of urine caused by a distemper of the kidneys in either heat or cold. It can arise from immoderate sexual intercourse, running, labor, or jumping. This urine is filled with fleshy resolutions and shreds, because the substance of the kidneys is dissolved by the intensity of the heat.

**¶ Arthritis.** Specifically, white and thin urine signifies this when accompanied by white, round, and tiny "atomic" resolutions, the details of which we shall assign in the individual chapters.

**¶ But it may be asked why the urine is discolored in arthritis.** **¶ And we answer:** that the matter of the urine is not contained in the liver, but around the extremities where the cause of the suffering lies. **¶ If it is asked again:** how those resolutions are mixed into the urine when the matter is contained in the foot? **¶ It is answered** that this is the cause: the "expulsive power" of that limb and the "attractive power" of others work through continuous passages. That is, by expelling, it helps other members in their attracting. And thus, from the expulsive power of that limb and the attractive power of other limbs through continuous passages, those resolutions return to the urinary ways and are mixed with the urine. Arthritis also arises from the dripping of <term>rheumatic matter</term> <note>flowing humors</note> from the brain to the lower parts, and especially to those which are more mobile and knotty, in which—by reason of mobility and knottiness—the attractive power is stronger.

**¶ Cholera: namely Black.** That is, melancholy. Thin and white urine signifies an excess of melancholy when other conditions are set aside. It is white because of the coldness of melancholy, for it is the nature of coldness to whiten. It is thin because of dryness, for it is the nature of dryness to thin.

**¶ Note that melancholy disposes the urine in two ways:** namely according to its quality, and in this way it makes it white and thin, or pale or white from coldness, and thin from dryness according to its substance. It also disposes the urine by its mixture, and then it makes it black and thick, as happens in the resolution of a <term>quartan fever</term> <note>a malarial fever where the paroxysm occurs every fourth day</note>.

**¶ Falling Sickness.** That is, <term>epilepsy</term>. White and thin urine signifies this specifically with a certain leadenness and obscurity of substance, which occurs because of the sympathy of the animate members. It is discolored in epilepsy because when nature suffers with the animate members and is not focused on the liver, digestion is left crude and the urine whitened.

**¶ Scotoma.** That is, a darkening of the eyes and dizziness. White and thin or pale urine signifies this, especially if it is very clear and bright with a certain greenishness and lucidity. For scotoma is said to arise from a melancholic humor, from which a thick and black smokiness is resolved, ascending to infect the brain and obscure the "visible spirit" <note>the medium thought to enable sight</note>. It is white due to much coldness, and clear due to excessive dryness.

**¶ Chill of the Liver.** That is, a distemper of the liver in coldness. Thus digestion is hindered; because of the coldness of the liver, watery and crude humors are generated, and so the urine is made white.

**¶ In a burning fever.** That is, in an acute <term>causonic fever</term> <note>a high, "burning" fever</note>. In the stage of increase, white and thin urine signifies death. But a distinction is made if it appears in the beginning, the increase, the peak, or the decline. If it appears in the beginning, it signifies the crudity of the matter, the weakness of the natural heat, and the long duration of the disease. Thus, from such a long duration, nature being afflicted and weakened, the sick person would succumb; therefore, a failure of the patient is to be feared, especially if other bad signs are present. But if nature is strong and other good signs occur, it does not signify death but health and a future termination through an abscess <note>original: *apostema*</note> formed in the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>original: *safragmate*</note>. If such urine appears in the increase or the peak, having been red before, it can signify two things: either it signifies phrenitis, or the extinction of natural heat due to the consumption of the <term>natural moisture</term> <note>the fluid "fuel" of the body</note>, which is annihilated when its nourishment fails. Thus the urine is discolored, and both are signs...

# Of the Colors

...is mortal. If such a urine appears during the decline of an illness, following a <term>Cretic determination</term> <note>a specific medical prognosis pattern named after the island of Crete or classical rhythmic patterns applied to crises</note>, it is a sign of health and similar outcomes.

¶ **In the elderly, a fragile strength.** That is, thin and white urine signifies a defect of strength due to old age and the weakness of the <term>natural heat</term> <note>the vital metabolic fire believed to drive digestion and life</note>. ¶ **Or a childish defect.** That is, a lack of nourishment in the limbs. ¶ **Lipothomia.** That is, <term>syncope</term> <note>fainting or sudden loss of consciousness</note> is signified by white and thin urine. This happens because of a thick vapor released from raw and melancholic humors. These vapors, breathing inward toward the spiritual passages, compress and suffocate the <term>vital spirit</term> in the heart. Once oppressed, the heart cannot bestow the benefit of heat or deliver it to the extremities. Consequently, since it does not ascend to the brain to temper the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>the refined substance believed to travel through nerves to enable sensation and movement</note>, sensation in the body and voluntary motion cease, and the animal’s body lies as if dead. White and thin urine especially signifies this.

¶ **In injuries to the shoulders or neck.** That is, for those beginning to have pain around the neck and shoulders, not from an external cause but from an internal one. Such pain rising suddenly while this urine is present signifies the dispersion and resolution of thick vapors; hence, it can be a certain sign of coming syncope. ¶ **Quartan fever.** <note>a fever that spikes every fourth day, traditionally linked to "black bile"</note> That is, white and thin urine signifies a fever originating from natural <term>melancholy</term>. But on the day following the onset, it should be pale or somewhat pale, and on the third or fourth day, it should be white or blue-gray. That it appears more colored on the following day happens because melancholic matter, being hard and compact, preserves its "ignition" or inflammation for a long time; thus, the effect of coloration appears more strongly the next day. Note that in a <term>quartan</term>, the urine is usually reddish or somewhat reddish, and sometimes sub-red.

¶ **Amphimerina.** <note>a quotidian fever that recurs daily</note> That is, white and thin urine signifies the resolution of a daily fever caused by <term>glassy phlegm</term> <note>original: *flegmate vitreo*; a thick, clear, cold humor</note>, specifically when the urine is initially sparse and globular at the bottom. If it is later poured out in great quantity and remains thin in substance, it signifies the resolution of the *amphimerina*. While the glassy phlegm was still raw and compact, it resisted nature's attempt to expel it, and because no resolution occurred, the urine was sparse. But once the phlegm is digested and the heat is strengthened, its resolution occurs through small particles, whereby the urine increases and thins.

¶ And note that every matter thickens the urine during its digestion, except for glassy phlegm. The agreement for this rule is found in <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>referred to as "Yppo."</note>, who says in the fourth part of the *Aphorisms*: "In those for whom the urine is white, sparse, and globular, not without fever, a following multitude of thin urine is beneficial." And in <term>Theophilus</term> <note>a 7th-century medical writer</note>: "White, thin, and abundant urine signifies a fading *amphimerina*."

¶ **Complaints of the womb.** That is, the passions from which women suffer, especially those arising from the retention of menses, particularly if they appear with scales and black resolutions, which signifies the retention of the melancholic humor (namely, the blood which is black and earthy).

¶ **Hemorrhoids and condylomas.** That is, diseases existing in the anus, or abscesses in or around the anus. "Hemorrhoids" is the name for both the suffering and the part. For certain veins are called hemorrhoidal, which, arising from the <term>chili vein</term> <note>the vena cava</note>, terminate at the pudendal circle. These veins sometimes swell and distend from much blood gathered in them, and sometimes they rupture so that blood flows from them uncontrollably; such a flow is called the flux of hemorrhoids. White and thin urine signifies hemorrhoids if vaporous and powdery resolutions appear at the bottom, and likewise for anal fissures and <term>condylomas</term> <note>small growths or warts</note>.

¶ **As a general guide.** Here is assigned the general significance of white and thin urine. If you wish to avoid falling into a fallacy of judgment, you must interpret such urine as signifying indigestion, the weakness of natural heat, and the accidents that usually emerge from indigestion. These include the trapping of wind (gas), tension of the <term>hypochondria</term> <note>the upper abdomen below the ribs</note>, inflation of the belly and sides, heaviness of the legs and hips, and a sluggishness of the whole body in both sensation and voluntary motion. It also indicates heaviness and a poor disposition of the head, and especially 

<column-break/>

of the left side. The trapping of wind occurs because, when the heat is weak, it breaks down the humors but does not consume those that are broken down. Hence, a turbulent, trapped wind is generated which, pulsing against the hypochondria and being drawn into them by reason of their emptiness, distends them. From this comes the inflation of the belly and the heavy pain in the sides. Because the spirits—whose motion provides lightness to the limbs—become torpid and dull, being hindered in their paths by the smoky cloudiness released from the raw humors. Alternatively, the superfluities generated in the nutritive organs from the lack of natural heat flow downward by their own weight, burdening the muscles of the hips and shins, making them feel like a heavy pack. Also, as vapors breathe toward the instruments of the senses, the organs and spirits are weighed down, and sensation and voluntary motion are hindered. These same vapors, breathing toward the brain, being thick and impetuous, cause a distension of the <term>meninges</term> <note>the membranes covering the brain</note>. From this distension comes a "solution of continuity" <note>a physical tear or separation of tissue</note>, resulting in a headache, especially on the left side, since that is the seat of melancholy due to its form. ¶ Note also that such urines appear during menstruation and in those with hemorrhoids. But then, small and black resolutions appear at the bottom, along with discoloration and thinness of the entire body.

But if it moves away from moderate thinness, it marks an excess of acetous phlegm, and so on.
