Urine reddish in color, thick in substance, and livid and granular at the top signifies an **aposteme** <term>aposteme: an inflammatory swelling or abscess containing pus</term> in the groin, or under the armpits, or in the genital organs. In these areas, because of the many nerves, the sensitivity of the pain is heightened. From the pain, an onset of rheums <note>The flow of humors or fluids.</note> is provoked, for every pain sharpens the rheum, as Galen asserts.

¶ **If frothy.** Another rule. Urine somewhat reddish <note>original: "subruffa"</note> in color, but with the redness fading: distinctly livid from the middle region upward: and appearing almost ash-colored: very thick or frothy in pleurisy—following an intense reddish color—it signifies the conversion of pleurisy into **peripneumonia** <note>Inflammation of the lungs, often seen as a progression from pleurisy.</note>. It becomes somewhat reddish because of the movement of the matter from a sensitive place to a nearly insensitive place, namely to a phlegmatic organ, the lung. From the middle upward it appears livid because of the occurring bubbling, from the corruption of the matter, and from its conversion into pus <note>original: "saniem"</note>. A part of this is transmitted to the urinary passages via the vena cava <note>In medieval anatomy, it was believed that waste fluids could travel from the chest to the bladder through the major veins.</note> and is purged through the urine. This bubbling, being smoothed and purged, and driven by the "spirit" <note>The breath or vital force.</note> toward the surface of the vessel, renders it such a color. It is ash-colored from the breaking down of the parts of the lung, for the lung is almost ash-colored; but it is frothy from the constant movement of the lung. ¶ **Fatty: a little reddish.** Another rule. Urine reddish in color, thick in substance—more so at the top than the bottom—when the hand is held behind it: livid and oily on the surface, with hair-like sediments <note>original: "crinoidibus resolutionibus"</note> over a long period, signifies the third species of **hectic fever** <note>original: "etbice"; a chronic wasting fever, often associated with phthisis or tuberculosis.</note> as it progresses over time. This is added because this fever, being constitutional, does not arrive except over a long duration. Such a color arises from the color of the organ itself; when a bubbling occurs in the organs, such a color is produced. That it appears livid arises from the corruption of the "substantial moisture" <note>The essential fluids that maintain the body's structure and life.</note>. That it appears oily arises from the fat being dissolved from the organs and floating on the urine. But the oiliness or lividity cannot be distin-

<column-break/>

-guished unless the hand is held behind the vessel, because of the small amount of fat and the thin color of the urine itself. 
<margin>Signs, that is, causes</margin>
Hair-like sediments <note>original: "crinoides"</note> are formed from the heat fixed in the organs and the dissolution of their parts. These accidents accompany it: namely a continuous color because of the continuous imbalance of the organs, though it is "slow" because it does not come from the [raw] matter but from the humors. Heat in the joints of the hands and feet arises from choleric vapors proceeding from the respiratory organs. Redness of the cheeks arises from choleric vapors inflaming them. Pain in the left shoulder blade occurs because, since it is bound to the respiratory organs, it is as if contracted and weakened. Thus the continuity is broken, and pain occurs. There is a variable cough—sometimes it is a dry cough due to dryness, and sometimes moist from some superfluity contained in the respiratory organs. There is a wasting of the whole body from the heat fixed in the organs, consuming and dissolving them. It also signifies a known quartan fever. And all these are discerned by the conditions considered, as shown in the following; hence when it is a simple tertian, then the urine is more red and thinner. But in a double tertian, the urine ought to be more red, thicker at the top, and almost approaching blackness. ¶ **This duration.** That is, because if the patient has labored for a long or short time, we can discern the four aforementioned sicknesses: whether he suffers from fevers, from heating of the liver, or from quartan fever. For if he has labored for a short time, with such urine persisting for a long time, then it signifies either an imbalance of the liver in heat or a quartan fever. <margin>Commentary</margin> ¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Clear and red.** In this chapter, rules are proposed concerning red urine with thin substance, with thick substance, and with moderately thick or moderately thin substance. Therefore, urine red in color, of moderately thin substance, shaded above, and thicker above than below, signifies a double tertian fever. Such a color arises from the intensity of heat and from the redness of the bile itself; and such a substance arises from dryness. ¶ Therefore, these accidents or symptoms ought to be present: namely, headache on the right side where the "mouth of the bile" is <note>Medieval anatomy often associated the right side of the head with the gallbladder and liver</note>, thirst, bitterness of the mouth, and ringing in the ears; but the significance of such urine varies because of the diversity of subjects, just as was said regarding reddish urine. For in a choleric person and in a youth, if such urine appears, it signifies a simple tertian. In a phlegmatic and melancholic old man, and in a woman at the start of the illness, such an occurrence signifies a simple tertian. In a child, it signifies a continuous fever over a long period. And if no fever is present, it signifies a heating of the liver; such also designates a known quartan fever. And all these are clearly distinguished solely by inspecting the circumstances. ¶ **Clear.** That is, thin in consistency. ¶ **Clouds.** Namely, in color. ¶ **Double Tertian.** That is, a double tertian arising from choleric matter putrefied in two places; it also simply signifies a simple tertian. And then it ought to be thinner, when a single and individual matter putrefies, such as bile; hence there is not such a great force of "boiling" <note>original: "ebullitionis," referring to the internal heat of the humors</note>. The same signifies a double tertian from double matter collected and putrefied in two places, which has distinct attacks daily with which it invades the patient. But we say it is more grave on the third day; if it has confused matter, it afflicts in the manner of a simple tertian, but makes the most severe assault because of the putrefaction of double matter; and the signs are the same as in the simple, but then it ought to be thin, because only a single matter putrefies. Hence there is not such a great force of boiling. In the double tertian, however, the urine ought to be more red <margin><unclear>Likely "Schon" or "Sign"</unclear></margin> and thickened more at the top, and almost approaching blackness. ¶ **Length of time.** For if the sick person has labored for a long time, the physician can weigh from that whether it is a fever, or heating of the liver, or a quartan fever. For if he begins to labor anew and such urine appears, a tertian fever is to be presumed. For if he has labored for a long time and such has persisted, a distemper of the liver or a quartan fever is to be presumed. But distinguish: because from a distemper of the liver it ought to be shaded on the surface and foamy with a certain yellowness, or be infused with blackness or greenness, which signifies the intensity of the heat. In a quartan fever, however, these symptoms are absent. ¶ **Clouds.** That is, cloudiness and darkness on the surface regarding a double

<column-break/>

tertian or heating of the liver. ¶ **Time.** That is, the time of the year, by which the disease can be confirmed. For if it was summer, such signifies a tertian or heating of the liver; if winter or autumn, a quartan. ¶ **Condition.** Regarding the complexion, which is essential to the person and which cannot vanish while the subject remains: for in a choleric body, such rather signifies a simple tertian; in a melancholic and phlegmatic body, a double one. ¶ **Age.** Whether it be a child or youth, or an old man. ¶ **Suffering.** Namely, whether the fever cycle is from the third day to the third, or from the fourth to the fourth, and whether he suffers with or without a periodic pattern. ¶ **Form.** Regarding the habit of the body: namely, whether the patient be lean, or fat, or fleshy. ¶ **Place.** Namely, whether in a hot region or a cold one; or it can refer to the region of the body: namely, whether he suffers in the right hypochondrium or in the left. ¶ **Sentence.** Namely, the definitive diagnosis. ¶ **With a stable foot.** That is, with an immovable and certain judgment. ¶ **Concerning all things.** That is, all the circumstances which have been mentioned, O physician, must be discussed by you.

## On red color with moderately thick substance.

¶ Turbid, slightly thick, infused with red liquid,
Provides a certain sign of a continuous tertian.
¶ If a livid cloud occupies the top,
It portends a middle hemitritaeus and the evil of pleurisy. <note>original: "brev." — likely a reference to a 'brief' or summary rule.</note>
¶ Thick and red [indicates] *synochus* if a film <note>original: "linoz," referring to a surface scum or membrane</note> covers the top.
¶ Thick and red figures *synocha* without the film.
¶ *Causon* <note>A name for an acute, burning fever.</note> if it is more thin than thick; reversed,
It is *synochis*. *Causon* shows thinness and fiery heat.
¶ Third: the form of red color is the witness.

¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **Turbid.** Here we treat red color coupled with moderately thick substance, and several rules are set down. <margin>Exposition</margin> The first rule: Urine red in color, in moderately thick substance, turbulent throughout, with impure and unequal substance, signifies a continuous tertian fever. The reason for this is given in the commentary. ¶ **If the top.** Another rule concerning red color with moderately thick substance. Urine red in color, in moderately thick substance, green in the upper part, signifies a middle hemitritaeus <note>A mixed fever combining the qualities of different cycles, often very dangerous.</note>. And if it is livid on the surface, it signifies pleurisy and middle hemitritaeus. And the middle hemitritaeus arises from bile putrefied inside the veins, boiling continuously, and from phlegm putrefied outside. In middle hemitritaeus, the greenness is not distinguished in the urine without placing a hand behind the vessel; but in pleurisy, it is well distinguished. What is pleurisy? It is a collection [of humors] made in the junction of the ribs and the diaphragm, and it happens most often from hot and sharp humors. The reason is stated by Hippocrates: "Those belching..." ¶ **Thick and red.** In this part, the author treats red or reddish color generally with thick substance, or moderately thick, or moderately thin. For these colors are uniform in judgment in certain cases. This is the rule: Urine red in color, or somewhat reddish, in thick substance and turbulent, livid above, and if it becomes foul-smelling upon being breathed upon, then it signifies *synochus*. <term>synochus: a continuous fever caused by putrefaction of the blood</term> *Synochus* happens from blood failing in quality. The reasons are given in the commentary. ¶ **Thick and red synocha.** Another rule. Urine red in color, or somewhat reddish, in thick substance and turbulent without lividity and stench, signifies *synocha*. <term>synocha: a continuous fever caused by an excess of blood volume rather than putrefaction</term> Now, *synocha* is from blood failing according to quantity. ### On Colors

<margin>
Sinochus has three species.
</margin>

*Sinochus* <note>original: "Sinochus"; a type of continuous fever thought to be caused by an excess or putrefaction of blood.</note> arises from an abundance of blood, but also from putrefaction. ¶ It must be noted: that *Sinochus* has three species: namely, the *homotena*, *augmastica*, and *peraugmastica* fevers, as recorded by Haly <note>Haly Abbas (Ali ibn al-Abbas al-Majusi), a 10th-century Persian physician.</note> in the second book of *On the Differences of Fevers*. He uses "sinocha" for "sinochus," not making a strict distinction in the name. ¶ Therefore, it should be noted: because as the species of *Sinochus* are diversified, so too is there a diversification in the urine. In the *homotena* <term>homotena: a fever that maintains a constant intensity from start to finish</term>, the urine appears uniform in color and in its substance, and its harmful quality persists from the beginning to the end. In the *peraugmastica* <term>peraugmastica: also known as epacmastica, a fever that begins at its highest intensity and gradually declines</term>, the urine itself appears red or reddish at the start of the fever. Afterward, the urine always proceeds toward lightening; it goes from bad to good just as the *peraugmastica* fever always proceeds by improving from the beginning to the end. In the *augmastica* <term>augmastica: a fever that starts mild and increases in intensity</term>, just as the fever proceeds by growing and increasing, so too does the urine. ¶ And note that here a certain general rule of urine is handed down: Whenever the urine appears red or reddish with a thick substance, if it afterward clears in the upper part, it is a good sign and a sign of health; the reason for this is found in the commentary. If, however, it clears in the lower part and becomes thin there, while it thickens at the top or remains thick, it is a bad sign and a sign of death; it signifies that the matter is being snatched away to the brain. In this, foolish doctors are deceived, believing the opposite of the truth. ¶ <margin>Causonides.</margin> Another rule concerning urine signifying *causonides* <note>A continuous fever caused by a mix of yellow bile and blood.</note>. Whenever you see urine that is red or reddish in color, and in its substance it is closer to thinness than to thickness, then you shall judge it to be *causon*. *Causonides* is a continuous fever composed of a double matter: principally composed of yellow bile, and secondarily of blood; therefore, the urine is more thin than thick. ¶ **The Reverse.** Another rule by the opposite of the former. Because red or reddish urine in color, approaching more toward thickness than thinness, signifies *sinochides*. *Sinochides* is a continuous fever composed of double matter: principally of blood, and secondarily of yellow bile, which is why it leans more toward thickness than thinness. ¶ <margin>Commentary.</margin> **Thin Causon.** Another rule regarding urine signifying *causon* <note>A "burning" fever (from the Greek 'kausis'), often associated with severe dehydration and yellow bile.</note>. Urine that is red or reddish in color, thin in substance throughout, and shining like fire, signifies *causon*. *Causon* is a very acute continuous fever, and it occurs from red bile putrefied in the veins near the opening of the stomach, the lungs, and the spleen. And therefore, it is called *causon* from *caumate* <note>original: "a caumate"; meaning burning heat.</note>.
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Turbid, thick, etc.** Here is placed the rule for red color with a moderately thick substance, which you may gather thus: Urine of a red color with a moderately thick substance, turbulent throughout with an impure and unequal substance, signifies a continuous tertian fever. Such a red color arises from the color of red bile, which by its boiling and redness is sufficient to clear and redden the urine. The urine is turbid throughout because of the disturbance and boiling produced in the vessels; and because some parts become thickened by the boiling—since those vessels are wider and their pores larger—thick, hot, and subtle parts are also emitted with the urine. Because the urine is disturbed, it is an impure urine of unequal substance. ¶ **Turbid.** That is, turbulent. ¶ **Slightly thick.** That is, approaching thickness. ¶ **If the top.** Another rule is placed regarding the red color with the same substance. For if it is red with the previous substance, but green on the surface, it signifies the *hemitritaeos* <note>original: "emittritum"; a semi-tertian fever characterized by overlapping cycles of different fevers.</note>. If, however, it is leaden on the surface, it signifies pleurisy. In the *hemitritaeos*, because of the bile continuously boiling inside the vessels, and from the phlegm outside, excessive boiling or burning occurs. Therefore, when the bile is emitted with the urine, being burnt and smoothed, it tends toward the surface of the urine

<column-break/>

and renders it green. But when there is only a little, the greenness is not distinguished unless the hand is applied <note>A diagnostic technique where the physician places a hand behind the glass to better see the color of the fluid.</note>. If, however, it appears without the application of the hand, or shows a distinct leaden color on the surface, it signifies pleurisy <note>An inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs.</note>, which is said to be a collection [of fluid] made in the junction of the ribs and the diaphragm; it most often arises from hot and acute humors. Whence Hippocrates says: "Belching happens... [and] they do not become very pleuritic." On account of the heat and the sharpness of the matter, and because the collection is in the warmer members—or those that are sensitive—and because they are in continuous motion, that matter boils and burns excessively. Therefore, through the branch of the vena cava, being diverted through the urinary passages, it is mixed in great quantity with the urine and renders it green. Because it is burnt and smoothed, it seeks the surface and makes it green; and because there is much burnt matter, the greenness appears without the application of the hand, or even a leaden color where there is not such a great cause of burning. ¶ **The top.** That is, the surface. ¶ **Hemitritaeos.** <note>original: "Medium... emittritum"</note> That is, the semi-tertian fever. ¶ **The bad pleuritic.** That is, pleurisy with a distinct leaden or green color.
¶ **Thick and Red.** In this chapter, he treats the red and reddish or sub-reddish colors generally under one heading, according to the combination of a thick substance, or moderately thick, or moderately thin. In these cases, all these colors will be uniform in judgment. At the beginning, therefore, the rule is proposed for red or reddish color with a thick substance, which you may gather thus: Urine that is red or reddish in color, thick and turbulent in substance—if it is leaden in the upper part, accompanied by difficult breathing, and a certain foul odor exhales from the vessel—signifies *sinochus*. It is such in color because it comes from the heat and color of the blood itself. For when blood is hot and red, verging toward impurity, it is not sufficient to purify the urine. And it is thick because of the moisture of the blood, whose property it is to thicken. And it is leaden because of the mixture of a little [burnt] blood. ¶ And it is stinking, which comes from the corruption of that blood. <margin>Causon</margin> *Sinochus* is a continuous fever from blood putrefied in the veins. It is called *sinochus* as if "co-habiting"—that is, having together <margin>It contains all fevers</margin> all the causes that run together toward continuity, which are three. The first is the continuous boiling of heat and putrefaction. The second is the continuous breathing of putrid smoke toward the heart. The third is the impurity of the blood. These three causes are found in a great fever so specifically as they are in *sinochus*; and therefore it is denoted by them. ¶ **Thick red sinocha.** Another rule. Urine that is red or reddish in color, thick and turbulent in substance, without the leaden color and stench, signifies a weak *sinocha*. *Sinocha* arises from blood that is abundant or "sinning" in quantity but not in quality <note>Meaning the patient has too much blood (plethora), but the blood itself has not yet turned "rotten" or putrid.</note>; and it is a species of ephemeral fever, although it arises from a humor. Because it is red or reddish, it happens from the qualities of the blood, as has already been said. That it is without the leaden color and stench happens because the blood is not corrupted nor putrefied, from the mixture of which the leaden color or foulness would be born. ¶ <margin>Species of Sinocha</margin> And it should be noted that since there are species of *sinochus*—namely *peraugmasticus*, *augmasticus*, and *homotenus*—the disposition of the urine varies according to the variety of the species. In the *peraugmasticus*, it appears reddish or red from the very beginning with other signs; afterward it appears red or reddish, moving from intensity to remission, so that a change occurs in the urine from bad to good. Just as the fever decreases and declines from the sharpness of the beginning, so too the intensity of the heat declines in the urine. In the *augmasticus*, the opposite happens. In the *homotenus*, the urine appears uniform <margin>General rule</margin> in color and persists in its bad state from beginning to end, just as the uniform fever requires. ¶ In this previous chapter, take this method and, as it were, a general tradition: Any urine that is reddish or reddish-orange in a thick substance, if afterward in the surface it begins without...

# Urine

to thin and, as it were, to clear: thus, if that turbulence and thickness begin to subside, it is a good and healthy sign. For through this, if the urine appeared thick throughout and now begins to purify at the top, it signifies that the motion of "ebullition" <note>original: "ebullitio"; the metaphorical "boiling" or agitation of humors during a fever</note> has now ceased. This boiling previously disturbed the humors throughout the body and threw the parts of the urine into a state of uniform thickness. But if it persists in thickness at the top, or appears thicker or more turbulent, while at the bottom it becomes thin or clear, it is a mortal sign. It signifies the seizure of the disease into the upper parts. Whence one must fear phrenitis <note>inflammation of the brain</note>, or lethargy, or mania. From this it happens that an unskilled practitioner, when he sees the urine thick in the beginning and afterwards thinning at the bottom, is deceived into judging it a recovery, when instead the disease is gaining strength against nature. **Sinochus.** That is, putrid. **Sinocha.** That is, inflammatory, from pure and sincere blood, but overheated. According to Constantine <note>Constantine the African, an 11th-century translator of Arabic medical texts</note>, the symptoms of the *sinochus* disease are these: a fixed headache emerging from the forepart of the head, redness of the cheeks, swelling of the veins (especially around the "spiritual" organs <note>the heart and lungs</note>), and a sweetness in the mouth. **Causonides.** Another rule is given concerning the colors red and reddish with a moderately thin substance and a moderately thick one, which you may gather thus: **Urine red or reddish in color and in substance approaching more toward thinness than thickness signifies *causonides*.** And *causonides* is a continuous composite fever from two different kinds of matter: principally from bile <note>original: "colera"; yellow bile</note> and secondarily from blood. Hence it approaches more toward thinness than thickness. **The Reverse.** **Sinochides.** Another rule is proposed through the opposite of the aforementioned. **For urine red or reddish in color, approaching more toward thickness than thinness, signifies *sinochides*.** That is, a continuous composite fever principally from blood and secondarily from bile. Hence it is closer to thickness than thinness. The symptoms appear mixed because of the mingling of blood and bile; the symptoms of the dominant humor prevail, and the opposites are perhaps contained by intermission. **Thin Causon.** Another rule: Urine red or reddish in color and entirely thin in substance, shining or like fire, signifies *causon*. *Causon* is a very acute continuous fever. Hence it is named from *cauma* <note>Greek for "burning heat"</note>, and it arises from multiple red bile putrefied in the very thin veins of the opening of the stomach, the liver, the lungs, and the spleen. Such a color comes from the heat and boiling of the matter itself, which putrefies in very hot places. It is thin and shining like fire because, since those vessels are too narrow, nothing exudes from them except what is most subtle and liquid; this, mixed with the urine, renders it thin and fiery. **These symptoms accompany it:** namely, a violent headache, so that it seems to the patient that a nail is being driven into his forehead. This happens because of the violent fumes and the bile resolved from the matter, which, stretching the *meninges* <note>original: "miringas"; the membranes covering the brain</note>, lashes the brain. Immoderate thirst is present, which is quieted by no drink; and this is due to the excessive heat of the bile burning the opening of the stomach. Sometimes blackness of the tongue is present due to the burning; sleeplessness from the drying of the brain; and dreams of lamps and ignited bodies. **The Reverse.** That is, disposed in the opposite way, such as thicker rather than thin. **The third is a witness.** Because when the heat is more intense, it suggests a greater fire.

### On the colors inopos and kianos.

**If the color is *inopos*, it brings harm to health.**
**In a continuous fever; it is less to be feared without fever.**
**For a caustic humor inflames the kidneys or the liver.**
**Either the *chyle-vein* is ruptured, or it seeps from a broken vessel.**
**Or dark blood is drawn from a woman's body.**

<column-break/>

**Leaping in a healthy body causes such a thing.**
**Or excessive intercourse, running, or immoderate labor.**
**Nor does *kianos* deviate from the law of the former.**

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
**Exposition.** If the color is *inopos* <note>original: "inopos"; a color like dark red wine</note>. After discussing the colors red and reddish, he here consequently deals with the colors *inopos* and *kianos* <note>original: "kianos"; a dark blue or livid color</note>; and these two colors are judged in the same way. The color *inopos* is like dark wine. But the color *kianos* has a deeper blackness, and also many colors, because in one part it is of a reddish color, in another black, and in another livid or green. **The Rule.** Urine of the color *inopos* or *kianos* in acute and very acute fevers is the worst and signifies death. This is because the symptoms of the illness are signified to be so finalized that they could not be finalized further while the substance of the body remains. Hence, if it first appears reddish or very red, and afterwards *inopos* or *kianos*, it is without doubt a bad and mortal sign. **It is less so without fever.** Another rule: if such urine, *inopos* or *kianos*, appears without fever, then it does not threaten as much danger. In that case, it signifies an abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note> in the liver or in the kidneys, or a rupture of the *chyle-vein* <note>original: "vene kilis"; likely referring to the vena cava</note>. If it is a rupture of the *chyle-vein*, then the greatest pain is felt in the seventh vertebra <note>original: "7. spondili"</note>, counting from the lower part, and then the urine appears more dreg-filled at the bottom. Such urine, whether *inopos* or *kianos*, can also signify dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note> if it appears thicker in the middle region. Such urine can also signify abscesses of the liver or kidneys, or pleurisy, or pneumonia; and these are distinguished by their own specific signs, as is sufficiently handed down in the commentary. **Or from a broken vessel.** Another rule: such urine, appearing *inopos* or *kianos* in women, either appears with fever or without fever. If without fever, then it signifies the eruption of the menses, and then such urine is not suspicious. But if it is with fever, then without doubt it threatens the highest danger, and it is even more so in men. **Leaping causes such.** Another rule: such urine sometimes appears in healthy people by reason of jumping, or also by reason of much intercourse, or running and great and immoderate labor; and this is known through the indications of the patients. **Nor is it deviating.** The author says here that urine in the color *kianos* is of the same and uniform judgment and significance as the color *inopos*, as has been said.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
**Commentary.** If the color. After the treatise on the red and reddish color, the author continues the chapter on the colors *inopos* and *kianos*; for they are of uniform judgment and the same consideration. The color *inopos* is like wine that turns toward blackness, such as the wine that comes from Calabria. *Kianos*, however, has a deeper blackness and even a manifold color, because the urine appears partly reddish, partly black, and partly livid or green. Such urine, whether *inopos* or *kianos*, in acute and very acute fevers is the worst and indicative of death. For it indicates the symptoms of the disease are so finalized that they cannot be finalized further while the substance remains. Hence, if it first appears reddish or very red, and thereafter *inopos* or *kianos*, such a process is without doubt the worst and a sign of death. This color is also accustomed to appear in women without fever due to the eruption of the menses; and then it is usually more thick, fatty, and dreg-filled at the bottom. Hence, urines of this kind are more suspicious in men than in women, unless such appears in women suffering from acute fevers by grace of the fevers themselves and not because of the eruption of the menses. For then the highest danger is presumed, even more than in men, in proportion as they are further removed from their nature. **Likewise, such urine appears in the rupture of the chyle-vein.** Whence the greatest pain is felt in the seventh vertebra, making the count from the bottom. Then the urine appears more dreg-filled at the bottom. There is however...

in a physician, the greatest of virtues is when, through such urine in such a place, he can truly predict the rupture of the aforementioned chyle vein. <note>original: "vene chilis"; referring to the vena cava or the "great vein" thought to carry chyle from the digestive system.</note>
¶ And note that when such urine appears thicker in the middle region, it can then signify dropsy. <note>original: "hydropisim"; a general term for swelling or fluid retention.</note> In such a case, distinguish: for if it is as if bloody, it can signify anasarca. <note>original: "hyposarcam"; swelling under the skin.</note> But if it is more livid, it signifies leucophlegmatia <note>a type of dropsy associated with pale, phlegmatic humor</note>; yet a judgment of dropsy must not be rushed into based on this sign alone. For a reckless and headlong discourse dishonors the practitioner and brings him shame. ¶ Likewise, such urine must signify or indicate an abscess of the liver, or pleurisy, or pneumonia, or an abscess of the kidneys; and it must be distinguished through other symptoms. One must investigate whether the patient suffers a piercing pain on the right side or on the left side, or a shortness of breath, or a weight and heaviness around the kidneys.
<margin>Abscess of the liver: how to distinguish it from pleurisy.</margin>Many authors distinguish an abscess of the liver from pleurisy in four ways according to Alexander. <note>Likely referring to Alexander of Trallian, a 6th-century physician.</note> Let it be on the right side; a distinction is necessary. **The first is according to the pulse.** For in an abscess of the liver, the body is more colored, and the color is much more persistent. But in an abscess of the vital organs <note>original: "spiritualium"; referring to the lungs or heart</note>, the body is always less colored, and especially with a color that is more fleeting. In an abscess of the liver, the cough is dry because its matter is beneath the diaphragm. But in a pleuritic patient, the cough is always moist according to everyone, because the matter is in the vital organs above the diaphragm and is easily brought out. ¶ Likewise, the pain is greater, and there is also a piercing sensation in pleurisy; this happens because of the location and the sensitivity of the diaphragm, which is composed of nerves. In an abscess of the liver, the pain is instead a sense of heaviness, since the liver is not a nervous organ. To these four aforementioned differences, another six differences are sometimes added, which are found in a certain letter from Galen himself to Glaucon the physician. ¶ And the first is: that an abscess of the liver is quite sharp <note>original: "acutum"; referring to the shape of the swelling</note> when the moon is in conjunction <note>likely a reference to the shape rather than astrology, though medical astrology was common</note>, but in pleurisy, the shape is round. ¶ Second: because in an abscess of the liver, the stools tend to be bloody, generated by the failure of the liver and the "sweating out" of blood from the liver; but in pleurisy, this does not happen. ¶ Likewise, thirdly, it is distinguished by the shape of the body. For in an abscess of the liver, the body is greatly and significantly wasted; but in pleurisy, the body is not wasted to such an extent. ¶ Likewise, fourth: the pleuritic patient lies better upon the painful parts because of the empty space, and because the abscess is not compressed by the stomach and intestines; but in an abscess of the liver, the patient cannot lie well upon the painful parts, because then the part that hurts is compressed by the stomach and the intestines, from which follows much greater pain. ¶ Likewise, fifth: it is distinguished by the location, because pleurisy can occur on either side, but an abscess of the liver can only occur on one side, namely the right. ¶ Likewise, sixth: it is also discerned by the urine, as was said previously. And here we have the ten differences of those abscesses just mentioned. ¶ Now let us return to the diagnostic signs of the aforementioned urine. Therefore, such urine, if a "leeching" breath <note>original: "sansugío anhelítu"; possibly a gasping or labored breathing</note> or orthopnea is present, and if it is somewhat livid at the top, signifies empyema <note>a collection of pus in the chest cavity</note>. The same urine, if it has a saffron-colored foam, signifies excessive heating of the liver and jaundice; which, if it occurs before the seventh day in an acute fever, is a very bad sign. It may also result from the failure of the matter, which, breaking out as a symptom, is diffused through the whole body, as if fluctuating from the internal parts and spreading to the exterior, and having become subcutaneous, it stains the skin, inducing jaundice. But if the force of nature expels the matter instead, and the jaundice arrives after the seventh day, it will be the resolution of the disease. Such urine also frequently appears in a healthy body from a leap, due to the rupture of a vein in the kidneys or in the bladder, or due to the "sweating out" of blood from the thinning of vapors caused by immoderate running, or sexual intercourse, or excessive labor. **Burning.** That is, gathered to form an abscess. **Chilis.** That is, the vein adjacent to the spine. **Or by a broken vessel.** That is, some vein.

<column-break/>

->On the color green.<-

> Severe jaundice, spasm, greater peril, and finally death,
> Are judged by urine stained with a leek-green color.

<margin>Exposition.</margin>
¶ Exposition. ¶ **Severe jaundice.** <note>original: "Agriacam"; a term for a severe, greenish form of jaundice.</note> After the colors *inopos* <note>wine-dark</note> and *kianos* <note>livid/dark blue</note> have been determined, we here treat the color green. Likewise, a green color in the urine signifies "adustion" <note>the scorching or burning of humors by excessive heat</note>. And there are three stages of adustion: namely, the first, the middle, and the complete. At the beginning of adustion, the urine appears in the color *kianos*, infused with a certain greenness or lividity at the top. In the middle, it becomes green and signifies the dominance of leek-green and verdigris-green colors. At the end of adustion, it turns black. Therefore, urine green in color appears sometimes in large amounts and sometimes in small. If it is green and small in amount, it signifies death, especially if the green or black color has stained the fingernails. When it is green and plentiful, very foul-smelling and dreggy, it signifies the rupture of an abscess in some noble organ, such as the liver, whereby the substance of the organ is dissolved and expelled through the urine. Whence in the first case, death is to come. Such urine also signifies jaundice from leek-green or verdigris-green bile. And note that there are three species of jaundice, as is held in the commentary. ¶ **Spasm.** This same urine appearing in an acute fever signifies a spasm from "inanition" <note>the depletion of vital fluids or humors</note>. ¶ **Greater.** So too, the urine signifies a "half-tertian" spasm <note>original: "emítritíū"; a complex fever type</note>, and thus threatens great danger. ¶ **Finally death.** So also the urine signifies, finally and in the last place, the mortification and extinction of natural heat. Lastly, there follows the color black. And because this was determined above in the first chapter, it is not necessary to repeat it here. ¶ And let these things suffice regarding colors. And thus the first principal part is ended.
<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ Commentary. ¶ **Severe jaundice, etc.** After the colors *inopos* and *kianos*, according to the appropriate order, we treat the color green. A green color in urine is a sign of adustion. Adustion is indeed enclosed in a threefold limit: namely, the first, the middle, and the complete. In the beginning of adustion, the urine first becomes *kianos*, infused with a certain lividity at the top; in the middle it becomes green and indicates the dominance of a leek-green color, whence it turns to verdigris; in the completion, it turns black. Urine which is green in color is sometimes plentiful and sometimes scarce. Green and scarce urine must signify death, and especially if the green, or livid, or black color has stained the fingernails of the fingers. When it is green and very foul-smelling and dreggy, it signifies the rupture of an abscess in some noble organ, such as the liver, whence the substance of the organ itself is dissolved, which, having been dissolved, is emitted with the urine. Whence in the first case, they discern that death is coming. Such urine green in color also portends jaundice from leek-green or verdigris-green bile which, having been diffused by its lightness to the surface of the body, stains the skin and induces green jaundice—that is, *agriaca*, which is also called *peraseleontos*, which is interpreted as "green" from the green weasel. For there are three species: green jaundice, of which we have just spoken; black jaundice, which is called *melanchirion* from *melon*, which is "black," and *chiros*, which is "hand," or *chiros* which is "humors." And saffron jaundice, which is called by the general name "jaundice," restricted to that specific type. ¶ Likewise, green urine appearing in an acute fever signifies a spasm from inanition because of the consumption of the substantial moisture for the reason aforementioned. The same urine signifies a greater "half-tertian" fever, and therefore it is very dangerous. ¶ **Agriaca.** That is, green jaundice. ¶ **Spasm.** From inanition. ¶ **Greater.** Namely, a half-tertian fever. ¶ **Finally.** That is, at the completion of the illness. ¶ **Death.** That is, the mortification of nature and the extinction of natural heat, as the fuel of nature fails. ¶ **Leek-green.** <note>original: "Prassino"</note> That is, green; for the horehound plant is called *prassium*, and then it is called a leek-green color; this is the meaning. ¶ **Stained with a leek-green color.** That is, composed of its potency drawn from leek-green bile, or a greenness emulating the leek-green color. And here the treatise on colors is ended. After green follows the color black, but that was dealt with in the first chapter on colors.

¶ On the contents

Urine

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
# On the contents of urine. This is the second principal part. Chapter II.

<note>A decorative drop cap 'S' featuring foliate designs within a rectangular border.</note>

> -> Often the appearance of color plays with the practitioner, <-
> -> And the judgment of the liquid frequently cheats his trust. <-
> -> In the contents, there is a settled law: a certain discernment, <-
> -> A constant rule of judgment, and true reliability. <-
> -> Setting aside other things, the author, conscious of nature, <-
> -> From here Hippocrates draws the firm seeds of truth. <-
> -> Now let the form of the contents be noted in order, <-
> -> So that their meanings may hold their proper ways. <-

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
**Exposition.** **Often.** Here begins the second principal part of this book. It continues from the previous part in this manner: previously, urine was determined by considering its colors and substances. Here, however, it is determined by the contents of the urine. Thus, the meaning of these two verses is this: Many times the color of the urine itself and its substance delude the physician and deceive him. The reason for this is that the color and substance of urine often appear in a way that does not testify to the humor which is the cause of the sickness. Because color is a superficial accident, it easily receives alteration. Furthermore, the substance of the urine—which ought to appear thin—appears thick; and when it should be thick, it appears thin due to the narrowness or wideness of the pores and passages, and also due to the digestion or indigestion of the matter. ¶ **In the contents.** This means that through the inspection of the contents, a certain and true judgment of infirmities will be obtained. The reason is that the contents are either contained within the organs themselves or are particles of those very organs, and thus a more certain and firm judgment is held. ¶ **Setting aside other things.** Here the author proves his point by the authority of the blessed Hippocrates, who in his book of *Prognostics* very rarely mentions the substance and color of urine, but hands down the teaching regarding the contents themselves: now concerning "bran," now "hair-like strands," now "scales." <note>Hippocrates refers to these sediments as signs of specific internal conditions; for example, "bran" (furfura) often indicated issues with the bladder or kidneys.</note>

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Often the practitioner.** Having completed the first part of his work, in which he dealt with urines according to the pairing of colors and substances, the author approaches the second part, in which a distinction is made regarding the contents. The faithful inspection of these is better for discerning the conditions of the internal organs than colors and substance. For color or substance is many times derived from elsewhere and does not testify to the humor which is the cause of the sickness. Indeed, color is a shadowy and superficial accident; therefore, it quickly vanishes due to any alteration of the body. The substance of urine is also changed due to the constriction or wideness of the pores, and due to the digestion or indigestion of the matter; hence, when the substance ought to be thick, it is sometimes thinned, and when it ought to be thin, it is thickened. But from the different types of contents, a more certain judgment regarding the sufferings of the body is chosen. Indeed, the contents in urines are either held within the organs themselves or are particles of those organs; therefore, they have a firmer consistency and significance. That the contents are more faithful messengers is proven by the authority of Hippocrates, who says in the *Prognostics* and in the *Aphorisms* (which are established as a kind of rule of doctrine) that he mentions the contents rather than the substance and color: now concerning bran-like particles, now hair-like strands, now hairs, now scales, now blood, now pus, now inserting "globes" into the discussion. He very rarely mentions substance and color, because those more often delude the practitioner, as color is a superficial accident and resides in the finer parts which quickly vanish from the internal and substantial things that persist more firmly in the composite whole. This can be seen in a rose: it is quickly deprived of its "rosiness" <note>original: "rositate"; its essence or color</note> when placed in boiling water or when smoked with sulfur. ¶ **Judgment.** <note>original: "Lesura," glossed as "iudiciū"</note> That is, the diagnosis. ¶ **Of the liquid.** <note>original: "Liquozis," glossed as "substātie"</note> That is, of the substance. For in children, the urine ought to be thick due to the humidity of their age, and yet it appears thin because of the narrowness of the passages working against it. ¶ **Cheats trust.** That is, it deceives. ¶ **Of nature.** That is, the cause of natural things, under which we understand whatever pertains to the lower sphere from a lighter globe. ¶ **Other things.** That is, color and substance. ¶ **Setting aside.** That is, regarding them as useless for judgments and the study of contents. ¶ **From here.** Namely, from the contents. ¶ **Now let the form of the contents.** After he has brought forward the proof of judgment regarding the contents according to the dogma of Hippocrates, the author acts to set down the number of contents. ¶ **In order.** <note>original: "Seriatim"</note> That is, arranged by reason; not from "serious," but from "series." ¶ **The meanings.** Namely, of the contents. ¶ **Ways.** That is, definitions.

¶ **Exposition. ¶ The rings.** Here Giles enumerates the contents appearing in urines, and according to this order of enumeration, he determines these in the following sections: first, concerning the ring.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary. ¶ The ring.** Now the author enumerates the contents according to their order, and in the same order, he will mandate the execution of those things which he enumerated in these four verses. And he declares the execution of each, starting first with the ring.

### On the thick and watery ring.

-> If the ring in the urine is thick and watery, <-
-> The posterior cell, weighed down by phlegm, suffers. <-
<note>In medieval "cell doctrine," the brain was divided into three ventricles or "cells." The posterior cell was associated with memory.</note>

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Exposition. ¶ Thick.** Here the ring is treated—not because the ring itself is a "content" in the urine, for it is the uppermost region of the urine, but because the contents begin to appear in the ring. And there is such a rule: urine appearing with a thick ring, in substance and color similar to water, signifies that the last cell of the head is burdened with phlegm, because it has its origin in that part.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary. ¶ Thick.** According to the series of the arrangement of the contents, he first deals with the ring. Not because the ring is a content of the urine—for it is the highest region of the urine—but because the contents begin to appear in the ring, and certain contents are distinguished by the ring. ¶ Concerning the ring, it can be asked: why is it appropriated to urine, since a ring appears in any liquid, such as water, wine, or oil? ¶ We respond thus: we do not appropriate the ring to urine so as to exclude it from other liquids. For any liquid makes a ring on the surface, and it is naturally generated on the surface from the more watery and more fluid parts according to the form of the containing vessel. Hence, in water or wine placed in a vessel, a ring stands out above, because the watery parts (and the more fluid ones, and those which have more of the air of the mixture) tend toward the surface, nor do they allow themselves to be compressed by the heavier parts. Also, the upper part of the liquid swells up from the proximity of the enclosed air, and for the same reason, a ring appears in urine. ¶ But here it does not seem that anything can be signified by the ring concerning the consistency of the brain or other members, since a ring can be continuous with any liquid. ¶ To this we say: as Isaac <note>Likely Isaac Judaeus (c. 850–950), a highly influential physician in the Middle Ages.</note> testifies, the brain—although it is cold and moist since it is of the nature of fat and marrow—is nevertheless actually warm. Thus, since it has a liquid and fluid substance, it requires similar nourishment. In the liver, however, there is a various and manifold generation of blood according to the diversity of the members to be nourished.

-> Giles on Urines. <-

<meta>This page continues the detailed examination of urine "contents," specifically focusing on the "circle"—the crown or meniscus that forms at the top of the urine in the vessel. It transitions from general theory about how blood nourishes the brain to specific diagnostic signs based on the circle's color and consistency.</meta>

### On the contents

Blood is therefore generated liquid and light: by its fluidity, it is sent to nourish the brain and seeks the higher parts. The excess of this blood is joined to its thickness and specific properties. From this, it becomes much more liquid, subtle, and lighter than the blood itself; therefore, when that excess is poured out, it tends upward toward the neighboring parts and forms a circle. <note>In medieval medicine, the "circle" or "crown" (Latin: *circulus*) at the top of a urine sample was believed to represent the head and brain.</note> For moisture possesses a movement from the center, creating width by spreading toward the circumference. Coldness has a movement from the circumference, inducing contraction; thus these movements are contrary. They run to the brain and determine whether the circle grows or shrinks, or whether the thickness or width of the circle increases or diminishes; this depends on whether the brain is nourished by blood that is more watery, drier, hotter, or colder. ¶ In the form of the circle, the consistency of the brain is principally reflected: whether it is nourished well or poorly, and whether it is disturbed by some other imbalance. For the circle serves the disposition of the "animated members"—that is, the brain and the meninges. <note>The "meninges" (Latin: *miringarum*) are the membranes enveloping the brain.</note> A circle that is thick in substance but faint in color declares a congestion of the brain, oppressed by the weight of phlegmatic matter, especially around the posterior part—that is, the occiput—where the seat and dominion or home of phlegm is located. Because the circle is faint, it arises from coldness, whereby the natural heat in the brain is weakened and cannot process excesses, which disturbs the brain. Because it is thick, this arises from moisture, which has a movement that spreads in width.
¶ **Thick.** That is, expanding and swollen in substance. ¶ **Watery.** That is, faint in color, as if it represents the color of water.

---

### On the purple and thick circle, and on the pale and thin one.

> *A thick, purple circle shows the blood afflicts the front.*
> *A pale and thin one signifies the left side is troubled by black bile.*

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **Purple.** A urine circle appearing purple and thick signifies that the front part of the head is afflicted. If such a circle appears, and there is a pricking in the nostrils, pain in the forehead, and fullness of the veins, and the sick person sees red bodies before their eyes, then it is predicted that blood will exit from the nostrils. ¶ **Left side.** <note>The original Latin uses *Lena*, a poetic term here interpreted as the left side.</note> A pale and thin circle signifies that melancholy <note>Black bile</note> abounds and causes affliction; for there the melancholic humor has its dominion.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Purple.** After the thick and faint circle, the author treats the purple and thick circle. Such a circle signifies an abundance of blood and that the front is troubled by it. In the "prore"—that is, the anterior part of the head—blood holds its principal domain. That the circle is purple arises from the heat of the blood; that it is thick arises from moisture. This signifies a great change in the brain, for while it ought to be nourished by cold and watery blood, burning and seething blood is sent for its nourishment. If there is a circle with pricking of the nostrils, pain in the belly, and fullness of the veins, and the patient thinks they see red bodies before them, it signifies a flow of blood from the nostrils. ¶ **Left side.** That is, the left part, etc. here he treats the faint and thin circle, which signifies that the left part of the brain is troubled and afflicted by the melancholic humor; in which left part of the brain the dominion of melancholy flourishes. Because it is faint, it is from coldness. Because it is thin, it is from the dryness of the humors. If such a circle persists, these symptoms ought to accompany it: namely, suspicion, faint-heartedness, fear, sleeplessness, and greed.

<margin>Signs of a future flow of blood from the nose.</margin>

### On the red and thin circle.

> *In the right part rages the sharp point of burning bile,*
> *If the circle should be thin and red.*

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **Right.** A red and thin circle signifies pain in the right part from the choleric humor <note>Yellow bile</note> abounding there. ¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Right part.** Next follows the intense and thin circle, which declares that choler is the cause and the right part of the head is afflicted. That it is red comes from heat; that it is thin comes from dryness. ¶ **Right part:** in which choler especially dominates.

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
### On the lead-colored circle.

> *It suggests the root of the senses is being put to death,*
> *The leaden circle: and from here harm is given to the branches.*

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **It suggests.** Here he determines the lead-colored circle. A circle that is leaden <note>Latin: *plumbeus*, a dull, greyish-blue</note> signifies epilepsy and a kind of mortification of the brain itself, which is the root of sense; and from there the malice is transformed to the remaining parts of the body.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **It suggests, etc.** Next follows the leaden circle, which signifies epilepsy and a kind of killing of the brain itself, and the spreading of malice to other parts of the body. ¶ **Root of sense.** That is, the brain, which is the root of the senses and the nerves. ¶ **Branches.** That is, the nerves, which are produced from the root of the brain.

---

### On the red circle appearing after a livid one.

> *If after a livid one a red circle is seen,*
> *The nature of the brain rises up: its vigor is restored.*

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **From a livid one.** A circle that is livid at first, if it later becomes red, signifies a conversion from evil to good, and that the power of the brain itself is strengthened and improved.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **From a livid one.** He treats the red circle not simply, but by comparison to a preceding livid color. And it is a comparative medium rather than an absolute one. For if in apoplexy or "inozi" <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek medical term for a brain disorder</note> a livid circle appeared first in the urine, and on the second or third day afterward a red one appears, such a change is most excellent: a conversion from mortification to the strengthening of life, and from the extinction of heat to its restoration. ¶ **Nature.** That is, the governing power. ¶ **Rises up.** That is, it signifies a resurrection.

### Next follows the green circle.

> *If it takes the form of burning heat in a water-fever,*
> *The bilious humor succeeds to the motion of frenzy.*

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **If the form.** He determines the green circle, which, appearing in an acute fever, brings fear of frenzy <note>Latin: *frenesis*, a term for brain inflammation or delirium</note> and of the rushing of matter to the brain.

<margin>Commentary.**
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **If the form.** Next follows the green circle, which signifies a certain agitation in an acute fever; whence one must fear a future frenzy arising from an excess of bile. ¶ **Bilious.** That is, choleric.

### On the trembling circle.

> *If it should be trembling, the spinal members are weighed down.*
> *If it should be black: it either kills or burns,*
> *Preceding the poison, or distinguished by lividity in both.*

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **If trembling.** A trembling circle signifies a heaviness in the spinal members. ¶ **If black.** A black circle signifies two things: either mortification and the extinction of natural heat, or "adustion" <note>Extreme overheating or scorching of the humors</note>. If it signifies mortification, then a livid color preceded it. If it signifies adustion, then a green color preceded it.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **If trembling.** Next follows the trembling circle, which signifies pain in the posterior parts from the "nucha" <note>The spinal cord or nape of the neck</note> all the way to the tail; which also signifies that around those parts there is a great "nervosity" and thus pain, which, exiting with its part of the urine and ascending upward, agitates the circle, whence the trembling occurs. ¶ **If black.** Here the author treats the black circle, which signifies mortification and adustion, or the completion of adustion. But it is distinguished thus: if it is preceded [by...]

<meta>This page continues the diagnostic analysis of urine, moving from the "circle" (the meniscus) to the "ampulla" (bubbles on the surface) and "granules" (beads of foam). It explains how these features indicate the maturity of a disease and the flow of humors from the brain to other parts of the body.</meta>

...[if] green [precedes], it signifies the completion of combustion; but if a livid color precedes, it signifies the detriment of mortification. <note>original: "viridis... liuidus." In medieval medicine, colors like green or livid (leaden/blue-black) in the urine's circle were grave signs of internal "burning" or the death of tissue.</note>

### On the bubble.

> A non-settling bubble, swelling, viscous, and clinging, 
> Makes the causes of disease crude and prolongs the illness. 
> It generates kidney disease and troubles with brain pain. 
> It marks rumbling, vomiting, and a loose belly.

<margin>Explanation</margin>
¶ **Explanation.** **Non-settling.** Having spoken of the circle, we must now speak of the bubble; this bubble follows the order of the enumeration made above. The bubble is a swelling of foam adhering to the circle: inflated, distended, and dilated. It is of two types: persistent and non-persistent. The non-persistent bubble is not determined in medicine, as it is transitory and caused by the pouring of the urine or any other liquid; this the author calls a "settling bubble." The non-persistent bubble is this: one that lasts and remains for a long time after the urine is poured, because it proceeds from an intrinsic cause. It is generated from a disturbance of the humors and from windiness <note>original: "ventositate," referring to gas or "vapors" trapped in the body's fluids.</note> trapped within. Therefore, because such a bubble signifies the disposition of the human body, it is discussed in medicine. This bubble is called "non-settling" by the author, meaning it remains for a long time. The rule for this bubble is as follows: A bubble in the urine that lasts for a long time, remaining swollen, dilated, and distended due to trapped windiness, being viscous and clinging to the circle—so much so that if a stick wrapped in flax is placed in the urine glass, it can only be removed from the circle with difficulty—then such a bubble signifies the "crudity" <term>crudity: the state of humors that are "undigested" or "un-cooked" by the body's natural heat</term> of the disease and its long duration. ¶ **And kidney disease.** This same bubble signifies a passion of the kidneys. The reason for this is found in the commentary. ¶ **And of the brains.** This bubble also signifies a headache because of the smokiness <note>original: "fumositatem," the vaporous waste of digestion</note> released from the crude matter, which ascends to the brain and inflates its membranes; thus pain is produced in the head. ¶ **Rumbling.** The same bubble signifies rumbling generated by windiness, as well as vomiting and a loose belly.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** **Non-settling.** Once the treatise on the circle is finished, he deals with the bubble, which follows the order of the enumeration. The bubble is foam adhering to the circle, quite swollen and dilated by much distension. Of bubbles, some are settling and others are non-settling. The settling kind is that which quickly vanishes, and it is generated by the force of pouring. Thus, from any liquid—such as water or especially wine poured forcefully into a vessel—a bubble is generated. But after a little time has passed, it is quickly annihilated and retains no trace of its former state. Regarding such a bubble, since it is transitory and does not remain, the author does not treat it, because it is not necessary for demonstrating the condition of the human body, as it does not arise from any disturbance of the humors but only from the external air. The non-settling bubble, however, is that which remains long after the pouring of the urine, because it arises from an internal cause, namely, from the disturbance and movement of the humors and trapped windiness. He deals with such a bubble here because it designates the disposition of the human body. Hence, this rule is given for the bubble: A bubble in the urine that remains for a long time, swollen and dilated, distended by trapped windiness, viscous and clinging to the circle—so that it can hardly be removed from the circle by a stick wrapped in flax—signifies the crudity of the matter, the length of the disease, kidney disease, and headache. It is "non-settling" because the permanence of the cause and the rooting of the malice are signified by this. It is "swollen" and "dilated" because it signifies the trapping of thick windiness. It is "clinging" because it proceeds from the viscosity of the matter. Such a bubble, therefore, portends the crudity of the matter. For crude and cold matter, when it cannot be fully cooked and digested by the action of heat, is resolved into thick windiness; this windiness, once released and not consumed by weak heat, is trapped in the moist parts

<column-break/>

and, approaching the liver through the continuous passages, it is mixed with the superfluity of the second digestion. Afterward, it is purged with the urine. The same bubble signifies the length of the illness; for where there is crudity of matter, length of illness follows. It also signifies <term>nephresis: an old term for kidney disease or inflammation</term>. For when crude humors are shown to be the cause, they have a similarity with the kidneys; for the kidneys are cold and removed from the source of heat. Since they are cold and the matter is cold with the gravity of substance and similarity of temperament, that matter is drawn to the kidneys along with the blood meant to nourish them. Since it cannot be consumed, because there is much of it and the heat in the kidneys is weak, it remains as an excess beyond nature and induces kidney disease. This same bubble also shows a headache, because it indicates trapped windiness; for the smokiness released from the crude matter breathes upward by its own lightness, induces head pain, and distends the membranes of the brain. We derive this rule and method from Hippocrates in the seventh book of the *Aphorisms*. For Hippocrates says: "Those who have bubbles floating on top of their urine have a sign of kidney disease and that the illness will be long." <note>original: "Quibuscūqʒ ampulle in vzina sugnantanť..." This is a reference to Hippocrates, Aphorisms 7.34.</note> ¶ **Non-settling bubble.** That is, remaining for a long time after the pouring of the urine, to distinguish it from those created by the force of pouring, which are not useful for prognosis regarding the human body. ¶ **Swollen.** That is, turgid or inflated. ¶ **Windy.** That is, distended by much windiness. ¶ **Clinging.** That is, stuck to the circle. ¶ **Prolongs.** That is, makes lengthy.

### On the granules.

> Granules are always messengers of a rheumatic cause. 
> If fixed granules are held in the sequence of the circle, 
> A secret confusion of disease lies hidden in the brain. 
> If they remain slightly depressed and, when moved, 
> Do not hasten back to the head, the humor seeks nearby places. 
> The flow becomes more prone toward the weaker part.

<margin>Explanation</margin>
¶ **Explanation.** **Granules.** Having determined the bubble, he consequently determines the granules. Granules are certain small grains of broken foam, divided into many parts within the circle. The rule is this: Granules signify a flux of humors <note>original: "fluxuz humoꝛ," referring to the movement of fluids like catarrh or bile</note> descending from the head to another lower part of the body. When "rheum" <note>original: "reuma," a flow of fluid, often from the head</note> flows and descends from the brain—a cold and moist member—it takes its name according to the weak part to which it flows, as is explained in the commentary. ¶ **Of the circle.** If the granules remain fixed in the circle, then this signifies that the matter of the disease resides in the brain. ¶ **If they remain depressed.** If those granules remain below the circle and do not ascend to the circle when the urine glass is moved, then depending on whether they are more or less depressed below the circle, this signifies pain in members closer to or further from the head. ¶ **More prone.** Here a cause is given on the part of the receiving member, which is the weakness of that member; for since the member itself is weak, it certainly cannot repel the matter to another place. We can also understand the strength of the propelling member by this. This is the first cause according to Johannitius in the commentary; the second and third causes are the abundance of matter and the wideness of the pores. <note>Johannitius (Hunayn ibn Ishaq) was a major translator and author of medical texts used in the Middle Ages.</note>

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** **Granules are.** After the bubble, the author deals with granules. Granules are certain grains of foam, cut off and separated in the circle; that is, divided into different parts. These granules testify to "rheum"—that is, the flow of humors from the head to another part. For since the brain is cold and moist, and of the nature of fat and marrow, it is nourished by cold and moist nutriment. Hence, much watery and fluid humidity often overflows in the brain, part of which is purged through the mucus of the nostrils, and another part is emitted through spit and coughing. If it happens that these superfluities abound in the brain, a headache is produced from such fullness; and neither the natural heat nor the auxiliary heat can manage to act upon that matter, breaking it into tiny parts...

->Gilles on Urines.<-

# On the contents

...dividing. Those particles from incontinence flow down as rheum <note>original: "reumaticant," referring to the medieval concept of "catarrh" or the flow of excess humors from the brain to the body</note> to the lower parts: and especially to those that they find to be weaker, nearby, and situated below. Therefore, if the matter moves to the narrowing of the nostrils, it causes a cold <note>original: "coryzam"</note>. If to the eyes, it causes ophthalmia. If specifically above the eyes, it causes pain in the eyebrows. If to the ears, it causes ringing and windiness, and prepares the way for deafness. If to the uvula <note>original: "vuam"</note>, it causes its relaxation and hoarseness. If to the mouth and tongue, it causes ulcerations of the mouth and tongue. If to the maxillary nerves, it causes pain in the teeth and tongue. If to the throat, it causes nodes and "bronchi" <note>original: "brancos," likely referring to swollen tonsils or throat glands</note> in the throat. If to the channels of the lung and the windpipe <note>original: "tracheā artariā"</note>, it causes a cough. If to the lung, it causes asthma and dyspnea <note>original: "dūniā," a corruption of the Greek term for difficulty breathing</note>. If to the intestines, it causes lientery or diarrhea, and then the excretions should be foamy. One of Hippocrates' sayings: *For those whose excretions are foamy, phlegm flows down twice from the head.* If to the mouth of the stomach, it causes pain, inflation, and indigestion; for in such cases, the urine's circle should be granular. Overall, granules signify a rheumatic distillation of matter to the parts near the head, and especially to the weaker ones, which are not sufficient to repel the force of the rheum, or cannot expel it. For no other member should be harmed, there can be three causes as Joannitius <note>The Latinized name of Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a translator and physician whose work was foundational to medieval European medicine</note> asserts. 1st: the strength of the member expelling; 2nd: the weakness of the one receiving; 3rd: this is the primary cause. The second is the abundance of the matter. The third is the width of the pores. But distinguish this: because if the granules lie in the circle <note>the meniscus at the top of the urine sample</note>, and when the urine is shaken they are pressed down but return to the circle, it shows the cause remains in the head. If however they are pressed below the circle and do not return to their circle, it signifies the weight and pain of the lower parts near or far from the head, according to how much or little they were pressed down. <margin>And the Circle.</margin> That is, fixed in the circle: so that if they were pressed down, they return to the circle.

### On the cloud.

> The spiritual cloud of the airy body
> Indicates a fault of the injured liver and heat.
> It is windy: or it becomes the foam of scorched heat
> A messenger continued in its own particles.
> This the color of urine proves, as does the substance of the foam.
> Spirit thickens it and heat thins it.
> Remaining divided, distinct with small heavy [parts]
> It strikes weak members with heavy rheum.
> It indicates jaundice: or portends the liver is being burned.
> If it is black: or green: or as if tinged with saffron.

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Explanation.** **Of the airy body.** Having spoken of the granular, we likewise treat the cloud <note>original: "nubecula," a suspension in the urine that looks like a light, floating cloud</note>. The cloud is a certain smoky and vaporous superfluity generated by the action of heat, having a certain obscurity. And thus the nebula <note>cloud</note>, since it is light, tends to the upper part of the urine and makes the urine itself shadowed. This nebula therefore signifies two things: namely, a distemper of the spiritual members <note>the heart and lungs, which medieval medicine believed managed the "vital spirits"</note>—and then there should be a certain lividness—and it signifies the heating of the liver, and the foam should be saffron-colored.

<margin>Multiple types of foam.</margin>
¶ **It is windy.** Here he treats of foam, which is indeed manifold. For one type is granular, which was discussed in the chapter on granules. And another is bubbly <note>original: "ampullosa," like a vial or large bubble</note>, which was discussed in the chapter on the bubble. And there is another continuous foam, which is treated here. This continuous foam signifies two things: namely, windiness <note>gas or vapors</note>—and this is known if the color of the urine is discolored, or if the substance of the urine is thick. It also signifies the vehemence of the heat of boiling—and this is known because the color of the urine is red and the substance thin. Saffron-colored foam is a sign of heating. Whence foam has significance in its color: for some is saffron, some green, some black; and according to this, it signifies different things.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** **Of the airy body.** After the granules, the author treats the cloud. Now, the cloud is a certain smoky, vaporous superfluity generated by the action of heat, participating in obscurity: which, since it is light and airy, being emitted with the urine, shadows it. Such a

<column-break/>

cloud appearing in the urine signifies a distemper of the spiritual members; and it occupies the surface <note>original: "suspiciē," likely "superficiem"</note> of the urine, which is called the airy body, and makes the urine participate in a certain lucidity. Such a cloud appearing also suggests the heat of the liver, which is more fully confirmed by a saffron color. **Of the airy body.** That is, on the surface. **Of the offense of the spiritual [parts].** That is, a passion of the spiritual members, which are the furnace and chimney of all heat. **Of the liver.** That is, the liver. **It is windy.** After the cloud, the author treats foam. Say therefore that by "foam" we understand foam lacking bubbles. Of bubbly foam, he spoke before. For foam is manifold. One is disjoined and cut off, and distinct with certain granules, of which the author treats in the chapter on granules; and here he repeats the same by chance of division. There is also another windy and bubbly foam, of which he proposed above in the chapter on bubbles. There is another third foam, neither granular nor bubbly, but continuous; and such signifies a union of viscosity, or the violence of heat and boiling. Here he distinguishes by the heat of the urine and the evidence of boiling: when it is one viscous-colored thing, it is an increase of indigestion and vice. Likewise, if it be thin and stretched too much, this is from heat. If it is perceived with saffron color, it provides a faithful argument for burning. Likewise, some foam varies according to color: for some is black, or green, or saffron. For black signifies melancholy <note>the "black bile" humor</note>, or burnings of the liver. Green signifies "agriaca" <note>an intense, bitter bile</note>. Saffron signifies saffron-colored jaundice. **Windy.** The bubbly kind of which it was said: a messenger of windiness. **Intense heat.** That is, of burning. **Spirit.** Windiness thickens the foam by its enclosure. **Thins.** That is, heat thins the enclosed windiness. **Intercisa.** <note>Divided or interrupted foam</note>. This has been spoken of: for it signifies black jaundice, or green, or citrine.

### On pus.

> Effused pus confesses ulcers of the bladder.
> Or a scab of the kidneys if a heavy odor is present.
> From the region of the liver flows a pussy sediment.
> This, pain and the injured action of the part teaches.

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Explanation.** **Ulcers.** Here he determines about pus <note>original: "sanie," a discharge of blood and pus from a wound or ulcer</note>, which pus emitted in the urine signifies an ulceration of the kidneys, or bladder, or liver. And he distinguishes: for pus emitted from the kidneys or bladder has a heavy odor, and in those parts pain is felt. But if pus is emitted from the liver, then the pain and heaviness are in the right hypochondrium <note>the upper abdominal region on the right side</note>, and the digestive power is hindered.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** **Ulcers of the bladder.** In this chapter he treats of pus, which, when effused with urine, signifies an ulceration of the bladder, or the liver from some superfluous matter collected in its region. But whether it is emitted from the kidneys, or the bladder, or the liver, distinguish thus. For from the kidneys or bladder, that which is emitted portends a heavy odor, and pain is felt in those parts and adjacent places. But from the liver, not at all. Instead, in the right hypochondrium, a pulsation of pain and a certain weight is perceived, and the operation of the digestive power is hindered. Therefore, let us elicit this from Hippocrates, who at the end of the fourth particle says: *If one urines pus, and it is thin and the odor is heavy, then it signifies an ulceration of the kidneys or bladder.*

### On fat.

> A fatty resolution preceding the form of oil.
> With a fever, it dissolves the whole; without fever, the loins.

<margin>Explanation.</margin>
¶ **Explanation.** Here he determines about fat appearing in the urine; and the author says that the fat appearing in the urine is either with fever or without fever. If with fever, then it signs the dissolution <note>the breaking down or wasting away of the body's tissues</note> of the whole body. If without fever, it signifies the dissolution happening from the kidneys. Concerning fatty urine and oily unctuosity which signifies the solution of the whole body, or the dissolution of the kidneys. And in how many ways the dissolution of the whole body [occurs]...
