C 3

...distinguished from the dissolution of the kidneys is best placed in the commentary.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ Commentary. ¶ The preceding text. After the sound follows the chapter on fat. By the name "fat" <note>original: "pinguedo," referring here to oily or fatty-looking substances floating in the urine</note> is understood a certain fatty and unctuous substance resolved from the limbs: which is emitted with the urine; the urine appears more or less fatty or oily according to the greater or lesser quantity of resolution, and according to the progress of the heat in the preceding resolution. For at the beginning of the resolution of the fat itself, the urine appears oily, having as it were the color of oil; in the "increase" stage, however, it is as if it were oil itself.

<margin>Froth of fat</margin>
In the "state" <note>original: "statu," the peak or height of a condition</note> however it is like fat itself or oil itself. Urine which has the color of oil in the beginning declares a liquefaction that is almost watery; that which is like oil has in itself the perfection of the mixture of oil. Such is the case in the "increase" stage: it signifies the process and increase of liquefaction. But that which is oily both in color and in substance, appearing just like oil itself, signifies the peak state of resolution and the ultimate dissolution caused by heat. Such urines are indeed familiar to hectic fever <note>original: "ethice febris," a chronic, wasting fever often associated with tuberculosis</note>. ¶ But note: that such urine appears either with fever or without. If with fever, it signifies the dissolution of the entire body, since fever is a universal movement of the body's humors. If without fever, it signifies a particular resolution of the kidneys and loins. For much fat is wrapped around the kidneys and loins and covers them; when this fat is resolved and passes out with the urine, the emission of oiliness is more copious than if it were emitted from the whole body. Nor is it located far from the urinary passages. And therefore, since it is abundant and placed nearby, and there is no consuming heat present (because it is without fever), once it begins to be resolved, it is purged more copiously. But that which is emitted from the whole body is in a smaller quantity: both because there is febrile heat present, which diminishes the quantity by consuming it, and because it is remote from the urinary channels. ¶ This we draw from Hippocrates, in the last section where he says: *In whomever the fatty sediment <term>hypostasis<gloss>the solid matter that settles at the bottom of a urine sample</gloss></term> is gathered into globules, this signifies that an acute kidney illness will occur in the form of a hectic fever.* The fat of urine is distinguished by its parts on the surface; it is found in a fleshy man who is not excessively heavy. In the second species, it occupies the whole surface of the urine like a spider web. In the third species, the fat is diffused throughout the whole. Whence urine poured upon a stone makes a dull sound, just like oil.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
¶ Fat resolved from the kidneys is distinguished in three ways from the fat of the whole body: first, because the fat of the body is not so abundant except perhaps in the third species of hectic fever. Second, it is distinguished because the fat of the kidneys appears immediately after the urine is passed; because it is difficult to mix, and being separated from nearby parts, it does not blend with the rest. Therefore, it appears unmixed in the urine, whereas fat separated from the whole body is thoroughly mixed by the force of "cooking" <note>original: "decoctōis," the metabolic process of the liver</note> in the liver. Thus it becomes less visible because it is not concentrated in one part. Third, it is distinguished because the fat of the kidneys does not cause the urine to become more intense in color unless perhaps the liver is also heated. But fat resolved from all the members occurs with an intensity and thinness of the urine.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
### On raw humor.

> Let humor in urine be at the top, middle, or bottom.
> It harms the upper, middle, or lower members.
> Sitting sediment causes strangury, kidney disease, and tenesmus.
> The middle burdens the nutritive organs; the top, the diaphragm.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
¶ Exposition. ¶ Humor. Here we treat the "raw humor" <note>unprocessed or undigested bodily fluids</note> that is emitted with urine. There are three things that have a similar appearance: namely, raw humor, putrefaction, and sediment. But how they are discerned is well explained in the commentary. Raw humor emitted in urine sometimes occupies the upper part of the urine, sometimes the middle part, and sometimes the lower; according to this, it testifies to various regions of the human body. If it occupies the highest part, then it signifies a sickness of the chest, of the "spiritual members" <note>the lungs and heart, responsible for the "vital spirits"</note>, and a compression of the diaphragm. If it occupies the middle part, then it signifies a fault of the stomach due to an excess of superfluity, a twisting of the belly, and 

<column-break/>

rumbling of the intestines. If it occupies the lower part, then it declares a suffering of the kidneys and loins and adjacent parts: such as strangury <note>painful, drop-by-drop urination</note> or nephresis <note>kidney inflammation</note>.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ Commentary. ¶ Humor, etc. After fat, he treats the raw humor that is purged with urine. ¶ And it should be noted: there are three things that present the appearance of sediment: namely, putrefaction and raw humor. It must therefore be diligently distinguished thus: If the urine is shaken and the sediment breaks into small particles <term>hypostases<gloss>sedimentary deposits</gloss></term>, it is true sediment and has a more even, less interrupted form. This sediment is the waste product of the "third digestion" <note>the final metabolic stage where nutrients are absorbed into the body's tissues</note>. If, however, the shaken urine dissolves into fatty and oily streaks, and the urine itself is fetid and of a bad odor, it signifies that the humor is putrid. Furthermore, such sediment is pus-like, uneven, and tasteless. If the urine is shaken and dispersed into certain "atoms" or tiny particles, the rawness of the humors is understood. Raw humor thus emitted with urine occupies either the upper, middle, or lowest part. If it holds the upper part, it declares a fault of the chest and spiritual organs and a compression of the diaphragm, such as asthma or "dysma" <note>dyspnea or difficulty breathing</note>, or a condition of coughing up blood. If it holds the middle part, a fault of the stomach from an excess of waste, or a twisting of the belly, or inflation and rumbling of the intestines is indicated. If it holds the lowest part, a suffering of the kidneys, loins, and adjacent parts—such as tenesmus <note>a distressing, continual urge to evacuate the bowels or bladder</note>, kidney inflammation, strangury, and pain in the shins and knees—is manifested.

### On bloody urine.

> From a fault of the liver is drawn the passing of blood.
> Or from the bladder or kidneys, or the chyle vein: for you the full
> And provident doctrine of the remaining signs makes it clear.
> The bladder pours out clotted, heavy, and spotted blood,
> Which settles at the bottom and has a slight stench.
> The rupture of the chyle vein is pure blood from a break,
> And the seventh part of the spine <note>likely the seventh vertebra from the bottom, in the lumbar region</note> pains heavily from the end.
> If it flows from the loins, it runs pure and without clots;
> The kidneys testify to this, and a stinging sensation accompanies it.
> Pain tortures the right side if the flow comes from the liver,
> And pure, clear blood flows, seeking relief through fomentations.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
¶ Exposition. ¶ From a fault. Here it is determined concerning blood exiting with the urine, which signifies four things: either a fault of the liver, the bladder, the kidneys, or a rupture of the "chyle vein" <note>original: "vene chilis," referring to the vena cava or a major vessel carrying nutrient-rich fluid</note>; this is what is said up to that point. ¶ *For you the full.* Here he provides specifications along with other conditions, specifically regarding what proceeds from the bladder. ¶ *It pours out clotted.* Here it is specified when blood proceeds from the bladder: because that blood is clotted into a ball-like shape, has a heavy and fetid odor, and resides at the bottom. Such blood is thicker and heavier. The reasons for these are explained sufficiently in the commentary. ¶ *Mixing.* Here it is specified when blood proceeds from a rupture of the chyle vein: because then the blood is pure, and the greatest pain is felt in the seventh vertebra, counting from the lower part. ¶ *If it flows from the loins.* Here the blood exiting from the kidneys is specified: because then the blood is pure and is not clotted, and pain and a stinging sensation are felt in the kidneys. ¶ *Right pain.* Here the blood exiting from the liver is specified: that blood is pure and clear, and a vehement pain is felt in the right hypochondrium <note>the upper-right area of the abdomen, below the ribs</note>. ¶ *Kidneys and bladder.* Here he determines the nature of the "small sands" <note>gravel or kidney stones</note> which signal illnesses of either the kidneys or the bladder. They are of the kidneys if they appear red in color; of the bladder if they appear white; they take the color of the organ from which they derive. It should also be noted that red sands sometimes appear in patients with a "double tertian" or simple fever <note>types of recurring malarial fevers</note>. Especially in those with "dry" kidneys due to visceral fever, red sands of calculus <note>stones</note> appear. What a stone is, how it is generated, and what the causes of its generation are, is made manifest enough in the commentary for anyone who looks.

It maintains the diagnostic framework linking the appearance of these substances to specific organs like the liver, kidneys, and bladder.</meta>

# On the Contents
<sig>D</sig>

blood: whenever it is emitted with the urine. Blood thus emitted with the urine either proceeds from the liver: and then it appears to be pure and sincere <note>original: "sincerus"; meaning unmixed or clean</note>, and it is felt in the right hypochondrium <note>the upper region of the abdomen, just below the ribs, where the liver is located</note>. And such blood, since it is hot, mixes perfectly with the urine. Or, it proceeds from the bladder: and then it appears to be clotted blood in the shape of a globe, of a heavy odor, and residing at the bottom. Because it is then cold—being destined for the nourishment of a cold member <note>the bladder was considered a "cold" organ in medieval physiology</note>—it is more impure, thicker, and heavier. Being received within the cavity of the bladder, which is a cold organ, it clots further and becomes corrupted, because the bladder has weak heat; therefore, the blood cannot be purified of its superfluities. Because it is cold, it is globular and heavy, descending to the bottom; thus it also has a heavy odor and does not mix with the urine. From this, one can tell it originates from the bladder. A piercing sensation is felt around the pubic bone, the peritoneum, and around the end of the penis during the emission of urine. Such blood can be turned into stone <note>original: "petrificari"</note> in the urine, both by its own globosity and its coldness, and also by the property of the place containing it, which facilitates petrification—a condition from which many have perished. And as Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a famous 10th-century Persian physician</note> reports, such blood is sometimes emitted through the penis in the manner of a leech. If it takes its origin by being drawn from the loins, it is pure, and pain and a piercing sensation are felt in the kidneys. If it comes from the rupture of a containing vein, it is similarly pure, and a vehement pain will be felt in the seventh vertebra, counting from the lower part. We draw the firmness of this dogma from Hippocrates <note>original: "Hypo."</note>, who says: "If someone passes blood, or a small amount of blood like dust, it is from the kidneys" <note>original: "Si sanguinē mingat qz: aut puo q̃si puluerulētū sanguinē ad isiam puri"</note>. And afterwards he adds: also scales, by which he signifies an ulceration of the bladder; and there is a pounding and a heavy burning, from which the corruption of the blood occurs, and then indeed it signifies an ulceration of the bladder. Likewise, Hippocrates says: "If they pass blood and have clots and strangury <note>painful, drop-by-drop urination</note>, and pain falls into the pubic area and the peritoneum, it signifies pain around the bladder." For from these things, a suffering of the bladder is indicated. Hippocrates determines the same when it proceeds from the kidneys, saying: "Whoever passes blood spontaneously, this signifies a rupture of a vein in the kidneys."

### ¶ On Sands.
Sands testify to a stone of the kidneys or bladder.
If red, it is of the kidneys; if more white, of the bladder.
Let the form of the content be a rival to that of the container.

<margin>Explanation</margin>¶ Exposition. ¶ Of the kidneys. Seek this commentary in the commentary said above, where it says: ¶ Of the kidneys and bladder. Here it is determined what small sands signify.

<margin>Commentary</margin>¶ Commentary. ¶ Of the kidneys. In this chapter, the author treats of small sands which are sometimes emitted with the urine, and of the sufferings of the bladder. They attest to "nefresis" <note>kidney disease</note> in the kidneys, or show that "lithiasis" <note>stone disease</note> will be in the bladder. But sands are either red, white, black, or darkish. If they are red and soft, they are considered to come from the kidneys. For the kidneys are red, soft, fleshy, and contain blood; therefore, the sands generated there, following the form of their container, are considered to be of a reddish type. If they are white, they rather come from the bladder, for the bladder is white; and according to the form of the container, it changes the content. For every thing is drawn to its own origin: either from the place of its generation, or from the acting or suffering thing. From the place, just as abscesses must be such as the places where they are born, like phlegms in an idle place. If they are black, it was melancholic matter, and these are the worst of all, because they are of thicker matter. But those which are white can be dissolved more quickly, because they are generated from phlegmatic humors that are crude, undigested, and congealed. The calculus <note>stone</note> which is made from black sands glued together is the worst of all. If it is large, it cannot be cured except by incision. But if it is from white sands produced from phlegmatic matter, unless it has been greatly scorched, cooked over a long period, and hardened, it can be more easily cured by the benefit of diuretics and antidotal medicines. ¶ And note that in children, lithiasis occurs more frequently because of the viscosity of the humors abounding in them; in youths, however, nefresis occurs more

<column-break/>

frequently because of the dryness of the kidneys. Wherefore the blood dries out, and the subtle parts are consumed; the earthy parts remaining are therefore hardened. ¶ It is known, however, that one should be cautious whenever you see red sands appear in the urine; do not immediately rush to a judgment about a stone, because in those suffering from a double or simple tertian fever <note>a fever recurring every third day, often malaria</note>, and especially in those having dry kidneys, red sands appear because of the febrile dyscrasia <note>an imbalance of bodily fluids caused by fever</note>. ¶ Also note: that there are three causes for the generation of a stone: namely, an abundance of superfluities, their viscosity, the narrowness of the passages, and the weakness of the expulsive virtue. These causes are stronger in children; therefore, they are more familiar with this suffering. ¶ Sands appear for three reasons: either from a stone, or from arthritis, or a long quartan fever. In arthritis, it is from the hardening of humors; in quartan fever, from the drying melancholy which hardens the humors, as found in Alexander of Tralles <note>original: "Alexādro de pnisco"</note>, who spat out a stone that had been generated in the channels of the lungs from the hardening of humors. ¶ And note that sands sometimes signify a confirmed stone, and sometimes a diminishing one. If, not having appeared before, they multiply more and more every day until less appears, it signifies the stone is being diminished. If, where many appeared before, they decrease more every day, they signify the stone is being confirmed <note>solidifying or growing</note>; when they do not appear at all, and the passages have not been purged, then they signify a confirmed stone.

### ¶ On Hairs.
The form will be similar to hairs, or it will be a shedding of flesh,
Or a part of the humor dried by the file of heat.
From this, you may prove the harms of the kidneys or of the whole.

<margin>Explanation</margin>¶ Exposition. ¶ The form. Here it is determined concerning hairs. Hairs are certain long and slender resolutions <note>dissolved particles</note> resembling hairs; they are emitted with the urine and signify either a dissolution of the kidneys and loins, or a dryness of the humors from the sharpness of the drying heat, and this is held in the commentary. ¶ Note that these hairs appear either with fever or without fever. If with fever, it signifies the dissolution of the whole body. If without fever, it signifies the dissolution of the kidneys and loins.

<margin>Commentary</margin>¶ Commentary. ¶ The form. In this chapter, the author treats of hairs. Hairs are certain long and slender resolutions in the manner of hairs which are emitted with the urine. They proceed from the dissolution of the kidneys and loins, or they are made from dried humors, which are distinguished thus: if, when rubbed between the fingers, one feels a sort of solidity of flesh in such a resolution, then it is considered to be from the substance of the kidneys; and it signifies a pain of the kidneys and loins from the sharpness of heat dissolving them, and thereafter killing the body; such things appear in diabetics. Wherefore Hippocrates says in the Aphorisms: "Those in whom small pieces of flesh or hairs come out while the urine is fatty, these things come from the kidneys." If, however, those hairs when rubbed between the fingers yield to the pressure and do not immediately vanish, so that there is some solidity beneath, they are signified to be made of phlegm and hardened humors. And these long resolutions appear somewhat thick; they signify an obstruction of the kidneys and loins, sometimes of the right kidney, sometimes of the left, and sometimes of both. If of the right, numbness and tingling <note>original: "formicatio"; the sensation of ants crawling on the skin</note> are felt in the right foot. If of the left, in the left foot. If of both, it is felt in both. For from such an obstruction the nerves are compressed, and through their compression the animal spirits <note>the subtle fluid believed to flow through nerves to provide sensation and motion</note>—whose property it is to run through the nerves—cannot bestow sense and voluntary motion to the extreme parts. Thus the animal spirit cannot pass freely through the nerves because of the aforementioned compression; hence numbness or tingling occurs. ¶ And note that hairs appear in the urine either with fever or without fever. If with fever, it signifies the dissolution of the whole body. If without fever, it is judged to be a shedding from the substance of the kidneys specifically.

### ¶ On Scales and Bran.
By thin scales and bran mixed in, there is noted
A scabrous condition of the bladder; or if fever accompanies it,
-> of the whole <- <note>This catchword "Totius" indicates the next page begins with "of the whole body"</note>

<summary>This page discusses the diagnostic significance of blood, sand (sediment), and hair-like fibers found in urine. It details how the color, texture, and physical sensations associated with these substances point to specific ailments in the liver, kidneys, or bladder.</summary>
<keywords>hematuria, kidney stones, lithiasis, bladder health, medieval pathology, Hippocrates, Haly Abbas, animal spirits, diabetes, urinary sediment</keywords>

--- Page 37 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical examination of urinary sediments, moving from blood and stones to various types of "resolutions"—solid particles shed from the body's internal members. It maintains the systematic diagnostic approach common in medieval medicine, linking physical appearance to the severity of wasting diseases like hectic fever.</meta>

# Urine

While the integrity of the whole once existed, the body is now thinned.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **Through scales.** In this place, the author determines the nature of scales and bran-like flakes. Scales <note>original: "squame"</note> are certain flat and round resolutions similar to fish scales; these are indeed scraped from the surface of the members. They are called "leaf-like scales" <note>original: "squame petaloides"</note>. When these scales appear in the urine, they sometimes signify the dissolution of the entire body—specifically if a fever is present. If, however, there is no fever, it signifies a localized dissolution and an irritation <note>original: "scabies"; often meaning a rough skin condition or ulceration</note> of the bladder. ¶ Bran-like flakes <note>original: "furfura"</note> are certain resolutions resembling bran, which are torn and scraped away from the members by the violence of heat. Those that are bran-like are white, because the members from which they fall are white. They are also thicker than scales because they are dissolved from deeper within the substance of the member. Such bran-like appearances in the urine signify either the dissolution of the whole body or only of the bladder. If, therefore, a fever is present when they appear, it signifies the dissolution of the whole body. If they appear without fever, they signify the dissolution of the bladder alone. This is also recognized through whether digestion or indigestion is present.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Through scales.** Next follows the discussion of scales and bran-like flakes. Scales are certain flat and round resolutions which are torn and scraped from the surface of the members by the action of heat. They are like small leaves <note>original: "petala"</note> or small fish scales. Hence they are called leaf-like scales. These resolutions, once separated from the members, are sometimes purged with the urine; they indicate the dissolution of either the whole body or the bladder. If a fever is present when they appear, they signify the dissolution of the whole body, as happens in hectic fever <note>original: "febre ethica"; a chronic wasting disease, often associated with tuberculosis</note>. If they appear without fever and with indigestion, then a localized dissolution and an ulceration of the bladder is demonstrated. Hippocrates confirms this in his *Aphorisms*, where he says: "If they pass scales and there is heavy pain, it signifies ulceration of the bladder." ¶ Bran-like flakes are resolutions arranged in the manner of bran, falling from the members due to the violence of heat. They are white because the members themselves are white. These are emitted with the urine and are thicker than scales because they are not scraped so superficially; rather, they are plucked more deeply from the substance of the members by internal heat. Urine having bran-like resolutions, therefore, signifies either the dissolution of the whole body or the bladder alone. Thus, the distinction is made by the presence or absence of fever, and by digestion or indigestion. Hippocrates, however, says in his *Aphorisms*: "Those who pass bran-like flakes in oily urine have an irritation of the bladder." Leaf-like scales and bran are dissolved from the bladder, but not hair-like strands <note>original: "crinoides"</note>, because the bladder is not a solid body but is thin and filmy. The aforementioned substances sometimes flow from the humors when heat takes up liquid parts or coldness condenses them. But with other signs, leaf-like scales appear in the first stage of hectic fever, bran-like flakes in the second, and hair-like strands in the third.

### On Hair-like Strands

> Certain faith is found through hair-like strands, which is the third fever.
> It is a species of hectic fever, hidden too deeply within.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **Certain.** Here he determines the nature of hair-like strands <note>original: "crinoides"</note>. Hair-like strands are certain thick resolutions which are plucked very deeply from the substance of the members by the violence of heat; they are larger than scales and bran. For hair-like strands have three large dimensions: namely, width, length, and depth. Therefore, hair-like strands appearing in the urine signify the third stage of hectic fever.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Certain.** Under one heading we have dealt with scales and bran. In this chapter I am about to treat hair-like strands. These are certain thick resolutions separated from the members by the violence of intense heat outside the members; they are larger than bran and leaf-like scales in three dimensions. Namely, they increase greatly in width, length, and depth, by which it is signified that the substance of the members is being dissolved more extensively and fully. They are called *crinoides* from *idos*, which is "form," and *crina*, which is "two," as if presenting a double form. Furthermore, *crine* or *crina* are thicker parts or particles of wheat which are divided from the integrity of the whole grain during the process of softening and grinding at the mill.

<column-break/>

Such hair-like strands appearing in the urine designate the third stage of hectic fever. Since they are so round, they do not proceed from the bladder. For the bladder is better suited to the resolution of bran and scales than to hair-like strands. Sometimes such strands appear red or blackish in an acute fever because of the infection of the blood, and this is a very bad sign; sometimes they testify to a disease of the solid members. Hence Hippocrates says in the final part: "In those for whom hair-like strands occur in the sediment <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> of the urine during a fever, it signifies a long illness," that is, hectic fever.

### On the Resolutions of Atoms and Small White Particles

> It is hinted that the gout reigns through small white particles.
> If it be a woman, another sign will not be lacking:
> Either she has conceived, or she is prone to illness.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **It hints.** Here he determines the nature of atom-like resolutions and small white particles. These resolutions appearing in the urine of both men and women signify the vice of gout <note>original: "gutta"; literally "the drop," a term for joint pain and metabolic disease</note>. And according to the region of the urine they occupy, they signify that the corresponding region of the human body is afflicted. For if they are in the upper part of the urine, it signifies the upper parts of the body suffer from gout; if in the middle, the middle; and if in the bottom of the urine, they signify gout in the inferior parts of the body. ¶ It is nevertheless to be noted that if these atom-like and white resolutions appear in the urine of a woman, and they are oily, residing at the bottom like the washings of starch <note>original: "loture amili"</note>, and after a short time they cluster together, such resolutions signify that the woman has conceived. If they appear reddish and round, they signify she has conceived a male. If they appear white or leaden <note>original: "liuide"</note> and flat in shape, they signify she has conceived a female. If, however, the woman has not conceived despite all the aforementioned signs, then it signifies gout, as was said, or a humorosity of the womb, and then the urine is thicker.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **It hints.** Next follows the treatise on atom-like resolutions and small white particles, which are the same thing. Atom-like and white resolutions signify the vice of gout in both men and women. But if they appear at the bottom, they signify gout of the inferior parts. If they appear in the middle region, they signify the vice of gout in the middle parts, namely from the region of the genitals up to the diaphragm. If they appear in the upper part, they signify gout of the superior parts. But if they are diffused through the entire substance of the urine, they signify gout in all members. Such resolutions, if they appear in the urine of a woman and it is oily—especially residing in the inferior part like the washings of starch and clustering together after a short time—signify the woman has conceived. If they appear reddish and round in shape, it signifies she has conceived a male; for they are red or reddish because the natural heat is sufficient to give them such a color. If, however, they appear white or leaden and flat in shape, they signify she has conceived a female. Through such a color and variety, the weakness of the natural heat is signified, being insufficient to attribute a perfect color to them. If the woman has not conceived and such resolutions appear, it signifies she has "conceived" pain and is about to give birth to darkness <note>a metaphorical way of describing severe illness or a false pregnancy</note>. The vice of gout alone is signified without other signs in a woman, because such resolutions are ambiguous <note>original: "equocant"</note>: either signifying conception, or arthritis, or a humorosity of the womb, and then the urine is thicker. These are the various urines—namely those of women—which most often deceive the practitioner.
<margin>The urines of women are fallacious.</margin>
Concerning such urines, to give a judgment is dangerous, since they may pertain to either of the things mentioned. Thus, the truth regarding them is unknown, whether on account of the fetus or on account of the woman. In men, however, such urines with small white particles are safer to judge; in them, the manifest truth shines. But the urines of women are cursed <note>original: "execrabiles"</note> because of the possibility of a fetus and in respect to the body containing it. Resolutions of this kind appearing in the urine of a man, signifying gout, are white, small, and round. They are white because they are resolved from white members; thus they imitate the color of the members from which they fall. They are small because when natural heat acts on the matter of gout to digest and dissolve it, a small part is resolved from the member; since the member is solid and the action of heat is small, that which is resolved is small. And therefore the resolutions are small.

It also notes that "white minute" particles can indicate gout in men but are notoriously difficult to interpret in women, as they may also signify pregnancy or uterine conditions.</summary>

Of the contents

They are round: because heat acts upon that matter from all sides, dissolving it in a circumferential manner, and thus they appear round. Or, they are round because, by their nature, granules are round, just as they are rounded during their descent like falling hail. The same is seen in a drop of rain, which is rounded during its descent.

### On the signs of conception.

->The womb is dry: Venus is put to sleep: the flow is retained.<-
->A discolored state: vomiting: compression of the member.<-
->Heaviness of the breasts: and disturbance of the belly.<-
->The signs of conception are proven by honey-water.<-

<margin>Exposition</margin>
**Exposition.** Here the author determines the signs through which we can recognize conception incidentally. The sign of conception that is found through the urine was discussed just recently. But there are other signs of conception which are enumerated in these aforementioned verses. ¶ **The womb is dry.** Because the "door" (the opening of the womb) is now closed; hence they do not emit the menses <note>original: "menstrua"</note>, which usually moisten the vulva, but rather they are retained for the nourishment of the fetus. ¶ **Venus is put to sleep.** Another sign of conception. If the desire for Venus <note>desire for sexual intercourse</note> is put to sleep and extinguished, it is because the womb, which was empty, is now filled. ¶ **Retention of flow.** Another sign of conception; the menses are retained so that the fetus may be nourished from them. ¶ **A discolored state.** Another sign of conception. A varied and multiform appetite; for now she craves sharp flavors, now sour fruits, or charcoal, and such similar things <note>This refers to "pica," the craving for non-food items or specific flavors often associated with pregnancy</note>. And this happens from the melancholic menstrual blood itself overflowing to the mouth of the stomach and infecting it. ¶ **Vomiting.** Another sign: because that blood infecting the mouth of the stomach moves it to vomit. ¶ **Compression of the member.** Another sign of conception, as is held in the commentary <note>The text suggests a physical sensation of tightness or resistance felt by the male partner during intercourse</note>. ¶ **Heaviness of the breasts:** because blood overflows to the spongy tissue of the breasts, which causes them to grow large. ¶ **And disturbance.** Another sign of conception from Hippocrates in the 4th part of the *Aphorisms*: "If you wish to know if a woman has conceived," etc.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
**Commentary.** **The womb is dry.** In this chapter, which is like the finale and completion of his work, the accidents and signs of celebrated conception to be signified through urine are assigned, following the intention of the preceding chapter. Therefore, to have full knowledge of conception, the author placed the signs of conception at the conclusion of his work. ¶ **The womb is dry.** Because the internal orifice is closed, the womb is no longer moistened by the emission of menses; nor is the vulva moistened by the smearing of menses, because the menses are retained to nourish the fetus. By this name "womb" <note>original: "matricis"</note>, its extremity—that is, the vulva—is understood. Or the vulva is dry because, as the womb is now filled with the male seed and already "minted" <note>original: "monetato"; a metaphor likening the formation of a fetus in the womb to the striking of a coin in a mint</note> within, the pleasure of the womb is no longer so diffused by the allurements of Venus, nor does it dissolve into venereal tears <note>likely referring to vaginal lubrication</note>. For its thirst, which previously could not be stilled, is extinguished; this happens because it is now full, and burdened by the internal weight, it is less able to be free for the venereal itch. For the sensitivity of the womb flourishes from emptiness; from greater sensitivity, the womb is more greatly disturbed by the pleasantness of Venus. ¶ **Venus is put to sleep.** Not entirely...

<margin>Whether the appetite for intercourse is greater before or after conception.</margin>
...on account of the aforementioned reason. But the seducers and lechers <note>original: "subagitatores z lenones"</note> and those accustomed to Venus grumble, saying this is false: because by many women, intercourse is craved more greedily and insistently after conception than before. They even say they have seen some women who, before conception, closed the door of shame to their adulterers, but once conception occurred, they relaxed their navel and their legs. **We respond** that this is more likely for the sake of security <note>i.e., they no longer fear becoming pregnant</note> than for the sake of heat and pleasure. Nevertheless, I do not deny that from the doubled heat of the fetus the kidneys are warmed, and from the heat prickling or weighing upon the orifices of Venus, a "tickling" <note>original: "pruritum"</note> is induced. But it is not as pleasurable as that which was before conception or during conception. For then, the whole womb opens itself, applauding the temperate nature of the seed, and lets it into the "mint" of conception—that is, the form. ¶ **Another commentary.** **The womb.**

<margin>Another commentary.</margin>
Since he treats of "atomosis" <note>the resolution of tiny particles</note>, which sometimes signify conception and sometimes not, he adds here the signs through which a distinction may be made. And first he places general signs, second specific ones. When the womb has followed what it desired and obtained what it hunted, it congeals. And therefore it is closed so that it may retain what it desired, and upon its acceptance, its neck and the vulva are dried, because that which used to flow no longer flows; hence the vulva becomes less moist. ¶ **Venus is put to sleep.** Since the womb was created for the sake of conception, once the end for which it was made is obtained, it then rests in it naturally; hence it does not desire to copulate further. However, from the boiling later produced in the womb itself—especially if the child to be generated is of a choleric nature—the womb also becomes like it in complexion. There are certain "combative" women who crave intercourse vehemently because their kidneys are warmed by the flow, especially since the vulva does not receive into itself the dissolved moisture; and because of this, she craves intercourse more, perhaps so that her vulva may be moistened. The womb craves intercourse most of all out of necessity or utility, for nature stimulates the womb with a vehement dryness to crave intercourse. ¶ **Retention of flow.** That is, of the menses. Hence the menses are promptly turned into nourishment for the fetus on account of the closing of the internal orifice.

<margin>Another commentary.</margin>
**Another commentary on the aforementioned verses.** **The womb.** This property comes from the things said before, because it tightens the neck of the womb to retain the matter of generation. ¶ **Affect.** That is, appetite. ¶ **Discolor affectus.** That is, varied and multiform. For now she craves sharp things, now sour fruits, now chalk, now charcoal and such things; this happens from the melancholic and contagious menstrual blood overflowing to the mouth of the stomach and infecting it. Hence they crave things similar to their infection. But this happens most in the novelty of conception on account of the retention of menses; for the menstrual blood is still in motion. However, in the 3rd or 4th month, once the fetus is confirmed, such appetite ceases. ¶ **Vomiting.** From the same cause; but it happens most in the novelty of conception. ¶ **Compression of the member.** From the narrowing of the internal orifice of the womb. Whence it seems to a man when he copulates with a woman that the member is "fled" by the vulva, especially when the member is long. ¶ **Heaviness of the breasts.** From the overflow of blood to the sponginess of the breasts, whence they distend and grow large. For there are continuous passages <note>original: "meatus"</note> from the womb to the breasts, through whose continuity the transition of derivation to the mammary regions and the breasts occurs. ¶ **Disturbance.** This sign is elicited from Hippocrates. For it is said in the 5th part of the *Aphorisms*: "Women, if you wish to know..." etc. When she is about to sleep, give her <term>mellicratum</term> <note>a mixture of honey and water, also known as hydromel</note> to drink; and if she indeed has cramps <note>original: "tortiones"</note>, she has conceived. If not, she has not. But it is not a completely truthful sign: for upon taking the honey-water, they feel cramps, yet they do not always prove a conception has occurred on account of this. If, however, in the body of the woman upon taking the honey-water there is an absence or privation of cramping, it is a certain sign that conception has not occurred.

### On the signs of conceiving a male.

->The brightness of the face suggests the conception of a male.<-
->Lightness of the limbs: the thickening of dense milk.<-
->And a round swelling of the belly on the right side.<-
->Contrary signs represent a female fetus.<-

<margin>Exposition</margin>
**Exposition.** ¶ **Conception.** These are the signs of conceiving a male: because if a woman was discolored before conception, and once conception occurred she has a well-colored face, one has from this a sign of a male conception. ¶ **Lightness of limbs.** If, after conception, the woman has a lightness of the limbs, this is a sign of a male conception. ¶ **Thickening of dense [milk].** That is, the coagulation and thickness of the milk. ¶ **And swelling.** Namely, of the belly. ¶ **On the right side round.** Because that is the place for the conception of males <note>Medieval medicine often held that males were conceived on the warmer right side and females on the cooler left</note>. ¶ **Female.** Signs contrary to these which were said signify the conception of a female.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
**Commentary.**

<meta>catchword: Another</meta>

<summary>This page outlines clinical and physical signs of pregnancy, such as cravings, vomiting, and physiological changes in the womb and breasts. It also provides traditional diagnostic markers for determining the sex of the fetus, associating male conception with the right side of the body and a healthy complexion.</summary>
<keywords>conception, pregnancy signs, womb, pica, cravings, honey-water test, male fetus, female fetus, medieval obstetrics, Hippocrates, breastfeeding physiology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of signs of pregnancy and fetal sex determination, moving from general signs to specific physiological indicators such as facial complexion and the consistency of breast milk. It then transitions into the medical analysis of "spermatic resolutions" (seminal discharge) and "powdery" sediments in urine, which indicate various conditions from sexual activity to systemic illness.</meta>

<margin>Commentary</margin>
**Conception. Conceiving.** After the treatment regarding the general signs of conception, the author joins to it the specific signs. **Brightness of the face.** He returns to the prior consistency of the woman. If, however, before conception she was accustomed to being less colored, and after a short time following conception a flushed or illuminated face appears, by this you may weigh the conception of a male. For he is conceived from hotter blood and in a hotter part of the menses; from which natural heat is struck into the body of the woman and a better digestion is procreated. For from good digestion, a good color is born in the face. **Lightness of the limbs.** From the same cause: for from good vigor comes good nourishment and a good restoration of the spirits <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" refers to the subtle vapors that carry life and movement through the body</note>. Once these are sufficiently restored, the strength and vigor of the bodies themselves are provided, and the limbs are made light. **The curdling of thick milk.** That is, coagulation. Because the milk is more digested and cooked, the wateriness has been removed by the power of the heat. If a drop of it is placed upon a nail, or upon marble, or upon another earthy thing, it does not flow; instead, its lateral parts are reduced into a heap, and this signifies the conception of a male. **On the right side.** Which is the place for the conception of males. **Round.** Because the parts of a male body, since they are stronger, cohere to themselves more strongly, and are not distended by a certain fragility in the menses. **Contrary signs.** For the effects are of contrary causes. **The second commentary**

<margin>Another commentary.</margin>
**on the aforementioned verses. Conception.** Here he determines the specific signs of conception: for the conception of a male is more specific than that of a female. The author posits that the sperm of the man stands in the place of the maker and the agent, but the menstrual blood in the place of the matter. And although every man is hotter than every woman, yet certain women are hotter than certain men; but this is understood regarding the viscous and material heat. All men, however, are hotter in the active and formal heat, and therefore men are stronger than women. **Brightness of the face.** Because from the hot matter which boils in the womb, hot fumes or vapors are elevated to the liver, by which it is heated. And similarly to the heart, by which it is heated. From these members thus heated, hot vapors are elevated to the face and to the head. Whence the face shines; the redness is from the flower of the blood purified by the power of heat, and from this comes the lightness of the whole body. Heat causes things to become thin and subtle, which are the principles of lightness; for a hot thing is quickly mobile. **Thick curdling.** Which is made by a strong heat that consumes the wateriness and strongly binds the spirit together. Whence we see that cooked meats are firmer, because heat overcomes moisture and binds it, and it coagulates by the abstraction of the moisture previously existing. But it should be noted that a gathered heat is stronger than a scattered one. And therefore small men are never humble, because their heat is gathered together. Whence they are strongly mobile and elevated, because heat always spreads and elevates; and therefore they are bolder and more clever. The contrary happens in large men on account of their thickness. Whence if you see or find a large man who is wise, or a small man who is humble, give praise to God. **And the swelling.** Because the heat and moisture strongly bind together, it becomes rounded, just as was tasted above. And this it also does on the right side of the womb, because that side is hot; and therefore the swelling is rounded when a male is conceived. Contrary signs appear in women. **And note that** the brightness of the face most especially certifies the conception of a male, if before conception the face was pale.

## On Spermatic Resolutions.

> Urine marked with spermatic signs confesses
> Enticing intercourse; that the genital members are burdened.
> The ferment of Venus <note>original: "fermento veneris", referring to semen as a leavening agent for life</note>, the vain mockeries of sleep.
> Either gonorrhea, or the member's strength dissolved.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
**Exposition.** Here he determines the matter of sperm appearing in the urine. The Rule: Urine appearing with spermatic resolutions that are residing or tending toward the bottom signifies that intercourse has preceded, or a nocturnal illusion <note>A nocturnal emission or "wet dream"</note>, or the will and desire for venereal acts without the act itself. And then it signifies a repletion of the generative members. **Either gonorrhea.** Such urine, if it occurs frequently, signifies <term>gonorrhea</term> <note>In this context, gonorrhea refers to any involuntary discharge of semen, not necessarily the modern infection</note>, or a paralysis <note>original: "parafesim," likely a corruption of paralysis or a loss of functional control</note> of the generative members.

<column-break/>

**Commentary.** **Spermatic.** In this chapter the author treats sperm in the urine, because sometimes spermatic resolutions are sent out with the urine. Whence the urine appears with certain spermatic resolutions. There is, therefore, such a rule: Urine appearing with spermatic resolutions tending toward the bottom or residing signifies that intercourse has preceded, or a nocturnal illusion, or concupiscence, or the affection for venereal acts without the conscious act. It also signifies a repletion of the genital members and the <term>didymi</term> <note>The epididymis or testicles</note> from the sperm that is present, because it overflows in the testicles and is emitted with the urine through incontinence. Such urine also signifies, if it occurs frequently, gonorrhea or a paralysis of the genital members. **Now, gonorrhea is** an immoderate and involuntary effusion of sperm, which is a most shameful passion, from which a not-small multitude—or some at some time—perish, because they blush to confess such a sickness. Whence the malice of the disease is more strengthened. This passion happens from an excessive abundance of blood. Whence the sperm increases on account of too much abundance of the collection. It also happens sometimes from a weakness of the retentive power, and sometimes from a smoothing <note>lubrication or loosening</note> of the seminal vessels. Whence the seminal vessels are lubricated, and thus the sperm, through such lubrication, since it has no coherence in the receptacles, slips out involuntarily. **This passion is signified** in those who have a paralysis in the genital members, just as it is in epileptics and apoplectics. For in those, urine and seed are emitted involuntarily, and thus the sperm goes out involuntarily on account of the weakness of the nerves and on account of other intrinsic causes. **With spermatic notes.** That is, with spermatic resolutions. **Written.** That is, poured out. **Enticing intercourse.** As for the celebrating of intercourse—that is, when someone has celebrated intercourse. Whence from the remains of the resolved matter not sufficiently led out because the expelling spirit was weak, therefore such urine appears. **Genital members.** The second signing: the genital members are said in this place to be the testicles, the penis, and especially the <term>didymi</term>. **With ferment.** That is, with the sperm by which the testicles swell, just as dough grows and is amplified by leaven. **Vain mockeries of sleep.** That is, nocturnal illusions from venereal offices or works; those things which, for example, present themselves to the sleeping, and they dream or sleep with an improper mind. **Gonorrhea.** That is, an immoderate and involuntary effusion of sperm. **Or [the strength] dissolved.** That is, paralysis, which happens from the dissolution of the members. **Another commentary follows on the aforementioned verses.** **Spermatic.** Sperm is emitted either on account of the multitude of matter, or on account of a defect in the retentive power, or on account of the weakness of a muscle softened according to paralysis. **Enticements.** Because the matter is moved too much and the testicles become too hot. Whence they strongly attract the sperm generated there, which they emit. It is thinned by the preceding movement in excessive intercourse. **Genital members.** On account of the multitude of spermatic matter, which swells from heat and movement. **Mockeries.** Because in such an opposition, the cavities are not well-modified by the sperm. **Gonorrhea.** That is, an involuntary emission of sperm. **Or dissolved.** That is, the contentive power, failing to retain on account of the softening of the muscle.

### On contents

...powdery resolutions: which are emitted with the urine in the likeness of dust. There is, therefore, a rule: Urine pale in color with powdery resolutions residing at the bottom signifies an ailment of the lower members, such as the kidneys and the loins, and earlier [it signifies] the lower parts. ¶ **From atrices.** <note>atrices: Small sores, fissures, or growths near the anus.</note> In those suffering from *atrices* and *fici* <note>fici: Soft, fig-like growths or warts.</note> and in those suffering from hemorrhoids and inflation of the spleen, such urine sometimes appears. ¶ **Or when the menses.** Such urine also appears in women when they suffer from a retention of their menstrual flow.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Lomentum.** <note>original: "Lomentum," a term for bean-meal or a washing powder, used here metaphorically for sediment.</note> ¶ **Under the form of ash.** Here he places another chapter concerning powdery resolutions: which are sometimes emitted above and settle at the bottom in the form of powder. From this, the following rule is gathered: Urine pale in color with powdery resolutions residing at the bottom, which are black or livid in color, signifies hemorrhoids. It also signifies *atrices* or *prodilomata* <note>Another term for condylomata or genital/anal warts.</note>. Such urine also signifies a defect of the spleen, and in women, it signifies sexual intercourse; or if such urine appears, it signifies the retention of the menses.

<margin>What hemorrhoids are</margin>
¶ **Hemorrhoids.** ¶ Hemorrhoids are five veins which, proceeding from the <term>vena chili<note>Original: "vena chili." The vena cava or the great central vein, believed to be the primary vessel for distributing nutrients.</note></term>, terminate in a circle toward the private parts. ¶ Therefore, these veins are sometimes filled and weighed down by <term>melancholic blood<note>One of the four humors; associated with earth, cold, and dryness. An excess was thought to cause heaviness and "black" diseases.</note></term>, which especially abounds in the *vena chili* adjacent to the spine. The spine, moreover, is cold, since it is the posterior part of the body. Therefore, on account of the coldness of that part, the melancholic blood has its origin in those veins. When the aforementioned veins are weighed down and overfilled with melancholic blood, they distend and swell strongly in that place, and they are inflated so that various tumors appear at their heads. Whence a heaviness and weightiness is felt around the lower parts, and there is a sluggishness of the whole body and a discoloration of the face. However, those veins sometimes rupture, and blood is emitted in great quantity. These veins are ruptured either due to the abundance of blood and due to incontinence, or from excessive heat due to sharpness and corrosion, or from external coldness due to compression. Note that this passion is especially familiar in those who are accustomed to sitting upon marble. "Hemorrhoid" is the name of both the member and the passion, for those veins are called hemorrhoids, through which this passion comes, which is called hemorrhoid. Whence the ailment arising from those veins is called hemorrhoids. "Hemorrhoid" comes from *haemo*, which is blood, and *rhois*, which is flow <note>Etymology from Greek: haima (blood) + rhoia (flow).</note>. Therefore, they are called hemorrhoids because they are a flow of blood. In hemorrhoids, the urine ought to be pale in color. For when melancholic blood abounds in the body, the natural heat is weakened. Whence the digestion is rendered "crude" <note>Undigested or incomplete.</note>, and from the crudity of digestion, the urine is discolored. It appears with powdery resolutions, which, resolved from the black and earthy melancholic blood, are derived through continuous passages to the bladder and emitted with the urine; and because they are heavy and earthy, they settle at the bottom.

<margin>What atrices are</margin>
¶ **Atrices** are collections made around the anus from melancholic blood that is disturbed in those parts, inducing a viscosity.

<margin>What fici and condylomata are</margin>
¶ **Fici** <note>Literally "figs."</note> are soft collections around the anus, distinguished by certain grains in the manner of fig seeds.
¶ **Condylomata** are hard, solid, and round collections around the anus in the manner of acorns; they are called condylomata from *condylon*, which means round. Whence in the poet Maximianus it is found: "with fingers bent into a *condylon*," that is, into a round shape.
¶ Therefore, in those with *atrices*, *fici*, and *condylomata*, the urine appears similar to the former and is disposed according to such a color for the same reason. ¶ And such resolutions appear from a vice of the spleen after medications have been given, especially due to the action of dissolution, the same pale urine appears with powdery resolutions. Similarly in the retention of menses. For when melancholic blood is retained through the menses, certain livid parts are resolved from the blood itself, which are as if scaly, and these are indeed emitted with the urine. ¶ **Ash-like.** That is, powdery. ¶ **Lowest members.** Such as the kidneys and the loins and the lower 

<column-break/>

parts, which are troubled by a shared suffering of the system, as has been said.

### ->On hypostasis<-
<note>hypostasis: The sediment or "settling" at the bottom of a urine sample, considered a key diagnostic indicator of the body's final stage of digestion.</note>

> *The color, substance, and time inform the sediment.*
> *The shape and the place: the color is white, the substance is like gypsum*
> *Continued in its parts; its shape figures a cone.*
> *The lower bottom is its place; its time is constancy.*
> *White, continuous, residing, constant, and pine-shaped.*
> *If such a sediment is made, let digestion be good; the virtue*
> *Of strong nature flourishes in its triple movement.*
> *It whitens, cleanses, accumulates, condenses, and unites.*
> *Heat thins the windiness and absorbs the vapors.*
> *Virtue retains what is good and repels what is wicked.*
> *Nature either cuts or alternates these acts.*
> *By these signs, the certain showing of health is clear.*

If the fever has been secreted, the discussion of the disease is brief.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ In this place, he determines the nature of hypostasis. Hypostasis, therefore, is the superfluity <note>Waste product or surplus.</note> of the **third digestion** poured out in the urine. Hypostasis in the third digestion is separated from the nourishment of the members and is emitted with the urine. Whence here is placed the description of "laudable" (healthy) hypostasis, and there are five conditions of it: namely, the **color**, which is white; the **substance**, which ought to be continuous without interruption or division; the **place**, which is the bottom of the urinal; the **time**, which means the hypostasis perseveres in its goodness for many days; and the **shape**, because it ought to be in the manner of a pyramid or a pine cone, so that it begins broadly and tends toward a point on all sides. And concerning the quality of these differences, it is determined singularly and very well in the commentary. ¶ **White, continuous.** In this little verse are contained the five differences of natural hypostasis: namely, that it be white in color, continuous in substance, residing at the bottom according to place, constant as to time, and pine-shaped as to form. And if such a sediment appears in the urine with these conditions, it signifies that digestion is good, and the virtue <note>The innate healing or functional power of the body.</note> is strong, and that the action of nature flourishes with a triple motion. ¶ Whence it must be noted that the motion of nature is threefold: namely, **alterative**, **local**, and **retentive**; this is declared at the end of the commentary.

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Informs.** He proposes another chapter on hypostasis, where it must be seen what hypostasis is and its properties. For hypostasis is the superfluity of the third digestion poured out with the urine. Every digestion, therefore, has its own superfluity. **The first digestion** <note>In the stomach and intestines.</note> has for its superfluity stool and windiness. **The second digestion** <note>In the liver and veins.</note> has urine. **The third digestion** <note>In the tissues and organs.</note> has hypostasis and sweat. Hypostasis in the third digestion is separated from the nourishment of the members. Whence, since digestion occurs in all members and all members are nourished by any nourishment, hypostasis is separated; but not all hypostasis that is separated from nourishment is purged with the urine. For due to the length of the ways and the narrowness of the passages, the whole cannot arrive at the bladder. For a certain part is consumed by the heat of the body; another is cleansed through sweat. Another part is thinned and expires through smoke and vapors. Only that portion which adheres to the vessels and is closer to the urinary paths descends to the bladder. For when they adhere to the urine, they enter the vessels through the rarefied openings of the pores by heat, and are derived through continuous passages to the liver; from the liver, however, it descends through the capillary veins to the bladder and is emitted with the urine. However, in the urine of the healthy, hypostasis does not appear, because by the strength of the heat and the virtue of the members, the hypostasis is consumed. Also, the members in the healthy are better nourished, and the superfluities of the members from nourishment are very small; whence there is little or no hypostasis. ¶ There are four origins of hypostasis: color,

# Urine 18

<margin>Color.</margin> **Color, substance, location, and time.** Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 832–932), a highly influential Jewish physician whose "Book on Urines" was a foundational text in medieval medicine.</note> in his book on urines adds a fifth differential, which is **form**; and following Isaac, we include that fifth differential here. The natural color of the sediment <note>original: "hypostasis." This refers to the matter that settles at the bottom of a urine vial.</note> is white; for every natural sediment ought to be white. All similar members <note>In medieval anatomy, "similar members" are tissues like bone, nerves, or membranes that appear uniform throughout.</note> of the human body are generally white, even though flesh appears to be red. But that is not the true color of the flesh; rather, it is the color of the blood dispersed through the pores of the flesh itself. Thus, if flesh is cooked and squeezed, as the Irish do, it is whitened, and it returns to its proper color. Therefore, nourishment is not incorporated into the members unless it is first whitened. Moreover, nutrition is the conversion of the nourishing thing into the nature of the thing being nourished. Therefore, since the members are white, the nourishment is white. And since the sediment is separated from such matter, it ought to be white in color. For every superfluity <note>A byproduct or waste of a biological process.</note> ought to be an emulator—that is, similar to and imitative of—that from which it is separated. Therefore, no sediment is praiseworthy unless it is white. This signifies the perfect assimilation of nourishment according to the nature of the members, and the strength of natural heat prevailing in digestion. A red sediment, however, is less good. It signifies the duration of an illness and the crudeness of the matter. Thus, the digestive power does not prevail in the <term>third digestion<note>Medieval medicine identified three stages of digestion: the first in the stomach, the second in the liver, and the third in the individual tissues and members.</note></term> in performing the digestion of the nourishment; yet it signifies a likeness of <term>eucritia<note>From Greek "eukrasia," meaning a healthy balance of humors.</note></term>—that is, well-terminable—because it is made of pure and sincere blood. Therefore, this humor is a friend to nature and very familiar to it. A sub-red sediment is worse than a red one, because it is made of watery blood. Thus, it threatens a longer illness due to the crudeness of the blood. A livid sediment is blameworthy, as it signifies mortification <note>The death of tissue or loss of vital spirit.</note>. Green or black is the worst, for it signifies adustion <note>Over-heating or "burning" of the humors, often associated with melancholy or toxic states.</note> and death. Let these remarks on the color of the sediment suffice.

<margin>Substance.</margin> ¶ The substance of the sediment is **continuous**, for it ought to be without division or interruption of its parts. By this, it is signified that the third digestion of the matter is perfect, and that it has no "windiness" <note>original: "ventositatem." Medieval doctors believed gas or air trapped in the body could disrupt digestive processes and cause pain or displacement of fluids.</note> whose presence could pull apart the continuity of the sediment. The tearing apart of the sediment occurs from windiness in the third digestion. Let these remarks on the substance of the sediment suffice.

<margin>Location.</margin> ¶ The first and natural location of the sediment is the **bottom**. For the sediment ought to be subsisting at the bottom of the urinal; and such subsidence signifies that the second digestion <note>The process occurring in the liver, where chyle is turned into blood.</note> was not disturbed nor hindered by any windiness. For if the second digestion had been windy, that wind, emitted with the urine, would propel the sediment either into the middle part of the urine or into the upper part, if the windiness were greater. There are three differences of sediment according to location. For if the sediment subsides at the bottom, it is properly called **sediment** <note>original: "sedimen."</note>. If it is propelled into the middle region of the urine, it is called **eneorema** <note>original: "eneozuma" / "eneorema," from Greek, meaning "suspended."</note>, as if hanging. And if it is propelled all the way to the surface of the urine by a greater impulse of windiness, it is called **nephelis** <note>original: "nephilis," from the Greek for "cloud."</note>—that is, a cloud—by a metaphor for clouds. Let these remarks on the location of the sediment suffice.

<margin>Time.</margin> ¶ The time of the sediment is its **permanence** in such urines through many days. Such permanence is equality over time, by which the greatest strength of nature is signified; for it does not fail in its good work but is sufficient to continue its labor. For if a sediment appears on the first day with good signs, but on the second day it appears with bad ones, the debility of nature is signified by such inconstancy, as it cannot persevere in a good work. ¶ And note that equality in a good sediment is best, but equality in a bad sediment is worst. Therefore, inequality in a bad state is good, but inequality in a good state is bad. Let these remarks on the time of the sediment suffice.

<margin>Form.</margin> ¶ The form of the sediment ought to be **pronoides**—that is, in the manner of a pineal form—so that it begins broad and extends perpendicularly from all sides into a sharp point, as if in the manner of a pyramid or a pinecone. Isaac calls such a form **pineated**, as if tending toward a point in the manner of a pinecone. Such a form signifies perfect digestion. Thus, the heavy parts of the sediment remain at the bottom and establish its base. The medium parts, which are not as heavy, occupy the middle. The lighter parts, which are fiery and airy, tend toward the top. The letter speaks for itself. ¶ **With its own meanings.** That is, with its own connections, so that it has coherence of parts.

<column-break/>

¶ **Tall.** That is, it starts from a broad base and tends toward a point in the manner of a gall-nut. ¶ **Location.** Is its bottom; that is, staying in the lower part. ¶ **Constancy.** That is, its permanence through many days. ¶ **White and continuous.** Here is placed the description of a good sediment, and he shows what it signifies. ¶ **White.** In color. ¶ **Continuous.** Regarding its substance. ¶ **Residing.** Regarding its location. ¶ **Constancy.** Regarding time. ¶ **Pineated.** This refers not to the pine tree itself, but to the form of the pinecone. ¶ **Good digestion.** Not just because it is white. For whiteness alone is not enough to suggest perfect digestion; it could appear white but be propelled or torn apart. But good digestion is signified by the fact that it is white along with the other following signs. ¶ **The power of digestion thrives with a threefold motion.** There is a triple motion of nature in the third digestion: the **alterative**, which occurs in the whitening of the nourishment; the **local**, which occurs in the rounding and transposition of parts; and the **essential**, because it occurs through other differences which are noted below or prolonged. ¶ **Whitens.** Behold the alterative motion. ¶ **Cleanses, densifies, and unites.** Behold the local and essential motions. ¶ **Windy heat.** That which is signified through continuity—that is, through the consistency of the sediment—it repels through vapor. ¶ **And also.** That which is signified through the continuity and consistency of the sediment.

### On sediment that is deficient in good qualities.
> The sediment harms and shows crudity in whatever [prior traits] it lacks.
> A dissonant and varied motion making distinctions,
> If, while the rest are preserved, it hangs or seeks the height,
> Digestion is proven harmed by a windy blast.
> Even if the right of location and law of color are kept,
> A windy force moves the sediment, its connection loosened.

<margin>Exposition.</margin> ¶ **Exposition.** ¶ Previously the author set down five signs of a praiseworthy sediment. Here he determines the nature of a sediment receding from the praiseworthy and says: that any sediment failing in any of the five aforesaid signs is tainted; in that much, it falls short of a praiseworthy sediment. For example: A sediment white in color, but failing in location because it is a cloud (*nebula*) or *nephelis*, falls short and recedes from the praiseworthy sediment. For by this, the windiness of the second digestion is signified, which by reason of the propelling windiness seeks the upper part and becomes a cloud or *nephelis*. And therefore it should be noted: that according to the three locations it occupies in the urine, the sediment receives three names. If it occupies the bottom, it is called **sediment** (*sedimen*). If the middle, it is called **cloud** (*nebula*) or **eneorema**—that is, as if hanging. And if it is propelled to the top by reason of a greater windiness pushing more strongly, it is called **nephelis**. And thus the sediment, in as much as it is elongated from its natural place, is made unnatural. ¶ **Even if the right of location.** If the sediment keeps its place and color—that is, it is white in color and at the bottom in location—but has a torn substance and is not continuous, it is an unnatural and blameworthy sediment; and it signifies that the third digestion was disturbed by windiness. ¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Harms.** ¶ The author specified the good and legitimate sediment with its proper signs according to location, color, substance, time, and form. Now he shows that if the sediment errs in any of these differentials, or in several, it is unpraiseworthy and against nature. For if the color and continuity are preserved but the location is changed, and it becomes an *eneorema* or *nephelis*, it is blameworthy, because it signifies that the second digestion is hindered by excessive windiness. If, however, the location and color are kept—so that it is white and subsiding—but the substance is changed, so that instead of continuous it is torn apart, it is blameworthy; for it signifies a perturbation of the third digestion occurring from windiness, so that the windiness falling upon the sediment removes its connection and continuity. ¶ **In whatever of them.** That is, whatever change is made from the prior differentials. ¶ **Making distinctions in motion.** That is, making the sediment differ from the praiseworthy sediment. ¶ **Dissonant and varied motion.** Because of the change made in its proper state, such a motion or such a perturbation harms and "incrudates" the sediment—that is, shows it to be vicious and infamous. ¶ **While the rest are preserved.** That is, the color...
