...substance. <margin>Explanation.</margin> ¶ **If it hangs.** That is, if it becomes a suspended cloud <note>original: "eneorema," a cloud-like suspension in the middle of the urine vial.</note>. Or if it becomes a mist <note>original: "nephele," a thin cloud floating at the top of the urine.</note>. ¶ **Saving the right.** That is, with the substance remaining and the whiteness generated in the third digestion <note>The final stage of digestion where nutrients are converted into body tissue.</note> persisting. ¶ **A windy force.** Generated in the third digestion. ¶ **It moves.** That is, it pulls apart and signifies an interrupted continuity; and lest one understand by this movement a simple push rather than a dispersal, he adds: ¶ **With the structure loosened.** That is, discontinued.

## Concerning Red and Sub-red Sediment

->¶ Sub-red, when it comes from watery blood,<-
->Is worse than red, though closer to white.<-
->¶ The red designates that there will be a long, well-determinable fever<-
->Since the cause of the ill is the humor, son of nature,<-
->Gentle and well-digested, soluble, and moderate.<-

<margin>Exposition.</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** The author compares red sediment to sub-red <note>A pale or diluted red.</note>, saying that sub-red sediment is more blameworthy than red sediment. The reason is that sub-red sediment is formed from watery and somewhat undigested or "crude" blood. Therefore, it signifies the rawness of the matter, and consequently a long duration of the disease, and through this length of illness, it threatens a failure of vital strength. ¶ **Though closer.** Although in terms of color sub-red sediment is closer to white than red sediment is, it is nonetheless further removed from a good state, as the commentary states. ¶ **Designates.** He determines the nature of red sediment and says that among all types of sediment, after the most praiseworthy white sediment, red is the best. This is because it is formed from good and well-digested blood, which is easily converted into the substance of the limbs during the third digestion. Thus, it signifies an illness that is easily terminable and healthy, though long-lasting; the reasons are made clear in the commentary.

<margin>Commentary.</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** ¶ **Sub-red.** He adds a note on sub-red sediment. It seems contrary to nature that sediment should ever be sub-red or any color other than white, especially since it is the superfluity of the third digestion, separated from the nourishment of the limbs. For the limbs are white, and the nourishment itself is white. And what falls away from that nourishment ought to be white, because no sediment should be any color other than white. Why then do authors say that some sediment is red or sub-red? We answer: while sediment is truly the superfluity of the third digestion and we grant that it should be white, sometimes by the name "sediment" we understand in a vague and general sense anything that resides at the bottom of the urine, whether it be crude humor, blood, pus, discharge, or a buildup of "sand" <note>Sedimentary deposits or stones in the urinary tract.</note>. According to this understanding, some sediment can be red or sub-red.

<margin>How sub-red sediment is said to be worse than red.</margin>
Sub-red sediment is said to be bad because it signifies it was made from crude and watery blood. Hence follows a long duration of illness due to the rawness of the matter. Yet it does not threaten immediate danger because it is made of sanguine matter, which is tempered compared to the others. ¶ But it is surprising that the author says: **Sub-red is worse than red.** For white is the best. Red is further from white than sub-red is, and sub-red is the middle point between red and white. One cannot pass from red to white except through sub-red by means of digestion. Therefore, since sub-red is closer to white than red is, it should be less bad than red, even though the author says it is worse. ¶ To this we say: sub-red sediment is further from white than red is in terms of the *nature of the cooking* (digestion). Sub-red does not occur as a middle stage of digestion between red and white; rather, it comes from crude and watery blood which, because of its rawness, could not be perfectly "cooked" or reddened, nor could it fully take on the appearance of blood. Red sediment, however, is closer and more related to white because the blood has already proceeded further; it is "cooked," and from this cooking, it can easily be assimilated into the limbs. ¶ **Though closer to white.** This "closeness" is to be understood in terms of color only, and not in terms of the progress of digestion. ¶ **Designates the red.**

<column-break/>

He determines regarding red sediment that after white, it is the most praiseworthy and reversible <note>Meaning the patient can easily return to health.</note> among the types of sediment. However, it signifies a long illness because of the abundance of matter and its rawness. ¶ **Easily determined.** <note>original: "Eucrita," from the Greek *eukritos*, meaning a favorable or easily judged turning point in a disease.</note> That is, having a good outcome because of its balanced temperament. For it is made of pure and sincere blood, which is friendly to the limbs. For the limbs are "sweet," and blood is sweet, and the limbs are nourished by such blood. ¶ **Easily determined.** That is, well-digested; from *eu*, which means good, and *crasis* <note>The mixture of humors.</note>. Thus *discrita* <note>dyscrasia</note> signifies the opposite. ¶ **Son of nature.** Because of the friendliness it has with the limbs; this is a poetic description of blood. ¶ **Gentle.** Because it has soothing qualities and a soft, warm substance. ¶ **Well-digested.** That is, processed; this is indicated by the moderate consistency of its substance. For if it were crude, it would come out watery; if burned, it would be thick. Because it is well-cooked and legitimately digested, it is moderate. ¶ **Soluble.** That is, fit to be dissolved and digested in the third digestion; this is due to the suitability of its qualities. For it is hot and moist, qualities which favor digestion. ¶ **Moderate.** This can refer to the balanced temperament of its qualities, or to the balance of its quantity. The qualities are established, but a moderation of quantity is also necessary. There is a moderation and proportion in the cleansing of the quantity: for example, there is twice as much blood in the human body as there is phlegm; twice as much phlegm as choler; and twice as much choler as melancholy. This can be clearly seen by those who observe carefully.

## Concerning Black Sediment

->¶ Black sediment brings mourning to nature's work,<-
->And overthrows the peak of vitality from on high.<-
->¶ Whether it holds the top or the middle, it is less faulty.<-
->In many things it offends, while the other offends in one.<-
->¶ The black mist <note>original: "nephilis," referring to a cloud at the top of the vial.</note> sins more in number; yet not because of that<-
->Is black sediment at the bottom worse, unless it sins more in number;<-
->The violence of the cause compensates for the lack of number.<-
->Bad circumstances of the disease aggravate and pile up the ills.<-

<margin>Exposition.</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** Here the author determines regarding black sediment. He says that among all species of sediment, black sediment is the worst and most blameworthy, because it signifies the "death" <note>original: "mortificationem"</note> and overthrow of heat or vitality. There are three types of black sediment according to the three places it occupies in the urine: namely, the bottom, the middle, or the top. ¶ **Whether it holds the top.** He says here that black sediment appearing in the middle of the urine or in the upper part does not signify as much evil as sediment settling at the bottom. That which settles at the bottom is the ultimate in being unpraiseworthy and evil.

<margin>The third author [Gilles]. Commentary.</margin>
¶ **The teaching.** Here he says that black sediment existing in the middle or upper part of the urine "sins" or errs in many ways: in color, being black, and in location, being high up. Black sediment at the bottom sins only in one way: namely, in color alone. In location it does not sin, because it holds the proper and legitimate place of natural sediment. However, the author's statement contains a falsehood when he says black sediment at the bottom sins only in one way; for in truth, it sins in many ways: in location, in substance, and in color. In location, because if it were in the middle of the urine, it would not be as bad. Therefore, it errs according to its location. And he says it holds its legitimate place, which is false. It sins in substance more than the suspended or high sediment. That black sediment at the bottom is of a thick and earthy substance, which could in no way be thinned by heat. Therefore, it sins more in its substance. Aegidius <note>Gilles de Corbeil, the author of the primary verses.</note> did not consider this. It also sins in color, as has been said. Therefore, black sediment at the bottom does not sin in only one way, but in many. Thus it is concluded: among all species of sediment, black sediment is the worst, and even more so when it is black at the bottom. Let these things suffice for the considerations of urines.

->¶ Commentary.<-

# Urine

<margin>Commentary</margin>
¶ **Commentary.** **Of nature.** In this last chapter, the discussion concerns **black sediment**, which is more detestable than all other types of sediment because it signifies mortification <note>The death of tissue or "dying" of the natural heat.</note>. If black sediment occupies the bottom of the vessel, it is worse than a black suspension <note>original: "eneozyma," referring to a cloud-like substance suspended in the middle of the urine.</note>, as is evident. However, a black suspension is faulty in more ways: namely, in color (because it is black) and in location (because it is elevated). The solution is this: although a black suspension is faulty in more respects, black sediment is a greater fault even if it lacks the specific fault of the black suspension's location. Quantity sometimes overcomes number in its malice. Therefore, black sediment is worse because it signifies that the cause of death is more abundant. Hence, such sediment, out of the abundance of its malice and its "earthiness," is pressed downward. That which signifies a cause of death that is less abundant tends to rise upward.

Alternatively, it can be understood that black sediment signifies that the natural heat is entirely extinguished. Thus, no "resolution" <note>The breakdown of humors into vapor or spirit.</note> can be made from it. Because no resolution occurs, no windiness <note>original: "ventositas," a vital gas or spirit generated by heat that moves substances within the body.</note> is generated in the body; and because no windiness is generated, there is no cause by which the sediment can be propelled into the upper part. This is due to the ultimate extinction of natural heat. Since the lack of resolution means no windiness is generated, it is a mortal sign and the greatest danger. A black suspension, even if it shows the extinction of natural heat, signifies some slight vigor of natural heat because the impulse was made from windiness; the windiness proceeded from a resolution that pushed the sediment up. ¶ **The explanation is clear.** ¶ **Not therefore more.** That is, in quantity. ¶ **And the light of vigor.** That is, height, or a pyramidal form. For when heat becomes strong, it elevates its food, just as we see that young men walk upright because of the multitude and strength of their heat. Old men, however, are stooped because of its defect. Heat of this kind renders the virtue vigorous. ¶ **Of vigor.** That is, of virtue. ¶ **Higher.** That is, deeper: because it is in its root and its center.

<margin>3 Anchor</margin>
¶ **O highest.** The cause of this is now declared. Since this black sediment, when suspended and high, indicates more faults than residing black sediment, it indicates windiness, which residing sediment does not. But it seems he wished to imply that black sediment at the bottom is in its natural place. But we said before that that place is the proper and natural place for natural sediment <note>original: "hypostasis," the normal white sediment found in healthy urine.</note>. But the natural and the unnatural will not naturally have the same place. Because of this, the opposition of reason is well enough understood: in this way, floating or suspended sediment, which is called a suspension <note>original: "eneozyma"</note>, is faulty in its location due to windiness, which weakens the natural heat and scatters and dissolves its continuity. Hence it is faulty in two ways. Residing sediment, however, is faulty in only one. 

But certainly, if you wish to examine the truth of the matter subtly, the author's speech is simply false: because residing sediment signifies a greater defect of natural heat than suspended sediment. For suspension signifies a fault in the substance, for the substance in it is divided. But sediment at the bottom does not. And I say that residing black sediment is more faulty in substance than suspended, because it is in no way refined by heat. The suspended, however, is refined in some way. But here he looks only to the extremes, and considered the windiness and lack of continuity in the suspended because he found neither in the other. Therefore he placed more faults in the suspended than the residing, though the former is suspended because of windiness and the other has the property of nature or sediment. Thus you will be able to defend the author somewhat, though he creates a stupor in his listeners with his manner of speaking. ¶ **Residing in one.** Such a thing in one place. Or say according to him: that if it is faulty in location, since it is very heavy, he proves this. ¶ **Mist, etc.** <note>original: "Nephilis," referring to the thin cloud at the top of the urine.</note> It signifies more faults in number, yet it signifies its vice in quantity: and according to the truth, it is not as much as the residing sediment. The rest of the speech is understood. And thus is the end, to the praise of God and the blessed Virgin Mary and all the inhabitants of heaven. Amen.

¶ **How Egidius seals his completed work. Last Chapter.**

Now, my Muse, the labor being complete, breathe;
Tighten the wheel; check the course; restrain the floods.
¶ Close the torrential waves of Musandinus’s river.

Or obscure the brightness of your beauty with stains; may it fix clear spears.
¶ Do not reveal your chaste face to the lewd populace.
Let the hem be shown, which they are not worthy to touch.

<margin>Exposition</margin>
¶ **Exposition.** ¶ **Now my.** Having completed his work and set down his doctrine concerning urine and its significations and contents, the author, narrating the style of his work in the manner of those who write metrically, invokes his Muse. First, assigning an end to his work, he seals and closes it. Second, he authenticates and approves this little book by the authority of other upright men whose opinions he has imitated. Third, he reproves and reviles the doctors of Montpellier <note>original: "pessulano monte," the University of Montpellier, a rival to the Salerno school.</note> and their followers because of their errors. The second part begins there (**Close Musandinus**). The third begins there (**Wayward and biting**). 

¶ And this third part is divided into three sections. First, he rebukes those doctors. Second, he reconciles with the masters of Montpellier, lest he speak ill of it. Third, he disdains the common people, the idiots, and the ignorant, or the talkative students. The second section is there (**Lest it tear**). The third is there (**To the lewd populace**). ¶ **Now my.** The literal exposition: ¶ **My Muse.** That is, the doctrine. ¶ **Breathe.** That is, put an end to it. ¶ **The labor being complete.** That is, the book being finished. ¶ **Tighten the wheel.** That is, stop the mobile genius of Egidius, which is capable of all things, just like the circular shape of a wheel. ¶ **Check the course.** That is, finish the study, in which there is no rest, just as in a race. ¶ **Restrain the floods.** That is, the canons and rules handed down in this book. 

¶ Note that he rightly compares science to a river, because just as a river continually flows and changes, so the science handed down by teachers in their opinions is continually—or daily—diversified and renewed. ¶ **Close the torrential waves of Musandinus’s river.** That is, the inundations of the teachings of that man who was called Petrus Musandinus <note>A famous teacher at Salerno and mentor to Gilles de Corbeil.</note>, whom Egidius imitated. ¶ **Do not spread further the treasures of Salerno’s horseman.** That is, you, Muse, do not extend further the treasury of the science of the noble doctor of Salerno, who was called Master Salernus. Hence "Salernus" is said equivocally of this man and of the city in which he lived. ¶ **Nor spread the heights of Visonis, nor the dogmas of Maurus.** That is, do not exceed the limits of the science of Master Visonis and Master Maurus <note>Influential Salernitan masters.</note>, who also treated urines. 

¶ **Soberly.** That is, you, my doctrine. ¶ **Close the hearth.** That is, impose an end. ¶ **Fearing the eye of envy.** That is, the "small eye," because it is the custom of those envious of another to squint and make the eye small with which they look at the good of others, so they may pretend as if they do not see such good things. ¶ **Of envy.** That is, the envy of those of Montpellier. ¶ **A contrary sect.** That is, the envious ones of Montpellier who envied Egidius for such a brilliant work. ¶ **Duel.** That is, war. ¶ **The wandering mountain of Montpellier.** That is, the pride of the wandering doctors of Montpellier. ¶ **Wayward.** That is, of diverse and false opinions. ¶ **Biting.** Goading. ¶ **Vehement.** Powerful in speaking evil. ¶ **Clamorous.** That is, a shouting sophist. ¶ **Empty.** That is, Egidius concerning urines.

### On the method of judging urines.

<note>A woodcut decorative initial 'I' featuring a physician in scholarly robes holding a glass uroscopy flask (matula) up to the light to examine the clarity and color of the urine.</note>
This is the method of judging urines, from which one must proceed in this way: first regarding color, second regarding substance, and third regarding contents. This method is such because first you must know whose urine it is: that is, a man's or a woman's. ¶ Likewise, whether they are young or old, or of whatever age. ¶ Likewise, if they are sick: how they fare, or not; that is, if the illness has arisen recently or is old. Then the judgment follows by this method. This urine is colored with an excessively citrine color <note>A lemon-yellow color, often associated with red choler/bile.</note>; therefore it testifies to red choler. It is turbid and shadowed from putrefied matter from the vessels; and therefore it is emitted as a single or double labor <note>Referring to the difficulty or frequency of urination.</note> from putrefied choler in the vessels of that man or woman whose urine this is. And this I say ¶ also regarding the color and substance. ¶ The ring <note>original: "circulus"; the upper layer or surface ring of the urine in the flask.</note> is thick and black, and it signifies a headache in that man or woman whose urine this is. ¶ Likewise, there are grains in the ring, and they show a rheum <note>original: "reumatismum"; a flow of excess humors or catarrh.</note>; hence the lord complains of headache from rheum in that man or woman. There are other grains there which are distant linearly below the ring, and they return slowly to the ring; they show a flux of humors descending from the head to the chest in that man or woman whose urine this is. Hence, one must ask about chest pain and heaviness, and by compassion <note>Meaning a sympathetic or radiating pain.</note> about stomach pain in that man or woman whose urine this is. Likewise, there is a cloud with grains there, and they show dryness of the chest in that man or woman, etc. Likewise, bran-like resolutions <note>Small, flake-like particles.</note>, that is, scaly ones like "petaloides" <note>resembling petals</note> and "crinoides" <note>resembling hairs</note>, which are like a fourth part of the grains throughout the whole body of the urine; they show the ultimate dissolution <note>A sign of approaching death or the breakdown of the body's tissues.</note> of the one whose urine this is. Likewise, there is a certain black "arthomofum" <note>A type of sediment.</note> content, and it signifies pain under a certain hypochondrium <note>The upper abdominal region under the ribs.</note>, that is, the right or the left. Hence, the lord complains of pain in the hypochondria. Likewise, there is a certain spermatic and troubled content which has an elegant hair-like shape, and it signifies pain in the joints of the one whose urine this is. Here there are no other resolutions, nor other contents except those which have been said, except for some that are in the bottom in the form of ash, some of which turn toward yellowness and some toward blackness; they have a manifest adherence and show the retention of menses in women. Hence, one must ask about the retention of menses in that woman, etc. These same things show in men an obstruction of the passages of the liver and spleen. Hence, one must ask about pain in the spleen and liver. Likewise, there are other contents which are black and obstructive, which sometimes appear with certain scaly resolutions in the bottom of the urine, and they show a great fullness of the intestines with constipation of the belly of the one whose urine this is. And because a few things suffice for a wise man, let these suffice for the present, because the same method and the same course are observed in all other contents, in whatever urines they may appear.

### On the contents of urines, color, and substance.

<column-break/>

<note>A woodcut decorative initial 'C' showing a seated scholar or physician in a high-backed chair, possibly teaching or in contemplation.</note>
The color and substance of the urine signify the disease itself. ¶ The content <note>original: "contentum"; the physical particles or clouds seen in the urine.</note> signifies in which member the matter of the disease resides. ¶ Likewise, a long spermatic content in the form of a hair with a thick root testifies to pain in the joints, that is, it signifies gout <note>original: "artheticam."</note>. ¶ Likewise, a thick, white, and troubled content in the bottom of the urine, and when it is a fleshy mass, it signifies a dissolution from the kidneys, or a descent, and it is an incurable disease of the kidneys: that is, in the substance of the kidneys. Because the urine passing through the kidney, since it is biting or stinging, dissolves more than medicines can consolidate. Hence, it is incurable. ¶ Likewise, a cloud hanging on the surface signifies pain of the spiritual parts <note>The organs of the chest involved in breathing.</note>. A green color appearing with the urine signifies a continuous fever and shows frenzy <note>original: "frenesim"; a state of delirium.</note>. ¶ Likewise, every thick and very viscous bubble appearing broadly with weak urine shows pain of the kidneys. When there is only one, and small, it shows the crudity <note>Immaturity or lack of "digestion" of the humors.</note> of the urine. ¶ Likewise, a grain in the ring with foam in the middle shows rheum. Appearing above with grains, it shows an affliction of the chest. ¶ Likewise, if blood appears in the whole body of the urine, it shows a rupture of a vein in the liver. If it is a little with some fatness, it shows a rupture in the kidneys. But if it is a little and troubled with spermatic, troubled resolutions, it shows a rupture of a vein in the bladder. ¶ If it is sandy or ashy residing in the bottom, it shows "nephresis" <note>Kidney stones or kidney disease.</note>. If it is with an oily substance, it shows hectic fever. If, however, it is with radiant urine, it shows a cleansing of the spleen and liver. If, however, it appears with urine signifying salt phlegm, it shows the "scabies" <note>An itchy skin condition.</note>. ¶ Likewise, a hair appearing in the whole body of the urine: if the urine is weak, it shows the thinness of the whole body. ## The sufficiency of the colors of urine.

<margin>sufficiency of colors</margin>
<note>A decorative square initial letter U containing stylized foliage and floral motifs.</note>
**It is asked** concerning the sufficiency <note>In this context, "sufficiency" refers to a complete or exhaustive classification.</note> of the colors. It is said that colors are caused by the humors. But every humor is either simple or composite. Color is caused either from a simple humor or a composite one. If from a simple one, we thus have one color from each humor: from blood, the color red; from yellow bile <note>original: "colera"; one of the four humors.</note>, the color citrine <note>A yellowish-green or lemon-like color.</note>; from melancholy <note>Black bile.</note>, the color glaucous <note>original: "glaucuz"; a greyish-blue or sea-green color.</note>; from phlegm, the color white. ¶ Likewise, humors can be mixed; the mixing of some humors is possible, and of others impossible. It is possible, such as blood and yellow bile; blood and phlegm; phlegm and melancholy; melancholy and yellow bile. The mixing is impossible for phlegm and yellow bile, though they may be mixed when they are in neighboring places, such as phlegm in the mouth of the stomach and yellow bile in the bottom. There is also an impossible mixing of blood and melancholy. If however phlegm is mixed with melancholy, that mixture will be either equal or unequal. If equal, the color will be honey-colored <note>original: "karopos"; a bright, yellowish-grey or amber-like color.</note>. If unequal and phlegm is superabundant, the color will be milky. If melancholy is superabundant, the color will be glaucous. ¶ Likewise, if a mixing occurs of yellow bile and phlegm, it will be either equal or unequal. If equal, the color will be citrine. If unequal and phlegm superabounds, the color will be pale or sub-pale. If yellow bile superabounds, the color will be sub-citrine. ¶ If it is asked why, when yellow bile superabounds, it is called "intense," when the mixture is equal. ¶ It must be answered: that the color is not called citrine from that equal mixture itself, but by reason of temperament <note>Balance of qualities.</note>, since phlegm tempers the heat and dryness of yellow bile; and the color citrine is more tempered than all other colors. And because of this, citrine color comes from such a mixture, not by reason of intensity or weakness, but by reason of temperament. If a mixture occurs of yellow bile and blood, it will be either equal or unequal. If equal, it will be tawny <note>original: "ruffus"; a reddish-yellow.</note>. If unequal and yellow bile superabounds, it will be sub-tawny. If blood superabounds, the color will be red. ¶ Likewise, a mixture can occur of burnt <note>original: "aduste"; humors that have become overheated and "scorched," considered highly toxic.</note> yellow bile and burnt blood. That mixture will be either equal or unequal. If equal, it will be wine-colored <note>original: "inopos"; a deep, dark red like wine.</note>. If unequal and blood superabounds, then the color will be ruddy. But if yellow bile superabounds, then the color will be sub-ruddy. ¶ Likewise, the color blue <note>original: "chianos"; from the Greek "kyanos."</note> is generated from a mixture of all corrupt humors. Green and livid colors are caused by white and black. If black overcomes white, the color will be green. If white overcomes black, the color will be livid. And this is the sufficiency of all colors. ¶ But if it is asked: why is there no color from other humors which can be mixed? ¶ It is said: because they do not agree except in passive qualities, and color is caused only by active qualities. And thus is the end, to the praise of almighty God, and His mother, and all the inhabitants of heaven. Amen.

## Preface to the Treatise on Pulses.

<margin>The Pulse</margin>
<note>A large decorative square initial letter Q. The interior of the letter contains a circular medallion featuring a woodcut portrait of a male figure wearing a physician's or scholar's cap and cloak, pointing upwards with his right hand.</note>
**There are four** principal organs <note>original: "membra"; parts or limbs, but here referring to internal organs.</note> by which the machine of the human body, strengthened by firm bases and foundations, stands: namely, the brain, the heart, the liver, and the testicles. They are called principal not because the destruction and death of the animal follows upon the interruption of any of these. For if the testicles were removed from the human body, although the body would be deformed and degenerate into a feminine nature, it would not die, nor would the state of its substance be destroyed. But they are called principal for this reason: because they rule and govern the whole body according to its disposition and according to the moderation of its virtues <note>original: "virtutũ"; the vital powers or faculties of the soul acting through the body.</note>. They rule according to disposition because, if the perfect temperaments <note>original: "crafes"; mixtures of qualities.</note> of these principles run together in one, the whole body is disposed according to them. They rule according to the moderation of virtues because the motive and sensitive virtue is centered in the brain; and the vegetative and spiritual virtue is principally founded in the heart. In the liver rules or dominates the augmentative and nutritive virtue; in the testicles, the propagative and generative virtue flourishes and takes joy. ¶ Of these four common virtues, the most useful and most widely extending beyond the others is the nutritive, and it is prior in nature. For it experiences its movements in the body before the infusion of the soul. Since the human body is fluid and subject to dissolution, it would necessarily fail unless the nutritive virtue restored what was lost; it operates throughout the entire time of the union of the soul to the body, and is committed to the universal existence. Whence it is the inseparable companion and partner of nature, and more intrinsic and faithful. Since the nutritive virtue cannot operate without a foundation upon which it rests, and the liver is its principal subject or foundation, it is fitting that the liver be formed before the other organs. And the edifice of the body rises from the liver as if from a primary foundation; therefore, the liver is judged to be the first root of the body. ¶ The vegetative virtue is more noble because it brings the body to a higher place or degree, illustrating it with vegetative splendor; yet it is later in nature, nor is it coequal to the body. And if it operates before the infusion of the soul, it executes its action only weakly and incompletely. Before the infusion of the soul, the body lives not by the soul nor by animation, but by vegetation, just as trees are enlivened by the spirit of greenness; but during the whole time of the union of soul and body, the spiritual virtue provides life or acts upon the organ in which it is founded; and that virtue is of high dignity or eminence in the heart, but later in nature and the time of formation. ¶ The motive and sensitive virtue is more excellent than the preceding ones by its precedence in dignity; for it serves the soul alone. ¶ Likewise, it proceeds from the soul, but it is later in time and nature. For before the infusion of the soul, this virtue is hindered and is not able to operate; therefore, it is drawn together by the infusion of the soul. Just as the sensitive virtue is later by reason of time and condition of nature, so also the organ which is the foundation of this virtue was formed afterward. ¶ The fourth virtue, which is propagative and generative, is less noble than the other virtues, and later in nature and time. It is less noble because it is not substantial to the body, nor so necessary, nor does it belong to the essence of nature like the other virtues, without which and their effects existence cannot be continued. And it can be called prior from the nature of the human complexion and composition, but posterior in time and nature because such a virtue is not moved to act in the body before the infusion of the soul, nor after its infusion, except at the time of puberty, when the bones are filled with marrow and growth...

# Preface on the Pulse

...with the humors: by the strengthening of natural heat and the widening of the passages; by the cause of sexual intercourse; and by the concurring heat of youth. In such cases, this power <note>The "virtue" or biological power of reproduction.</note> is provoked to the administration of its operation excellently and remarkably due to the readiness of these causes. However, this operation is unbridled, just like other powers. For when this power continues its action with an unbridled course for any length of time, the body is unnerved and wastes away, and the body falls into deficiency. Whence it is certain that this operation of the power is not as substantial or necessary to nature as others, since its continual action produces a defect in the body; whereas the animal body continually and without end breathes out, breathes in, and respires, is enlightened by the vegetative soul, and the limbs continually digest, desire, and retain, and are moved continually to cleanse the body of superfluities. Therefore, the effects of this [reproductive] power are more unbridled and more violent, and are by no means the effects of a general power, whose operation is suspended in many—those "little ones" who are dashed against the rock of continence. <note>A biblical allusion to Psalm 137:9, here used metaphorically to describe those who practice celibacy.</note> In others, however, such action is hindered because of the coldness or thickness of the testicles, or they are deprived of it by the causes concurring with intercourse. Hence it is that this power is not suited to nature except for the sake of propagation, so that the kinds of things are preserved through the multiplication of individuals, lest they perish. For man does not last continually; it is necessary, therefore, that through the successive power of propagation, he claims for himself a form and species that is similar, conforming, and—though less worthy than the other principal members and later in time—perpetuates the lineage.

¶ Since, therefore, the heart and the liver are preferred with such a prejudice of principality—that is, according to the physical disposition of these members, as Haly <note>Haly Abbas (d. 982), a famous Persian physician. The "Tegni" refers to Galen's *Ars Medica*, on which Haly commented.</note> testifies in his commentary on the *Tegni*—the whole body is disposed by them. Galen asserts that the whole body does not draw its disposition from the brain, nor from the testicles, but this is owed only to the heart and the liver. Hence it is that the studious intention of the ancient philosophers labored greatly to investigate the natures and conditions of these members. But these could not be better weighed or more expressly investigated than by the judgment of the pulses and the discernment of urines. For one [urine] elucidates the disposition of the liver and the members communicating with it by faithful testimony. The pulse, however, declares the condition of the heart, the tenor of life, and the presence of the vital spirits. Regarding the doctrine of urines, various and manifold treatises are found, but because of their confusion, we have constructed a small book of a new edition, compiled under a volume of brevity, so that we might consult the instruction of our scholars and serve the common utility. This book [on urines] escaped from us uncorrected and unpolished. For it suddenly came forth into the light and, not waiting for the legitimate time of publication, it was born an abortion. <note>The author uses the metaphor of a premature birth or "abortion" (*abortiuus*) to describe a book published before he could properly finish it.</note> Nor could it now be easily recalled, since it has already come into the hands of many, worn down by bad copying; and it disdained to be hidden, being nurtured among the people of Montpellier. <note>original: "montipedensibus"; referring to the famous medical school at the University of Montpellier.</note> It is on the lips of everyone; and though some may openly disparage it with the habits of envy, they nevertheless enrich their own poverty and penury from it and refresh the dryness of their own intellect.

¶ Regarding the doctrine of pulses, few or none have given a perfect or complete science. Galen, indeed, induced confusion and disturbed the truth through the great length of his volumes, the variety of his books, and his wordiness. For "all confusion is the stepmother of truth." Constantine <note>Constantine the African (11th century), who translated Arabic medical texts into Latin.</note> in his *Pantegni*, intending to teach the doctrine of pulses, proposes many variations and differences which, through their multiplicity, can scarcely be grasped by the speech of human reason.

¶ Philaretus, <note>A 7th-century medical writer whose work on pulses was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note> however, studied to narrow the confusion of the aforesaid authors under a volume of great brevity; but wishing to flee the Charybdis of confusion, he fell into the Scylla <note>A classical metaphor for avoiding one danger only to fall into another.</note> of obscure brevity, which obscurity is an enemy to teaching. Whence the book of Philaretus, in my judgment, is worthy to be cast out from the company of these books and the art.

<column-break/>

However, we, choosing a better path and abhorring both brevity and confusion, have composed a small book on the differences of pulses, making a temperament <note>A "temperament" or "middle way" refers to the medical concept of balance.</note> of both, so that, by maintaining a middle course, we may serve the understanding of our scholars who are fed by the food of our doctrine.

¶ Moreover, we write in the artifice of metric position <note>The text is written in verse/poetry to make it easier for medical students to memorize.</note> without sacrificing reason, so that the words, bound by the ties of poetic feet, may be more faithfully locked under the seal of memory and a more certain doctrine may be produced. From the vestibule of this work, we banish the wandering and false-running monks who, abusing the rule of religion and putting aside their monkly skin, presume to meddle in the mystery of this art. To such as these, the secrets of this work are by no means to be disclosed; "neither are pearls to be cast before swine," <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6.</note> nor are the mysteries of philosophy to be divulged to the unskilled. We therefore remove all such people, so that those who cannot grasp it with their intellect may be seen as unworthy to read it.

¶ Those things which are usually investigated in the introductions of certain books also occur for investigation at the beginning of this work: namely, what is the author's intention; what is the cause of the intention; what is the utility; to which part of philosophy it belongs; what is the mode of acting; what is the title of the book; what is the order of treatment.

¶ The **intention** of the author in this work is to hand down the doctrine of pulses by composing and showing the change of pulses, and the causes of the changes, and the types, and the differences.

¶ The **cause of the intention** is common to all: namely, utility, and the lack of Latin literature concerning the doctrine of pulses.

¶ The **utility** is the knowledge of the present dispositions of the human body, the foreknowledge of future ones, and the remembrance of past ones; and this is true in the healthy as well as in the sick and those in between.

¶ This book for the most part belongs to **philosophy**, and through philosophy to natural science: namely, to **physics** <note>In the medieval sense, "physics" refers to the study of nature and the human body.</note>.

¶ The **mode of acting** is definitive and divisive. **Definitive**, because it defines all types of pulses and determines the significations of the differences, since defining belongs to teachers. ¶ **Divisive**, because it partitions all types of pulses into various parts, and the causes of changes are distributed into various species in a three-fold reading.

¶ Therefore, this book is **divided** into three portions. In the first, it treats generally of the ten types of pulses by defining them, and of the five considerations by which the differences of the pulse are discerned. Second, of the species of types, and of the circumstances and causes from which the pulse is named. Third, it treats principally of the significations of the pulses. However, each partition has its own special and proper order of treatment, which will be manifest from the text.

¶ Regarding the **Title**, I am ashamed to set it forth, because: *"Envy feeds on the living; it rests after death, when each man's honor protects him according to his merit."* <note>original: "Pascitur in viuis livor..."; a quote from Ovid's *Amores*, 1.15.39.</note> But lest the authority of this book be converted into the praises of a detractor by an unspeakable change of the title, and lest another presume to collect the grain which he did not sow, we submit the title with a humble face and modest brow, so that a false-writing detractor cannot stamp the coinage of our genius and labor with another image and an adulterous likeness. Let the title, therefore, be as follows: ¶ **Here begins...**

## ¶ Here begins the book of Master Gilles on pulses, composed in verse.

The powers of the mind are unequal to these modest attempts;
A heavy subject ends, entangled in metaphors.
Arduous, difficult, knotted, impassable for the small—
We undertake an arduous task attempted by none of our predecessors.
We, wishing to cross the steep precipices of so great a sea,
Do not rely on the service of a boat, nor the use of an oarsman,
But proceed on metrical feet, and on dry heels. <note>original: "pedibus metricis: & sicco calce vadam⁹." Gilles is making a pun: he is writing in poetic "feet" (meter) rather than prose, comparing prose to a boat and poetry to walking across the water or through the shallows.</note>
The unharmonious subject refuses the touch of a faithful craftsman,
And words not articulated with a decent joint
Shudder to be constrained by the poetic measurements of a metrical frame.
The weightier the matter, and the less suited to be resolved,
The more it deserves to be inclined toward forgiveness.
The gravity itself shall rule: if the author should sin in anything,
It lightens the offense of the fault and absolves the guilt.

## ¶ Here begins the commentary of Master Gentile da Foligno upon the treatise on pulses by Master Gilles.

**The powers of the mind.** The author, in the manner of one writing correctly, prescribes a preface for his work, in which he decently pays the readers what is due in a preface. For he captures the goodwill of the listeners when he shows that the subject can scarcely be treated in metrical speech. This treatise is very useful for instruction. ¶ **A heavy subject.** He rouses attention here, where he suggests the arduousness and lengthiness of the matter. In both, he hunts for a receptive mind, as we perceive from the text. The subject matter concerns the diversity of pulses. ¶ **Burdened.** That is, heavy, and compressing the mind with the difficulty of the treatment. ¶ **Metaphors.** <note>original: "Figuris." In this context, it refers to rhetorical figures or complex symbolic descriptions.</note> That is, distinguished by various prayers in the mutations and significations of the pulses, by which the matter itself is shaped. ¶ **Entangled.** That is, he brings back the matter as intricate and involved. ¶ **Arduous, difficult.** All these words emphasize the difficulty of the work, and here he rouses attention. ¶ **Attempted by none.** That is, none of our predecessors dared to approach the lengthiness of so great a work, nor to bind its arduousness in metrical feet. ¶ **The steep precipices of so great [a sea].** That is, the depth of the matter, which is compared to a sea because of its vastness. ¶ **Not relying on a boat.** That is, on prose speech. Prose speech is likened to a boat, and metrical speech to walking through the shallows on feet. The matter of pulses is deep and is compared to a sea through a certain metaphor. For just as a sailor on the sea, being in a very sturdy ship, penetrates the deep of the sea safely, whereas he would fail if he presumed to go on foot; so the mind, treating the sea of such a vast matter by the rowing of prose speech, crosses over better and more safely than if it should attempt to travel through that same matter on the feet of metrical speech. ¶ **The unharmonious [subject] of the lute.** Another metaphor through which the difficulty of the work is given or shown; it is drawn from the lute and the fiddle. If these have dissonant and discontinuous strings, neither well-prepared by the craftsman’s plectrum nor properly tuned, they return no harmony to the touch. So also this matter has such disharmony and discontinuity of words that the resonance of metrical speech can scarcely result from them. ¶ **The weightier the matter.** Through this, he asks for forgiveness if he should sin in anything during the treatment, excusing himself by the difficulty of the matter.

<column-break/>

### ¶ On the complexion of the heart: its form, composition, and office.

The heart, the seat of life, the faithful dwelling of vital heat,
The basis of nature, the unique sun of the microcosm. <note>The "microcosm" refers to the human being viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>
The throne of the life-giving chamber and the inner sanctuary of vigor.
In which a little fountain bubbles up, which with pure fuel
Governs the stars, gives life, increases, disposes, and burns.
Here, seeking again stable numbers and physical bonds,
By which the foundations of human life consist.
From seed-like causes, an indwelling power inhabits this,
And the fiery force renders for itself a twin seat.
Whence a species kindred to heat is given to the limbs.
The apex rises in them; the terrestrial parts provide the foundation.
And they build the base; the lighter parts are carried upward.

¶ **The heart [is the seat] of life.** Having finished the preface, he approaches the principal proposition: to treat the matter of pulses. But before he approaches his subject of the distinction of pulses, he places certain preambles and antecedents to the main point, by which the reader may approach the understanding of what follows more promptly and easily. First, therefore, he discourses on the <term>complexion of the heart</term> <note>Complexion refers to the specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> and on its form, composition, and office, which draws its origin from the complexion and form. ¶ And note that the supreme Craftsman <note>God.</note> providently arranged all things and established the heart just as he placed the sun in the middle of the microcosm. He made it very hot, fiery, round, and hollow, and established it as a youth; because it is the foundation of natural and vital heat, the domicile of the spirit, by whose benefit the whole body is heated and enlivened. For every hot thing—according to the testimony of Philaretus—is by nature swiftly mobile. For it was necessary for the heart to yield to mobility so that through its motion the vital spirit might be infused into the limbs, the infusion of which has the task of enlivening and vivifying the entire body. And it is round, but not perfectly so; rather it remains shaped in the manner of a cone, because a round form is friendly and conducive to motion. For the expert perceives that everything round is by its nature mobile or rollable. ¶ Likewise, a round form is more perfect and closer to incorruptibility because of the lack of corners. For Constantinus <note>Constantine the African, an 11th-century translator of Arabic medical texts.</note> says in his book on the eyes that a round form is smooth on the sides and sloping all around, having no corners in which superfluity might be contained to cause injury. If it had corners in which the stain of superfluity adhered, the heart would be a triangle or some other shape, and the "rust" adhering in the corners would provide a cause for dissolution. The heart is youthful and hollow so that within the cells of its cavity it might receive the blood with the natural spirit sent to it from the liver, and might more freely contain the vital spirit within itself. Also, so that it might more promptly draw in the air breathed from the lungs to temper the heat of its innate seething. For if it were solid inside and devoid of hollowness, the interposition of the middle parts would prevent the constriction from which the dilation arises. If dilation and constriction were forbidden, no blowing out of the vital spirit through the arteries would occur, and thus the heart would necessarily fail in its natural office within. ¶ **The heart of life.** That is, the universal seat, the domicile of the life-giver. ¶ **Faithful dwelling.** That is, a faithful habitation. ¶ **Of vital heat.** That is, the spirit from which all limbs are heated. ¶ **Unique basis.** That is, the foundation; for just as a foundation is that upon which a building rests, so the entire machine of the microcosm is strengthened by the heart as by a firm and principal basis. ¶ **Unique** [does] not [mean] only, but principal. There are indeed other bases of the microcosm, but this one is more excellent, as we taught from the beginning—that is, in the preface—where we discussed many things regarding the four principal organs. ¶ **Sun of the microcosm.** For just as in the greater world, which is called the macrocosm, all things [live] by the benefit of the sun...

# On the dispositions of the heart

They are irradiated, illuminated, warmed, and comforted; and those things meant to be increased are increased; the things born of the earth are called toward conception and birth. But when the sun is absent from us in the opposite region, and is sent away to the antarctic pole, and when clouds by their opposition steal its sight from us, the lower things are cheated of its benefit, and the sad and misty air is condemned by the absence of warmth. In a similar way, from the sun of our body—that is, the heart—all the members are warmed; they are quickened toward nourishment and invited toward the restoration of lost parts. And if a cloud of smoky vapor should darken it, or some other sudden cause change it, the human body hastens toward an eclipse and is deprived of the light of growth. 

¶ **The bridal chamber of life.** <note>original: "Viuifici thalamus."</note> In a bridal chamber, men live in luxury and rejoice; they behave wantonly, and the sad are refreshed; they stay away from the inconvenient and the superstitious. Similarly, in the bridal chamber of the heart, in which the nuptials of the soul and nature are celebrated—with the life-giving spirits serving as intermediaries like servants and household slaves to the marriage of the soul and nature—nature, rejoicing in the delight of temperance, becomes cheerful and is encouraged to "marry." It eliminates melancholy and resentment, and by means of pure and sincere blood, it obtains the richness of its own recreation. Therefore, the heart is rightly called the bridal chamber of the vital spirit and of vigor. 

¶ **The Throne.** Because just as kings preside on a throne, so natural heat reigns and holds its empire in the heart. 

¶ **The Secret Chamber.** <note>original: "Penetrate," likely a variation of *penetralia*, the innermost part of a temple or home.</note> This is the most secret part of a house, and the heart is the more secret part of the human body, to which—as if it were more enclosed than other parts—the force of death breaks in more slowly after the other parts have been extinguished. Whence death is described as the "extinguishing of natural heat in the heart"; for in this way life cannot be defeated unless its principal tower is seized. The other members are like huts and appendages to the castle; if they are broken off, the sovereignty of life is not diminished. 

¶ **In which.** That is, in the heart. 

¶ **It gushes.** <note>original: "Scaturit."</note> That is, it boils up and seethes. It is the nature of streams and waters to gush from the earth, which leap and break out from the ground with force. For water that is foul and bound by the viscosity of mud does not gush. Indeed, the heat in the heart gushes in the likeness of leaping water. 

¶ **Behold the little fountain.** <note>original: "fonticulus."</note> That is, the vital spirit with pure, cleansed blood; a fountain continually flowing, leaping into the life of the body; nor can it dry up unless it is dried by the violence of death. This little fountain rules the members as the "protector" and patron of the body, and the heart sustains them. 

¶ **It quickens.** <note>original: "Vegetat."</note> That is, it makes alive by its infusion, or by nature mediating through the members. 

¶ **It increases.** Because by the vigor of the vital spirit, and by such nature mediating, it nourishes and increases the body. For when the body is dead and destitute of the vital spirit, it is not nourished. As to how it nourishes the body in the infusion of the soul, and the question of the vital and animal spirit before the infusion, let us leave that to be solved by the "foot-draggers" <note>original: "motipedensibus," likely a disparaging term for those who are slow to understand or follow.</note> so that they may exercise themselves a little therein. 

¶ **It disposes.** That is, it assimilates and forms the whole body to its own complexion, so that the whole is accepted as a totality. For bones cannot be changed from their own nature first, since they are cold and dry, but parts common to the whole body are changed, which must be discussed more fully in the section on the "realm." 

¶ **It ventilates.** <note>original: "Aduarat," likely *adventat* or *evantat*.</note> That is, it airs and cools, and tempers the body by the softness of the attracted air; for the whole body would glow from the vehemence of the seething heat unless the air attracted by the heart and breathed in by the lungs, by the fan of its ventilation, soothed it. 

¶ **From.** That is, from the heart itself as if from the foundation of nature. 

¶ **You should seek.** That is, search out physically. 

¶ **Stable numbers and physical bonds.** That is, firm proportions which are observed in numbers, and physical modes, and invisible joints <note>original: "gumphos," a technical term for a bolt or nail.</note> by which the soul is entangled in the body. For there is a certain measure and a certain boundary of proportion in which the quality of the heart in the whole body, and the heat in any of the other members, ought to exceed; if it stops below that boundary more than nature can sustain, or if it crosses 

<column-break/>

its boundary, life is destroyed. 

¶ **Physical bonds.** These are the natural, vital, and animal spirits by which the soul is joined to the body. For those spirits, although they have their generative power in discrete places, receive their strength and reinforcement from the heart. Also, because of the heat of the heart, and the natural spirit being purified by the power of heat, the vital and animal spirits are found in the heart. 

¶ **From its seeds.** He had said the heart was the sun of the body and the foundation of natural heat; now he assigns the reason why this is so. 

¶ **Because a fiery power.** That is, natural heat contracted from the first components, which are the seminal and original causes, inhabits this seat of the heart, and by a certain treaty of brotherhood, it devotedly embraces that seat. For although heat is in every part of the body as the governor of the whole, the heart nevertheless appropriates for itself a firm and stable mansion. 

¶ **Whence it gives.** He proves from the shape of the heart that the heart is the habitation of natural heat. It has a pointed shape <note>original: "pincatam," possibly *pineatam*, like a pine cone.</note> and is similar to a cone: thick and round at the bottom, spread out in a certain circular width, but tending toward a point at the top. This shape is suited to the thing because, by the power of its "fire-ness," fire by its natural motion tends toward the heights or toward a point. Therefore, from the thicker and more watery parts having more bulk and earthiness, the heart is wider at the bottom; the watery parts, hindered by the earthy ones, do not follow the motion of the fire's constriction. Thus, from the contradiction of either part, its lower part is rounded in a thick circularity. The fiery and airy parts, however, are snatched upward by the impetus of the heat; ascending by the snatching of their own lightness and tending toward a point, they constitute the summit of the heart in the manner of a cone or pyramid. 

¶ **But it is objected:** Why is the heart in the human body arranged so that, according to its disposition, the heart is thick at the top and pointed below? Whence, by this arrangement, the aforesaid reasoning is overturned. 

¶ **To this we say** that according to the Greeks, man is called *anthropos*, as if "turned upward," and is likened to an **inverted tree**. <note>The "inverted tree" is a classical philosophical concept where humans are rooted in heaven (the brain) with branches reaching down (the limbs), whereas plants are rooted in the earth.</note> For just as an inverted tree has its root established at the top and branches proceeding downward from the root, so man has the brain, which is the root of the whole body, originating at the top. The other members, proceeding from the brain as if from a root by means of the nerves, are established below. Thus, according to the disposition of this order, the heart is blunt in the upper part and pointed in the lower part with respect to this order. But if the natural order of position is inspected—since every root ought to be placed below and the branches raised—then according to this order of nature, the heart will be pointed at the top and thick and blunt at the bottom. 

¶ **The base.** That is, the foundation of the substance of the heart, which is composed of earthy parts residing at the bottom.

# Of the Heart

...slow: and where it begins, it knows not how to cease until it is completed. Thus, we rebuke the error of certain men who asserted that the motion of the heart occurs through certain nerves descending from the brain to the muscles of the chest, which these nerves move. These moved muscles then move the chest <note>the thorax</note>, and draw the lungs with them; the moved lungs then stir the heart. This I judge, from the hall of my speculation, should be blown away <note>original: "insufflandum," meaning to be rejected or dismissed like breath</note>. For the motion of the heart, as Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a Persian physician whose "Royal Book" was a standard medical text</note> says, is natural; it is not in our power to delay it, as we can with the motion of the soul. The motion of the soul is voluntary; it is subject to the will and moderated by reason, and it is administered through the nerves and the animal spirit, which is the servant and herald of the soul. This motion we can delay and retard as we wish, just like the motion of a hand, a foot, or another limb. 

There is a third motion, which is intermediate: that of the lungs and the chest. It is partly natural—wherefore it cannot be entirely stopped, for necessity imposes the law of motion—and it is partly voluntary. Thus it can be delayed for a time, and the will follows judgment when we hold our breath or cease from breathing in. In that which can be delayed, it proceeds from the soul and is voluntary; but in that which cannot be delayed entirely, being forced into action by the necessity of breathing, it proceeds from nature and is universal. 

Therefore, the motion of the heart is not proportional to the motion of the lungs; for the motion of the heart is doubled or tripled before the motion of the lungs or chest completes a single cycle. The motion of the chest is proportional to the motion of the lungs, but the motion of the heart does not correspond to the motion of the lungs. This is true: if you apply your right hand over your left hand, or if you discern the nature of the pulse in the arteries, you will find a threefold motion of the heart before the motion of the lungs is completed once. 

But the motion of the arteries is proportional to the motion of the heart. For when the heart moves, the entire artery moves, just as when a staff in the hand is moved, the hand is moved, and also the staff at its tip, in its middle, and at its beginning. It seems to some that the artery moves later than the heart, since it does not move except by the motion of the heart. For the vital spirit, which dilates the heart and the arteries, cannot be in the heart and the arteries at the same instant; but in the passage of time, it is diffused from the heart into the arteries. Thus, the dilation of the arteries seems to be successive to the motion of the heart, which solves the problem of the "mountain-feet" <note>original: "montipedes," likely a technical or corrupt term referring to the transmission of motion through the limbs or "steps" of the pulse</note>.

<margin>The motion of the heart is twofold.</margin>
The motion of the heart, therefore, which according to the assigned reason is unrestrained and necessary, is twofold. One is simple, the other composite. Simple motion consists only in dilation, or only in constriction. That which consists of both dilation and constriction is composite, and it consists of contrary movements. **Diastole**, **dilation**, and **arsis** <note>Greek for "lifting up"</note> are the same thing. **Systole**, **constriction**, and **thesis** <note>Greek for "setting down"</note> are the same thing. Diastole is the motion of the heart toward its extremities. Systole is the reduction of the surrounding parts back to the center. Therefore, the impetus of the heart and the vehemence of the spirit in those parts performs the dilation; and the motion of dilation lasts as long as the impetus of heat and the vehemence or violence of the pushing spirit permits. Thus, heat induces a boiling <note>term: ebullition; the medieval idea that blood "boiled" in the heart to create pressure</note> and the pushing spirit performs the diastole. When the violence of the impulse ceases or weakens, the motion of dilation subsides. And then, from the earthy substance of the heart—because of the vehemence of the extreme parts and their weight—there occurs the compression of the heart and the reduction of the extreme parts toward one another.

<margin>Four causes of heart motion.</margin>
The causes of the motion of the heart are various and different; they are said by us to be four. First, the hot complexion of the heart. Second, its form and composition with earthy substance. Third, the spirit innate with smoky superfluity. The fourth cause can be said to be the spiritual power <note>virtus spiritualis</note>, which proceeds from the three preceding ones. But we shall show more fully how dilation is made by the pushing spirit as the servant, and by heat as the craftsman. Blood, through the "hollow vein" <note>the vena cava</note> from the liver, enters the heart with the natural spirit through the right auricle of the heart and is administered to it. In the hidden depths of the heart, the received blood, finding an extremely hot place, begins to boil; and boiling, it is resolved and rarefied into smoke and spirit. But smoke differs from spirit.

<column-break/>

<margin>Smoke and spirit differ.</margin>
For spirit is more subtle, while smoke is coarser. Spirit is intermediate between fire and air: blunter than fire and more subtle than air. Smoke is intermediate between water and air: coarser than air and more subtle than water. Thus, smoke and spirit generated in the heart through the process of rarefaction occupy a larger place and fill the concavity of the heart and distend it. From this comes the dilation of the heart. That every rarefied body occupies a larger space can be proven by authority, reason, and example. For Aristotle says that from one handful of water, many handfuls of air are made; and the same is true for other things. 

A primary argument can be brought forward: If a whole chestnut is placed in ignited ash, the heat of the fire resolves the moisture of the chestnut into smoke. The resolved smoke is much greater in quantity than the mass from which it was generated. Therefore, it occupies a larger place and fills and distends the space between the shell and the chestnut. And since it cannot be contained inside, because it strives for vaporization, it moves upward with a certain violence and carries the chestnut with it, nor does it allow it to be pushed back down until it evaporates after the shell has burst. In a similar way, the dilation of the heart occurs from the smoke and spirit occupying a larger place than the blood. But the constriction of the heart is effected by its weightiness alone, just as the gravity of the chestnut alone seems sufficient for its falling back down. 

Since the motion of the heart according to diastole and systole has a threefold cause—hot complexion, composition, and spirit with innate smoke—it should be known that the operative power, which is the fourth cause, proceeds from these three. It is described thus: "The motive power is the motion of the heart and arteries," etc. An objection is raised regarding the compression of the heart: it seems that it is not an operation of power. For when compression begins, the power ceases to operate, nor does it exercise any motion. Likewise, power cannot operate except through some mediating spirit; but in compression, the spirit does not move, nor is the compression made through it, but rather from the coherence of the parts of the heart, which, being of heavy substance, is pressed downward by the power of its own gravity. Therefore, the operative power is not the motion of the heart and arteries according to both diastole and systole, but according to diastole alone—which contradicts the Author. Let us leave this argument to be solved by those who trade in such matters, so that they may have something to argue about.

Having explained these things, let us interpret the text. **Unrestrained** <note>original: "effreno"</note>: that is, violent, necessary, and natural; it refers to the composite motion that brings the parts together, as it adds: **Now**. That is, sometimes, **to rise**. **Into Arsis**. That is, into diastole, from the heat creating the boiling and from the pushing spirit. **Now**. That is, sometimes, when dilation is complete and the impulse of the spirit ceases. **Thesis**. That is, systole. **Adverse**. Because it is the contrary motion of diastole. **Presses it**. Namely, the heart, from the coherence and weight of the parts. **Of the beast** <note>likely an error in transcription for a technical term</note>. I say: **Rival**. That is, familiar and friendly. **Of the center**. That is, of the convexity of the heart. 

**Continuously**. He said the heart is snatched by an unrestrained and violent motion. Therefore, since it is hot and agitated in a ceaseless and unrestrained motion, it could be inflamed and grow white-hot, especially since it is hot and fiery. For it is a physical principle that solid bodies, especially when hot, are heated by motion—and not only hot things, but even those that are cold and earthy. In chariots and mills, around the axle where the wheel turns, we see fire ignited by the impetus of unrestrained rotation. If this were to happen in the heart, the human body would fail and incur the danger of dissolution. Lest this happen, nature—provident, discrete, and diligent in all her operations—acting as a dispenser, established the lung as the servant and chamberlain of the heart. The lung, with the bellows of conceived airiness, tempers the heart’s fervor and soothes its fiery face with the fan of gentle ventilation. **The moist lung**. As it is the receptacle of phlegm, and it moistens with much liquid. **And of raw blood**. That is, of phlegm, which is raw humor and the first stage of blood.

<summary>This page explains the mechanics of heart motion, refuting the idea that it is controlled by the brain and instead attributing it to "boiling" blood (rarefaction) causing expansion (diastole) and its own weight causing contraction (systole). It also identifies the lung as a necessary cooling mechanism to prevent the heart from overheating due to its constant, violent motion.</summary>

### On the causes of the heart's motion.

**The heart’s form, thickness, smoke, and spiritual force,**
**The handmaid of power, providing breath to the limbs.**
**These are the causes of the art; but the falling <note>original: "thesis," here referring to the downward stroke or contraction known as systole</note> by gravity alone**
**Is perfected, while the substance is weighed down by itself.**
**The rule of nature governs and celebrates this motion,**
**Whose power, infused into the limbs of the soul, rouses**
**Vigor, and tempers the other uses of virtue.**

¶ **The heart's form.** Regarding what the causes of the heart's motion are, he says those whose distinction claims their light from the preceding sections. ¶ **Form.** As to its roundness; which form is suitable for mobility, for everything round is mobile by nature. ¶ **Thickness.** That is, its hot complexion; for everything hot is by nature swiftly mobile, just as everything cold is slowly mobile. ¶ **Smoke.** Generated from resolved blood through sudden rarefaction; whence, occupying a larger space, it inflates the heart and dilates it. ¶ **Spiritual force.** That is, existing in the heart itself. ¶ **Handmaid of power.** The vital spirit, as a minister, carries the operation with it and the spiritual power. ¶ **Providing breath.** That is, pouring the breaths of life into the body. Not all the aforesaid are causes [of the same thing]. ¶ **Of the art.** That is, of diastole <note>the expansion of the heart</note>. ¶ **But the falling.** Which is the reduction of the extreme parts to the center. ¶ **Is perfected.** From gravity alone, and coherence, and the earthiness of the substance. ¶ **While it is weighed down.** That is, in the motion of its own gravity, with no impulse of the spirit working toward this. ¶ **Governs and celebrates this.** The author had said the heart's motion is unrestrained and necessary, because it is caused by nature alone. Thence it seems to some that the motion of the heart should be attributed to nature alone, and that it is entirely foreign to the soul's power. Therefore he shows that although it happens principally by nature, yet it derives vigor for its formation from the soul. ¶ But he proves that the motion of the heart nevertheless proceeds from the soul. Constantine <note>Constantine the African, the monk-physician who translated Arabic medical texts into Latin</note> says in the *Pantegni* that one power pertains to nature alone, and is called 'natural.' Another is that which pre-vivifies the heart and dilates both the heart and the arteries, and likewise constricts them; this pertains to the soul and is called 'spiritual.' The third is that which perfects sense and voluntary motion, that is, 'animal' <note>from "anima," meaning soul</note>. From this it appears that the spiritual power, which works the heart's motion, nevertheless proceeds from the soul. ¶ To this Constantine says, when he says the spiritual power pertains to the soul, he does not say it for this reason: that it takes its life and the beginning of its essence from the soul; but because from the infusion of the soul it executes its action more perfectly. For before the infusion of the soul, it was present only in potential, but after the soul is infused, it is present in act. Whence from the infusion of the soul, all powers of the body exist more strongly in fulfilling their actions.

**And drive far away the shadows of the smoky cloud,**
**So the spirit can be restored by worthy fuel.**
**From heat and falling <note>expansion and contraction</note> the motion of the heart is forged,**
**Which makes the pulse, and becomes harmonious with life.**

**¶ In the pulse resound the tenors and harmony of life,**
**The melodies of the vital union and the heart's love,**
**The innermost tempering, and the secret will of the soul.**
**¶ The increase, the paroxysm, the standstill, and the periodic error,**

**It certifies the faith; the pulse confirms and unites.**
**Censure reduces the genus of judgment into a species,**
**But with a doubtful pulse, the physician's mind wavers.**

¶ **Innate.** What the motion of the heart is, and by what occurring causes it happens, and what works the heart's motion—whether it be the limbs or nature—he has said; because the pulse proceeds either from the motion of the heart or from the causes working the heart's motion. Therefore, he provides an introductory description of the pulse. ¶ Since the entire teaching of this work consists of pulses, he provides a deep and worthy description by way of reasoning out its property. It is described by the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> thus: "Pulse is the motion of the heart and arteries," etc. This definition is not to be understood by essence, as are many definitions of this art.
<margin>Pulse</margin>
For the pulse is not that motion which is in the heart, since that is singular, whereas the pulse is in the arteries far from the heart. However, the motion of the heart is the cause of that motion which is in the arteries and which is the pulse. Just as from the motion of a tree follows the motion of the leaves and fruit, yet they are not one and the same motion, but one is made by the other; so it is in the pulse. For the heart moves and dilates, from whose motion the vital spirit is impelled; and once impelled, it moves the arteries. Since this is entirely the pulse, we can define it thus: "Pulse is a motion composed of various movements in a hollow and arterial limb, made by the motion of the heart and certain arteries, proceeding from an operating power by means of the spirit." It can also be said that the physical definition is through essence, such that the pulse is a motion composed of the motion of the heart and the motion of the arteries. For from various motions, one composite motion can be established. This motion of the heart was the motion which is the pulse, and the motion of the arteries was similarly a part of the same. He, therefore, who touches the pulse, feels the parts; he does not feel the motion of the heart directly, but deduces it from the knowledge of the motion of the arteries. ¶ The text is explained thus. ¶ **Such a motion.** Which makes the pulse is composed of the motion of the arteries and the heart. ¶ **Is forged.** That is, composed. **From heat and falling.** That is, from dilation <note>diastole</note> and contraction <note>systole</note>. That is, the motion of the heart and arteries is considered as composed of diastole and systole. It follows: ¶ **So that the soothing.** Here he assigns the utility of the pulse. Whence this clause is not part of the definition, but is annexed to express its utility. Just as in a physical definition, this clause is added: "for the cooling of the innate heat." For the utility of the pulse is so that the body may be warmed by its motion, and from the air inspired by the lung, the vital spirit may be restored. For a part of that attracted air evaporates through the pores of the body; some is consumed by heat; some is expired from the lung by the constriction of the heart; some, being retained, is refined and purified, and from it—once annexed and joined to the vital spirit—the vital spirit is restored. And this is: ¶ **So that the soothing breeze.** That is, the inspired air. ¶ **May recreate.** That is, soothe and temper. ¶ **Innate heat.** That is, natural heat, which otherwise would seethe and catch fire. ¶ **Not because of shadow.**

For example, a lion’s skin, although it is dead, is yet choleric and hot in the fourth degree <note>in Galenic medicine, the highest degree of a quality</note>; if taken into the body, it dissolves and provokes fever.
