<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the heart’s interaction with air and the vital spirit, specifically addressing why constant breathing is necessary to prevent the "smoky" superfluities from thickening the spirit and causing death.</meta>

...produced from those things flowing in: and by the infusion of spirits and humors: and it exists in action, though it leaves the substance; this is recreated by the air and becomes distempered, and no other. 

¶ **Smoky shadows.** <margin>Two causes of animal death on the part of the heart.</margin> That is, the superfluities which, when received into the body, would cloud and overshadow the vital spirit. 

¶ **Let them be expelled.** That is, let them be blown out from the heart to the lung, and from the lung emitted to the exterior. 

¶ Here it can be asked: when we suspend our breathing, by what means does the heart attract air, or by what does it expel superfluities? 

¶ It is said that in breathing, an attraction of air occurs; this air is transmitted through the *trachea arteria* <note>The windpipe</note> to the lung and is received in the small cavities of the lung. Not all of that air is transmitted to the heart for two reasons: first, because the heart would not be capable of holding all the air attracted to the lung, of which the lung is capable as it is a thin member; second, because the heart contains a part of it within itself. Thus, even if air is not attracted from the outside, the heart finds air in the lung which it can attract. And although the lung is filled with air and the heart has sufficient air within itself by which it can be cherished—from which it would seem that air could be held for a long time without the immediate help of external air—nevertheless, this cannot happen. This is because the heart, always in constriction <note>systole</note>, which follows dilation <note>diastole</note>, emits smoky superfluities. If these were transmitted to the lung and could not be blown out, nor contained in the heart, they would return and be reciprocated back to the heart, thickening the vital spirit, which by nature ought to be subtle <note>refined or thin</note>. When the spirit is too thickened, an excessive dilation of the heart occurs, and the extremities are prevented from returning to the center. 

Indeed, if there is an excessive thinning of the spirits, it is a cause of death for some. Thus, those raised in thick air, if they were to pass into a hot region where the air is purified, would quickly die, because the vital spirit becomes too refined and weakened beyond its nature; nor can it fully dilate the thickness of the heart, and from this they suffer syncope <note>fainting or heart failure</note>, and in fainting, they are suffocated. This is why fish, nourished by the thick air of the water, die when extracted from the water into the air itself, which is thinner. Some die more slowly, like eels; some more quickly, like herring; some in a medium time, like pike and barbel. Let the scholars investigate why this happens. 

Similarly, I say that an excessive thickening of the vital spirit beyond nature causes death to occur. Hence, men of Libya, if they were to pass into thick air, would not live long; nor could we live long in their air, for the same reason: because the vital spirit, through the thickening which it undergoes contrary to nature, is corrupted. Therefore, when the thickened spirit fills the sides of the heart, the heart dilates immoderately. 

<column-break/>

When it exceeds the limit of its dilation, it is hindered in its constriction, leading to the interruption of the animal life. There are, indeed, two causes of immoderate death: dilation and constriction. For just as the body of an animal cannot live unless it has a proper dilation followed by constriction, and dilation succeeding constriction, so too from the impediment or immoderation of dilation and constriction, the danger of death is incurred. And for the human body to live, inspiration is not enough unless it also breathes out. These things happen according to the alternation of the dilation and constriction of the heart. 

<margin>Why someone dies from excessive joy.</margin> 
From this it follows that from laughter and excessive joy, many suffer syncope due to immoderate dilation, and if the syncope persists, they die. For while, through immoderate dilation, the smoky superfluities are not blown out because constriction is hindered, but are instead retained in the heart; being retained, they thicken the vital spirit, which ought to be subtle. This thickened spirit, deprived of motion, is extinguished. Just as ethereal fire, igniting the air, is extinguished when the motion of ignition descends into thicker air; for while it thickens, the nature of its subtlety departs and it is put out. Similarly, a fire kindled in flax and held in the mouth of a performer is kept there, but by the blowing and breath it is thickened, and before it can exit, it is extinguished. For the same reason, a fire in air that is too moist and rainy can hardly burn, because it is thickened by the rainy air. Also, from joy, syncope happens for another reason: because when exhalation is hindered, the vital spirit cannot be restored to the animal; when this fails, voluntary sense and animal motion cease. Natural heat in the heart is also annihilated by the retained smoky superfluities. 

<margin>Why one dies in terror and strong sadness.</margin> 
Just as syncope and death sometimes happen from joy because of the immoderation of dilation, so it happens from sadness and great terror <margin>Who faints more easily or with more difficulty from joy or sadness.</margin> because of the immoderation of constriction. For when the lateral parts of the heart are immoderately constricted, excluding all emptiness, no air is received into the heart, nor does the respiration of air occur, which is necessary to temper the heat of the heart and recover the vital spirit. 

¶ Now, all these things vary, being intensified or relaxed according to the state of the heart. In some, the heart is soft and tender and has a fleshy substance; such a heart, when joy supervenes, dilates further and more vehemently because of the obedience of its parts. People with such a heart suffer syncope more easily and more severely. And if they are placed in an air-bath lacking vents, they are quickly thrown into syncope. 

Those, however, who have an earthy and compact heart suffer syncope from joy more slowly, because the hardness of the heart resists immoderate dilation. But from incoming sadness, they suffer syncope more quickly and severely, because the hardness and heaviness of the parts aid the excess of constriction. People with very hard hearts, if they enter a furnace where the air is very refined due to the smelting of metals, incur severe syncope from a lack of dilation; because the vital spirit in a hard heart ought to be thick, and being made very thin by the extremely refined air, it cannot propel the sides of the heart to the measure of proper dilation. From this, it happens that children suffer syncope more quickly than men. 

¶ **It resonates in the pulse.** Having introduced the definition of the pulse, it is necessary to declare the utility of the pulse. Namely: the declaration of the consistency and habit of a tempered body, or its distemper; or the discernment of the passions and affections of the soul; the clarification of the seasons and of acute illnesses; the distinction of future crises, whether for good or for evil; the knowledge of life and death; the eradication of frauds and delusions; and the certification of urine. All these will become clearer from the meaning of the text. 

¶ **Of times.** That is, the stability of life and its integrity, and the continuity of its process according to the natural law of the body itself. 

¶ **They resonate in the pulse.** That is, they are made manifest through the pulse. For just as the clarity of metal is declared by sound, and the goodness or malice of a cymbal, so through the pulse, as if through a certain sound (because in it the arteries are pulsed by the motion of the impelling spirit), the distemper or temper of the human body is declared. And not only are these known through the pulse. 

¶ **But love.** That is, the general consideration of the parts. 

¶ **Syzygies.** <note>original: "sinzugie," referring to the union or yoking of elements</note> That is, of human life, which consists in a certain syzygy or proportional concord of the four elements in the body. By "vital syzygy," one can understand the admirable joining and matrimonial complexion or bond between the body and the soul. 

¶ **Modulations.** That is, the temperaments not only of the heart but of the internal members, which, when the heart is well, are stronger and more tempered, just as when it is unwell, they languish and grow weary. 

¶ **Secret will.** <margin>On the pulses of the passions of the soul.</margin> That is, the passions and affections of the soul, such as joy, anger, sadness, animosity, fear, greed, and liberality; for they change the pulse and are declared through the pulses, although the distinction of such is difficult. 

¶ For in **joy**, because the heart dilates moderately due to the temperament of the affection, and because the blood is a tempered humor which moves in joy, the heart diffuses gradually and temperately from the interior to the exterior. Hence the pulse increases in magnitude with a tempered process, and claims for itself a middle ground between strong and weak, and fast and slow. For not much cooling is necessary because of the temperament of the heat. 

¶ In **anger**: because heat is impetuously diffused from the interior to the exterior, and the bile is burning because it is moved in anger. Therefore, from anger, the pulse suddenly rises in magnitude, and provoked by the impetuosity of the bile, neglecting fear, it assumes speed and frequency. Hence, if such a pulse is made beyond the nature of the body without a fever, without a wandering mind, and without physical exercise, it can be gathered that it arises from anger and signifies anger—especially since anger is a boiling of the heart. In which, from the desire for revenge (since revenge happens through exterior things), the furious heat bursts outward. This pulse which arises from anger becomes strong, large, frequent, and fast; yet it remains moderate between softness and hardness.

¶ **The Increase.** Not only are the passions of the soul made known through the pulse: but also the four stages of acute illness: the qualities of the pores: and the quantities of the periods <note>The recurring cycles of a fever or disease.</note>.

<margin>On the pulses of the stages of illnesses.</margin>

In the beginning of an acute illness, the pulses are large and swift: yet less so than in the "augment" <note>The period when symptoms increase.</note> because of the rawness of the movement.
¶ And because the heat, being oppressed by much matter, is not sufficient to fully resolve it: in the augment of the illness, the heat being now mature and the matter beginning to be more fully dissolved as the heat regains its strength: larger and stronger pulses occur. In the "state" <note>original: *status*; the peak or plateau of the illness</note>, the pulses reach their maximum size and speed because of the sharpness of the heat. In the "decline," as the heat cools down, the pulses diminish: and become slow.
¶ Moreover, you will know that the decline is happening in this way: if a crisis has preceded it: or if it is without any crisis, the matter has been consumed: because it often happens that it is consumed by the febrile heat without any other purging: and then the sick person begins to be master of himself. Then the decline of the disease is nothing <note>meaning, the disease is ending</note>: and such pulses are good. If, however, none of these have preceded: and the patient becomes mentally stunned and weak: and there is a diminution of sensibility: such pulses are the worst: because they do not arise from the lack of disease: but from a lack of strength, as Philaretus says. Rare pulses are always difficult.
¶ **The Increase.** That is, the augment of the illness. In the augment, understand the beginning: and the paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or increase in symptoms.</note>. That is, the exacerbation of the illness: specifically, when it is in acute cases: because they are used sharply. That is, acute. Therefore they have paroxysms: because the pulse indicates the urgency of the paroxysms: because then it will be more distressing and more vehement.
¶ **The State.** That is, the peak of the period.
¶ **And the periodic error.** That is, the intermittent onset compared to the continuous: which resolves partial and periodic movements.
¶ The pulse signifies an intermittent fever: because it maintains its speed and frequency. But at certain times it provokes and at certain times it grows strong: it serves to signify the intermittent state.
¶ **The determination of diseases.** That is, the determinations of acute cases: which are called crises.
¶ **What the fates portend.** There are three fates: that is, the three Fates: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos <note>In Greek mythology, the Moirai who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note>. Clotho is the motion from non-being to being: and it is generation. Lachesis is the production through the continuity of existing. Atropos is corruption. That is, the departure from a substantial state: or the turning from being to non-being. The whole power or faculty of the Fates exults in the pulse.
¶ **The deceptions of urines.** Here is placed the final utility of considering the pulse: because judgment is not certified through it alone: but through it the deceptions of urine are opened, and the truth revealed. For urine, when considered alone, deceives the physician: unless its judgment is certified through the pulse. For if the pulse agrees with the urine: then the judgment of the urine is good. But if it disagrees, the judgment is bad. For the proportion of the signs unites the judgment: that is, reduces it to a unity of judgment.
¶ **From genus to species.** Sometimes urine appears red: and turbulent in color and substance: and signifies a distemper of the body: namely, heat: and signifies illness in general. But because such an appearance can arise from many causes: such as from fever: or an aposteme <note>An abscess or swelling.</note>: or from a ruptured vein: or from a heating of the liver: or from immoderate exercise: with blood flowing more than is right: although they signify illness

<column-break/>

in general: nevertheless they do not signify it in a determinate and definite way. But when the significance of the pulse is applied to the consideration, it specifies the genus: determines it: and declares: what the illness is in its species, whether it be a fever or something else: and if a fever, whether it be continuous or intermittent.

[...sparse]ness. i.e., rare: frequent and moderate. ¶ Constantine <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a physician and translator who brought Arabic medical knowledge to Italy.</note> says in the *Pantegni* <note>original: *Pategni*; Constantine’s major medical encyclopedia.</note> that the seventh type of pulse is based on the rest period: and he cites the authority of Galen, who says: The pulse has two rests, one in dilation <note>systole</note> and one in constriction <note>diastole</note>. One rest occurs when the pulse, at the peak of its expansion, strikes the fingers: he calls this the "outer rest," and we can barely perceive it with our senses. The second rest occurs when the pulse returns toward its center in constriction: and this rest is not sensible, because it is not easily known or perceived by the sense: but the delay of the constriction is known through the dilation. ¶ The fourth consideration concerns the comparison of the apparent movements to the hidden proportion between them. If there are more apparent movements than hidden ones, it is called an **incidental pulse**: that is, falling into the notice of our senses because of its increase. If, however, there are more hidden movements than apparent ones, it is called a **deciduous pulse**: that is, falling away from the notice of our senses. And this is the eighth type: which arises from the fourth consideration: namely, incidental and deciduous. ¶ And note: so that the incidence or falling away of the pulses may be determined, it is not enough to consider eight or nine movements: but one must proceed in observation up to the **hundredth beat**: so that the comparison of the rests to the movements—the hidden to the apparent, the strong to the weak—may be better weighed. For if one strong movement follows, and then another weak one, and again a third strong and a fourth weak: the pulse is not to be judged "deciduous" simply because the first was strong and the second weak. For by that same reasoning, since the second is weak and a third strong one follows, it would be an "incidental" pulse, because the weak tends toward the strong: and thus it could be proven that the same pulse was both incidental and deciduous. To this we say: judge the pulse by that consistency in which it is seen to remain the longest. For you will know it thus: if the pulse is felt in ten beats and fails in the eleventh: then count from that eleventh: if it fails again at the fourth beat after the eleventh: it is called deciduous: and such a pulse, tending toward failure by certain degrees, signifies death <note>original: *mortem*; though the text here uses a shorthand for "death" or "end of movement".</note>. But if it fails at the eighth beat, and then fails at the eleventh beat after that, and later is seen to fail even more slowly until the failure ceases: that is an incidental pulse: and it signifies that nature, previously afflicted, is now rising again and growing strong, having partially overcome the disease. ¶ The fifth consideration focuses on the change or consistency of the aforementioned observations: and from this consideration two extreme types—namely the ninth and tenth—proceed: which are not "principal" types, but are annexed and joined to the principals. For they are not observed as primary qualities, but lie adjacent to others: such as **equal** and **unequal** (the ninth), and **ordered** and **disordered** (the tenth). If a pulse is constantly strong, it is called equal. If some weakness is mixed with the strength, it is called unequal. But more will be said of these later. ¶ Note: that these types of pulses are not always opposites, since three or four types can sometimes exist within one and the same pulse. For sometimes a **large** pulse can also be **soft**, **fast**, **strong**, **thick**, **equal**, **ordered**, and **full**. But some are indeed opposites: like large and small: which are different types because they fall under one genus but are different distinctions of that genus; therefore they cannot exist together. Similarly, there are different types that are not contrary, but due to the contrariety of their causes, they cannot sustain each other: such as "large" and "weak." For an abundance of spirit makes a pulse large, while a defect of spirit and heat makes it weak. Similarly: strong and small: fast and weak: thick and small: slow and fast: rare [and frequent]. And to speak generally, no types can be mixed together in which a contrariety of causes intervenes. Ten types of pulses are described according to different reasons: namely, by movement, by the organ, and by multiple movements. ¶ Note that this general name "pulse" can be predicated of any of the lower types: for

In the second way, the pulse is called the **result**, just like the organ: and according to this mean-

-ing, two types of pulses are distinguished: namely, **soft** and **full**. These, however, pertain to the organ. For an artery is properly said to be soft, empty, or full. Indeed, a movement is said to be soft, hard, full, or empty in comparison: and if they are so called regarding the pulse, the description refers back to the property of the organ. **Hot** and **cold**—which is the third category of pulses—are said to pertain to the "thing being pulsed" <note>The "thing being pulsed" refers to the substance within the artery, such as the blood or vital spirits.</note>: and it can be seen that those three types of pulses are distinguished according as the thing being pulsed is the artery. For it can properly be called hot or cold. But some, considering that it is not hot or cold of itself, but rather from the coldness or the mortification of the vital spirit propelling it, say that a "hot" or "cold" pulse refers to the "thing repelling" <note>The force or spirit that drives the pulse.</note>: and this is the third meaning of pulse: that it be taken for the repelling force. This could be the case, were it not for what Philaretus <note>A 7th-century medical writer whose work *On Pulses* was a standard textbook.</note> says: that the ninth type is observed according to the heat which is returned through the whole body of the artery, in which the quantity of the underlying matter is considered. Through touch, the whole is perceived as an "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to a thing's nature, like its temperature.</note>: by which the author suggests: a hot pulse pertains to the thing being pulsed, not the thing repelling. For if it is said that the pulse is hot because of the hot spirit, it is not because of the substance or quality of the artery. Similarly, a soft, full, or empty pulse should not be said to refer back to the substance of the organ, but to the qualities of the humors flowing into the artery. For an artery is felt as soft, hard, or full because of the underlying humor: for a large amount of watery phlegm makes an artery soft or full, but dryness makes it hard and empty. But Philaretus testifies that full, soft, hard, or empty are observed according to the consistency of the organ, or according to its shape. If, therefore, full, soft, hard, and empty pertain to the consistency and shape of the organ, so do hot and cold. For who would deny that an artery is hot by its own quality or shape? For it is hot or cold by its own quality as a formal cause: and it is hot or cold by reason of the spirit, with the quality of the spirit acting as the efficient or material cause. Whence Constantine says in the *Pantegni*: The heat of the artery comes from the matter contained within it: that is, the spirit and the blood. In the fourth way, "pulse" is called a **collection of many beats**, according to which four types are distinguished: rare, frequent, incidental, deciduous, equal, unequal, ordered, and disordered. ¶ **Skill** [Solertia]: That is, prudence. ¶ **Of the craftsman** [Artificis]: That is, of the physician. ¶ **Tests** [Probat]: Examines and judges. ¶ **Pulse** [Pulsus]: Understand this generally—not for the movement, nor for the repelling force, nor for the thing being pulsed, but now for the collection of many beats: and he shows how he tests them. ¶ **In five ways**: That is, by five distinct considerations. ¶ **From which**: That is, from these considerations. ¶ **He elicits**: That is, he proceeds. ¶ **The number**: That is, the ten types of pulses: which stand in a double proportion to the five considerations. <header>Of [Pulses]</header>

Philaretus <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century Byzantine physician often called Philaretus in Latin texts.</note> puts the ninth <note>original: "nenuȝ," likely a scribal error for "nonum"</note> pulse as the hot one; he is a disturber of names and meanings. And Constantine <note>Constantine the African</note> calls it the sixth. ¶ **From these.** That is, attribute it to the last ones. ¶ **From the first.** Those elicited from the first consideration. ¶ **It arises.** That is, it is completed. ¶ **A series of six.** That is, six types. ¶ **Thick.** Here he assigns the origin of the seventh type: which is frequent and rare. ¶ **Delay.** That is, according to the delay and space that exists between two dilations, it is observed as "thick" or "frequent." This is what Constantine says arises from the time of the touch <note>original: "getis," likely an abbreviation for "tangentis"</note>; Philaretus says it arises from the quantity of the touch. This is also the sixth type according to Philaretus, but the seventh according to Constantine. Whence these types of pulses arise, by what causes they are proven, and what they signify, we shall say in the following sections with the author himself. ¶ **Who with a dactylic foot.** He sets the origin of the eighth: which is the **incidental** and **deciduous** pulse; Philaretus calls it the ninth, while Constantine assigns it the eighth. This type is observed according to the comparison and proportion of delays to delays, or apparent movements to hidden ones, or strong to weak. The **apparent delays** are those of the pulse itself. The **hidden delays** are those of the touch existing between two pulses. The quantity of the incidental and deciduous pulse is determined by the proportion of time to time: if the delay of the preceding pulse is less than the subsequent pulse, it is called **deciduous** <note>falling away</note>. If the delay of the following is greater than the preceding, it is called **incidental** <note>falling upon</note>; which is to be understood according to the logic assigned. ¶ The deciduous pulse is compared by the author to a **dactylic foot** <note>A poetic meter consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones</note>; because just as a dactyl, beginning from a long and fit whole syllable, declines into shorts, so the deciduous pulse moves from apparent delays toward hidden ones. ¶ **Everywhere.** That is, it is pressed up and down. ¶ **From on high.** That is, from entirely apparent delays. ¶ **And with a dactylic foot.** That is, in a dactylic rhythm. ¶ **And that which is failing.** This is the assignment of the incidental pulse. ¶ **It arises.** ¶ **Failing before.** ¶ **And recovers strength.** <note>original: "Airet qȝ resumit," likely "viresque resumit"</note> That is, moving from hidden differences into apparent ones, until it fails in nothing; it is the judgment of nature rising again and strength being recovered. ¶ **It is noted.** That is, it is observed regarding its origin. ¶ **From the comparative theses.** That is, the proportion of delays, which are the delays of dilations and "theses" <note>the lowering or resting phase of the pulse</note>. For those delays are observed and weighed according to **systole** and **diastole**. ¶ **As if the chief ones.** Having assigned eight types, which are the first and principal ones, he assigns the origin of the two extremes: namely, the ninth and tenth, which are accidental and joined to the principals. ¶ **Joined.** The ninth is **equal** and **unequal**; the tenth is **ordered** and **disordered**. Philaretus puts "equal" as the seventh and "ordered" as the eighth. ¶ **Discordant or consonant.** <note>original: "Dilcoz," likely "discors"</note> That is, equal or unequal. ¶ **One order.** Regarding the ordered pulse. ¶ **Or adverse.** That is, disordered. Truly, the ordered or disordered state is considered according to the logic of numbers and calculations. For two weak pulses, or three, or four, or one disordered pulse, do not just interfere with two large and strong ones, but in many other differing ways, according to the diversity of numbers, various pulses of several other types are interposed. And therefore we said that the "ordered" and "disordered" must be observed according to numerical logic. What an equal pulse is, what unequal, what ordered, and what disordered—and whether an ordered pulse is equal or not, and whether every disordered pulse is unequal, and how many species of unequal-disordered pulses there are—will appear below, where the definitions and meanings of each type will be set down.

### On the Large, Small, and Moderate Pulse.

Increased three-fold dimension makes a **large** pulse.
**Small** if the dimension is small; **moderate** if moderately increased.
In length, width, and height, the large pulse rises.
The small falls into the hidden, the narrow, and the receding.
That which follows the middle is rightly held to be **moderate**.

¶ Having assigned the types of pulses based on their origins, so that a clearer doctrine of the types of pulses may be established, he puts this definition for each type. And first he defines the **large pulse**. A large pulse is one that is observed according to the quality of three dimensions: **length**, **width**, and **depth**; it is called "large" because it transcends the normal measure. For a pulse to be large, it must be long, wide, and deep. The **small pulse** is understood by the opposite: that which is not long, wide, nor deep. The text is clear. ¶ **Small if small.** That is, a diminished triple dimension makes a small pulse; it suffers a loss of quantity in length through shortness, in width through narrowness, and in depth through "residence"—that is, according to its uncertain revolution. ¶ **Middle.** That is, a moderate pulse is created by a triple dimension that is **moderately increased**. That is, it maintains a middle ground, not exceeding in any dimension.

### On Long and Short, Wide and Narrow, High and Deep Pulses.

A **long** pulse will occupy the tips of four fingers.
The **short** stops short; and the **moderate** is equal to all.
The **wide** pulse holds the fingers in width; the **high** stands out.
The **slender** meets the touch; the **narrow**; and the **deep** pulse resides below.

¶ He had defined the large pulse by the excess of the triple dimension—namely, length, width, and depth. Therefore, so that it might appear more clearly what "large" is, he defines what it is to be long, wide, and deep. Once these are known, the nature of the "large" pulse, which is composed of them, is perfectly understood. For once the parts are investigated, the nature of the whole is declared. A **long pulse** is that which... ¶ **Will be.** That is, it exceeds or fills... ¶ **The ventricles.** That is, the tips and summits... ¶ **Of four fingers.** Stretched out over the length of the artery. For since it is felt in the tips <note>original: "ventriculis," referring to the fleshy pads of the fingertips</note> of four fingers, it could even be felt in five or six if they were placed there. ¶ Having set the definition of "long," he sets the definition of "short" <note>original: "curti"</note> as its opposite. ¶ **Stops short.** That is, it is fallen short of by the tips of the four fingers. For it is felt in the first, second, and third, but not the fourth. ¶ **Mutilated.** That is, it is short, when it is shortened in its length. ¶ **Middle.** That is, let it be moderate between the extremes. **To all.** That is, to the fingers. ¶ **Equal.** Insofar as it does not exceed, nor is it exceeded by, the tips. He defines the **wide** pulse, which together with the "long" quickly runs toward making a "large" pulse. ¶ **Wide holds the fingers.** When it occupies the tips of the fingers in its width. ¶ **High.** A pulse which is considered by its height; when, namely, the artery raises itself much, receding from the center of the arm by a vehement impulse of the spirit. ¶ **Stands out.** That is, it is elevated, prominent, and forceful. ¶ **Meets.** That is, it does not move in width; it does not occupy the full width of the fingers, but is fallen short of, meeting the touch like a slender cord. ¶ **Deep.** That is, hidden, which is the opposite of high. ¶ **Resides.** That is, it is near the center, with a perceived moderateness between the extremes—namely, it does not exceed in width, nor is it exceeded. ¶ And note that these differences can be described in many ways, such as "long with narrow" or "long with moderate." ¶ Likewise, "wide" and "narrow" are compared. ¶ Likewise, "wide" with "apparent" and with "hidden," or the "middle" between the two. But no short, narrow, or hidden pulse is considered "large."

### On the Strong and Weak Pulse.

Frequency joined with **large** constitutes the **strong** pulse.
The opposite species arises from opposite causes.

¶ He has dealt with the first genus of pulses, which includes large, small, and moderate according to the diversity of their compositions. Consequently, he deals with the second: namely, the **strong**, **weak**, and **moderate**, which relates principally to the quantity of the motion of the artery. Although this is the third genus according to Philaretus and Constantine, it is ordered thus by us because the constraint of poetic meter <note>The source text is a commentary on a verse poem</note> required such an order. He defines the **strong** genus as coming from two things: the "large" and the "frequent" (that is, the fast). For Philaretus says:

<header>Of Pulses</header>

Philaretus <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> says: taking frequency with magnitude makes a pulse strong: but by "frequency," velocity <note>speed of the individual beat</note> is understood. For if he meant frequency <note>repetition/rate</note>, since that arises from a weakness of the "virtue" <note>the body's innate vital power</note> and a strength of heat seeking the magnitude of refrigeration—a weak virtue which is not sufficient to draw in enough air at once to cool the body must supply the defect in quantity by the repetition and numerousness of the action—therefore a strong pulse could not tolerate frequency, because their causes are opposites. Thus, a strong pulse is composed of the **large** and the **fast**: large, because it elevates the artery greatly and forces it to move away from the center, spreading out in length along the side until it touches the fingers; and fast, because once the strike has begun, it completes its motion quickly. This is what is touched upon in the text.
¶ **The third species.** That is, the weak pulse. ¶ **It arises.** That is, it proceeds. ¶ **From opposite causes.** That is, from weak heat, feeble virtue, and a debility of the spirits.

### On the fast and slow pulse: and on the hard and soft pulse.

> Slowness produces a slow pulse, haste produces a quick one.
> If the organs <note>the arteries</note> strike the fingers with harsh stiffness,
> they constitute a hard pulse; if with weariness, a relaxed one.

¶ Here he provides knowledge of the second genus: that is, the fast, the slow, and the medium; which is assigned by us in the third place. This genus pertains to the quantity of the artery's motion and is observed by the time or the speed of the motion. Thus, a **fast pulse**, according to Constantine <note>Constantine the African</note>, is one which traverses its space in a small amount of time; namely, when the strike, once begun, is quickly completed. And a **slow pulse** is one which traverses a small space in a long time; namely, when the motion, once begun, is finished over a long duration. ¶ The **medium pulse** is the middle between these extremes, as in its own constriction. ¶ **If they strike.** Having declared the three genera of pulses that arise from the first consideration with their proper definitions, he now sets forth the knowledge and definitions of the others. First, he deals with those that arise from the second consideration, which pertain to the consistency of the organ <note>the artery wall</note>: these are the **hard**, the **soft**, and the **medium**; the **full**, the **empty**, and the **medium**; and the **hot**, the **cold**, and the **medium**. Thus, a **hard pulse** is one where, when touched by the fingers, the artery feels hard and rigid, almost as if stretched cords were being felt. ¶ A **soft pulse** is when the artery is felt to be soft. And a hard pulse might seem to be "strong," but it is not so. For a strong pulse, according to Constantine, dilates the vessels so that they seem almost emptied. A hard pulse is like a rough one, because the hardness of the limb does not obey the virtue <note>the vital power</note> so that it can be dilated. ¶ **If the organs.** That is, the arteries. ¶ **Strike.** Namely, the fingers and the pads of the fingers. ¶ **Hard with harshness.** That is, with the hardness and rigidity of distension. ¶ **If with weariness.** That is, it is felt with a certain kind of lassitude and softness. For so Constantine glosses it: so that the fingers seem to be penetrated by them.

### On the full and empty pulse.

> If it yields, it is empty; if it remains swollen, it is full.
> Arterial heat constitutes a hot pulse.
> A cold one occurs from the coldness of the underlying limb.

¶ He identifies by description what the fifth genus is: namely, the **full** and the **empty**. A **full pulse** is one which seems swollen with some redundant humor. An **empty pulse** is one that appears as if inflated, but immediately when touched, it is felt by the fingers to be empty. This fifth genus pertains to the shape and condition of the organ in its emptiness and fullness. ¶ **It constitutes a pulse.** He assigns the knowledge of the sixth genus: which is the **hot**, the **cold**, and the **medium**; which, along with the preceding conditions, pertains to the consistency of the artery. For the artery is of such a consistency that it feels hot or cold; although the heat of the artery is drawn from the glowing spirit and the blood contained within, nevertheless the quality found there is the disposition of the artery itself. ¶ **Arterial heat.** That is, a hot pulse, when the tips of the fingers feel the artery to be hot. The **cold pulse** is perceived in the opposite way.

<column-break/>

### On the middle pulses.

> Since other species are linked by some intermediate point,
> a strong pulse is joined to a powerful one with no distinction.
> Let him who unravels the hidden riddles of things solve the cause
> of this connection between the equal and the unequal.

<margin>Whether all species of pulses have a middle ground or not.</margin>
¶ Since in assigning the aforementioned genera the author assigned the "middle" of some extremes, yet placed no middle between other extremes, he shows in this chapter that this must be declared, investigated, and left to the examination and discussion of physicians <note>original: "phycǫ," abbreviation for physicorum</note>, whose task it is to solve enigmatic reasons and to untie and straighten out such ambiguities. What has been omitted by the author, we—who are his interpreters and his substitutes—shall supply the defect. ¶ I say, therefore, that all those extremes which are joined to a "distemper" <note>an imbalance of the four humors</note>, such as large and small, short and long, wide and narrow, open and hidden, fast and slow, frequent and rare, have a point of convergence. For from one difference to another, a transition is made through a **temperate middle ground**. A "large" pulse exceeding the medium in its three dimensions shows a distemper; a "small" pulse diminished beyond measure shows a distemper because of a defect of heat and feebleness of spirit. Behold, these pulses indicate distempered qualities: one an excess, the other a defect. Between excess and defect there is a middle, which is described by the negation of the extremes: it is neither in excess nor in defect. That is the **temperate pulse**, and thus it is the middle between the large and the small. Similarly between the short and the long, and between any other extremes applied to health; if a distemper is added, the "medium" will be the healthy state. If truth be told, the stronger a thing is, the healthier it is. And in strength there is no "excess," just as in virtue or in the goodness of the mind there is no "excess of mind" <note>meaning you cannot have too much of a good quality like health or virtue</note>. And it follows from this that one extreme exceeds that middle in temperance and health. But every "medium" passes between two extremes. If it is a true middle, it is more temperate and healthy than either extreme. ¶ Also, if there is a middle between the strong and the weak, that type would be neither strong nor weak, but outside the temperate range. ¶ Also, a pulse is never **strong** except by the tenacity of virtue; and it passes into the **weak** with no single middle point from the most strong, or it passes into the weak through many "less strong" mediums until the final lessening of strength. And that which is "less strong" is the mediator through which the "more strong" passes into the weak. A "strong" type is not a middle between strong and weak, because then it would be neither strong nor weak; for "strong" is a genus according to its own breadth. Just as there is no middle between virtue and vice, so there is no middle between the strong and the weak. ¶ Likewise, the **equal** and the **unequal** have no middle. For if one existed, it would be neither equal nor unequal; but whatever is equal to one is unequal to another. For the transition from equal to unequal happens with no intermediate, and vice versa. ¶ Likewise, to be "equal" is to be healthy and temperate according to nature (unless it be in a bad state, like equality in a sickly pulse). However, everything "unequal" is distempered according to nature, resulting from disease. Similarly, the **ordered** and the **disordered** have no middle. ¶ Likewise, the **incidental** and the **deciduous** <note>pulses that fall or strike unexpectedly</note> have no middle ground: because the incidental arises from the temperance and strengthening of virtue, while the deciduous arises from the opposite. Between the temperate and the intemperate, between strengthening and defect, there is no middle ground; otherwise, it would not be temperate.

->Gilles on pulses.<-

### On the frequent and rare pulse.

->If with a sudden snatch, in motion with a small distinction,<-
->The rising <note>original: "arsis," the dilation of the artery</note> multiplies: a numerous series constitutes<-
->A frequent pulse. The contrary species constitutes a rare one.<-

¶ Up to this point he has set forth the doctrine of six genera of pulses: of which three pertain to the property of motion—namely, one to quantity (large, small, and medium); two to quality (fast, slow, and moderate; strong, weak, and moderate). Another three pertain to the resistance of the organ or its shape: hard, soft, and moderate; full, empty, and moderate; hot, cold, and moderate. Now he defines the seventh genus from the time of rest, and he considers the interval between two diastoles <note>The diastole is the expansion of the artery as it fills with blood.</note>: which is the **frequent** and the **rare**. ¶ **If a sudden numerous series.** That is, a frequent and numerous repetition of dilations. ¶ **Multiplies.** It repeats by continually replicating. ¶ **Arsis.** That is, the diastole. ¶ **With a small distinction.** That is, a modest delay of rest interspersed between one diastole and another. ¶ **By a sudden snatch.** That is, by motion repeated rapidly. ¶ **Contrary species.** That is, the contrary disposition makes a rare pulse.

### On the incident and decadent pulse.

->The decadent, from strong and manifest rhythms,<-
->Degenerating from the sense, tends with a silent foot to the depths.<-
->It inclines into the hidden, struggling to escape the sense.<-
->The incident rises: breathing again, it tends toward the height.<-
->It deserts the hidden: it gains for itself the manifest.<-

¶ He provides knowledge of the eighth genus: namely, the **incident** and the **decadent**, which considers the comparison of delays to delays, hidden ones to open ones, and strong ones to weak ones. An **open delay** is when the pulse meets the sense <note>That is, the touch of the physician's fingers.</note>: i.e., when the artery dilates so that its motion is openly felt. A **hidden one** is when the dilation is so hidden and near to the center that it either escapes the sense or changes it very little. According therefore to the comparison of delays to delays, it notes "incidences" or "decadences," which we have expressly taught above in the tenth distinction of genera, which need not be repeated. ¶ If one objects regarding the "mouse-tail" pulse <note>original: "cauda foicina finitina," likely a corruption of "cauda murina" or "myurus," a pulse that gradually fades away like the tapering tail of a mouse.</note> that it is a decadent pulse: for the decadent pulse is perceived more broadly. For a decadent pulse can be found where there is no "mouse-tail" pulse: for instance, if after ten strong strikes one weak one occurs; then after eight strong ones one weak one; then after seven, then four, then two, until finally it fails entirely. In truth, a certain decadent pulse resembles the "mouse-tail" pulse. But the decadent pulse treated here has more delays and intersperses more weak ones gradually, until none run openly; whereas the "mouse-tail" rises as if from hidden depths into strong actions—but from the hidden it continually tends toward higher things. ¶ **By rhythms.** That is, by open motions. ¶ **Degenerating from the sense.** That is, gradu-

<column-break/>

-ally declining. ¶ **Incident.** That is, an "incident" pulse falling into the knowledge of the sense through its own increase. ¶ **It rises breathing again.** That is, to rise up or resurge into nature; and it signifies resuming breaths and strengths.

### On the equal pulse.

->Firm and fleeing the commerce of the opposite motion,<-
->It remains equal, the law of its tenor being preserved.<-

¶ After having treated the eight principal genera, he deals with the ninth and tenth, which are annexed and joined to the principals: namely, the **equal** and **unequal**, the **ordered** and **disordered**. The **equal** is that whose strike is equal and of uniform tenor in the tips of the fingers: such as if it is large, fast, strong, frequent, soft, full, and also moderate; receiving no diversity in quality, quantity, time of motion, or number of motion. ¶ **Equal is divided.** For one is "absolutely equal," which preserves quality in all the said differences, of which we have already spoken. Another is "equal in a certain respect" (*secundum quid*): such as being equal in magnitude, but sometimes felt as fast and sometimes slow. ¶ Likewise, one which is equal in smallness or weakness; such a pulse is equal in this respect, but is not absolutely equal. A certain **unequal** pulse receives the opposite difference: one is absolutely unequal, such as is unequal in all genera; another is unequal in one genus and not another; and according to that, it is called equal. ¶ **Fleeing.** That is, receiving no association with the opposite difference. And such a one is absolutely equal if it is preserved in good differences; but it can be equal in bad "pauses" <note>original: "pausionibus," referring to the state of the pulse during rest.</note> as in smallness and weakness. Such a pulse is not simply or absolutely equal, but "equal in this" or "equal in evil"; and he added this to exclude such qualities. ¶ **Firm.** For that which remains in uniform smallness is not firm by the firmness of nature, but rather from weakness. Therefore, whatever is firm from the firmness of nature and proceeding from virtue, and preserving a uniform tenor in all genera, is simply equal.

### On the unequal pulse.

->Degenerate, unstable, nor running in the same path,<-
->The unequal changes, moderated by uncertain reins.<-

¶ He describes the unequal. ¶ **Degenerate.** That is, degenerating from equality through its governance. ¶ **Unstable.** Because it does not preserve the state of one tenor. ¶ **Nor running in the same path.** Because it passes through the diverse ways of opposite genera. ¶ **It changes.** Namely, now slowing, now hurrying; it proceeds, wavering from large to small, from strong to weak. ¶ **Moderated.** That is, agitated. ¶ **By uncertain reins.** ¶ This is a metaphor taken from someone who does not know well how to rule and bridle a horse.

### On the ordered and disordered and deprived pulse.

->By distinct steps it is changed in right order.<-
->It passes into the opposite, which takes its name from order.<-
->Which is judged by the deprivation of the laws of order.<-
->It precedes in order; it is headlong and without law.<-

¶ He provides knowledge of the tenth genus: which is the **ordered** and **disordered**. ¶ And note that every equal pulse is ordered: for where there is equality, there is order; but the reverse is not always true. For of ordered things, one is equal and another unequal; yet every unequal pulse is not necessarily disordered. For of unequal pulses, one is ordered and another disordered. The disordered is unequal; the ordered unequal pulse is one which receives the opposite difference of a diverse opposite genus, yet it is ordered and, as it were, step-like, and according to the proportion of a uniform degree: when, for instance, the relationship of the following <margin>form</margin> strikes in its inequality and form and relationship to the preceding...

...rhythm: if there are eight pulses continuously strong and the ninth is weak, and again eight strong and the ninth weak, and if the condition of the pulses proceeds in this way for a long time, it can still vary in many other ways, provided the patterns of mutation appear consistent to themselves. This may also be called an **ordered unequal pulse**, which is due to a specific cause—namely, the "finishing" near-tail <note>original: "cauda scilicet vicina finitativa"</note> and the "rebounding" tail <note>original: "cauda retonativa"</note>. For in the finishing near-tail, the first percussion is large and strong, the second smaller, the third even smaller, and thus by a gradual path and proportionately it tends little by little toward failure, until it is no longer felt. Similarly, the "rebounding tail" can be considered an orderly progression from failure back toward magnitude. We place these types under the "equally ordered" pulse because they occur according to a consideration of order and habit; however, they rarely remain in that state, but more frequently become an unequal, disordered tumult through an indiscriminate confusion and lack of order.

The **disordered pulse** is one that transitions to the opposite difference in an extraordinary way, with no order of habit preserved, nor any discernible pattern in the confusion. **Inequality** and **disorder** are found in all the aforementioned types: as if there are two large pulses and one small, then another medium; or two small, one medium, then another small; or one medium and one large succeeded by a small. ¶ **Distinct according to orders and proportions of degrees.** ¶ **Which takes the name.** That is, "ordered." ¶ **Which by deprivation.** That is, it is named from "order" by its absence <note>The author is explaining that "disordered" is defined by the lack of order</note>. ¶ **The wandering, all-encompassing.** That is, confused and outside of order.

### On the species of disordered and unequal pulses.

> The final genus spreads into a number of species,
> Which borrow for themselves foreign names from things,
> Which comparative reason unites to itself in a pact:
> The spasmodic, the consumptive, the ant-like, and the worm-like,
> The branching, the floating, the hammer-like, and the goat-leap,
> The saw-like, the mouse-tail—whether straight or twisted.

¶ He divides the "unequal disordered" pulse into its species and soon enumerates them; these will be discussed in the following sections when their specific treatment begins. He names these species after animals, instruments, or other things with which they share a resemblance. For instance, he says "goat-leap" <note>original: "capricans"</note> from the goat, and "ant-like" <note>original: "formicans"</note> from the ant, and so with the others. The reasons for these names will be given below. ¶ **The final genus.** That is, the unequal disordered pulse. ¶ **Spreads.** That is, it distributes them in a scattered and varied way. ¶ **In a number of species.** That is, into many types which are enclosed under a certain number. ¶ **Which.** Namely, the species. ¶ **Borrow.** That is, they borrow names for themselves due to a poverty and lack of specific vocabulary. For the Latin language is poor in its choice of words <note>This is a common complaint among medieval scholars translating Greek medical concepts into Latin</note>. ¶ **Foreign.** Names of animals, instruments, or other things—not all things, but those similar and of one kind. ¶ **Which.** That is, the things. ¶ **Unites.** That is, assimilates and conforms to itself. ¶ **Reason.** That is, proportion. ¶ **Comparative pact.** That is, a comparison of similarity.

### On the causes.

> Form, thickness, sex, age, and pregnancy,
> Place and time, labor, food, fullness, and drink,
> The cause and type of disease, intercourse, and mental disturbance,
> And the position of the body—all vary the characteristics of the pulse.

<margin>Form.</margin> ¶ **Form.** Having distinguished the genera of pulses and their properties, he consequently deals here briefly with the causes of the pulse's mutations by enumerating them. The pulses are changed in three ways: by things natural, things non-natural <note>In medieval medicine, the "six non-naturals" were external factors like air, diet, and exercise that affected health</note>, and things against nature. Under "natural things," we include both those that are persistent and governing—such as complexions <note>The balance of the four humors</note>—and those that are inseparable and co-existent, such as the figure of the body, the distinction between male and female, age, and similar things. ¶ **Form.** That is, the habit of the body, which is divided into thinness,

<column-break/>

thickness, and the middle state. ¶ **Varies the pulse.** In lean people, the pulses are larger and stronger than in the fat and those who are overly full. **Thickness**, from an excessive congestion of flesh, causes a smaller and weaker pulse because the heat and the spirits <note>The "vital spirits" were thought to carry life through the arteries</note> in them become sluggish and lazy from the excess of flesh. But the pulse of thick people is unequal because of the weakness of the "virtue" <note>The body's innate power</note>. In lean people, the pulses are "fit" because the artery is exposed, or stripped and almost naked. In the fat, the pulse is hidden because the artery is deep and buried in the flesh, and thus it is hindered. In the slender, the pulse lies greatly under the touch—that is, it is easily felt by the judgment of touch, which is due to the exposure of the organ <note>the artery</note>. Some, however, explain this "lying under the touch" poorly, saying the pulse lies under the touch when it is weak; this interpretation is contrary to Constantine <note>Constantine the African, an 11th-century translator of Arabic medicine</note>. Moreover, one must investigate whether the leanness is natural or if it has proceeded from a previous thickness.

<margin>Thick.</margin> ¶ **Thick.** That is, the complexion determined from birth varies the pulse. For a hot complexion makes the pulse strong and fast for the sake of drawing in much air for cooling; but a cold one makes it small and slow because there is little need for cooling. A moist complexion makes the pulse soft, while a dry one makes it hard. And that the pulse is made fast by the complexion is proven by Philaretus <note>A 7th-century medical writer</note>, who says: for every hot thing is moved quickly, and every cold thing is moved slowly—which can be understood regarding animals alone. For some things are naturally hot, like pepper or orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note>, which are not mobile. In a hot heart, indeed, the hot blood boiling from the heat is quickly resolved into vapor; hence the motion of the heart and arteries is completed quickly, making them faster.

<margin>Sex.</margin> ¶ **Sex.** That is, the difference between male and female changes the pulse, as Constantine also says in the *Pantegni* <note>The *Pantegni* was a foundational medical encyclopedia</note>. The pulse is larger and stronger in the male than in the female, and for a better reason: for the male is of a hotter nature, stronger, and more prone to exercise. And the female's pulse is smaller, weaker, and more frequent. Smallness and weakness occur because women are weaker in virtue than men and possess less heat and exercise. In comparison to the male, the pulse is more frequent in the female due to the weakness of the virtue; for nature often impels by repeating in the female what it performs with one large pulse in the male. This is so that the air, through repeated turns, is drawn in for cooling in the same amount that one large pulse would draw in for the male. For the greater the heat, if the virtue is strong, the greater the speed necessary for nature, so that a large quantity of air may be drawn in a short time for cooling. But when the power of the work fails, it must be drawn in more densely; hence it happens that it is denser in women than in men. One might try to prove from the surface of the text in the *Pantegni* that the female pulse is faster, but this is not true. For speed arises from the strength of the virtue and the vehemence of heat; but there <note>in that text</note> we understand "frequency" by "speed," as when Philaretus says that frequency, by taking on magnitude, makes the pulse valid. ¶ **Note** that if other particulars are at odds with the sex—such as a cold complexion, thickness, rest, or old age—the pulse will be weaker. If the particulars align, the contrary will be larger and stronger. Understand the same regarding the male. Thus it is necessary for the physician, when he approaches the sick, to make a comparison of all parts and discern all accidents, so that he is not deceived in judging the pulses.

<margin>Age.</margin> ¶ **Age.** This changes the pulse because children have a faster pulse for the sake of cooling the heat, of which they have much. However, they have a frequency of temperate magnitude and strength, because the virtue—not yet complete in complexion and strength, nor firm enough to extract much air at once—is not sufficient to cool the natural heat. Young men <note>adults in their prime</note> indeed have a strong and large pulse, temperate in speed, which arises from their heat and their own virtue. Old men have a small, weak, and rare pulse because of their cold nature in relation to their age; hence it is not necessary for much air to be drawn in for cooling. Other ages related to these have pulses neighboring the qualities or heats of those ages to which they seem most akin. For while in children the pulse is fast and temperate in its magnitude and smallness, the pulse in the decrepit is smallest...

<meta>This page continues the examination of how external and internal factors—such as age, life stages, and environmental conditions—influence the quality and rhythm of the pulse. ...and most very slow: most rare and most deficient. In youths of perfect youth, the pulse is greatest and strongest: temperate in both its speed and slowness. It should be observed that the pulses of children increase greatly in speed, while they decrease in slowness. And the pulse grows larger until it reaches its perfect magnitude, where the pulse is at its greatest and strongest: temperate in speed and slowness, until middle age is reached. When old age gradually comes on, the opposites of the aforementioned qualities follow, until extreme old age is reached, in which the pulse becomes small, rare, and slow.

<margin>Pregnancy</margin>
¶ **Pregnancy.** That is, the impregnation of a woman changes the pulse. But a distinction must be made: for the pregnancy is either in its middle, its beginning, or its completion. In the beginning, the pregnant woman has a strong, large, and fast pulse, because the heat of the fetus increases the mother's natural heat. For the arteries of the <term>secundine</term> <note>The placenta or afterbirth.</note> and the arteries of the fetus are joined, and both sets of arteries in the woman are intertwined. This is proven by the newness of the retention of the menses; by the increased heat, the pulses become large and fast. They become strong because the <term>virtue</term> <note>The "vital virtue" or innate power governing the heart and pulse.</note> does not yet suffer any oppression due to the small size of the fetus, but persists in its power. Hence, the pulses are large and strong until the fourth month, or through the middle of the fourth. But from the fourth month onward, more or less, the pulses become variable, frequent, small, and weak, because the virtue is burdened by the increased size of the fetus, and the <term>operative virtue</term> fails toward the end for two reasons: because of a deficiency of blood and <term>spirits</term> <note>The "vital spirits" or pneuma believed to carry life through the arteries.</note>, since the blood goes toward the nourishment of the fetus; and the more that is spent on the nourishment of the fetus, the more the limbs of the pregnant woman are weakened by the lack of nourishment and its withdrawal. And it fails because of the expansion of the womb, which occupies more space, whereby the heart is compressed; and thus the operative virtue, which produces the pulse, is burdened. They become frequent, as Philaretus <note>A significant 7th-century Byzantine medical writer frequently cited in the Middle Ages.</note> says, because of the necessity of drawing in air for both the mother and the fetus. Hence there arises a threefold necessity for cooling: from the fetus, from the mother, and from the retained blood. And since the virtue is deficient, it must draw in air many times, since it cannot draw in enough at once to satisfy the need for cooling. Therefore, the pulses become frequent.

<margin>Sleep</margin>
¶ **Sleep** changes the pulse, but in different ways. For in the beginning of sleep, as the natural heat begins to be called inward and is not yet performing digestion, the pulse is small, weak, and slow due to the preceding dryness of being awake. But once the heat is strengthened within and the food is already digested and divided among the limbs, with the blood multiplied, the marrow increased, and the spirits repaired, the pulses at the end of sleep and around the middle become large and strong: moderate in speed and slowness due to the digestion of food. If sleep is prolonged so that the expulsion of the food's waste is delayed, the pulse will be small, weak, rare, and slow. Hence, after the food is digested, the sleeper should be roused from sleep to expel the waste: <note>original: "egestiōes: vrinā: sputa"</note> excrement, urine, and phlegm through their proper <term>emunctories</term> <note>Organs or channels that carry off waste.</note>. If someone is awakened from sleep suddenly, such as by a voice or any passion, or if they are startled by the wind, the nature of the pulse is disturbed; sometimes it is large and strong, sometimes fast and frequent, but not inordinately trembling. When the person who was startled rests, the pulse returns to its powerful state. ¶ Some have been misled by the superficial words of Philaretus, who says that in sleep pulses are only small, weak, and slow, not distinguishing the phases of sleep. For Philaretus says that in sleep the pulses become smaller, lighter, and weaker as the natural heat penetrates to the depths. They understand this to mean that the natural heat penetrating the depths of the stomach and liver becomes different. And thus, leaving behind the <term>spiritual members</term> <note>The heart and lungs.</note>, which are not deep because they are positioned above the diaphragm, the pulses are small in sleep. But in these people, the <term>nutritive members</term> <note>The digestive organs.</note> grow warm, and the spiritual members grow cold. Now, the condition of the spiritual members determines the pulse, not the nutritive ones. ¶ But it is certain that during sleep the spiritual members grow warm. For we see some sleepers who are not able to breathe enough air through the nostrils alone unless they also keep the mouth open, and they also make more forceful exhalations, which does not happen except in a great magnitude of heat drawing in a larger quantity of air for the greater need for cooling. It is therefore better to understand this according to the doctrine of the ancients, so that a distinction is made within sleep itself.

<margin>Location</margin>
¶ **Location.** That is, the region changes the pulse. Hence those living in a hot

<column-break/>

region, such as in Ethiopia, have a large and fast pulse, just like in summer. Those living in a cold region, such as in England <note>original: "Angella"</note>, have a pulse similar to winter: that is, rare and slow. Those living in temperate places, such as those staying on a direct line <note>likely referring to the equator or a specific temperate latitude</note>, have a temperate, moderate pulse, similar to a balanced temperament. Regions placed between these should be considered to have pulses according to which they are closer to. And what is said of the region should be understood similarly of the air. For a region is only changed by the grace of the air, and similarly for the seasons.

¶ **And time.** For Spring and Autumn, which are temperate in respect to the seasons, produce temperate and moderate pulses. The other two, namely Winter and Summer, produce exceeding pulses: either according to smallness or according to magnitude, fast and small. In Spring, because of the tempering of heat, the blood multiplies, and spirits are generated and multiplied more abundantly. Hence the pulses are large and strong: moderate in speed and slowness because of the retention of spirits; because the virtue is bolstered by the preceding winter, they become strong. In Autumn, though the temperament may be similar, this does not seem possible to happen, since in Autumn the bodies are as if thinned out through the whole summer, and their virtues are fatigued, dissolved by the heat. Hence, with the opening of the pores, the heat and spirits have already exhaled; large and strong pulses cannot be. However, we say that in Autumn the heat and spirits still flourish around the heart, and they are retained by the closing of the pores from the cold of Autumn. Hence, from the flourishing heat and the retention of spirits around the heart, the pulses become large and strong. In Summer, they are fast and hurrying because of the rapid resolution of blood into smoke and spirit; they are fast because of the great necessity of drawing in air for cooling; they are frequent. In Winter, they become rare and slow for the opposite reasons; namely, because of the constriction of the heart and because of the cooling of the air. From constriction, the pulses become small, slow, and rare. ¶ Note, however, that while the nutritive organs are warmer in winter (because "stomachs are warmer in winter and spring," etc.), the spiritual organs are colder because the air and the cold spirit are inspired freely to the heart and lungs. This does not penetrate to the nutritive organs because the intervening diaphragm only arranges the spiritual organs, and the pulse must be arranged according to the condition of the spiritual organs. Around the nutritive organs, heat is retained because of the constriction of the pores. Hence, with the pores constricted, the smoky and vaporous wastes cannot exhale and are retained in the body, and therefore those parts are warmer. In summer, for opposite causes, the conditions of the spiritual organs, nutritive organs, and the lungs become opposite.

<margin>Labor</margin>
¶ **Labor.** That is, the exercise of the body changes the pulse. From temperate exercise—because it dissolves the harmful wastes of the body, the limbs are strengthened, and natural heat is increased—the pulses become large, fast, strong in virtue, and moderate in frequency. But in exercise that is intemperate, when pain and fatigue already invade the limbs, the pulses become small and weak, or small and rare, because the virtue is now failing and the natural heat is now diminished; from much exercise, the humors are dried out. Hence, the pulses are rendered hard. ¶ Note that scattered exercises in their beginning produce large and strong pulses, but in their progress and end they produce small, weak, slow, rare, and hard ones. (¶ Location, time, and exercise, and others mentioned in this verse, are to be referred to as "non-natural things" <note>In Galenic medicine, the "six non-naturals" were external factors like diet, exercise, and environment that affected health.</note>).

<margin>Food</margin>
¶ **Food.** That is, food changes the pulse in quality and quantity. In quantity: because if it is much, it makes the pulse inordinately disturbed at first because of the burdening of the virtue oppressed by digestion; but with the heat excited, it becomes larger and stronger as the food begins to be processed through the limbs. And with the limbs strengthened by nourishment, because the food is digested well, the virtue is strengthened, the heat is excited, the pulse is magnified and made fast. With a small amount of food that is quickly digested and dispersed to the limbs, it makes the pulse less strong, smaller, and moderate between softness and hardness. By quality, food varies the pulse: if it is hot, it makes the pulse fast and frequent; if cold, the opposite; if moist, soft; if dry, hard. And you can combine the qualities and the differences of the pulses.

<margin>Bathing</margin>
¶ **Bathing.** That is, a warm bath of sweet water, which is called "repletion" <note>original: "repletio"</note> by another name, because it fills with vapor from the temperate air, because it fills from within, and from the warm water of a sweet-water bath. Used in a moderate way with temperate heat, it makes the pulse large, fast, strong, soft, and frequent.

Column 1:

<margin>dense</margin>
**Dense.** For [the bath] increases the vital power by dissolving superfluous humors; and by heating the body, it makes the pulse fast. It makes it soft and dense <note>In this context, "dense" (spissus) refers to a high frequency of beats with short intervals between them.</note> due to the moistening effect. A long-lasting bath makes the pulse smaller and weaker than before, though the speed and density remain; this happens because of the vital exhaustion of the body's moisture as its heat increases, but it remains moderate in terms of softness and hardness. If, however, one stays in the bath so long that the virtue is dissolved and the heat is diminished, the pulse becomes small, weak, and slow, just as in those who have over-exercised. Conversely, a moderate cold water bath used on a stout, youthful body makes the pulse large, strong, and fast, because the natural heat is gathered together inside and strengthens the virtue; but if one stays in it until the natural heat fails or flees, it makes the pulse small, slow, and rare <note>A "rare" pulse (rarus) is the opposite of a dense one, meaning there are long intervals between beats.</note> because the virtue is suffocated. But in a thin and slender person, it makes the pulse failing and slow, for in such a body the coldness meets no resistance. Hence, penetrating quickly to the interior, it soon intercepts and extinguishes the heat and diminishes the virtue. From this, the pulse becomes
<margin>pulse</margin>
slow and rare. It also becomes weak and hard, because the organs are constricted by the cold. But from a long stay in such a body, it makes the pulse extremely deficient, hard, and rare, as the cold strikes the principal limbs and the heat flees to the innermost parts. ¶ **Drink.** This changes the pulse in quality and quantity, according to the different types of drinks, just as was said regarding food—except that food nourishes and strengthens more.
<margin>cause of disease</margin>
¶ **Cause of Disease.** This changes the pulse, and although this is distinguished in various and manifold ways by the authors, we can nevertheless divide it into two branches. For one cause of disease is contrary to nature, which is a dissolution or dissipation of nature; the other is a weighing down and constriction. The cause that dissolves and dissipates the virtue is the removal of nourishment, the worsening of any disease, as well as accidents of the soul <note>Emotions or psychological states.</note>, extreme pains, or excessive evacuation. The cause that weighs down and constricts is an excessive multitude of humors, a hot or cold <term>aposteme</term> <note>An internal swelling or abscess.</note>, and the like. Let us first look at the dissolving causes. ¶ Dissolving causes make the pulse small, weak, fast, and dense. The more these dissolving causes are intensified and prolonged, the more the pulse increases in weakness and smallness, until it becomes "vermicular" <note>Worm-like (vermiculosus): a pulse that feels like a crawling worm.</note> and "formicular" <note>Ant-like (formiculosus): a pulse so tiny and weak it feels like an ant crawling under the skin.</note>. The latter is the most deficient, smallest, and worst of all. This also happens when the virtue is suddenly dissolved, as in an excessive flow of blood
<margin>Miscarriage/Hemorrhage</margin>
from a vein, or from <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>Bloodletting.</note>, or from an artery, or from blood flowing from a wound, or from a loosening of the bowels; this occurs when the vital spirit suddenly falls, as we see in syncope <note>Fainting.</note>. This is the pulse that arises from a failure of the virtue. ¶ And note: the vermicular pulse necessarily precedes the formicular. The extreme worsening of a disease in its final and consuming stage produces the vermicular pulse. ¶ Regarding the "accidents of the soul," although they are among the causes that dissolve and dissipate the virtue, we shall speak of them at the end of this chapter. **Pain**, if it be in any limb, makes the pulse terrible, as in the liver or stomach. If the pain is extreme even in a non-principal part, such as the hand or foot, it makes the pulse 
terrible; just as a moderate pain in a principal organ, or any pain whether in a principal or non-principal part, makes the pulse fast, strong, and dense. This is because nature exerts itself against the pain to expel it, which moves the vital virtue and natural heat. But if the pain persists and the virtue vanishes, the pulse becomes weak, small, fast, dense, and irregular. This irregularity happens because the pain increases at times and decreases at others. ¶ **Causes that weigh down and constrict** arise from an excessive abundance of humors. If these abound in one limb, they create a disease according to the nature of the humor and the function of the limb; hence, diseases
<margin>Repletion</margin>
arising from fullness are more numerous than those arising from emptiness. The pulse resulting from diseases that weigh down the virtue is small and weak. Due to the failure of the virtue under the weight of the humor, it is "full" because of the abundance; it is dense because of the need for cooling; and it is irregular because the virtue is conquered by the humors—much like a fire overwhelmed by too many logs, which is sometimes buried and sometimes emerges and subsides. When the virtue is heavily weighed down, it must necessarily produce a variation either in magnitude, or in speed, or in two, or in more, or in fewer of these qualities. But when the virtue is equal to the humors, the pulse is equal in its diversity,

<column-break/>

Column 2:

because it balances the large beats with the small. If the virtue is conquered by the humors, the beats become small and failing, and many such continue 
before a strong one occurs; if the opposite is true, the result is the opposite. Sometimes the virtue, due to certain sudden harmful movements, strikes the fingers all at once and then the pulse rests; this extra stroke seems superfluous. The cause is that while nature is resting, some harm supervenes; hence, she moves against her will to defend herself from that harm. Sometimes the virtue fails during the time of movement, making it necessary for the virtue to rest. Because of this, one stroke may be less apparent between two or three others. ¶ **A particular pulse arising from fullness** is like the pulse from blood pouring through the whole body: it is large, fast, full, and midway between hard and soft. The cause is evident in itself. If it arises from red bile <note>Cholera.</note>, it becomes fast, dense, very hot, hard, and irregular due to the impetuousness of the bile. Similarly, the pulse of a phlegmatic person can be tracked according to its own qualities. ¶ Pulses vary and intensify according to the humors: when they putrefy, they intensify, and they subside according to the abundance of humors, which creates a greater irregularity in the pulse. Therefore, as the disease arises from different humors and is established in different limbs, the pulse is diversified accordingly. Later, we shall speak of the variation of pulses due to the causes of diseases in their proper place, and regarding the change of the pulse due to the types of diseases.
<margin>Intercourse</margin>
¶ **Sexual Intercourse.** If it is moderate and occurs at proper intervals according to one's personal constitution, it makes the pulse fast, large, and strong. If it is immoderate, though it may be large and strong at first, it afterwards becomes weak and small.
<margin>Disturbance</margin>
¶ **Disturbance of Mind.** That is, the passion of the soul, such as joy, anger, etc. **Anger** makes the pulse fast and dense because of the heat suddenly bursting outward from the excessive desire for vengeance; it remains temperate in terms of softness and hardness. **Joy** makes the pulse large and moderate—between strong and weak, and between slow and fast—because with temperate heat, much cooling is not required. **Sadness** makes the pulse small, weak, and rare, because the heat is gradually drawn back to the interior; if this persists for long, it makes the pulse vermicular and then formicular.
<margin>Bodily positions</margin>
¶ **Bodily Positions.** The placement of the body and ways of lying down; for example, if someone lies on their left side and compresses the left arm, the blood will be restricted by the compression of the arm at the narrow point. Thus, the pulse appears hidden and as if failing. Therefore, if an improvident person, unaware of such compression, feels such a pulse, they might be deceived, judging the patient to be dying. A physician must, therefore, check the pulse in the other arm; if he finds that one strong, he should realize the other pulse was changed by compression. If not, he may despair. All these things change or vary the pulse—that is, they alter it in various ways as has been said. ¶ **Idioms.** That is, the differences of the pulse, from *eidos*, which means "form." For every difference arises from a form.
