The author puts forward some necessary chapters for understanding what came before and what follows, just as he did in the first part. First, he uses a transition, joining what has been said to what is about to be said. ¶ **Arduous.** <note>original: "Ardua"</note> That is, difficult. ¶ **Part of the purpose.** <note>original: "Pars ppositi"</note> That is, the laborious work which we have proposed concerning the doctrine of pulses. ¶ **Exhausted.** <note>original: "Exhausta"</note> That is, completed and put into execution. ¶ **Another now.** <note>original: "Altera nunc"</note> That is, a division. ¶ **It remains.** <note>original: "Supereest"</note> It remains to be treated. ¶ **Of which.** <note>original: "Cuius"</note> Namely, of the division. ¶ **Distinction.** <note>original: "Distinctio"</note> That is, the execution of making the distinction. ¶ **It pushes forth.** <note>original: "Trudet"</note> That is, he studiously intends and opens the intention of this division and shows what he is studying. ¶ **To shape the prescribed species.** <note>original: "Informare pscriptas spēs"</note> That is, the aforesaid ten kinds of pulses and their species. ¶ **With certain.** <note>original: "Certis"</note> That is, manifest and secret. ¶ **Figures.** <note>original: "Figuris"</note> That is, significations.

# In which arteries the pulse is to be considered.

> The pulse ought to be discerned in honorable arteries:
> Exposed, long, straight, and near to the heart.
> Where the left hand, since it is bordering the heart,
> Is proven by judgment to be better known for the pulse.
> There is certain faith there, and the constancy of true motion.
> A truthful pulse: the faithful servant of nature.

¶ Here the author teaches in which arteries the pulse ought to be considered. For while it is to be considered in the arteries, it is not so in all of them, but only in the arteries of the left arm, which are specially designated for investigating the pulse and exploring the conditions of the body. ¶ Some arteries are lower, as in the length of the back; others are deep in the flesh, as in the hips; others are covered by bones, as in the chest; others are too remote from the heart, as in the soles of the feet and the heels; others are too short, as at the bridge of the nose; and others are tortuous, as in the temples and ears; others are indecent, as around the private parts, and especially in women. Others, though they may share some of the preceding characteristics, are nonetheless equivocal and ambiguous, such as the arteries of the right arm. The first are rejected because of their posterior position, since the movement of heat flourishes more in the anterior part of the heart than in the posterior. The second because of the oppression of the flesh, as they are not exposed but placed underneath and entangled in the flesh. Others because of the placement of bones; hence the movement of the arteries cannot reach the surface of the bones, and therefore remains insensible and hidden. Others because of their extreme distance from the heart; for the motion of the heart tires and fails sooner in remote parts than in nearby ones, and grows faint in the process of such a long journey. For the force of mortification <note>In medieval medicine, "mortification" refers to the loss of vital heat or the dying off of tissue.</note> invades the extreme parts sooner than the nearby ones. Just as the heat of a fire is destroyed by action sooner in the far corners of a house than around the parts near or neighboring the hearth, so it must be judged regarding natural heat. Others are rejected because of extreme shortness, for they cannot receive the placement of four fingers. And thus in such arteries the knowledge of magnitude and strength—which are the chief differences of the pulse—is hindered and will not be known. In such places, it cannot be discerned whether the pulse is long, or small, or short. The common people, however, believe that by such a pulse at the bridge of the nose, a judgment of death or life is certified; and if they do not feel a pulse there, they judge it to be death; if the opposite, they do not despair. Others, even if they are sometimes touched, are avoided because of their tortuosity, for they cannot receive four fingers in a straight line. Others are to be avoided because of the shamefulness of the private parts, for it would be indecent to uncover the genitals, especially of women. Others, even if they can be conveniently investigated, are not as faithful and truthful because of the proximity of the heat of the liver; they are not as frequently used because of the fallacy of ambiguity implied in them, as is clear in the text. But the arteries of the left arm are chosen because they are long, straight, exposed, 

<column-break/>

running, and near the heart; they are faithful. ¶ **Honorable.** <note>original: "Honestis"</note> To distinguish them from those that are indecent. ¶ **Exposed.** <note>original: "Expositis"</note> That is, naked and open, to distinguish them from those covered by flesh and bones. ¶ **Long.** <note>original: "Longis"</note> To distinguish them from short ones. ¶ **Straight.** <note>original: "Rectis"</note> To distinguish them from tortuous ones. ¶ **Near the heart.** <note>original: "Cordiqz ppinquis"</note> To distinguish them from the unfaithful ones that are distant from the heart and deceiving based on false opinion; for the arteries of the left arm possess all these qualities. Hence I say that in such things one must consider them as was said before. ¶ **Wherefore.** <note>original: "Vnde"</note> That is, for this reason you ought to consider the arteries of the left arm. ¶ **Left.** <note>original: "Sinistre"</note> That is, the arteries of the left arm; and he shows the cause. ¶ **Since there.** <note>original: "Cū ibi"</note> That is, in those arteries. ¶ **Certain faith.** <note>original: "Certa fides"</note> That is, a certain and faithful judgment and condition of the heart because of proximity; for no prejudice is taken from them by the heat of the liver.

# Why the pulse is not to be considered in the right arm.

> The right side: because it is more fervent, because more fully
> The life-giving vapor radiates upon it; and the lamp of the heart
> It receives more freely: where the maker of pure blood,
> The liver reigns, the gentle persuader of tender love.
> The fuel of evil, where the gall-bladder seethes,
> Makes the pulse equivocal; confused by such great heat,
> It entangles errors and adulterates the examination of the art.

¶ In this chapter, he assigns the causes why the pulse is not to be considered in the right arm; and he assigns a cause, namely, the manifold abundance of heat. For there is a predominance of heat in the right part of the body: both because of the liver located on the right side, which is a hot organ and the foundation of the nutritive power; and because of the gallbladder having its home in that part, from which all the seething of anger proceeds; and because of the heart's breathing out into that part. For although the heart has its domicile in the left side, it nevertheless breathes its spirit and vital heat into the right side. ¶ **More fervent.** <note>original: "Feruidior"</note> That is, a dominance of prevailing heat, which can be weighed by strength, mobility, and the vigor of defense. For in defending the body, the left side is like a servant holding the shield, while the right, like a strong soldier, raises the unsheathed sword to strike. And because he said the right side is more fervent, he proves it first through explanation when he adds: ¶ **Because the dominance of heat is more fully** in the right side; he puts forward the cause which is drawn from the breathing out of the vital spirit into the right side. ¶ **Life-giving.** <note>original: "Viuificus"</note> That is, the vital heat proceeding from the heart. ¶ **Radiates.** <note>original: "Irradiat"</note> It kindles and illuminates like a ray bursting and proceeding from the sun. ¶ **More fully.** <note>original: "Plenius"</note> That is, more perfectly. ¶ **Receives more freely.** Because of its breathing out into the right side. ¶ **Where the maker of blood.** <note>original: "Vbi sanguinis actor"</note> He posits another cause, which he draws from the explanation of the liver, why it is hotter. ¶ **Maker.** <note>original: "Actor"</note> That is, the fabricator and generator. For in the liver, all blood is generated. ¶ **Gentle pulse.** <note>original: "Blādus pulsus"</note> Because of the heat of the liver and the tempering of the blood. Whence the limbs are refreshed, they become playful and joyful, and the enticements of love are suggested. ¶ **Fuel.** <note>original: "Incentina"</note> He assigns a third cause why the right side surpasses in heat, which is taken from the gallbladder; since it is the domicile of choler and the habitation of anger, it is situated on the right side. ¶ **Gallic.** <note>original: "Fellea"</note> That is, of the gallbladder, which contains the bitterness of anger and rancor. ¶ **Makes equivocal.** <note>original: "Equiuocat"</note> That is, it makes the pulse ambiguous and suspect to the person touching the right arm: whether such a pulse comes from the heart’s heat or the liver’s. Therefore it is equivocal. ¶ **Entangles errors.** That is, of fallacies and illusions. ¶ **Adulterates.** That is, because of an adulterated conception, it renders the indication of this art untrustworthy.

# How the pulse should be touched by holding the hand.

> Let the glad hand of the physician hold and guide the patient's [hand];
> The weak part requires the help of a supporting force.
> Which, if it should guide itself, confused by a slight tremor,
> It would deceive the craftsman, and an error of the examination would occur.

<meta>This page continues the practical instruction on pulse diagnosis, specifically moving from which artery to choose to the physical method of handling the patient and the physician's own technique. It establishes the necessity of physical support to avoid false readings caused by the patient's weakness.</meta>

## Here he instructs the physician on how he ought to hold the patient's hand.
The patient’s left hand must be supported by the physician's left hand; and he assigns the reason why. Otherwise, an error in the examination would occur. Because such a tremor can sometimes happen in an entirely healthy body due to a lack of regulation and a failure of support because of the weakness of the nerves, a physician not paying attention to the cause might believe that this tremor happens because of a lack of <term>spirits</term> <note>The "spirits" (spiritus) were believed to be the vital subtle substances that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> and the onset of death; and thus being deceived, he would judge the patient to be dying. But if the tremor is felt even when the arm is supported, it is certain: either that part is paralyzed and the nerves are greatly weakened, obstructed, or weighed down, and the spirits are intercepted or lacking; which, in persistent acute fevers where nature is weak, is a fatal sign. Therefore, so that the physician does not fall into a fallacy while touching the patient's pulse, he should always support the arm.

# Concerning the instruction of the physician in touching the pulses.
> But take care that the patient does not compress his fingers into a fist.
> Nor let them extend too much: lest the upper arm be compressed
> By the weight of the side: let an order of <term>arrangement</term> <note>original: "scomatis"; refers to the Greek "schema," meaning the physical posture or arrangement of the limbs.</note>
> Be present, so that the moderation of the limbs removes any ambiguity.

## Here he instructs the physician through another caution: namely, that the physician should consider when he touches the pulse whether the patient holds their fingers closed and folded into a fist, or extended in the palm. But see that no violence is done to any nerve or artery, either by extension or compression. For when the hand is held in a relaxed and simple manner, the nerves and arteries and spirits perform their course more freely through their channels.

## On the side. <note>original: "L'ateris"</note> Here he places another caution: which concerns the lying position. Care must be taken lest the patient lie upon their side and keep the arm compressed. For if the physician is prudent and touches the pulse with the arm compressed, he may not be able to feel it; he will then judge the person as perhaps not being healthy, or that he is failing the physician. Therefore, the physician, if he does not feel the pulse, ought to ask if the patient has been lying on their left side; if it is so, he must touch the right arm, because the pulse is not felt in a compressed limb. The reason is: because there is an attraction of blood to the compressed place. Just as when someone's hand is bound with a lace or rope, immediately the blood runs more vehemently from the pain, for it is attracted in great quantity. Hence, the movement of the spirits is suffocated by such a proportion of blood, and the pulse is not felt. This is also why "numbness" <note>original: "dormitationes"; literally "sleepings" of the limbs.</note> happens in the feet, becoming insensible from the vehemence of pressure. And thus, judgment should not be hindered by compression.

## Let order be present. <note>original: "Adsit ordo"</note> He presents considerations on the moderate and the disordered.
**Arrangement.** <note>original: "Scomatis"</note> That is, the position of the limbs. It is, moreover, the ordered positioning of the limbs. If the patient lies on the right side more frequently than on the left for the recreation of the right side, making no compression of the arm. And why.

## As moderation. <note>original: "Ut moderatio"</note> That is, a moderate position. **Let it remove the ambiguous motion.** That is, let it remove illusions and ambiguities which arise from a weak and hidden motion in a compressed limb.

# With which hand the pulse ought to be touched: and how much it ought to be touched: and in what way.
> The right hand: since it excels in the investigation of the senses.
> And to it is given a more vivid experience of touch.
> Let him apply his fingers to the artery. Let the manifest things be noted
> With fingers applied lightly, and the hidden things with them pressed.
> Nor should he stop before the hundredth
> Motion is made: which number serves nature; and by the
> Judgment of this number, the sentence of truth becomes clear.

## Here the author shows with which hand the physician ought to touch the pulses: and he says with the right hand: because in it, due to the dominance of manifold heat, just as in the pulse, a vivid experience of all sensitivity reigns.

## Let him apply his fingers to the artery. That is, let him use the tips of
<column-break/>
four fingers along the length of the artery: so that from such an application he can investigate the pulse through its length, width, and height.

## Manifest things. <note>original: "Mãifesta"</note> Here he presents a certain caution: that in a wasted or thin body, where the artery is manifest and exposed, and not buried in the flesh, the pulse ought to be touched lightly and superficially; because the artery is swollen and does not need compression. In a fat body, and one with much flesh, because the artery is compressed by soft flesh and entangled in deep pores, the pulse ought to be touched with a compression of the fingers. Otherwise, indeed, it would not be felt; and so it must be done in the strong and the weak. For a weak pulse must not be pressed down.

## Nor should he stop before. <note>original: "Nec pius absistat"</note> Here the author presents another instruction: that the physician, in the discernment of the pulse by the placement of fingers upon the arteries, ought to continue until the hundredth stroke. For within this number, he will be able to weigh all the differences and diversities of the pulse: whether it is <term>incisive</term> or <term>decisive</term>, or ordered or disordered, and what kind of disorder, and so on for others. For the <term>centenary</term> <note>The number 100.</note> is a preeminent limit of number or numbers, and fertile and pregnant with the service of much perfection, both in natural and theological matters; and so it is preferred above others.

# Concerning the significations of a large pulse according to nature.
> A large pulse is that which moderates itself by the number of nature.
> Which neither the cause of evil nor the force of a <term>symptom</term> <note>original: "synthomatis"; likely referring to a specific pathological complication.</note> urges.
> It indicates one who is a spendthrift, unstable, and greedy for popular favor.
> He undertakes arduous things; he reveals the secrets of his mind.
> To this pulse is joined a companion: virtue intensified by heat.
> An abundance of spirits, a form suited to the limbs.
> Prone to dilation, and fit to be moved.

In this second portion, having premised certain things necessary for the understanding of the doctrine of pulses, he here approaches the principal proposal by beginning the treatise on the significations of pulses. He begins from the first: which is considered according to the triple dimension, namely, concerning the significations of a **large pulse**. First, he shows the significations of a large pulse according to nature; afterwards, the large pulse beyond nature. A large pulse according to nature signifies strength and an abundance of spirit impelling the artery, and a manifold use of natural heat, and also the softness of the organ, and its obedience and capacity for dilation. Hence, every large pulse is naturally soft: or, being tempered in softness and hardness, it signifies prodigality; because the motion of heat is from the center to the circumferences, and it disperses all things. Hence, the nobilities of the soul are strengthened by the motion of heat in the disposition of things; it also indicates instabilities and a lightness of mind. For everything hot is swiftly mobile.

<margin>
Otherwise: the morals are formed by the motion of heat in the dispersal of things.
</margin>

> **Popular favor.** <note>original: "Aure pplaris"</note> That is, the seeking of empty glory. For heat tends upward, and in a hot body the blood naturally boils and the spirit seethes. Hence, through the motion of heat, the habit of the heart, the motion of the spirits, and the quality of the <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determined a person's physical and mental constitution.</note> are known; and it draws its own affections. Hence, thoughts are of glorious and magnificent things, and praise is favorably embraced for great things. And from the same cause, it signifies much hope, and a manic confidence in difficult things, and the undertaking of uncontrollable works, and the revelation of secrets. And this is especially so in a heart of short stature, in which, because of the proximity of the heart and the brain, there is a rapid recurrence of the spirits.

For these are born from coldness of the heart and a failure of spirits. ¶ **But naturally.** That is, this refers to a pulse that is naturally short, not one made short by disease, about which he adds below.

# On

saying: which signifies the onset of external and internal heat. ¶ **Abnormal.** <note>original: "discola"</note> That is, a disturbance of the humors: which causes schism and discord in the city of the human body. ¶ **Snatched.** <note>original: "raptu"</note> That is, with a hurried and rapid motion. ¶ **Discordant.** <note>original: "diffoni"</note> A slow pulse happens according to contrary causes and contrary significations and it happens to it by the opposite. ¶ **Discordant.** That is, difficult. ¶ **Distant from the extremes.** That is, middling between the fast and the slow.

### On the hard and soft pulse.

->Hardness of the vessels: of the heart: rigor: a dry humor.<-
->A stay too harsh: the mysteries of the hard pulse.<-

After he has dispatched the treatise on the significations of the three types that are observed according to the property of the movement of the artery, he subsequently continues with the significations of the other three types which pertain to the consistency of the organ. <note>The "consistency of the organ" refers to how the artery wall feels to the touch—hard, soft, or medium—rather than the speed of the beat.</note> First, however, concerning the hard, soft, and middling pulse. A pulse is either hard naturally, or outside of nature. The naturally hard pulse signifies dryness of the vessels, and hardness and tension of the artery from natural dryness; it signifies dryness of the heart, austerity of the mind, and stubbornness. The hard pulse outside of nature arises from sanguineous <note>blood-based</note> or choleric humors flowing into certain limbs, creating in them, from excessive fullness, a tension of the veins and arteries, and of the nervous parts. Hence, in the swellings of the nervous and arterial parts, due to the trapping of smoke <note>original: "fumi conclusionē"; referring to "sooty vapors" or waste gases the body needs to expel</note>, the blockage of pores, and excessive tension and pressure, there occur hardness, smallness, weakness, density, speed, and sometimes a **saw-like** <note>term: "serrina"; a pulse that feels jagged or uneven, like the teeth of a saw</note> irregularity. It is hard due to tension; small due to the hardness of the organ, which cannot be dilated because of the defect of the artery's power under such excessive hardness. Therefore, every hard pulse is small, fast, and dense because of the great necessity for "refrigeration" <note>The medieval belief that the pulse's primary job was to draw in cool air to vent the heart's heat.</note>. For since the weak power cannot pull enough at once, <margin>The pulse of inflammations.</margin> it is necessary to repeat the action frequently, as it cannot fulfill its requirement in a single stroke. The irregularity and diversity arise from the distress of the vital power, which, being greatly afflicted and occupied, cannot maintain order, but dilates now more, now less, according to the motion and boiling of the cause. ¶ In such **abscesses** <note>term: "apostematibus"; used here to mean any internal inflammation or swelling</note>, their pulses vary at different times. In the beginning, the hardness is less, the strength is greater, and the pulse is larger in quantity, yet there is no irregularity. In the beginning, the abscess is small and causes modest tension of the parts; hence the power is still strong and can better dilate the vessels. The heat is great, which is why the pulse is fast and dense. The irregularity is slight because the hardness of the artery is modest and the power is not yet so oppressed. These signs occur according to the progression of time: through the increase and the peak, they grow larger; and he especially notes this: that fullness accompanies it, because with hardness (that is, tension of the arteries) there is a greater increase of the inflammation and greater compression of the parts, and a thickening of the vapors. In the decline, however, <margin>In hard inflammations.</margin> the inflammation recedes, the humor dissolves, the inflammation ends, and the pulse is restored to health. ¶ However, from the dissipation of thin humors and the hardening of thick ones in hard and blocked inflammations, the pulse becomes harder and thinner, because the organs do not dilate in width or depth due to their hardness. It is less fast and dense because the heat is less and does not require as much refrigeration as before. Indeed, if such hardness should persist after the dissolution of the matter, it signifies danger: namely, the hardening of an inflammation that is difficult to dissolve, and thus the prolongation of the disease, signifying a failure of nature.

<margin>In inflammations of the brain.</margin> ¶ If the inflammation is in the membranes of the brain, as in **phrenitis** <note>An acute fever marked by delirium.</note>, the pulse becomes hard, small, fast, strong, and dense; hard because the inflammation occurs in nervous places. Why it is small or dense is clear from the points above, but it is somewhat stronger than in other inflammations because the power is stronger in these cases. Hence some sick people in these diseases rise up quickly, and become more talkative and garrulous, and can hardly be held back by men, because it follows from the agitation or corruption of the mind. The irregularity arises from the inconsistent dilation of the organ along with the hardness of the effusion and the strength of the vital power; hence it happens that one part dilates while another does not. The hardness of the pulse is less in an inflammation of the liver and that which is in nervous places, because these members are not of such hardness, nor do they create such tensions as the nervous and arterial members. ¶ In places closest to the heart, <margin>In inflammations near the heart.</margin> inflammations create pulses similar to those that arise from an inflammation in arterial places; for the veins of the liver and the arteries are likened to the heart. ¶ From a choleric inflammation <margin>In melancholic inflammations.</margin> based especially in a noble member such as the membranes of the brain, or the diaphragm, or around the heart—since an abscess cannot form in the heart itself—if it occurs in the liver or stomach, the pulse becomes very hard. If it happens in other members, such as the foot or the hand, the hardness is not so great unless it is in arterial locations. ¶ From a melancholic inflammation in the same members, there is hardness and thinness in the pulse. ¶ **Quinsy** <note>original: "Squinā tū" (Squinantiam); an inflammation of the throat/tonsils.</note>: because it occurs in the muscles of the throat which are partly nervous and cord-like, it makes the pulse hard, rigid <note>original: "tbetanofuz" (tetanofum)</note>, saw-like, small, weak, and dense; the reasons are clear from the above. If such a pulse from such a sickness increases in hardness, rigidity, and the diversity of the saw-like beat, it announces a future spasm, because the nerve is forced to grow from the inflammation, and from the nerves of the brain because of the connection of the nerves to it; hence it is necessary that a spasm should arise. If, while the same hardness remains, it should fall from rigidity into rarity <note>a slow, infrequent beat</note>, it signifies the patient is being suffocated or weakened. For such rarity happens because of the freezing of natural heat. ¶ In **pleurisy** <margin>In pleurisy.</margin> "red bile" makes the pulse hard and very dense. And such a pulse in pleurisy signifies that red choler is the cause. For the caustic humor signifies something very mobile and very furious; hence it signifies either **peripneumonia** <note>pneumonia</note> or a future fainting <note>syncope</note> because of the instability and thinness of the pleuritic matter, if in peripneumonia it changes into syncope. It leads to mania or failure, which happens from the proximity of the heart or the lung to the site of the disease. If in pleurisy there is smallness and density, and a lessened hardness, it signifies that the pleurisy arises from phlegmatic matter, and it announces a future alienation of the mind, or a future apoplexy. For the cold and moist humor ascending to the brain causes these diseases. ¶ **Empyema** <margin>In empyema.</margin> <note>A collection of pus in the cavity between the lung and the chest wall.</note> before the dissolution of the matter makes the pulse hard and very saw-like, fast, and dense. If the matter is changed into rot, is digested, and is emitted, then the patient's pulse becomes soft, wide, weak, and rare; soft and wide because of the moisture of the matter in the members; weak from sudden emptying; rare from the great desire to draw in air. ¶ In **peripneumonia** <margin>In pneumonia.</margin> whether it arises from a hot inflammation of the chest—where the moisture from the proximity of the heart dries out, and the arteries and foundations of the chest simply dry up—or from a bad hot and dry proportion in the whole body, in which dryness persists; because of the use of hot and cold things it changes into coldness, and the substantial moisture of the body is dried up. And when the body is decrepit, the pulse becomes hard, weak, small; weak because the power fails over a long time; small from the failure of the power in dilating the organs; hard from the failure and desiccation of the whole body; fast and dense because of the necessity for refrigeration. ¶ A hot inflammation in the mouth of the stomach <margin>In the colon/stomach.</margin> makes the pulse hard, rigid, dense, fast, and saw-like; the saw-like beat reveals it; later it is rigid from the nervous quality; weak from the failure of power; which failure, if prolonged, makes the pulse slow and rare. A cold inflammation of the stomach makes the pulse hard, weak, and small. ¶ **Tympanites** <margin>In dropsy.</margin> <note>A condition where the abdomen is bloated with gas or fluid.</note> makes the pulse hard, rigid, and dense; hard from dryness, and dense from the failure of power.

### On the hard pulse in pleurisy.

->The hardness of the pulse in pleurisy is perilous.<-
->The dry matter is earthy: it is proven raw.<-
->Difficult to dissolve: from which the dispersal of the disease<-
->Is prolonged: the strength is oppressed: nature grows weary.<-
->And life succumbs, exhausted by the long duel.<-

Because while it can arise from blood, rarely from phlegm, and often from choler <note>yellow bile</note>; due to the hardness of the pulse and its thickness, it signifies that there is pleurisy caused by choler, which is more dangerous when made from this matter. This is because of the mobility of the matter, its fury, and the easy turn into pneumonia <note>original: "pipleumonia"</note> due to the proximity of the location. A hard pulse also signifies excessive tension of the organs from dryness and a multitude of illnesses. ### On the significance of the naturally soft pulse.

> In a pulse to which nature grants softness,
> The substance of the heart and artery are equally soft.
> The interior of the body is thick and humid; the mind womanly,
> Wax-like, flexible, pious, flattering, and not very faithful.

An arriving softness, by which a rhythmic <note>original: "fynhromatic'" likely referring to a specific fever rhythm</note> impulse urges. It dissolves the humors and softens the vessels. It follows concerning the soft pulse. Therefore, a soft pulse according to nature signifies humidity of the body and natural softness of the organs, which soften from the humid temperament of the heart. As for character, it signifies womanliness of soul: a wax-like and flexible mind, pious and unfaithful. All of this happens from humidity, which among qualities is particularly liable to change and is the worst. Softness that "arrives" signifies a softness beyond nature. A pulse soft beyond nature signifies an abundance of humid nature and its unnatural dissolution. Whence the organs are moistened; once moistened, they soften. From abscesses <note>original: "apostematibus"</note> which are mostly phlegmatic if they occur in fleshy and naturally humid places, the pulse becomes soft. Hence in apoplexy and lethargy the pulse is soft, and also slow and rare: stormy in its variation because phlegmatic humor abounds and is born in the brain. Whence it is transmitted from other members to the brain. The brain itself is also humid by nature, because humors are made from much humidity; a weak pulse must be slow and rare from weakness of the power, with much humidity and stormy variation.

### On the full pulse.

> An abundance of spirits is noted as full through the full [pulse],
> A flood of blood filling the vessels most abundantly.

He follows with the significations of the fifth genus: which pertains to the consistency of the organ, that is, the full and the empty. Therefore, a full pulse signifies a multitude of blood received in the cavity of the heart: which blood, resolved into smoke and vapor, moves the heart and the arteries are moved. Such a pulse appears in those suffering from *synochus* and inflammatory *synocha* <note>types of continuous, non-intermittent fevers</note> and those laboring from a repletion of watery humors. And note that every full pulse is broad: since fullness and breadth happen from the same cause, namely, from an abundance of humidity. But it must be known that if phlegmatic humor abounds too much in the body, and especially outside the vessels, the blood is diminished. From the lack of blood in the vessels due to the multitude of phlegm, a full pulse does not occur.

### On the empty pulse.

> In the empty [pulse] the veins thirst. The power
> Of the vegetative air, absorbed, perishes; the fountain of living blood dries up,
> Which the dryness, the file of foreign heat, drinks up.

He deals here with the significations of the empty pulse, which corresponds to the full in the third way and is described by contrary significations. Thus, an empty pulse signifies a lack of blood, a consumption of humidity, and a failure of the spirits. Whence when the fingers are applied over the artery: immediately the artery yields to compression; it returns no humidity enclosed <column-break/> above or would return it. But immediately the pulse, because of the emptying of its organ which is vacant, vanishes. Now an empty pulse is either with heat or with cold. If with vehement heat: it signifies the onset of wasting <note>original: "synthesim"</note> and hectic fever <note>original: "ethyca"</note>. If with cold, it signifies the extinction of natural heat, because cold is a state of mortification; the empty pulse announces the loss of spirits and substantial humidity.
<margin>In lethargy the pulse is empty</margin>
In the lethargic person, an empty pulse appears because it overflows from phlegmatic humor snatched above. Whence lethargy happens; and with blood diminished in the veins due to a failure of digestion from the multiplication of the other humor in the arteries, an empty pulse occurs. He does not treat the empty pulse here according to nature, because all emptiness is unnatural, since it is from a failure of humors and spirits. In the empty pulse the veins: Which are the vessels of the blood. Thirst: That is, they are emptied and dried up because of the lack of blood and consumption. Vegetative: That is, the vital spirit, whose job it is to help and enliven the members. The fountain of living blood: From which, as if from a certain fountain, the members drink, are moistened, and restored. The file of heat: That is, the core and provocation of burning in the human body. For just as a whetstone sharpens iron, and through a file it is made sharper and more cutting, so through dryness the natural heat is made more fervent: which appears in dry wood, which obeys burning more than if it were green. A fever that arises from this is sharper than that which arises from another humor. Whence this does not happen except through the "file" of dryness.

### On the hot and cold pulse.

> And the hot [pulse] whose biting sting burns
> The fingers continually: from this comes acute fever.
> If the hot [pulse] burns the fingers at intervals,
> It is called interval-like and deceptive.
> The hot pulse joined with the empty is a witness to hectic fever.

He continues with the significance of the seventh genus: which is hot and cold. This likewise pertains to the consistency of the organs along with the two preceding ones. Therefore, a hot pulse signifies heat of the organ and a distemper of the spirits and humors flowing in the arteries themselves. But a hot pulse is either hot from blood, or from choler, or from heat fixed in the members, consuming and drinking up the blood in the veins. For if it is hot from blood, it ought to be accompanied by fullness, softness, and greatness, being middle-range between fast and frequent. Fullness comes from the repletion of power. Softness from the humidity of the blood; greatness from the great resolution of blood into smoke and spirit. It is middle-range between fast and frequent from the moderate necessity of needing refrigeration. For the humidity of blood is the tempering of heat and restrains the need for cooling; but if it is hot from choler, it is discerned by slenderness and hardness, by frequency and other symptoms which appear accompanying it in the body. If it is from heat fixed in the members, whence there would be emptiness, it signifies hectic fever and phthisis <note>a wasting disease like tuberculosis</note>. Also, another division of the hot pulse is made. For one hot pulse is continually hot, burning and biting upon the application of the fingers; it signifies a continuous fever. Another is at intervals and intermittent, without the stinging and biting of the fingers; it signifies an intermittent fever.

### On the cold pulse.

> It proves the setting of the spirits, and the lamp of life
> It lightens and extinguishes, the icy [pulse] of the heart's breath.

He continues with the significations of the cold pulse. A cold pulse signifies the extinction of natural heat, the annulment of the spirits, and the prominence of mortification. I do not say much more, except that the physician should stand near the sick person when such a pulse appears. For then the cross and the lights, and the incense, and the hair-shirt, and the holy water should have their place. <note>The author suggests that at this stage, the patient is beyond medical help and requires religious last rites.</note> Setting: That is, failure. Lamp: That is, the vital spirit, which is the lamp of the microcosm <note>the human body viewed as a miniature universe</note>.

## The third part begins concerning the significations of the other kinds of pulses.

> Now you may take a breath, my little novice Muse.
> A sweet recreation restores tired strength.
> It is enough now: away with delays: gird yourself for the return.
> Receive this: but take care that your feet do not stumble. <note>The author uses a play on words here: "feet" refers both to the feet of the traveler and the "metrical feet" of the poetry he is writing.</note>
> The heat is coming. and many thousands [of miles] remain.
> Perhaps a clandestine enemy lies in wait within.
> The celebrated plague of envy: the little ant of fame
> Scattering the worst weeds among the pure grains.
> So that the journey may be safer: and the envious man
> Might spare you, along with the mockeries of the foolish old commoners.
> Let the words remain seasoned with the flavor of Musandinus. <note>Petrus Musandinus (12th century) was a famous master of the Salernitan medical school and teacher of Gilles de Corbeil.</note>
> Present to all the title of the equivocal Salerno.
> Marked with the clear seal of Alphanus the Prelate. <note>Alphanus I (d. 1085) was the Archbishop of Salerno and a crucial figure in translating medical texts from Greek to Latin.</note>

Our author approaches the third distinction of his work, in which he follows through on the significations of the other kinds of pulses. He sets down their distinctions—at least some of them—which he had not placed in the second part. He begins with a prologue in which he speaks to his Muse, inviting her to a rest of recreation as she is exhausted from the present work. **Little novice.** That is, unrefined and new. **It is enough now.** etc. Because a long rest gives birth to sloth and weakens vigor, he immediately orders her to interrupt that rest so she may approach the work begun. **Lest your feet stumble.** That is, when you stretch your feet and are carried by the "feet" of metrical speech, beware lest any obstacle meet your feet. **Many thousands remain.** That is, many miles remain to be traveled. i.e., various chapters and various rules which still remain concerning the kinds of pulses; the intellect of the practitioner must travel through these rules as if through a certain road and path. **Lies in wait.** Here our author warns his Muse to beware of flatterers and detractors, who gnaw at the well-spoken words of others with a canine and satirical tooth; because they cannot do it themselves, they defraud others out of a certain malice of mind, and they turn the praises of others toward themselves by changing the titles. They scatter and sow the black seeds of envy and the weeds of detraction where they ought to sow the seeds of praise and favor. **Flavor of Musandinus.** That is, with the flavorful and sententious authorities of Peter Musandinus, who was the patron and supreme craftsman of this faculty, who had no equal nor shall have a successor. **Equivocal Salerno.** Salerno is "equivocal" <note>In medieval logic, an "equivocal" term is one that has multiple meanings.</note> because it refers both to the city and to the master who is the teacher of this art. **Alphanus.** That is, that supreme and unique master in the science of physics <note>The term "physics" (physica) here refers to the study of medicine and natural philosophy.</note>. **The Prelate.** That is, the Archbishop of Salerno; trusting in such great patrons, you can face the malicious enemies.

### On the significations of the frequent pulse.

> He who recalls and repeats his stroke very often.
> By a fragile force it is contracted; and by the strong heat
> Of the heart, a foreign vapor is adopted, so it may be refreshed.
> It can be sufficiently soothed by the breathing of the air.
> Lest the air be given to it all at once as much as it requires.
> The oppressed force refuses. Therefore, the complex force pays back
> In multiple numbers what it previously formed in one.
> And the repetition of the frequent pulse makes up for the deficiency of the quantity.

Our author follows through on the significations of the other kinds

<column-break/>

of pulses which remain from the six previously mentioned. First, he explains the significations of the **frequent** and the **rare** pulse, which is the seventh kind. This is measured by the time of rest that occurs between two dilations <note>original: "diastoles"</note>, as was said in the first part. Therefore, a **frequent pulse** signifies the strength and vehemence of external and unnatural heat, and the weakness and affliction of the **vital force** <note>original: "virtutis"</note>; because the heat is strong, it requires a great attraction of air and cooling. Whence there is a great necessity for humid cooling and ventilation to temper the fervor. If the vital force is weak and afflicted, it cannot sufficiently draw in a quantity of air in a single stroke as much as the necessity of the burning heat requires. Thus it is certain that through a numerous and frequent action, that which was lacking in the quantity of a single attraction is restored and supplied. Therefore, when these aforesaid causes concur—namely, strong heat and weak vital force—a frequent pulse occurs. If, however, a strong vital force concurs with strong heat, the strong force draws a sufficient quantity of air according to the necessity of the burning; then the pulse does not become frequent, but stays in the middle between rare and frequent. **Very often.** That is, repeating the motion very frequently. **Adopted vapor.** That is, external and unnatural heat, which the heart "adopts" due to the violence brought upon it by fever, or exercise, or pain, or any compression or change. **Soothed by the air.** That is, the air, by the attraction of which the internal parts are softened. **What it previously formed in one.** That is, the quantity of a single attraction.

### On the significations of the rare pulse.

> In a rare pulse, the heat is weak, and the vital force is infirm.

He establishes the causes and significations of the **rare pulse** and says: that a rare pulse signifies weakness of heat and infirmity of the vital force. Because the heat is weak, there does not remain much necessity for drawing in air for cooling. Even though the vital force is infirm, it can sufficiently administer air to respond in one attraction because of the weakness of the heat. But this was previously found in the *Pantegni* <note>The *Pantegni* was a massive medical encyclopedia translated/adapted by Constantinus Africanus.</note>. For Constantinus says: a rare pulse is made from a weak force and strong heat. And Philaretus <note>A 7th-century Byzantine medical writer.</note> says: a rare pulse comes from weak heat and an infirm vital force. The solution to this doubt is: when Constantinus says a rare pulse comes from a weak force and strong heat, he says this with respect to certain healthy bodies which are disposed toward a cold complexion; because of the weakness of their heat, they require little cooling. And their vital force, since it is strong (because the bodies are healthy and oppressed by no sickness), can sufficiently draw in with one stroke that which can cool the weak heat. Whence in them, a rare pulse occurs. But what Philaretus says—that a rare pulse comes from weak heat and an infirm vital force—he says this regarding the bodies of the sick. For in a person with a fever, a rare pulse signifies a very great hindrance to the operating vital force, because it signifies the extinction of natural heat through the consumption of humidity and the nullification of the spirits. Whence, if in a person suffering from an acute fever there suddenly appears a rare pulse—where previously the pulse was very fast, frequent, and large—and this happens without any resolution of the disease or mental wandering of the patient, it signifies death.

### On the incident and decadent pulse.

> By the pulse thrust from within, the vital force is repaired.
> Health, thus captivated, is set free; the languid becomes strong.
> It restores weak powers; the oppressed rises again.
> Life is reformed, the disease conquered by the symptom.
> But through the decadent pulse, as the evening of life is now made,
> The vegetative splendor of the air verges toward its setting.
> The weakened force perishes; and to the one drawing sparingly,
> Atropos insults, so that she may cut short the use of life. <note>Atropos is the one of the three Greek Fates who cuts the thread of life.</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of pulse diagnostics, moving from the physical texture of the artery to the "significations of other kinds," focusing specifically on rhythmic patterns known as the "incident" and "decident" pulses—terms used to describe the increasing or decreasing strength and frequency of the heartbeat as a prognostic indicator of life or death.</meta>

# Concerning the Pulses

Here the author treats the eighth kind of pulse, which is called the **incident** and the **decident** <note>original: *incidens & decidens*. In medieval medicine, these terms describe pulses that seem to "fall in" or "fall away" in strength or frequency.</note>, and he demonstrates its significations. Therefore, the **incident pulse** is observed by a comparison and weighing of the movements against the pauses: of the hidden against the open, and the strong against the weak (and vice-versa). An **open pause** is so-called because it produces the pulse during dilation <note>The *diastole*, or the expansion of the artery.</note>; a **hidden pause** is that which occurs during constriction <note>The *systole*, or the contraction of the artery.</note>. Therefore, the pulse is called incident or decident based on the comparison of the duration of dilation to the duration of constriction. For if the duration of constriction is shorter and the duration of dilation is greater, it is called an **incident pulse**. If, however, the duration of dilation is shorter and the duration of constriction (which is between two dilations) is greater, then it is called **decident**. If it is equal between the two pauses, it will be a pulse midway between the decident and incident.

This pulse can also be observed by the comparison of many pauses according to many subsequent and succeeding beats. For "incidence" sometimes takes place in a single beat, and sometimes across many. In a single beat, it occurs if a comparison is made of several pauses, constrictions, and dilations succeeding each other through many beats. If, therefore, it happens that the pulse continues for five strong strikes, and the sixth occurs weak or somewhat failing; and afterward ten strong ones follow and the eleventh is weak; and afterward twenty strong ones occur and the twenty-first is weak or failing; and the pulse proceeds thus by multiplying the strong strikes until the weak ones do not appear at all: such a pulse is called **incident**. It signifies the strengthening of the vital force, convalescence, and a full **crisis** <note>In ancient medicine, a "crisis" was the "turning point" of a disease, leading either to recovery or death.</note> to come.

Similarly, the **decident** can be understood in two ways, as was said of the incident: either in one beat or in many. How it is said to occur in one or many is clear: for if ten strong strikes precede and eleven weak ones follow; and then six strong ones are followed by seven weak; then four strong by five weak; then three strong by four weak; and so on gradually until the strong strikes vanish through the multiplication of the weak, then such a pulse is said to be **deciding** (or falling)—that is, falling away from the notice of our senses because of its diminishment.

¶ And note that the incident pulse includes the "fictitious tail" and "rebounding tail" <note>original: *caudam ficitinam, retonatinam*. These refer to specific secondary vibrations felt at the end of a pulse beat.</note>; the decident, however, can contain the "fictitious tail" and the "ending tail." Take heed that by a decident or failing pulse occurring on a critical day, the hour of death can be distinguished; and by an incident pulse, the good sign of convalescence can be signaled. Suppose, then, that some sick person has a decident pulse. You shall know whether they must escape from that illness in this way: you must calculate from the first failure of the pulse to the second, noting in which hour of the day it happens, how many beats are in the first failure, and how many in the second. For example: if between the first and second failure thirty strong strikes occur at the third hour of the day; but since it is troublesome for you to always be there, you should return the next day at the same hour to calculate the number, and count the strikes of that pulse between one failure and another. And if you now find the failure at the eleventh strike—meaning you have lost fifteen strong strikes, since you previously had thirty—it is a sign that as the other hours pass, the person will lose the other fifteen strikes and will die in that same hour. You can do the same for the incident pulse, and a crisis toward a good outcome is designated. If someone has a falling pulse, calculate from the first incident (which is somewhat stronger) until the second incident, noting at what hour it happens and how many beats are between the first incident pulse and the somewhat stronger ones. For example: if thirty strikes occur between the first and second incident at the third hour; afterward, coming on the second day at the same hour, calculate as on the first day. If you find fifteen movements between the first incident and the second, you have found the incident pulse. By proceeding thus, you can predict the coming crisis according to the great and small hour, and the calculation of hours and strikes.

¶ **Incidui.** That is, of the incident.
¶ **Having accepted the prize.** <note>original: *Accepto bravio*.</note> Meaning the prize of the crown after the weakness of the illness.
¶ **Through the decident.** That is, the falling. The literal meaning is plain.

<column-break/>

## Concerning the equal and unequal pulse; the ordered and unordered.

> A good thing joined to a good thing becomes a whole good.
> When touched by the left hand <note>In this context, "left" implies the sinister or unfavorable.</note>, it takes on the form of the bad thing joined to it.
> Inequality in a good state is to be rejected; in a bad state, it is to be praised.
> For of the two things proposed to you which are to be desired:
> Choose that which remains fixed in stable goodness.
> Of the two things proposed to you which are to be fled:
> Choose the more changeable; flee that which stands more constant.
> In every kind of pulse, equality or inequality can be found;
> but it is not equally "equal."
> A single observation of one thing alone makes the pulse.
> If a large pulse continues itself and keeps its own tenor
> undisturbed, it falls into full equality.
> When an alien kind enters, it is not called equal
> simply, but in this respect: since it is not equal in all things.

The eight kinds of pulses having been assigned and their accidents followed through, the author now treats the two extreme kinds which are accidents joined to the two principal ones mentioned before: namely, the **equal** and **unequal**, and the **ordered** and **unordered**. Yet he does not treat the ordered and unordered except by the distinction of their species and parts. Thus, an **equal pulse** is one whose strikes have a uniform and similar pattern, occurring uniformly at the tips of the fingers—as if the strikes were large, and equal in their magnitude, not small, not rare, not thick, not weak, nor diverse in any way. And this is called an **absolute equal pulse**. An **unequal pulse**, however, is one whose strikes vary: whether in movement (such that it is now thick, now fast, now slow) or in the quantity of dilation (now large, now small) or in strength (now strong, now weak). Just as there is a certain absolutely equal pulse preserving equality in all things, so there is a certain absolutely unequal pulse preserving inequality in all strikes. And there is a pulse unequal only in quantity or strength, while in other things it varies; that is called unequal, but in some respect it is termed equal.

¶ And note: every equality in a good state is good, and in a bad state it is bad. Inequality in a bad state is good <note>Because it indicates a change from a stable morbid state toward recovery.</note>. The author suggests this diversity according to the division in the present chapter. Nor does this division have a place only in the consideration of pulses, but also regarding the "middle space" of the veins.

¶ **Pantas.** That is, equality.
¶ **Sinistro.** With the left and bad differences.
¶ **Imparitas.** That is, unequal.

## Next follows concerning the pulse called the "rebounding tail" and the one called the "ending tail."

> The rebounding tail pulse <note>original: *cauda retonatina*.</note> is first perceived as a soft strike.
> In the next it faints; the third movement becomes light.
> To the judgment of the sense, the fourth manifests itself more.
> The fifth flourishes; the sixth is confirmed with valid vigor.
> From the shadows of the sense, and from the fainting of the sense itself.

<meta>This page continues the classification of irregular pulses, moving from the basic "incident" and "decident" types to more complex rhythmic variations named after animals and mechanical motions. > It creeps toward excess, proceeding by a gradual path. 
> Nature reciprocates the accustomed strikes with this pulse. 
> The "fining" pulse begins its motions from a high point. 
> Gradually it is depressed, it declines, it is softened. 
> And from being clearly felt, it sinks into the depths. 
> This brings the heralds of approaching death.

Here he treats the species of the unequal and inordinate pulse <note>original: *pulsus inequalis & inordinati*. An irregular pulse that lacks a consistent rhythm or strength.</note>, of which there are many types: namely, the **fining mouse-tail**, the **returning mouse-tail**, the **caprizant** (goat-leap), the **martelline** (hammer-like), the **muscular** (mouse-muscle), the **fluctuating** (wavy), the **spasmodic**, the **phthisical**, the **formicant** (ant-like), the **vermicular** (worm-like), and the **gazelle-like**. 

First, he discusses the **fining mouse-tail** and the **returning mouse-tail** <note>original: *cauda soricina finitina & retornatina*. These pulses are named after the shape of a mouse's tail—gradually tapering or thickening.</note>. Although these can be species of an "ordered" and "equal" pulse, they are nevertheless contained under the "unequal" and "inordinate" categories, because sometimes the fining and returning mouse-tail pulses proceed in their strikes according to an inordinate inequality, and sometimes according to an ordered one. For where there is a disturbance of the natural causes, an ordering of the resulting inequality can scarcely be fully maintained. However, Constantine <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a physician whose translations of Arabic medical texts, like the *Pantegni* (The Total Art), revolutionized Western medicine.</note> in the *Pantegni* subordinates these species to the ordered and equal pulses. 

Therefore, the **returning mouse-tail pulse** begins as if from hidden and nearly insensible strikes and, little by little, proceeding by a gradual path in an ordered manner, it increases from the smallest beats to small ones, from small to somewhat open, from somewhat open to more manifest, and so it continues and proceeds orderly until it regains strong motions. This pulse is called the "returning mouse-tail" because just as a mouse's tail, at its final extremity (which is furthest from the animal's body), begins with extreme thinness and proceeds continuously toward thickness and greater bulk until it reaches the animal's body; so also this pulse, by reason of similarity, proceeds by increasing little by little from weak strikes to less weak, from less weak to somewhat strong, and from strong to stronger strikes. 

The **fining mouse-tail** can be understood by the opposite: because starting from stronger strikes, it passes through less strong ones, thirdly through weak ones, and fourthly through weaker ones; finally, it descends from there through degrees of weakness until it is no longer felt. This is likened to the "fining" mouse-tail, for a mouse's tail is thicker where it is inserted into the animal's body and proceeds by gradually thinning until the end. The **returning tail** signifies the strengthening of nature and the return of health; the **fining tail** is a precursor of death.

### On the consolation of the physician when the patient dies.

> Pack up your bags and flee, O bringer of medicine. 
> Your expenses are worth nothing; your help is of no use. 
> Losses cannot be repaired when death is already near. 
> **Atropos** <note>The Fate who cuts the thread of life.</note> excludes **Lachesis** <note>The Fate who measures the thread of life.</note>; she breaks the vitals. 
> She dissolves the threads; she casts away the bonds and life itself. 
> Let the modesty of your brow remain safe; lift up your face, 
> Lest the approaching death bring shame upon you. 
> Let your judgment anticipate the death-bringing falls, 
> Retaining the office of a seer and the name of a prophet. 
> A physician does not always heal, nor does an orator always persuade. 
> But nevertheless, he concludes his office with the final end, 
> Doing each thing he ought, if he observes the contingencies. 
> Let him dictate with a stable judgment life for the one who will live, 
> Or death for the one who will die; what fault then is the healer's? 
> The common duty is hard: the curing of disease. 
> A common action is scarcely completed by one man alone.

Because a physician might perhaps despair due to the imminent death of a patient and fear for his own life, believing he will be blamed by the patient's friends, the author therefore consoles him and strengthens and confirms his friends, showing that there is nothing to fear. And when he has foretold the patient's death, glory and honor will be joined to him rather than shame or ambition, and he will be regarded as a prophet among men, because he is warned by prognostic signs alone.

<column-break/>

### On the caprizant pulse.

> From one descent the **caprizant** <note>original: *caprizans*. Derived from *capra* (goat), describing a "leaping" or double-beat pulse.</note> doubles its leap 
> In the manner of a leaping goat, which first strikes the air twice 
> Before it seeks to fix its course upon the ground. 
> In this species, the first progression yields to the second. 
> If such a species results when nature dictates its origin, 
> By this sign, the substance of the vessel is hard and rebellious. 
> A weak vital force is noted by the ear. 
> The sense is dull, the speech headlong, the mind disturbed. 
> Resolved in many ways so that it might suggest words, 
> It releases the concept of the mind with a mutilated voice. 
> Thus the caprizant will be a pulse without law or order. 
> The cause is a mixture of evil and a diverse diet, 
> Dissonant matter, and a great resolution of vapor.

In this chapter, the author defines what the caprizant pulse is and explains its significance. For the **caprizant** is that which, beginning with speed, seems to fall before the strike of the fingers, and afterward is moved by an incomplete dilation; it is called caprizant in the likeness of a young goat. For when a young goat begins to be swift in its leap, it seems to make a leap into the air, and afterward, in completing its course and completing its leap, it is swiftest. Such a pulse, before it returns to the center, has two dilations: the first smaller, the second larger. Just as a goat leaping in the air first lifts its feet once, then lifts itself again a second time before placing its footprint on the ground. The caprizant pulse is therefore sometimes according to nature, and sometimes beyond nature. The author explains in this chapter which significations are natural and which are not.

### On the martelline pulse.

> When the hammer strikes the anvil twice, and the mass 
> Of the metal object is forced to rebound by persuasion, 
> And thus the strike is divided, yet in itself it is a single blow. 
> So the limbs, shaken by hard rigor, rebound. 
> And thus the **martelline** species <note>original: *martellina*. From *martellus* (hammer).</note> stretches the fingers, 
> Nor does it return to the center until it has doubled the strike. 
> From which a fiery spirit is signaled from birth, 
> A dry heart, a discordant presumption of mind, and pride. 
> In a continuous fever where the martelline pulse dominates, 
> The moisture of the heart is consumed by the febrile burning.

Next follows the **martelline pulse**, which is named after the hammer (*martellus*). For just as the strike of a hammer upon an anvil falls into several subsequent strikes because of the rebound of the hammer from the hardness of the anvil; so also the martelline pulse in its dilation, before it returns to the center, seems to strike the fingers twice from the striking of the spirit and the hardness of the organ <note>The artery.</note>. The **hammer-like** <note>original: *martellinus*. Also known as the "dicrotic" pulse; it feels like a double strike.</note> pulse occurs because of the hardness of the organ's substance. This happens due to an overabundance of the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*. In medieval medicine, "spirit" refers to the vital pneuma or gas that was believed to carry the life force through the arteries.</note> by which the artery is moved; because of the hardness of that spirit, it is struck back again, creating a second rise. Therefore, Philaretus <note>Philaretus (7th century AD) was a Byzantine physician whose work on pulses was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note> says: the hammer-like or "double-striking" pulse occurs when the spirit runs violently and comes to a second percussion, just as a hammer strikes an anvil. There is a difference between the caprizant and the hammer-like: in the caprizant, the spirit is not "struck back" as in the hammer-like; rather, before the strike reaches the fingers, it seems to almost fall away, only to be violently summoned again after an incomplete dilation. 

Thus, if the hammer-like pulse occurs according to nature, it signifies a stubbornness of the heart and a persistence of the mind resulting from dryness, or pride resulting from an abundance of spirit. However, if it occurs "beside nature" <note>original: *preter naturam*. Meaning a pathological or diseased state.</note>, it signifies an inflammation of the heart and a failure of the **humors** <note>original: *humoris*. The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance determined health.</note>, as happens in acute fevers.

### On the branchy pulse.

> The **branchy** pulse is split into branches and organs:
> Striking with a four-fold motion, it runs through the fingers at the bottom.
> Two-colored in its beat: just as the confused
> Voice of the harp resists when strings are touched all at once.
> This species, by the command of the thick humors, figures
> A mobile purpose: the changeable will of the heart.
> If such a thing happens by the force of an evil symptom,
> The matter of the disease becomes discordant: a clashing cause
> Wages war: the **virtue** <note>original: *virtus*. The natural healing power or vital force of the body.</note> strikes back at the symptom equally.
> Life is reformed: nursing nature rises again.
> As the cloud of evil expires, the breeze of health returns.

¶ Here he provides the definition of the **branchy** <note>original: *ramosi*. A pulse that feels as if it is splitting or moving in different directions under the physician's fingers.</note> pulse and shows its significations. The branchy pulse is that which appears one way to the first fingers of the person touching it, and appears unequal to the remaining fingers. For example, it might appear fast to one finger, slow to another; thick to one, rare to another; strong to one, weak to another; rising to one, and again falling or hidden to another. This is considered according to the quantity of the motion, the power of the movement, and the number of the motions. For this pulse cannot vary according to magnitude <note>size or volume</note>. Indeed, it is impossible for the pulse to be "large" under one finger in the same part of the organ while being changed to "small" under another finger during the same strike. A "large" pulse, by necessity, passes under all four fingers. 

Similarly, the branchy pulse cannot be judged based on variations in width or narrowness, heat or cold, hardness or softness, or emptiness or fullness. For never in the same strike can a pulse be perceived by different fingers as being simultaneously branchy, wide and narrow, hot and cold, soft in some parts and hard in others, or empty in one and full in another. However, it can be considered small and large in terms of speed, slowness, weakness, strength, rarity, and frequency. 

¶ One type of branchy pulse is according to nature, another is beside nature. That which is according to nature signifies a mutability of the heart. That which is beside nature, occurring in acute fevers, signifies a conflict of the humors; it signifies the convalescence of nature on the part of life, but also declares the labor and the end of the disease. According to Philaretus, the branchy pulse happens because of some superfluity contained in the cavity of the artery which resists the incoming spirit. Thus, because of the resistance of this superfluity, the whole artery cannot be totally dilated by the incoming spirit; instead, the motion of the heart and the motion of the spirit are shifted downward and to the left, as if they were diversified. 

¶ These things having been determined, the text becomes clear by itself.

<column-break/>

According to the same diversities, as Constantine <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a primary translator of Arabic medical texts into Latin.</note> testifies in the *Pantegni* <note>The *Pantegni* was Constantine's most famous compilation of medical knowledge.</note>, one may find the **forked-tail** <note>original: *caudam foriciana*. A pulse that tapers off unevenly across the fingers.</note> and the **inclined** pulse. The forked-tail is found across different fingers when the pulse is thick under the first finger touching the arm, smaller under the second finger, small under the third, and smallest under the fourth. Similarly, this "tail" can be understood in terms of strong and weak, or fast and slow. But this forked-tail differs from the other mouse-tail pulse we treated earlier with the author. 

¶ The **inclined** pulse is considered according to the diversity of percussions under the four fingers: for instance, if it is thick under the two middle fingers and thin under the two outer fingers; or open in the middle and hidden at the ends. The extremity appears to incline downward from above because of a defect in the **virtue** <note>vital power</note>, which is unable to lift the substance of the organ on the side of the arm. The cause of the artery's heaviness at the extremity within the hand is solely the failure of the virtue, which scarcely reaches that point. The inclined pulse is understood similarly in terms of strength, speed, and slowness; thus, the inclined pulse and the aforementioned forked-tail can be included under the category of the branchy pulse. For there can be many species of branchy pulses. 

¶ Under this same species is also contained the **saw-like** pulse <note>original: *ferrinus*. From *ferra* or *serra*, meaning a saw.</note>, of which more will be said in what follows. This pulse moves under one finger but is quiet under three; or it moves under the first two and rests under the others; or it is strong under one, weak under the second, weaker under the third, and weakest under the fourth, such that it is not felt at all. 

¶ And this is how the pulse called the "forked-tail" could be understood: when it proceeds by gradually weakening from the first finger to the second, the second to the third, and the third to the fourth. But if it does not proceed gradually in weakness through the fourth finger—for instance, if it moves under one and rests under the others, or moves under the first two and not the others—it should be called **saw-like**. It is named from "saw," because it is likened to the teeth of a saw.

### On the fluctuating pulse.

> The stormy pulse shakes the vessels with an enormous blow.
> It fluctuates: it overflows: it roars: it seethes: and
> It surrounds the pressed finger-chambers laterally.
> A part moves upward, and backward, and forward.
> Thence you may prove the sudden tumult of the mind and heart,
> And the motion of the billowing blood in a disturbed body.

¶ In this chapter he treats the **stormy** <note>original: *procelloso*.</note> or **seething** <note>original: *estuoso*.</note> pulse according to Constantine, which Philaretus calls "fluctuation." He proceeds to show what the fluctuating pulse is and what it signifies. The seething pulse occurs when the upper part of the organ placed under the pinky finger moves forward, while under another finger the lower part moves later and more slowly. A part of the organ is felt to move downward and to the left—some parts wide, some parts narrow—just as we see in a storm at sea. 

The fluctuating pulse, therefore, occurs from an abundance of watery humor filling the body of the artery more than it should. Thus, the spirit generated in the arteries moves the watery humor existing in the arteries more in one place of the artery than in another. Because of this, a kind of inundation or surge is perceived by the senses during the pulse. And for this reason, it is called the fluctuating pulse. Such a pulse is usually found in a certain species of **dropsy** <note>original: *hydropisis*. An old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid.</note> called **anasarca** <note>A condition characterized by widespread swelling of the skin due to effusion of fluid into the extracellular space.</note>, which is an equal loosening of the flesh. This pulse sometimes signifies a perturbation of the mind, or sudden anger, or sadness, or a sudden disturbance of the humors.

### On the spasmodic pulse.

> The **spasmodic** pulse stiffens in the manner of a 
> Taut rope: it serves the phthisic <note>those suffering from wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note> and the emaciated.
