It consumes the moisture of the body: it swallows it up in emptiness. 
A more plentiful spasmodic kind occurs when the organs are filled: 
Humor is poured into the rheumatic nerves. 
Smooth limbs are deprived of their moving vigor.

¶ Here the author treats the **spasmodic pulse** <note>original: *spasmoso pulsu*. A pulse associated with convulsions or tension.</note>: which the physician calls by another name: and he explains its meanings, both the physiological kind and the spasmodic kind resulting from "repletion" <note>original: *repletione*. An excess of bodily fluids or "humors."</note>. Therefore, the physiological spasmodic pulse is said to happen when the flesh is consumed and dried out by febrile heat. Whence the artery has no place to be positioned except in the manner of a tense string, and so it is stretched. Thus, when compressed by the fingers, it shifts from right to left. For this reason, the spasmodic and the "branchy" <note>original: *ramosus*. A pulse that feels like it has multiple offshoots.</note> pulses seem to be the same. But they differ because of different causes: for in the branchy pulse, the body of the artery spreads out; but in the spasmodic, the nerve is stretched, and much hardness is felt. Thus it is called "spasmodic" because of the tension of the nerve or artery, or because it signifies a future spasm. In the branchy pulse, however, such tension does not occur as it does in the spasmodic. Therefore, the spasmodic signifies a drying of the body, a consumption of the humors, a hardening of the arteries, and excessive desiccation. It also signifies a spasm from "inanition" <note>original: *inanitione*. Exhaustion due to a lack of nourishment or fluids.</note>. However, there is a certain spasmodic pulse caused by a fullness of humors, where the artery is felt to be very swollen.

### ¶ Concerning the ant-like and worm-like pulse.

> There are twin pulses: the ant-like and the worm-like.
> They occur rather in burning and very acute fevers.
> Faithful heralds of death; they report the approach of the tomb.
> In fever, the ant-like pulse is a swift messenger of the burial mound.
> It does not return to a better state, but puts life to sleep in death.
> These types often occur, except in the heat of fever,
> When the danger of death is not urgent: fainting brings them on.

¶ Here the author treats two types of irregular pulse together: namely, the **worm-like** <note>original: *vermiculoso*. A pulse that feels like a worm crawling under the skin.</note> and the **ant-like** <note>original: *formicante*. From the Latin *formica* (ant); a pulse so small and weak it feels like an ant crawling.</note>. The worm-like pulse moves in the manner of a boiling or surging motion, but the surging pulse is larger and stronger. The worm-like is smaller and weaker: yet it is faster and more frequent, because its cause is a failing of the "virtue" <note>original: *virtus*. The "vital power" or strength of the patient.</note>. And it is called worm-like because it is felt under the fingers like the movement of worms. The ant-like pulse moves just like the worm-like, but the ant-like is smaller, more deficient, and more frequent. For in this case, its strength is entirely taken away; it is called ant-like because it feels like ants under the finger. Just as an ant has a smaller movement than a worm, so the ant-like pulse is smaller and signifies a greater deficiency than the worm-like, since its movement is the smallest, just as the movement of an ant is smaller than the movements of other animals. If any pulse fails to the point of "formication" <note>The sensation of insects crawling on the skin.</note>, and this happens from the symptoms of an acute fever and from the consumption of the spirits, one must entirely despair of the patient's life. If, however, it fails only to the worm-like stage, let him remain with you; if it does not progress to the ant-like, he does not die entirely. And note that the worm-like necessarily comes before the ant-like. If there is a return from the ant-like to the worm-like, it is a good sign; but if, on the contrary, there is a descent from the worm-like to the ant-like, it is the worst sign. ¶ The ant-like and worm-like pulses sometimes occur from a sudden dissolution of strength, such as from a great loss of blood: as in a flow from hemorrhoids, or from the nose, or from an immoderate flow of the 

<column-break/>

bowels, or of the menses in women. Because of such a great consumption or dissolution of strength due to a lack of spirits and the withdrawal of nourishment, the patient is forced into **syncope** <note>original: *syncope*. Fainting or sudden loss of consciousness.</note> and has an ant-like or worm-like pulse. However, one should not despair over such a pulse, because it happens from such a temporary cause. We sometimes see many people in syncope in whom we perceive neither breath nor pulse, who nevertheless return to their former state through the application of cold water and the comfort of aromatics. Therefore, a physician should not despair of a pulse changed by such a cause, nor should he judge the patient to be dead. ¶ For **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> gives an example of a certain woman suffering from "suffocation of the womb" <note>original: *suffocationem matricis*. A historical diagnosis where the uterus was believed to put pressure on other organs, causing breathing to stop and the pulse to vanish.</note>, in whom no pulse could be felt. He placed a finely plucked tuft of wool to her mouth; the wool moved slightly and was warmed by her breath, by which he knew she was still alive; and after applying his care, he restored her to health. But if the ant-like and worm-like pulses occur in a body where the limbs are failing and dried out from acute fevers, and not because of a sudden change in nature, then one must despair, and by such a pulse, the sentence of death is determined.

### ¶ Following is the saw-like pulse.

> The saw-like species meets the first finger
> Weakly: in the rest it becomes languid; none follow.
> This pulse draws its related name from a saw.
> Whose action, driven by the first cut of the teeth,
> Is heavy: in the rest it is heavier; it is mournful with sighs.
> This fatal saw of the pulse cuts away the vigor 
> of the body, and a lethal cloud overshadows life.

¶ Here the author treats the **saw-like pulse** <note>original: *pulsu serrino*. A pulse that feels uneven or jagged, like the teeth of a saw.</note>: and it can be understood in various ways. For sometimes it moves under one finger while it is quiet under three; or it moves under the first two and is quiet under the others; or it is strong under one, weak under another, fast under a third, and slow under a fourth. It is called "saw-like" from the saw (*serra*), because it is likened to the teeth of a saw when it makes an unequal cut. According to this, it is classified as saw-like. The saw-like pulse can be contained within certain species of the aforementioned pulses. Let it be "saw-like" when, for instance, it is felt as weak under the first finger, almost failing under the second, and is not felt at all under the third. According to this estimation, the saw-like pulse will be a certain terminal limit of the "mouse-tail" pulse.

### ¶ Here the author addresses his Muse so that she may seal the work on pulses.

> Set the boundaries for your work. The meadows have drunk enough.
> The seeds flourish. The earth, previously dry to the farmer,
> Now smiles more fully, rejoicing in the rich manure,
> And bringing forth fruits for us from a wealthy vein.
> Now it shrinks from the sterile cultivation of Philaretus’s plowshare.

These prayers were recently reviewed by a learned man and corrected of all errors.

<meta>This page transitions from the previous treatise on pulses to a new work on urines. The author, Pierleone da Spoleto, justifies writing a new text on a subject already covered by ancient authorities like Hippocrates and Galen, arguing that he is organizing their scattered insights into a unified, logical system based on Galen’s own methods.</meta>

# On Urines

¶ Here begins the treatise on urines by Pietro Leone of Spoleto, the most excellent physician of our age.

### ¶ Preface:

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicts a scholar or saint seated at a desk with an open book, representing the authority and study behind this medical text.</note>

**Some will be amazed** when they first read the title of this little book: either thinking that I am raving, or that I am far too arrogant. They might ask why a treatise on urines should be written anew by me, when the subject has already been most perfectly published by many very famous men. They might argue that I am not fit to add anything to its perfection, and that one can scarcely interpret their existing words. Therefore, they will judge it a matter of presumption or madness to compose a new edition on urines. I would easily agree with them if Hippocrates and Galen—men illuminated by a certain divine light in the art of medicine—had published a separate book on the subject. Indeed, there is nothing regarding this material that a physician ought to consider which they did not fully and abundantly determine in various places, as the nature of the matter required. You will find that nothing was truly omitted, except that they did not collect into one place those things which were handed down dispersedly. Therefore, this tradition seems to lack only that completion. Concerning this matter, many have tried to bring these teachings together into one treatise; however, they either did not follow through, or if they did collect everything, they did not put them in the order that the nature of the subject seems to demand, or that Galen would have imitated. This, therefore, is what we promise in this new tradition: that those things which were said fully and abundantly by Hippocrates and Galen in different places shall be collected into one, in the same order and reasoning process that Galen himself would have used. If anyone doubts this, let him read the short works Galen published on pulses; in them, let him contemplate not just the words or particular sentences, but rather the craftsmanship <note>original: *artificium*. Referring to the systematic method or logic of the scientific practice.</note> and the way of proceeding. Once he recognizes this, he will understand that those things regarding urines which were cast about by Galen have been brought back to Galen's own order. For this reason, I urge those who read this book not only to think they can profit in the knowledge of urines, but to see that an entrance to many other things lies open to them. This will happen if they turn their minds not only to what is said, but more importantly to the *method* of saying it. If anyone perceives this, he will understand that he has prepared for himself an easy path to Galen's doctrine and to the full and complete way of investigating any medicinal term, so that he may see clearer than light how one must proceed in the knowledge of any medicinal matter. ¶ This, therefore, is my intention: to place before you a single universal model in which the logic of order in teaching appears according to the mind of Galen. From there, it will provide clear knowledge of urines, distinct in order and perfect in reasoning.

### ¶ Division of the work.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' shows a figure holding a circular vessel, likely a 'matula' or urine flask, used by medieval physicians for uroscopy, the visual inspection of urine to diagnose illness.</note>

**The whole work is divided** into three distinctions: the first of which will investigate the definition of urine itself and its related properties. The second will demonstrate the significance of every difference in urine. The third and last will describe the diagnostic urine for every treatable condition of the body over which the significance of urine is able to extend. ¶ The first distinction, therefore, which concerns the definition of urine, will

<column-break/>

contain as many chapters as there are things necessary for knowing its complete definition. ¶ It is necessary for a physician not only to scrutinize the definition of urine so that he may perceive through the intellect by which essential differences urine differs from everything that is *not* urine, but also—since he is a craftsman who works through the senses, especially in that part dealing with signs—to gather definitions by which the senses may recognize how human urine differs from other liquids that seem to have some similarity to it. ¶ This knowledge can not undeservedly be called a "definition," since a definition is nothing other than the restriction of any thing within its own proper limits; that is, it is called a "term" <note>original: *terminus*. A boundary or limit.</note> from the act of "terminating," named after the likeness of the markers placed between fields. As the Commentator <note>A reference to Averroes (1126–1198), the famous Andalusian philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says regarding the senses: "Ends or definitions are accepted from those who dwell in the fields. Those who use some boundary distinguish and discern their own fields for themselves; those who lack such a boundary and distinction lack a definition." When a definitive statement is extended or brought to a thing, those who do not know it by its own limits, markers, or boundaries cannot separate it from other things which it is not. ¶ Deservedly, therefore, the distinctive knowledge by which the physician separates urine from other liquids through the senses can be called "definitive." But since such knowledge cannot be conveniently had unless it is first certified that the urine exists in its natural state, it is first necessary to know how it is to be collected and also preserved. This is so that before this definition (of separating it from other liquids) occurs, the urine is not changed from its natural disposition. Therefore, it is necessary to interpose a chapter before this one, which will be about the conditions to be observed in the collection and preservation of urines. ¶ Let us gather, then, that there will be three chapters of this first distinction: the first of which will collect its proper definition and its related properties. The second will note the conditions which one must observe in the taking, keeping, and inspection of urines before a judgment is passed on it—whether in separating it from other liquids or in judging its meanings. The third and last will note the differences by which human urine is discerned from other liquids and from the urines of other animals.

### ¶ On the definition of urine and the explanation of the definition. Chapter I.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' shows a seated figure, likely a physician, carefully examining a glass vessel, highlighting the importance of visual observation in medical diagnosis.</note>

**Let us begin**, therefore, from the definition and the interpretation of its name, asserting that it is called "urine" (*urina*) either because it is "made as one" (*una*) in the kidneys, or from "I burn" (*uro, uris*), or from the Greek word *ulat* <note>original: *vlat*. Possibly a corruption of 'ouros' or 'oulon', here interpreted by the author as 'demonstration'.</note> which sounds like "demonstration" in Latin. In whatever way it receives its name, according to its essential definition, urine is nothing other than that which exits from a treatable body through the penis or a proportional instrument, emitted from the bladder, kidneys, and liver; generated in the liver from the work of the nutritive power <note>The "nutritive power" was believed to be the bodily faculty responsible for converting food into tissues and fluids.</note> and segregated from the blood, signifying the conditions of the treatable body—especially those which have a relationship to the nutritive power. ¶ Many will perhaps wonder at seeing this new and unusual definition of urine, since it was defined differently by ancient doctors. Some of them assert it is a "straining of the blood," such as Theophilus; or of "the blood and other humors," such as Isaac. Some call it the "wateriness of the blood"; others the "serosity of the blood," as Giles describes it by comparison to serosity <note>term: serosity (serositas). The watery part of a fluid, similar to whey in milk.</note> or the whey-like part of milk: that the one stands in the same relation to the blood and other hu—

<meta>This page continues the introductory discussion on the nature of urine, moving from the general justification of the work to specific medical definitions and the physiological process of how urine is generated in the body.</meta>

...ways <note>original: "mozes," likely "modos" (ways) or a reference to the authority Moses Maimonides</note> that urine is to blood as serum <note>The watery portion of a fluid, like whey in milk.</note> is to milk, along with its other parts. Although these various definitions may somehow correctly define the essence of urine, they do not fully express its nature in a way that suits our current purpose. Therefore, if one looks more correctly, setting aside trivialities, they will recognize that the following definition is better suited to our goal. 

And so that we do not seem to assert this without cause, it must be understood that not only urine, but also other things considered by a physician, can be encountered in two ways. One way is when such things are considered according to what they are in themselves, absolutely, according to the specific differences considered by the physician. The other way is when they are considered by the physician insofar as they can be signs of something significant within the healable body. 

In this second way, we say a physician considers the "complexion" <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's constitution.</note>: in one way according to itself and its own characteristics, and in another way insofar as it is considered as this or 그 type. This complexion is a sign for the physician to understand something about the healable body itself. Such a consideration of it is held in the doctrine of the humors, since it is a superfluity <note>An excess or byproduct.</note> of the humors, and especially of the mass of blood. Therefore, it rightly deserves the name "aquosity," or "filtrate," or "serosity," <note>original: "aquositatis," "colamenti," "ferositatis"</note> whichever of these one prefers, as each is appropriate in such a consideration. 

Moved by this reasoning, and not unwisely, I believe it is more commonly defined for the healthy and the strong in this way. In the other way—insofar as it is a sign for the physician of the dispositions of the healable body—it falls under the categories of signs, being an "issuing action" and a "quality." If these signs behave naturally, they are called signs of health; if they are changed from their natural disposition, they are called signs of sickness. Since urine is neither an action nor a quality, it is categorized as something "issuing forth." 

Rightly, therefore, since in this our treatise urine appears more as a sign for the physician than as what it is in itself and absolutely, it is more conveniently defined as: "that which issues from a healable body," and "a filtrate," or "superfluity," "aquosity," or "serosity" of the blood and other humors. 

And lest we seem to be inventing fables, Galen, as a most true and perfect craftsman, shows us this double treatment among his actions on pulses. He shows the first in his book *On the Usefulness of Pulses*, where, if we observe with diligent reasoning, we will understand the pulse was considered by him as to what it is in itself. He shows the second in his books *On the Differences of Pulses* and in his *Commentary on Pulses*, in which he demonstrated nothing except how the pulse signifies the dispositions of the healable body. 

Perhaps moved by this same reasoning, Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> in his third or second doctrine also omitted the definition of urine, recognizing that the one gathered from the treatise on humors did not suit his consideration here.

It was further said that it travels from the liver to the kidneys, and from the kidneys to the bladder, and is emitted from the bladder through the "rod" <note>The penis; original: "virgam."</note> or an instrument proportional to it. In this way, its exit differs from that of sweat and other things which, although they are "issuing forth," do not exit through these primary members. Although sperm also exits through the "rod," it is not emitted from the liver to the bladder and from the bladder to the "rod," but proceeds through its own pathways and the seminal vessels. Similarly, even if the menstrual flow has its exit through a specific instrument, the matter itself is not transmitted from the liver through the kidneys and bladder.

Next, it was said to be generated in the liver by the nutritive faculty, and thus separated from the blood. From this, authors took the opportunity to define urine as the "filtrate of blood." However, we must understand by "blood" not simply the primary blood separated from other humors—as that would be false—but rather the "mass of blood" which aggregates the remaining

<column-break/>

humors within itself. This is how Theophilus <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century Byzantine medical writer.</note> understood it in the definition he gave for urine. Isaac <note>Isaac Israeli ben Solomon, a 10th-century physician and philosopher.</note>, understanding this correctly, expressed it more clearly here, saying: "urine is the filtrate of the blood and of the other humors, produced by the actions of nature." The "efficient cause" and the "location" are natural heat or the nutritive faculty, and the matter is asserted to be the "chyle" of the liver.

<margin>
The mode of blood generation in the liver.
</margin>
But let us proceed and show that this "issuing forth" is generated in the liver by the nutritive faculty and sequestered from the blood. This will be easy if the mode of generation, the location, and the matter are first understood—both for the useful flow and the superfluity. The "useful" part is the blood and its mass, while the "superfluity" is the urine, since it is its aquosity or filtrate. 

The mode of blood generation is as follows: food and drink are masticated and ground by the teeth, prepared for digestion, and then brought into the belly or stomach by the attractive faculty of the stomach. Retained there by the retentive faculty, it is mostly digested by the natural heat of the stomach, with the help of other adjacent members. It is converted into a partial mass or "chyle." Once digested and converted into chyle, the "gatekeeper" <note>The pylorus; original: "portanarius."</note> at the bottom of the stomach opens, and the whole chyle mass descends first into the duodenum, then to the jejunum. From there, the earthy and dreg-like part <note>Fecal matter.</note> descends to the lower intestines. 

The thinner, liquid, and chylous portion is drawn through the meseraic veins <note>Mesenteric veins.</note> to the "gate of the liver" or the "milky vein" <note>original: "venam lacteam," here referring to the portal vein system.</note> by the expulsive faculty of the stomach. With the help of the liver’s attractive faculty, this matter is dispersed through the liver into its smallest veins and pores, communicated throughout the whole liver so that a more perfect digestion may be produced. Thus, the blood-making faculty of the liver, with its natural heat, works upon this chyle, transmuting it into blood and the other humors simultaneously, and into the "urinal aquosity," which is generated alongside the blood mass for the sake of penetration <note>To help the humors flow through the narrow vessels.</note>. Such, therefore, is the mode, location, agent, and matter of the generation of blood and other humors, as well as of urine.

<margin>
The mode of urine generation.
</margin>
From this, it is further particularly and clearly gathered that urine is generated in the liver by the nutritive faculty, and is separated from the blood therein. However, because of its confusion and mixing with the blood mass—which is falsely imagined as long as it remains in the liver and veins with the blood—some have taken the opportunity to assert that urine does not have a proper, distinct, and specific existence in the liver itself. Consequently, they claim it is neither generated nor separated from the blood there, but claims its proper and separate existence only in the kidneys.

<margin>
Whether urine is naturally in the kidneys, or separated.
</margin>
They argue that everything is separated from others and distinguished by its formal act. As Haly Abbas <note>original: "Daliabas," referring to the 10th-century Persian physician Haly Abbas.</note> says in the seventh book of his *Theorica*: "Thus urine is the aquosity of the blood, which the kidneys separate and purge from it." Gilles <note>Gilles de Corbeil (Egidius), a 12th-century physician.</note> says the same, asserting that urine is said to "become one" in the kidneys—that is, it becomes separated, distinct, and specific. 

To these we respond by asserting that urine, before it reaches the kidneys, obtains a proper and specific essence, even though it does not appear separate to us in its natural exit until after passing through the kidneys. However, in an unnatural exit, such as through the opening of a vein <note>Bloodletting.</note>, after the blood has settled, the "urinal aquosity" truly appears separate. This is called "prochor" <note>original: "procor," a term for the watery serum in blood.</note> by physicians, as stated in the *Second Book of Elements*. From this, it appears that there is no need to say, as the "Conciliator" <note>Pietro d'Abano, author of the *Conciliator Differentiarum*.</note> says, that there are two forms of urine: one essential and true, and the other accidental and apparent. The first is given to it in the liver, while the second is in the kidneys. He adds: "Since this second form is more manifest and sensible, and the physician is a craftsman of the senses, the physician considers this second and accidental form." Since this is completed in the kidneys, physicians say it is "proper" for it to be in the kidneys. He says the same thing as a proposition...

# On Urines

<columns>
...maintaining one form: and that it is essential: and that it is perceptible to the senses at the same time: and that it is produced in the liver. This is evident to all by signs, and it can be proven by logic founded upon those same signs, as follows: When the kidneys are diseased, but the liver and veins remain healthy, it happens that the urine appears "digested" <note>In uroscopy, "digested" urine is clear and well-colored, indicating that the body's internal heat has properly processed the humors.</note>. Since it was already digested before it ever reached the kidneys, this could not occur unless it had its own existence before arriving there—and this can only happen in the liver. Therefore, urine is generated in the liver. And this is what Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was the foundational text for medieval European medicine.</note> says: mature urine demonstrates the health of the veins, because illnesses of the kidneys do not prevent maturation.

It is confirmed: where a certain form of humor is initiated, its superfluity <note>A "superfluity" is a byproduct of the body's metabolic processes; medicine of this era viewed urine, sweat, and feces as leftovers from the three stages of digestion.</note> is produced by the same source, through the same production and digestion. But the humors are generated by the work of the nutritive virtue in the liver. Therefore, since urine is their superfluity, it must be generated in its own right in the liver by that same nutritive virtue.

The same can be argued from the "indigestion" of urine. It signifies, above all, the dispositions of the liver itself, as shall be said, because it is generated in the liver. For the consequence holds: origins bear witness to their principles. There, it is separated from the blood and other humors, just like other superfluities: for example, the frothy parts which are later carried to the gallbladder, and the dregs to the spleen. Thus, the "aquosity" <note>The watery portion of the blood.</note> glides through the vena cava <note>original: "chilin venam," referring to the great central vein.</note> with a small amount of blood to the kidneys, and from there to the bladder, and is finally expelled from the bladder.

<margin>The regions of the urine in proportion to the principal parts of our body.</margin>

This was the final point placed in the definition: it is a signifier of healable dispositions, especially of those parts attributed to the work of nutrition. And even if other things exiting the body share this trait—in that they signify the dispositions within the body—none do so as universally. Thus, urine is a signifier for many dispositions of the limbs. While urine, along with other excretions, relates to the digestion of all parts, those other excretions only represent the specific members of which they are the superfluity. For example, feces represent the first digestion and the members through which they pass, the stomach and intestines. Sweat signifies the third digestion and the fleshy members, muscles, and skin. Mucus signifies the brain and the chest. Even sperm, though it exits the body and its qualities could signify something, is called a "useful superfluity" because of its noble end—reproduction—rather than a "signifying superfluity." Therefore, it is not numbered among the excretions that define health.

Only urine among the excretions holds the primary place in the universality and certainty of its significance. This is much like the pulse among the actions of the body, because it signifies more certainly and universally than other actions. Urine signifies in many ways: by its color, its substance <note>The thickness or consistency of the liquid.</note>, and other factors, as will be made clear below, whereas other excretions signify through far fewer characteristics. Furthermore, urine signifies across all three digestions, although most principally the second digestion and its organs. Though some may doubt this, it will be proven by reason shortly, in the section where we determine the specific significance of the *hypostasis* <note>The sediment or "contents" that settle at the bottom of a urine sample.</note>.

Let us say, therefore, that urine generally signifies the dispositions of all members. While this is easily understood regarding the organs where it is generated or through which it is emitted, it is difficult to know how urine can certify us regarding distant or extreme members. Yet it can, if one considers the logic of the "regions" found in the urine. Through differences in color and contents in the various regions, we are certified in various ways regarding the dispositions of different members based on their location. By this reasoning, it is clear that any part of the urine, or any specific region, does not signify just any part of the body, but rather a determined region of urine signifies a determined member.

Physicians state there are four principal parts or members of the human body. First are the "animal" parts, located in the highest part. Second are the "spiritual" parts. Third are the "natural" parts, and fourth are the "generative" parts. Four different sites in the body correspond to these. The first is the highest site of the animal parts, and their principal member is the brain. The sec-

<column-break/>

-ond site is that of the spiritual parts, namely the chest and its contents, the principal of which is the heart. The third is the site of the natural parts, the principal of which is the liver. The fourth is the site of the generative or lower parts, among which the kidneys, testicles, and other lower members are numbered. To these four various sites of the members, four sites in the urine correspond proportionally, which physicians call "regions."

The first region corresponds to the animal members and their location; this is the **circle** <note>The "crown" or topmost ring of the urine in the glass.</note>. The second region bears witness to the spiritual parts, their location, and qualities; this is the entire **surface** or the "airy body" <note>The area just below the surface of the liquid.</note>. The third is for the natural parts, regarding their perfection or **substance**. The fourth is for the generative or lower parts, which is the entire **bottom** <note>The base of the flask where sediment collects.</note>.

From this comes the foundation of what is commonly said: that a thick "circle" at the top signifies a heaviness of the head. Regarding the second region: urine showing lines on the "surface" signifies a fault of the chest. Regarding the third: thinness in the "substance" of the urine signifies dryness of the liver, while its thickness signifies humidity. Regarding the fourth: small grains or "sand" portend a fault of *lithiasis*—that is, a stone.

And so that we may demonstrate the universal significance of urine over the dispositions of all members and the proportionality of its regions, let us assume that the members of our body differ in location, nature, and physical substance. Because of their fluidity and the continuous heat of our body, they require constant restoration from the blood or secondary humors lest they perish. They require nourishment that differs in nature and substance, just as the members themselves differ. Although the full diversity of the nourishing blood is only realized when it is finally carried to the members to feed them, this process must begin in the liver. Afterwards, the blood is transmitted proportionally to each part, and a substance similar to each member is sent by the common expulsive virtue, aided by the specific attractive virtue of each individual member. Therefore, it follows that in the whole mass of blood, there is a "trace" and an initiated diversity of these members. And since the "aquosity" of the urine is found mixed with the blood, it follows that in the urine, in its own way, a similar impression of this alteration is made, leaving a trace of those members and their qualities.

<margin>Members are the same in location, yet different in nature and substance, and they require different nourishment.</margin>

This is deduced even more strongly: the aquosity of the urine flows through the veins with the blood, as proven above, for no other reason than to make the blood penetrate more easily into narrow places. It is carried with the blood to the farthest members. Since the blood is diverse according to the requirements of the members it must nourish, the aquosity of the urine mixed with that blood will also be diverse. But blood is not only diverse in its "complexion" <note>The balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> and substance, but also in other distinctions, such as its location and thickness, because the members themselves are different.

Since the brain is light and of a subtle substance compared to other members, it is necessary that the blood which nourishes it be light and of a subtle substance. Otherwise, it would not be proportional to it, nor could it be carried or transmitted to the higher places—such as the head—unless it were of such a nature. The aquosity of the urine mixed with it to help it penetrate is, in a similar way, light and subtle, conforming to the complexion and nature of the brain. When it is later expelled as a superfluity—either partly through sweat, or by flowing back through the veins to the liver, then to the kidneys, and finally to the bladder—it follows that in the whole mass of urine, that portion which comes from the brain by this reflux will have a high and supreme position in comparison to the other portions coming from the other members. This is just as the brain holds its place among the other members. It will have traces impressed upon it in color, substance, and content that are proportional to the brain.

...matter: it was never in the brain. Therefore, it cannot carry a significance regarding the brain's disposition through its physical substance, nor can it hold the uppermost position in the urine flask by direct physical likeness to the brain. For as has been said, a certain portion of aqueousness <note>In the humoral system, "aqueousness" is the watery byproduct of the blood-making process.</note> always passes with the blood to the nourishing members. Since this does not convert into the actual substance of the organ—being a type of superfluity <note>A "superfluity" is an excess or waste product of digestion.</note>—it must necessarily be expelled, either imperceptibly through sweat and vapors, or subtly through the reflux to the proper channels of the urine. ¶ It can also be proven another way. The "spirit" existing in the brain is informed by the shape and property of the brain; it proceeds to the liver and there distinguishes a portion of blood proportional and suitable to the brain. It informs, alters, and changes that blood to the nature of the brain for the purpose of its nourishment. Since it is then certain that it changes the aqueous moisture mixed with that blood, that moisture receives an impression in its own way, just as the blood it is mixed with does. Thus, when it exits, it retains the "footprints" of the brain impressed upon it by the spirit. In this way, its position in the flask and other qualities are proportional to the brain. Consequently, the <term>circle</term><note>The "circulus" refers to the uppermost ring or surface of the urine in the glass flask (matula).</note>, since it is that specific portion, rightly signifies the disposition of the brain. In a similar way, this is to be understood regarding the other members of the body. ¶ As for the <term>spiritual members</term><note>The "spiritual members" traditionally refer to the heart and lungs, which were believed to be the seat of the "vital spirit."</note>, although they are naturally hot—even hotter than the brain because of their constant motion—they are nevertheless of a dense and thick substance. They require thick blood for their proper nourishment. Therefore, it is necessary that the portion of urine representing them, being mixed with such thick blood, should be proportional in disposition. Its place will be immediately inside the circle; because it is hot, it seeks a higher location (as heat rises), but because it is of a thick substance, it resides just below the circle. From its signs and impressions, we recognize the state of those same organs. ¶ The <term>natural members</term><note>The "natural members" are the digestive organs, primarily the liver and stomach.</note>, especially the nutritive ones like the liver, are also hot, yet less so than the spiritual members. They are also more humid and thicker. It follows that as their blood is proportional to their nourishment, so too is their superfluity. Because of the conflict between the heat moving it upward and its thick substance moving it downward, it occupies the middle position in the entire volume of urine. ¶ Finally, the <term>inferior members</term><note>The lower limbs and pelvic organs.</note>, being cold and earthy, require blood proportional to themselves, and must have a similar aqueousness. Therefore, the portion of urine proportional to them will hold the lowest place due to its gravity, and it will preserve within itself the impression of the complexion and nature of those members.

¶ Although it has been clearly demonstrated from these facts that urine is a universal sign of the disposition of all members, it does not certify each one equally. It provides certainty about different members to a greater or lesser degree. There are some members about which urine signifies directly, immediately, and manifestly: such as the liver and the veins, and especially the "hump" of the liver. This is because the urine, being generated there, carries the footprints of the <term>complexion</term><note>The "complexion" is the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an organ.</note>, humors, and virtues existing within it. This appears in the chapter on substance and content. The same is true for the large veins near the liver, the <term>vena chilis</term><note>The "vena chilis" refers to the vena cava, the large vein carrying blood to the heart.</note>, the urinary pores (ureters), the kidneys, the bladder, and the "chamber of the rod" <note>Original: "thalamo virge," referring to the urethral canal of the penis.</note> through which it passes; from these, it brings signs of their disposition, especially regarding what is contained within them. ¶ There are some members, however, for which it does not signify as primarily, such as the smaller and capillary veins. Since such aqueousness is mixed with the blood and transmitted through the veins, it often seeps back to the kidneys—either by the strength of the veins' expulsive power or the weakness of their retentive power, or by the kidneys' own attractive strength. Bringing with it the impression of those parts, it signifies upon them. Their significance is best observed in the <term>hypostasis</term><note>The "hypostasis" is the sediment that settles at the bottom of the urine flask.</note>. ¶ There are a third group of members about whose dispositions it is said to signify lastly and least directly, providing the least certainty: such as the extremities (hands and feet). For these, physicians have devised a way to weigh the diversity of the "regions" <note>The "regions" are the vertical zones of the urine flask (top, middle, bottom).</note>. For even if other things

<column-break/>

considered in urines—regarding the complexions of certain members, the abundance of humors in them, and the action of the vital virtue—can signify through the sediment, they can provide very little certainty about individual specific members. This is only possible by observing the various differences in color and content in the various regions, as was demonstrated above.

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'S' depicts a seated figure, likely a physician or scholar, within a square decorative frame.</note>
<margin>1st condition</margin>
**There are** fourteen conditions to be observed in judging urines. ¶ The first of these is that it should be taken in the morning after digestion is complete. Only then is the urine a true indicator of how much the natural heat is worth in digesting the humors, and in demonstrating other dispositions. For if it were taken at night or in the evening before digestion is complete, it would undoubtedly signify "indigestion." However, this would not arise from a defect in the power of the natural heat, but rather simply from the short time it remained in the body; it was not held long enough to receive the full impression of the natural heat. Similarly, if it were taken a long time after digestion was completed and after a long fast, it would show signs of "ignition" and overheating. This would not stem from an excess of natural heat, but from a lack of nutritional material for the heat to act upon and be tempered by. Therefore, the judgment of the urine would be deceptive if it were taken at any hour other than the morning hour. <margin>2nd</margin> ¶ The second condition: it must not sit for more than six hours after it has been passed, according to the common opinion of physicians. Avicenna, however, explicitly stated that it should not even pass one hour. The reason for this limit on the hours is that after that time, it is altered by the surrounding air, either in color, substance, or content. Because of this, the judgment is corrupted and its significance is weakened by the change in color or the dissolution and thickening of the sediment. <margin>3rd</margin> ¶ The third condition: it must not be saved from the night before. The reason for this is not only that digestion might not have been fully celebrated at that hour, but most importantly because even if digestion were perfectly complete, the night is cold. It is the nature of cold to condense, to make things "raw" (undigested), and to hinder the separation of parts. Therefore, becoming "raw" and lacking proper separation due to the impression of the night air, its judgment would be deceptive. <margin>4th</margin> ¶ The fourth condition: it should not be taken from a person who did not eat or drink on the preceding day. If they had not, the urine would be thinned and tinted by the inflammation of heat, and thus a correct judgment would be hindered. The same is to be understood, by contrast, regarding those who have overindulged, as will appear in the sixth condition. <margin>5th</margin> ¶ The fifth condition: the person from whom the urine is taken must not have previously consumed food or drink that tints the urine, nor should they have touched it with a staining substance. Because of such a color—impressed upon it accidentally—a false judgment would then be made regarding the disposition of the body. The specific things that tint urine are saffron (*crocus*), cassia fistula, and dyer’s madder (*rubra tinctorum*). Experience proves and the opinion of physicians <note>The text cites "Sal.," likely the School of Salerno or Galen.</note> confirms that each of these tints urine accidentally. Regarding dyer’s madder, the School of Salerno made mention; of cassia, Avicenna spoke explicitly. One can also reasonably say the same of saffron, wine, rhubarb, and many other things. Those things that tint urine perfectly are like henna (*alcanna*) and kermes (*bermis*), which one must also guard against in their own way. <margin>6th</margin> ¶ The sixth condition: it is not only from food and drink, as said in the fourth condition, but also that...

# On Urines

## Column 1

...and that it should not be notably or improperly altered by any of the <term>non-natural things</term><note>In medieval medicine, "non-naturals" were external factors that influenced health, such as air, diet, sleep, and emotions.</note> affecting the body; otherwise, the urine might be changed from its natural disposition and our correct judgment might be corrupted. These factors are primarily: anger, fear, joy, wakefulness, and excessive movement of the body, and the like. For all these things tint the urine toward a citron or red color, while their opposites cause a loss of color. Similarly, sport, bathing, and especially sexual intercourse greatly change the urine. Among these, intercourse not only alters the color of the urine but also makes its substance thick and notably changes its contents. The same judgment applies to notable evacuations of the bowels, vomiting, or <term>phlebotomy</term><note>The practice of bloodletting.</note>. Therefore, since all these things vary the judgment of the urine, it must be presupposed that the body from which the urine is taken is in a steady state regarding all these factors.

<margin>7th</margin>The seventh condition is that the entire urine should be collected, and not mixed from several different times. For if it were taken in parts, the proper form of the <term>hypostasis</term><note>The sediment that settles at the bottom of a urine flask, used to diagnose the health of the lower body.</note> would not be formed; and if it were taken mixed, the separation of parts would be totally hindered, and thus it cannot be judged correctly. <margin>8th</margin>The eighth condition: that it should not be judged at the very beginning when it is voided, but one should wait at least half an hour <note>original: "mediū bore" — likely referring to a specific interval or "middle of the hour" required for the urine to settle.</note>; for in that time the separation of the sediment will occur. If it has a shape, a firm disposition of color and substance will also be formed, by which it can be judged correctly. If by chance the substance should change from thin to thick, or vice versa, or from one color to another, the sediment could be changed. Then there is no doubt that a judgment delivered at the beginning would have been false, since those things which were to be present were not yet in the urine.

<margin>9th</margin>The ninth condition: that as far as possible, it should not be altered by any exterior thing, such as wind, sun, heat, or cold, lest its transparency be disturbed, or its substance and sediment be congealed, dissolved, or changed in color. Therefore, those who keep it near a fire err, since the fire, by its strong action, breaks up the sediment, thins or thickens the substance, and provides a tint; likewise, extreme cold has an effect. Thus, if someone judges the conditions of the body based on the dispositions found in the urine after such an occurrence, their judgment will be erroneous. <margin>10th</margin>The tenth condition is: that it should be received in a vessel of clear glass, or pure, bright crystal, of a suitable size and with a rounded bottom. For if the glass is not clear but has some other cloudy color, it would impart a similar color to the urine itself. Likewise, if it were not perfectly clear, the true color of the urine could not be clearly perceived. Similarly, if its bottom were not round, the shape of the sediment and its suspension could not be recognized; thus an error would occur in judging. From this, the error of those who wish to judge urine in glazed earthenware vessels, or in cups, vials, or ampoules, is gathered.

<margin>11th</margin>The eleventh condition is: that it should be inspected in a bright place, but not under a ray of the sun, nor where a ray is reflected, whether from the sun or another luminous body whose reflection might occur, representing a deceptive color in the urine. For in a sunbeam, the transparency, color, and substance of the urine appear much different than they are in reality. Therefore, one must beware of this, and similarly of the reverberation of things that impress a color.

<margin>12th</margin>The twelfth condition is: that less trust should be placed in the urines of children than in those of other ages, and especially those who are nourished by milk. This is because the tinting matter in them is quiet and submerged; for example, the color and perfection of maturation do not yet appear because of their very long sleep and superabundance of moisture.

<margin>13th</margin>The thirteenth: that it should not be moved from place to place, nor transposed from vessel to vessel, nor shaken, because the sediment is broken and dispersed and mixes with the substance of the urine, thereby hindering a true judgment.

<margin>14th</margin>The fourteenth and final condition is that, before a final opinion on the significance of the urine is delivered, one must distinguish between the urine of a human—not only from the urines of other animals—but also from other liquids that seem to have a likeness to human urine.

## Column 2

This teaching will be handed down in the following chapter through its own signs.

## On the assignment of differences by which human urines can be distinguished from other liquids having some likeness to urine, and also from the urines of certain animals.

### Chapter III.

<note>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'L' contains stylized foliage and floral motifs.</note>
The liquids that are not urine, yet seem to have a certain likeness to it, are these: syrup of vinegar, a decoction of figs, <term>hydromel</term><note>A mixture of honey and water.</note> (or honey-water), water tinted with saffron, and chickpea broth. These are known to be distinguished from urine by this reasoning: the more you bring them close to you and join them to your sight, the clearer they appear. But the further you move them from your sight, the more turbulent they will seem. The opposite happens in the urines of humans: the closer they are inspected, the thicker and more turbid they appear; but from further away, they seem thinner and clearer. The cause of this is assigned as such: in human urine, a great portion of <term>humors</term><note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that medieval doctors believed governed health.</note> is mixed in, which cannot be perceived from afar. In other liquids, it happens otherwise, since no humoral substance is mixed in them. Therefore, up close, turbulence and thickness cannot appear, though they may well appear from a distance.

From this it is gathered: that if a little beaten egg white is mixed with any of these liquids, or the dust of sticky earth, they cannot be discerned from human urine. And this is the difference that can be had on the part of the substance or the transparency. Besides this difference, there are others. For on the part of color: no urine is so deprived of odor that it does not have some, even if small, stench in comparison to these liquids.

And there is another sign of distinction on the part of the contents: and this first regarding the froth. In hydromel, the froth is citron-colored; in urine, however, it is never so, for it is either white or green, as in jaundice.

Secondly, regarding the content which is the sediment: human urine is separated from other liquids. For in a decoction of figs, in which the appearance of sediment is greatest among other liquids, it tends to descend to the sides of the bottom of the vessel and does not reside in the middle like true sediment <note>original: "hypostasis"</note>. Furthermore, it has an irregular motion and lacks a trace of color; these three conditions can by no means concur together in human urine, although perhaps sometimes one might easily happen without the other. For instance, the lateral descent of sediment can also happen in human urine. This is because, from the beginning of its collection, the sediment was pushed to the side of the urine by ascending fumes or vapors, or by dispersing windiness. But if its motion occurs, it will either be ordered, or some trace of color will appear in it.

The animals whose urines are encountered as needing to be discerned from human urines are these: the donkey, the horse, the ox, the pig, the sheep, the goat, and the camel.

<margin>Why the urines of donkeys are thicker than the urines of humans, but their milk is thinner.</margin>The urine of the donkey is similar to liquefied butter in the thickness of its substance, in turbulence regarding its transparency, and in whiteness regarding its color. In a human, such substance and transparency never coincide with such a color. The reason why this appears in donkeys is this: because it produces many thick superfluities in the second digestion by way of its blood, which is very thick and cold because of its cold complexion. It does not perfectly separate these from the blood because of its lack of heat and the width of the urinary passages, which cause the urinary wateriness to descend again mixed with many thick superfluities. In humans, however, because of the passages, it appears thinner, clearer, and more tinted in color. But it happens otherwise in the generation of donkey milk: because the vessels leading to the breasts are narrower, and the breasts themselves are colder than the breasts of a woman; thus it happens that the milk is more watery and thinner than the milk of a woman.

<margin>Why the urines of horses and many others are more citron-colored than the urines of donkeys.</margin>The urines of horses and mules, although they are very similar to these in substance and transparency, are more citron-colored than those of donkeys.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on distinguishing human urine from animal urine, specifically focusing on the differences between the urine of horses, asses, oxen, sheep, goats, and deer. # On Urines

...[These urines] are difficult to distinguish, as they are somewhat citron-colored. Furthermore, they are non-uniform in their **transparency**; for in the upper part they appear to be of a clear substance, but in the lower part they are more turbulent and thicker than those of asses. The reason for these two <note>Referring to horses and asses.</note> is this: since these two animals are by nature far warmer, by their heat they not only tint the urine more but also separate its parts better. Therefore, it is no wonder if they appear citron in color and non-uniform in transparency. This is why the upper part appears clearer, as the thicker parts are separated from it and descend to the bottom; the lower part, however, is more turbulent due to the descent of those thick parts. The urine of **oxen**, since it seems to hold a middle ground between the aforementioned asses and horses, must be distinguished from human urine by the same reasoning.

<margin>Why the urines of sheep resemble human urines.</margin>
The urines of **sheep** are indeed more similar to human urines in odor, substance, and transparency. For they are sub-citrine <note>original: "subcitrine"; a pale, lemon-yellow color</note>, thin, and clear; and this is because they are closer to the human <term>complexion</term><note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) within a living being.</note>, especially if they graze on good herbs. Nonetheless, in their substance, they are far thinner and have a sediment similar to the <term>dregs of oil</term><note>original: "amurce olei"; the watery, bitter sediment that settles from olive oil.</note>, which does not occur in the urines of humans, as they do not usually multiply such a surplus of humors. The urines of **goats** and **deer** are thinner in substance than the urines of oxen, and clearer than the urines of sheep, and they lack sediment; all of which proceed from the dryness and coldness of such animals, as well as the narrowness of their passages.

### In which the differences to be observed in urines are noted; the descriptions and meanings of these differences are gathered; of which there will be three parts. The 1st will note the substantial differences. The 2nd will explain their descriptions. The 3rd will demonstrate their meanings. Distinction II.

## On the classification of the categories of things from which significance in urine is drawn. Chapter I.

**H**aving dispatched these matters, the next step is to approach the subject itself more closely: namely, to treat the meanings of urines. This, however, can by no means be done unless we know the categories of things from which meaning is taken in urines, and the differences of those categories, until we arrive at the indivisible parts, and a name is assigned to each difference, and it is described by comparison, and afterward, the meaning of the same is denoted. This applies both to each difference taken by itself and to those joined with any other or others of the remaining differences.

Beginning then in order, let us say that the categories of things from which significance in urine is taken are eight: namely, **substance**, **transparency**, **odor**, **flavor**, **manner of voiding**, **color**, and **content**. All these, or most of them, ought to be considered in everything that exits the body, so that a certain indication can be taken from them. Hence, in the stool, mucus, sweat, and the rest, these things must always be considered. Urine is of the category of things that exit, as was proven above; therefore, these things must also be contemplated in urine, so that a correct and complete significance may be had from it regarding the dispositions of the members of the human body. The sufficiency of these eight categories can be understood by reason as follows. Whatever dispositions are found in urine are either in the liquid itself, or in the content <note>The sediment or floating matter.</note>, or in the urine by reason of the content. If in the urine itself and its liquid: then they are in its substance, or in its <term>accidents</term><note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is an attribute that does not belong to the essence of a thing (like color or smell).</note>, taking substance as we shall say below when we assign the descriptions of these terms. If in the first way, it is one category of things to be considered: which is the substance of the humors. If by reason of an accident: then it is either of its quantity, or quality, or its state or "having." If in the first way: it is **quantity**, and it is another category. If by reason of quality: then either

<column-break/>

of a tangible or gustable quality: and these are cast aside from the observation of the physician, although they are not excluded by my reasoning. If it is by reason of smell, it is another category: which is **odor**. Or if it is visible: and that visible thing is either proper <note>Specifically belonging to that sense.</note>, and thus another category is **color**. If it is a common visible <note>A quality perceived by multiple senses or general observation.</note>, it is **transparency**. If it is by reason of its state, or the way it behaves: since urine is nothing other than an exit, the **manner of voiding** will be observed in it, which constitutes another category. If, in the tenth place, we consider the disposition of the urine by reason of what stands within it: it will be the final category to be considered in the <term>hypostasis</term> or **content** of the urine, along with those things reduced to it, such as the circle <note>The ring at the surface of the urine.</note>, bubbles, and the like.

<margin>In each</margin>
In each of these categories, one must descend further by dividing them, so that all the differences of urines may be fully and perfectly collected. Let us say, then, that the **substance** of urine is threefold: one is thin or subtle; another is thick or fat; and the rest is mediocre. This category of content has these three differences. Unless one wished to divide these three differences further according to an assignment of degrees: thin, thinner, thinnest; thick, thicker, thickest; mediocre on the side of thin, mediocre on the side of thick, and simply mediocre. According to this method, it can reasonably be stated otherwise: dense, thinner, and mediocre; moderately dense, and moderately thin. There will also be a category of consideration from which significance is taken in urine, which is **quantity**; and let it be distributed into further differences in this manner: continuous and discrete quantity. Continuous quantity is distributed into the differences of **much**, **little**, and **mediocre**. This refers to the urine that is voided regarding its continuous quantity: it is either much, little, or of mediocre quantity; and this must be understood by making a comparison to the quality and quantity of things ingested. Discrete quantity likewise has further differences: for there is that which is voided many times and **frequently**, and there is that which is voided **rarely** and in few instances. The third category is taken from its **transparency** or translucency, the differences of which are clarity, turbulence (or darkness), and their mediocrity. And degrees can be assigned to these differences: clear, more clear, very clear; clear-turbid, more turbid, very turbid; mediocre on one side; clear and simply mediocre. The fourth category is **odor**, the differences of which are sharp, sweet, foul, and lacking odor. The fifth category is **flavor**, the differences of which are tasteless, salty, sharp, bitter, sour, and harsh <note>original: "ponticus"; a dry, astringent flavor like an unripe fruit.</note>. The diversity of these differences can also be assigned further by degrees: namely, intense, relaxed, and mediocre. However, it is known that while flavor is considered by the physician regarding sensory experience, it is not found in practice today; its doctrine is written not for sensory use and experience, but for a complete understanding of the things to be considered. <note>The author clarifies that while medical theory includes the flavor of urine, medieval doctors were moving away from actually tasting it, though the knowledge remained part of the diagnostic framework.</note> The sixth is the **manner of emitting urine**, or the manner of voiding, the differences of which are: easily and without labor; and with difficulty and effort. But after this, the difference still undergoes division into further differences. For that which is emitted without labor is either voluntary or involuntary; and further, that which is emitted involuntarily comes out either imperceptibly or with pain. By the same reasoning, that which is voided with difficulty and effort can be emitted with pain or without pain. Beyond this, it is not permitted to descend further into differences. The seventh category of those things to be considered in the meanings assumed from urine is **color**; and its differences are manifold and very difficult to know, both because of their multiplicity and even more because of the variety of authors in assigning the differences of colors and their number. For different doctors name the colors of urines differently, assign their differences in various ways, situate the same colors in order differently, and note their number in various ways.

<meta>This page continues the classification of urines, moving from the comparison of human and animal urines into a technical breakdown of urine colors and "contents" (sediment and floating particles) based on the authorities of Gilles de Corbeil, Maurus, Theophilus, and Avicenna.</meta>

# On Urines

Therefore, in this section, there is a need for the highest level of reasoning and a systematic approach, so that the knowledge of colors may be clear and the various opinions of the doctors may be brought into harmony. Regarding this, it must first be understood concerning the number of these colors: Gilles <note>Gilles de Corbeil (Egidius Corboliensis), a 12th-century physician.</note> lists twenty, while Maurus and Theophilus <note>Maurus of Salerno and Theophilus Protospatharius, influential Byzantine and Salernitan medical authors.</note> similarly set the number at nineteen. Avicenna, however, assigns thirty-two colors; and even more can be discovered if their differences are examined subtly according to the nature of the matter, as will be shown below. The differences among all these authors are reconciled as follows: Gilles, Maurus, and Theophilus, who proposed fewer colors, considered only those which can be perceived and clearly recognized by the physician’s senses, since the practitioner himself is a sensory craftsman. Avicenna and any others who assign more colors follow the nature of the thing itself. Gilles, through Maurus and Theophilus, enumerates these colors: white, milky, blue-gray <note>original: "glaucuz"</note>, saffron-yellow <note>original: "kropon"; from the Greek "krokos"</note>, pale, sub-pale, citrine, sub-citrine, reddish-yellow <note>original: "ruffuz"</note>, sub-reddish-yellow, red, sub-red, rubicund <note>a deep, healthy red</note>, sub-rubicund, wine-colored <note>original: "inopon"; from the Greek "oinopos"</note>, dark blue <note>original: "kyanon"</note>, green, lead-colored <note>original: "liuiduz"</note>, and black. When these are doubled <note>likely referring to the "sub-" variations or intensity levels</note>, they all fall into the count of twenty. If no logic for this partition and order is assigned by those doctors, I nevertheless believe the reasoning for the division and order to be this: that from one extreme, which is simply white, a transition is made to the other extreme, the color black, through intermediate colors up to the simple middle, which is reddish-yellow or sub-reddish-yellow; and proceeding from there through the others to the final extreme, as can easily be seen by anyone looking closely.

But there is another method of division, far more complete and technical, which follows the nature of the matter more than sensory recognition. It collects the numbers, names, and degrees or differences of colors in this way: Every color of urine is either **simple** or **composite**, as was expressed in Avicenna's own division. But afterward, the members of each category are assigned different distinctions. Thus, for the **composite** color, the distribution into its differences is as follows: Every composite color is either like meat-washings <note>original: "lotura carnis"; the pinkish-red water left after washing raw meat</note>, or oily, or fatty, or an oily color mixed with that which is like meat-washings, or it is flesh-colored, or it is mixed from red with blackness. However, the fatty color is threefold: for the whole urine may appear fatty, or only the upper part, or the lower part. Similarly, the oily color is threefold: either in color only, as at the beginning of an illness; or in substance only; or in both, as in diseases of the kidneys or in wasting conditions at the end. And so, in total, there are ten differences of composite colors: first, like meat-washings; then flesh-colored. Second, red with blackness. Third, oily mixed with meat-washings. Fourth following that. Fifth, fatty in the whole urine. Sixth, fatty in the upper part. Seventh, fatty in the lower part. The eighth is oily in color only. The ninth is oily in substance only. The tenth and last is oily in both; and this is the finished number of composite colors.

Again, the **simple** color undergoes its own divisions, which are as follows: A simple color of urine is either an extreme or a middle. And each is twofold: either truly middle and truly extreme, or middle and extreme by approximation. The middle color, which stands in the middle of the whole breadth of colors, is **golden**—similar to "Iantiensi" gold <note>original: "auro Jantiensi"; likely referring to a specific high-quality or pure gold coinage</note>—which is the middle between citrine on one side and fiery on the other. The simply and truly extreme colors are either white or black; and thus we have these three capital and principal colors: **white, gold, and black**. The other colors are either intermediate between white and gold, or intermediate between gold and black. For the first ones, which are between white and gold, still differ among themselves: some savor more of the nature of the extreme, namely white, and these are crystalline, mucilaginous, glassy <note>original: "vactuosus"</note>, and "egg-white" color <note>original: "albuginosus"</note>, milky, blue-gray, and saffron-colored

<column-break/>

which are seven in number. The remaining ones, which more closely approach the middle color, gold, are in ascending order: straw-colored <note>original: "palearis"</note>, citrine, yellow, reddish-yellow, citrine-blue-gray <note>original: "citrinũ. glaucuz"</note>, then an intense high citrine, and finally saffron-red <note>original: "zaffaranin⁹"</note>. These are all the colors on the side of whiteness, which together with the seven others enumerated above, number twelve. There are also other middle colors on the other side between gold and true black; and these are similarly twofold like the ones above: some are closer to the golden-citrine color, and the others, receding further from this middle, approach true black. Those closer to the middle are the reds, greens, and dark colors. Among the reds are these: rose-red, clear red, dark red, purple-red, dusty red, blood-red, blackish-red, turbid wine-red, and meat-washing red. After these follow the greens and darks, and these are: *prohisticinus* <note>a yellowish-green</note>, rust-colored, indigo, leek-green <note>original: "porcinus"</note>, and finally *promus* <note>a very dark green or brown</note>; all of these together with those immediately listed above number fifteen. Following these are the remainder, which by receding further from the middle approach blackness, and they are: black resembling citrine; black after *fussan* <note>a dark brown or dusky color</note>; black after dark green; black receding from indigo; and truly black. All these from golden-citrine to true black number twenty, including the extremes. The total integrated sum of all these, both simple and composite, extends to the number forty-two. Let this suffice for the number, names, order, and differences of colors. The remaining things pertaining to colors we shall explain later, just as we will for the other categories of things from which signs are taken, by describing below the differences of each of these categories and explaining their proper significance.

The eighth and last category of those things from which the signs of urine are taken is the "Contents" <note>original: "contentum"; substances held within the liquid</note>, a term taken in a broad sense, under which is included **hypostasis** <note>the heavy sediment at the bottom of the vessel</note>. Among the other things to be observed in urine, this is the first and principal, because through it the dispositions of the human body are more certainly judged. There are many differences of this "content," which are collected in the verses of Gilles, which are as follows: **Circle, bubble, grain, cloudlet, foam. Pus, fatness, food particles, blood, sand, hair. Scurf, hair-like particles, scales, atomic parts. Semen, ash, sediment reaching up from the bottom.** Therefore, these are contained in another list: hypostasis, clouds, *eneorema* <note>original: "eneozilma"; particles suspended in the middle of the urine</note>, circle, bubble, grains, foam, sand-grains, stones, atoms, scurf <note>bran-like flakes</note>, petals <note>original: "petala"; leaf-like flakes</note>, clots <note>original: "trumbi"</note>, hair-like particles, scales, pieces of flesh, blood, semen, phlegm, and fatness. There are some, however, who understand "hypostasis" as the name for the Contents itself, and thus they wish hypostasis to extend as a common genus to all or most of these. Then, by subdividing, they say one kind of hypostasis is **natural** and the other **unnatural**. They call "natural" that which appears white, even, pine-cone shaped, and hanging at the bottom. The "unnatural" is afterward called sandy, stony, atomic, scurfy, petal-like, clot-like, etc.—an opinion with which Avicenna seems to agree. But certainly the former partition is more convenient, because "Content" is better placed as the more general term, while hypostasis itself is placed as a part or species of Content. Nevertheless, it should be noted that any of these differences into which the Content is divided is further divisible. And since the teaching of any knowable thing is not complete until one arrives at the indivisible parts of that genus, in order that we may have a complete method of judging urines, it is necessary to further subdivide any of these differences until one arrives at differences or divisions beyond which it is not possible to proceed, as was perfectly explained above concerning colors and other things.
