<header>Of</header>

<margin>On the differences of the sediment.</margin>
¶ Let us begin first with the sediment <note>original: "hypostasis"; the solid matter that settles at the bottom of a urine glass.</note>, as it is the most important of the contents. Regarding the sediment, so that a physician may judge correctly by it, seven categories of things must be observed, from which a judgment of the clinical state is drawn. The first is its substance. The second is its quantity. The third is its quality, under which color is included. The fourth is the position of its parts. The fifth is its location. The sixth is the time of its appearance. The seventh is the mixture of its parts. An eighth might perhaps be added, which is its movement. Within these categories, there are several distinctions. ¶ Regarding the substance of the sediment, besides the distinctions we named above for the substance of the urine itself—namely, thinness, thickness, and mediocrity—there are others that are more closely observed in the substance of the sediment: these are rarity and density (along with a middle state), and uniformity and deformity <note>meaning consistency versus irregularity</note>, which are not found in the substance of the urine itself. ¶ In terms of quantity, the differences of the sediment are the same as those for the urine. In terms of quality, there is color and form, or whatever shape surrounds it. For taste and odor do not have a separate consideration in the sediment from that which is made regarding the odor and taste of the urine; but the distinctions of form are: pear-shaped <note>original: "pyrealis"</note>, round, flat, angular, and the like. ¶ The differences of color are entirely the same as those twenty differences of urine colors listed above. However, the reasoning for judging by the color of the sediment and the color of the urine is one thing for the former and another for the latter, as will be made clear below in its proper place; and so that they may be understood specifically, the colors proper to the sediment are described here: white, whitish, citrine, sub-citrine, reddish-yellow, sub-reddish-yellow, blue-gray, yellow, red, sub-red, rosy, purple, sea-green, dark green, leaden, indigo-colored, rainbow-colored, black, and sub-black. ¶ Regarding position, the differences are continuity and discontinuity, to which rarity and density may be added, or the closeness and distance of the parts from one another. ¶ Regarding location, the differences are the highest, the middle, and the lowest, or even the floor. This means that the sediment of the urine, in terms of location, is either in the highest part, the lowest part, the middle region, or residing at the very bottom of the urinal. According to these differences of location, the sediments are given various names. For when it is at the top, it is called <term>nephilis</term> <note>from the Greek for "cloudlet"; suspended at the top</note>; in the middle it is called <term>eneorema</term> <note>original: "enozima"; a suspension hanging in the middle of the fluid</note>; at the bottom it is truly called sediment <note>original: "hypostasis"</note>. ¶ The seventh category, which is the time of appearance, has the differences of appearing early, late, or at the proper time. ¶ The eighth, which is the mixture of parts, has the differences of uniformity or deformity of its parts in relation to one another; and these are all the differences of the sediment.

<margin>On the differences of foam.</margin>
¶ It remains for us to assign the differences of the other contents. Another content is foam, from which a judgment is taken regarding the conditions of the human body. Its differences are to be observed not only in terms of quantity, but also duration. Regarding its quality, it has the quantity of its aggregation, the differences of which are "much" and "little"; and the quantity of its extension in each individual bubble, the differences of which are "large" and "small." In terms of duration, the differences are: foam that breaks easily and is of short duration, and foam that is difficult to break and of long duration. ¶ Furthermore, granules are reduced to this category of content, the differences of which are in position and motion. In terms of position, they are either on the surface or within the substance of the urine. In terms of motion, the differences are "moving" or "standing." ¶ To this same category is reduced the <term>ampulla</term> <note>large, bell-like bubbles</note>; and thus we can divide foam another way, saying that one kind of foam is "bubbly," another "granular," and a third "frothy."

<margin>On the differences of the circle.</margin>
¶ The circle <note>the ring or corona that forms at the top of the urine against the glass</note> is another content, the differences of which are observed in substance and color: in substance, it is thick, thin, or medium. In color, it is watery, red, citrine, and green.

<margin>On the differences of sand.</margin>
¶ There is also another content, sand <note>original: "arenule"; fine sediment suggesting kidney stones</note>, the differences of which are also according to substance, quantity, and color. ¶ According to substance, they are fine or coarse. In quantity, they are much or little. In color, they are red or white.

<margin>On the differences of the stone.</margin>
¶ Counted among the contents is also the stone <note>original: "calculus"</note>, the differences of which are in quantity, color, and so on. In quantity—

<column-break/>

—if continuous, it is large or small. If discrete, one or many. In color, the differences are white and red. In shape: oblong, angular, oval, fragile, or hard as marble. ¶ Briefly, the other contents—namely atoms, bran-like flakes <note>original: "furfura"</note>, scale-like particles <note>original: "petala"</note>, hair-like particles <note>original: "crinoydes"</note>, waste <note>original: "scima"</note>, fat, sperm, pus, clotted blood, and phlegm—all these have differences according to substance, quantity, and quality, and especially regarding color. Their differences are: substance (thin or thick), quantity (large or small), and color, as above. ¶ But among all these, blood and fat have other specific differences. For blood is either mixed with the urine or separate. Fat either floats on the surface or is mixed into the substance of the urine; furthermore, it appears either early or late, and lasts for a long time or a short time. And let these things suffice regarding the simple differences of all the aforementioned categories of contents observed in urines.

---

->Chapter II. On the numbering of compound differences; that is, on the combination of one difference with another.<-

<note>A decorative initial "L" features floral scrollwork and stylized leaves within a rectangular frame.</note>
These, then, are the simple differences of these categories which are handed down to be observed in the judgments of urines. Besides these, many compound ones can be added from the combination of one difference with the others, or when several arise with several others; the manner of this is found to be manifold. ¶ For the first way is to combine the differences of one category with the differences of the same category, and so on until the end; for example, one difference of a content with the rest. For example: a thin circle with all the other contents, such as atoms, scales, foam, and the others. ¶ The second way is to combine the differences or species of one category with the species, differences, or species of another category, so that it runs through all of them. For example, a difference or species of "thin substance" combined with the differences of quality (odor, color, and taste), of quantity, of transparency, of the content, and others. And each of these two ways—especially the second—can be done by combining them in pairs, in threes, in fours, and so on. In this way, there are said to be innumerable differences of urines, which no author has not only never written down, but has not even imagined, as we shall show below, God willing. Although it is in a sense impossible to list every single one, we shall nevertheless express those we have found described and exhausted by ancient and modern authors in a more skillful way and a more convenient order; moreover, we shall add many about which no mention is found to have been made by anyone. And so that these may be understood more clearly, I thought one example should be demonstrated before we come to the significations, lest one difficulty be entangled with another. Let us take, for example, one species or difference of substance, namely "thick substance," and let us combine it in pairs with the individual species or differences of the other categories. ¶ Let the urine be described, then, as follows: one whose substance is thick and in quantity "much"; thick and <margin>What the urine is.</margin> quantity "little"; thick and passed frequently; thick and passed rarely. Thick and clear in transparency; thick and turbid; thick and medium. Thick passed easily; thick passed with difficulty; thick passed insensibly; thick passed with pain. Thick lacking odor; thick and stinking. Thick and sweet; thick and sharp; thick and tasteless; thick and salty; thick and bitter; thick and sour; thick and watery; thick with the taste of healthy urine. Thick and white, crystalline. Thick and slimy; thick and oily; thick and pale. Thick and yellow; thick and reddish-yellow; thick and tile-red; thick and rosy; thick and clear red; thick and dark red; thick and purple. Thick and red like dust; thick and red like blood; thick and red as if black; thick and red like a very turbid thing. ...like citrine: thick and black after being tawny; thick and black after dark green; thick and black from an indigo-like state. # Here begins the second part of the second distinction: in which the descriptions of the differences or species already enumerated are set forth.

## On the description of the differences of all categories except color and contents. Chapter I.

<margin>What urines are.</margin>
<note>A decorative initial "N" depicts a scholar or physician seated at a desk, surrounded by books and perhaps a lectern, representing the authority of the medical tradition.</note>
**Now that** the categories and the differences of the categories from which the meanings of urines are to be taken have been fully enumerated, it is time for us to approach their descriptions, the interpretations of their names, or perhaps their definitions. For the previous material requires this. It is not necessary here to hunt for exquisite formal and essential <note>original: "quidditativas"</note> definitions, but only to denote these categories and their differences through similarities, figures, and descriptions. For this knowledge is purely sensory, having very little or nothing of the intellect compared to other parts of medicine. Although each individual part does not transcend the substance, this part is nevertheless most perceived by the senses; therefore, its knowledge requires those definitional inquiries by which the differences of urines become known to the senses. ¶ Let us begin, then, and proceed in describing them in the same order we followed in dividing them. The first category of things to be observed in the judgments of urines was the substance. "Substance," therefore, among physicians, is not usually taken as a term for "primary substance" <note>A reference to Aristotelian metaphysics where substance is the fundamental essence of a thing</note> as they distinguish it among other primary things—which is divided into matter, form, and the composite—but rather for the "corpulence" or density of a thing. And thus, applying it to urine, "substance" is only the wateriness and liquidity of the urine, or the way it holds itself in its corpulence, or a certain quality which the sight perceives in the urine in terms of thickness, thinness, and mediocrity. And this is what a certain Theophilus <note>Theophilus Protospatharius, a 7th-century Byzantine medical writer whose work on urines was fundamental to the medieval curriculum</note> had expressed when he said: "For the substance of urine is the humidity itself." And many of the wise physicians have noted this humidity as the "outpouring." A thin or sub-

<column-break/>

-tle substance is the disposition of the liquid because it is easily and suddenly penetrable by the sharp edge of sight. The thick substance, however, is that which is penetrable with difficulty and slowly; the medium substance is that which holds a middle way between these. The other degrees, which were assigned above within these three differences, can be described by the same logic: namely, by their approach to or departure from the mediocrity of the substance or from one of the extremes.

<margin>What is quantity.</margin>
¶ The quantity of urine is nothing other than its measure or mass; its differences, as has been said, are "abundance" and "paucity" regarding the continuous part; and "frequency" and "rarity" of urinating regarding the discrete part, along with their middle states. This category and its differences do not need description, as they are understood by themselves from the force of the name.

<margin>What is transparency.</margin>
¶ And the third category is transparency <note>original: "dyaphanitas"</note> or clarity, because it is nothing other than a "double appearance": one, namely, on the surface, and the other in the depth. For "diaphanous" is said from *dia*, which is "two," and *fanos*, which is "appearance," as if it were a double appearance. Or otherwise, the diaphanous is that which is not visible in itself except by reason of the color found in it. ¶ "Clarity," which was its difference, is nothing other than the free and easy appearance of a thing within. ¶ "Obscurity," however, or turbulence, is a difficult appearance because of what is within. ¶ "Mediocrity" is that which holds a middle way in the ease and difficulty of appearance. The remaining degrees that can be further assigned ought to be described in the same way by a greater or lesser approach to one of the extremes or to the middle, as was said above concerning the substance. ¶ Take note, however, that clarity and turbulence are not the same as thinness and thickness, since they are of entirely different categories. For it is possible for a urine to be thin and turbid, or thick and clear—just as the white of an egg or glass is thick and clear, and turbid water is thin, yet it is still turbid. From these things, you clearly gather that transparency is a different category to be considered in urine from the substance itself, since the species are varied and distinct.

<margin>What is odor.</margin>
¶ Odor is a "fumable" quality and an evaporation perceivable by the sense of smell. ¶ Urine "lacking odor" is when such an evaporation is not felt by a healthy body with a well-disposed organ of smell. ¶ The "sharpness" or "acridity" of the air is that fumable evaporation with a certain sharp stinging in the organ of smell. ¶ "Sweet" is a certain mild evaporation; a "fetid" odor is a horrible or putrid evaporation.

<margin>What is taste.</margin>
¶ "Taste," which is another category to be attended to, is a quality of a moist body affecting the sense of the organ of taste with a certain opening or closing stinging. ¶ An "acute" taste is a quality by which the tongue seems to be pierced by a strong stinging. ¶ "Bitter" is a quality that stings the surface of the organ with a roughness and even abrades it. ¶ "Salty" is that which stings and abrades less than bitter. ¶ "Sweet" is a quality that soothes and delights the taste. ¶ "Vinegary" <note>original: "acetosus"</note> stings and pierces less than acute.

<margin>What is the manner of urinating.</margin>
¶ The manner of urinating is the ability and form of urinating. ¶ One urinates "easily" when one expels it without labor. It is "difficult," however, when effort is made and it cannot exit freely; furthermore, that which one emits voluntarily and without labor is a species of urinating easily, just as one can also emit urine easily without will, and when it exits involuntarily it does so easily without pain. There is another manner, when this can also happen with pain.

## On the description of color and its differences. Chapter II.

<note>A decorative initial "C" featuring floral and leaf scrollwork patterns.</note>
**Color** may be understood in two ways: namely, as a quality proper to a bounded body in the manner taken from *The Sense and the Sensate* <note>A work by Aristotle</note>; or for everything that can be perceived in any way by the sense of sight, and the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> explains this mode in *On the Soul* when he says: "Color is the movement of sight according to the action of the transparent medium." Nevertheless, it is to be taken here in the first way, but in the second way...

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of urine, moving from the physical substance of the urine to a detailed catalog of its colors and their diagnostic meanings. It synthesizes the teachings of Greek, Arabic, and Salernitan authorities like Theophilus, Avicenna, and Gilles de Corbeil.</meta>

# On...

<margin>Description of colors according to Theophilus, on illnesses, etc.</margin>

...regarding the substance and transparency, which are categories distinct in themselves from color. ¶ In assigning the descriptions of the differences between colors, I believe this order should be observed: first, the twenty differences upon which Maurus, Theophilus, and Gilles <note>Gilles de Corbeil, the 12th-century author of the verse treatise *De Urinis*</note> agree—as we expressed above—who received their interpretations from Salernum and Hippocrates, should be set down. After that, the colors assigned by Avicenna <note>original: "Auicẽ."; refers to the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> and those enumerated for reasons beyond the aforementioned should be included. In this way, the teaching will be complete in every respect. ¶ Let us therefore begin with **white** in this manner. ¶ A color is called **white** when it is, so to speak, deprived of all dye. ¶ It is called **milky**, however, because it has a likeness to milk; here, you should not understand "milky" as having the actual thickness of milk's substance—which is thick and turbid—but only the color of milk within the substance of urine, just as it might more properly be said to resemble whey <note>original: "sero"; the watery part of milk that remains after curding</note>. ¶ **Lactis** <note>original: "Lacti."; likely a shorthand reference to the milky category</note>. ¶ **Pale-white** urine, or the color **glaucous** <note>original: "glaucus"; a pale, greyish-blue or sea-green</note>, is a varied color that tends from simple white toward citrine, and sometimes seems to receive more dye than white or milky urine. It is called *glaucus* after the likeness of the color found in the cornea of the eye, or after the likeness of white horn when it is well-polished and transparent with a slight leaden hue. ¶ The color **karopos** <note>original: "Karopos"; from the Greek *charopos*, often meaning amber or camel-colored</note> recedes further from white and receives more dye than glaucous; it is called *karopos* after the likeness of camel hair, or after the color of the urine found under the tongue <note>An ancient diagnostic practice involving sublingual inspection</note>. ¶ **Pale** and **sub-pale** colors are similar to the broth of half-cooked meats. ¶ **Sub-citrine** and **citrine** colors are those tending from the extreme of white toward the true middle; they are so named for their likeness to an unripe or well-ripened citron <note>The *citrus medica*, a lemon-like fruit used as a standard for yellow hues</note>. ¶ For **sub-citrine** is compared to an unripe citron, while **citrine** is like a well-ripened citron. On this point, we do not follow Theophilus entirely, because the prefix "sub" is found among doctors to be used in two ways: sometimes it signifies a more intense color, but we use it to denote a more diminished color, where it signifies a step or degree. Thus, "sub-citrine" is the same as a color more faint than citrine. ¶ **Sub-tawny** and **tawny** <note>original: "Subzuffus ꝛ zuffus"; likely a variant of *rufus* (reddish-gold)</note> are colors that, according to Theophilus and Haly <note>Haly Abbas, another major Arabic medical authority</note>, are situated in the middle of the extremes of white and black. They are slightly more intense than citrine because they have something more—namely, a small trace of redness. Thus, sub-tawny is like bright gold or "Genoese" gold. ¶ **Tawny**, however, is like a more fulvous gold, specifically like the gold of the Januenses <note>referring to the high-quality gold coinage of Genoa</note>. Theophilus expresses these two colors with other terms: he calls sub-tawny "like gold-colored *orichalcum*" <note>A golden-colored brass alloy</note> and tawny "like Genoese gold," which means the same as what was explained above. ¶ **Sub-red** and **red** are colors receding from the middle ground toward black, participating more in redness. **Sub-red** is like garden saffron, the seed of which is called *carthamus*. ¶ **Red**, however, is like true or field saffron. ¶ **Sub-ruddy** and **ruddy** are colors similar to a watery substance into which has been mixed a quantity of clear, bright, and transparent blood. ¶ **Inopos** <note>original: "Inopos"; wine-colored</note> is a color like clear dark wine, or purple blood, or scarlet. ¶ **Kyanos** <note>original: "Kyanos"; dark blue or cyan</note> is like bright blood that is beginning to putrefy, or like something dyed with red gall. ¶ The **livid** color participates more in blackness combined with a dusky hue. ¶ The **green** color is the color of "adustion" <note>A medical term for the "burning" of humors by excessive internal heat</note> or of mortification <note>Death of tissue</note>; it is named for its likeness to the "flower of brass" <note>verdigris, the green pigment that forms on copper or brass</note>. ¶ The **black** color is either from extreme adustion by way of heat, or from extreme mortification by way of cold.

<margin>Description of colors according to Avicenna.</margin>

¶ These colors are described differently in their placement, order, and variety by Avicenna in this manner. For he said that some colors are **simple** and some are **composite**. A simple color is one that appears singly and apart from others. A composite color, conversely, is one where—to a diligent observer—not just one color appears in the same urine, but several and diverse ones. Thus, urine like the "washings of meat" <note>original: "loture carnis"</note> is a composite color of urine, composed of white and red. This can be understood by looking at water in which meat has been washed: parts of the blood are mixed with the water, in which the color is perceived.

<column-break/>

<margin>Red color is found in urine in three ways.</margin>

At first glance, it seems to be one color, yet in truth and to a very diligent observer, two appear: one, namely red, which is derived from the bloody parts; and the other white and clear, which is derived from the transparent parts of the water. ¶ On this point it should be further noted that the color **red** can be found in urine in three ways. First, when the urine is truly red, and there is only that one color in it; this is caused by a great deal of blood perfectly mixed with the substance of the urine. Second, red color is found in urine not throughout the whole, but in specific regions—namely, at the bottom, as happens in the rupture of veins in the kidneys or the bladder. Third, the red color is found when the urine appears red in its entirety, yet it is not so in reality; for if it is diligently inspected, the red color can be discerned from the white in tiny, divided particles of the urine. In this way, we say the red color is mixed with white in the composite color "similar to the washing of meat." Note that what is said here specifically about red and white can be said generally of all composite colors. Therefore, hold this general rule: mixed and composite colors are either so composed that they appear composite throughout the whole urine and seem to make one color (though different colors appear if inspected attentively, yet they seem like one at first glance due to the proximity of the parts); or they are so composed that one appears in one region and another in another—for instance, one in the upper part and the other in the lower. ¶ The **oleagineous** <note>oily</note> color is a composite color; it is called oleagineous because its color, substance, and stillness are similar to common olive oil. But it is called composite for two reasons: first, because the color is a mixture of citrine and green throughout the whole substance of the urine. Thus, while appearing at first glance to be one, it is called composite because it is composed of a color properly so-called (citrine) and a "color" improperly so-called (brightness and transparency).

<margin>The colors flesh-colored, ash-colored, etc.</margin>

¶ **Flesh-colored** <note>original: "Carninus"</note> is a composite color; it is that which is similar to meat. It is composed of citrine and black, or of citrine and ash-colored. ¶ Regarding this, note that these two colors—citrine and black—can be seen to be composed together while both remain in their own form, but mixed; or one of them remains in its proper form and the other takes the form of ash. Because this can happen indifferently to both, it is called **ashy-leaden** or **ashy-black**. ¶ The fourth composite color is that which is composed of **red** and **black** colors throughout the whole substance of the urine. ¶ Regarding **simple** colors, it should be understood that although Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note> and Avicenna list many colors, they sometimes establish five principal ones: namely, **white, citrine, red, green,** and **black**. The others are less principal and can be reduced to one of these five, as can be seen by the observer in the process. ¶ It should also be understood that these five principal colors can be taken in two ways: commonly and broadly, or properly and strictly. Taken commonly, they are verified in the other degrees associated with them; taken properly, they are verified only in that which is truly and properly such, and which is placed exactly in the middle of its degrees. ¶ Although this is said generally of all five, it is said more particularly and properly of **citrine** and **red**. Thus, while it could be said of white, green, and black, it is more truly said of citrine and red. ¶ For **citrine** can be taken first very broadly; if so, it is verified for any color tending toward the glaucous, whether it participates more in or tends toward whiteness or toward citrine. For this reason, it is called "straw-colored citrine," though it tastes much of the nature of whiteness. It can also be taken less broadly as the color citrine itself for everything verging more toward citrine, whether it be from the side of whiteness or redness; and thus we say both "citrine" and "fiery" are citrine. It can be taken a third way, more properly and strictly, for the true citrine color, which is similar to the first ripe citron. ¶ The same can be said in its own way regarding the color **red**: it is first taken very broadly for every color contained within its degrees; and thus it is called "broadly red" whether it has redness or some degree of whiteness...

<summary>This page catalogs the diverse colors of urine used in medieval medical diagnosis, citing authorities like Theophilus and Avicenna. It explains the physical characteristics of hues ranging from milky white to "burning" black and distinguishes between simple colors and composite mixtures like "meat-washings" or "oily" urine.</summary>
<keywords>uroscopy, color theory, Theophilus Protospatharius, Avicenna, medieval medicine, humors, diagnosis, Gilles de Corbeil</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of urine colors, moving from the definitions of white and pale shades into the nuances of red, green, and black. It concludes with the start of a new chapter on the 'contents' (sediment and bubbles) found within the urine.</meta>

...with whiteness or with turbulence; we call it both "red" and "rose-colored," as well as "dusty." Secondly, we use the term **red** properly for that which signifies the true degree of redness, which is similar to **scarlet**. Avicenna <note>original: "Auī."; the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> alludes to this double usage. First, when he says: "Degrees of redness exist." Second, when he says: "Just as red," etc. The same can be said for the remaining colors: white, green, and black. ¶ What has been said here regarding this multiple understanding of colors serves not only this section—where we intend to describe individual colors—but will be far more useful for what follows. For through this distinction, the great diversity among doctors can be brought into harmony, both in naming these colors and in situating or grading them, and even more so in assigning their meanings. Hence, it sometimes happens that one and the same color is not only named differently by various doctors, but is even named differently by the same doctor. Avicenna, for instance, uses all these interpretations in different places; sometimes he says there are many degrees of **citrine** <note>a yellow-gold color common in medical texts</note>, and then he takes "citrine" in a broad sense to include them all; at other times, he takes it in the proper sense, as it is verified when it is specifically called "citrine."

<margin>The color of straw</margin>
¶ Having seen these things, let us proceed to the designation of the simple colors according to Avicenna's sequence. And let us speak first of those which pertain to **citrine**. ¶ **Straw-colored** <note>original: "palearius"</note> is the color resembling the color of grain-straw existing in a field, not yet fully ripened and harvested; this color participates in a certain whiteness and greenness. ¶ **Citrine** <note>original: "Citrinus"</note> is to be understood as the likeness of a well-ripened citron <note>a large, fragrant citrus fruit</note>. ¶ **Yellow** <note>original: "Flauus"</note> is a color similar to the moistened hair of a youth, or similar to the outer hairy husk of chestnuts. ¶ **Ruddy** <note>original: "Rufus"</note> is a color similar to gold not perfectly purified from the mine, according to Theophilus. ¶ **Orange-citrine** <note>original: "Citrūlarie"</note> is a color declining more toward red than ruddy; it is the color of a pome, a citron, or an orange that is not yet well-ripened. ¶ **Watery** is the color similar to the color of water in which **saffron** <note>original: "crocus"</note> has been dissolved. ¶ **Saffron-colored** <note>original: "Croceus"</note> is the color similar to pure saffron—that is, the threads. It is also called **clear red**. These are the colors which are graded within the "citrine" category by Avicenna and Theophilus. Maurus and Gilles <note>Gilles de Corbeil</note> grade only four in the citrine range: namely, sub-citrine (which includes yellow and citrine), orange-citrine, sub-ruddy (fiery), and clear red. ¶ The colors, however, which pertain to **redness** are situated by this argument and described in this manner. ¶ **Absolute Red** is a true red, clear and without whiteness, like the color of scarlet. ¶ **Rose-red** is a red color declining toward whiteness more than absolute red, and it is similar to the color of a pale-red rose. ¶ **Dark Red** is a color participating in much darkness, but not entirely. ¶ **Dusty Red** is a red color with a dusty blackness throughout, yet with some clarity in certain parts. This same color is called **cyanic** <note>original: "kianos"; likely a deep wine-red or bluish-red</note> by others and is described above as being similar to red wine that tends toward blackness, as if the dust of red bricks were mixed with water, or like red sandalwood. ¶ The colors that approach **greenness** are described in this fashion. ¶ **Pistachio-colored** <note>original: "fisticatus"</note> is so named for its likeness to the pistachio nut. ¶ **Verdigris** and **zinc-colored** <note>original: "eruginosus & çinçarinus"</note> are named for the likeness of copper rust; it is greener and blacker than pistachio-colored. ¶ **Lily-colored**, or **iris-colored**, or **sky-blue** <note>original: "celestinus"</note> is similar to the color of the flowers of the blue lily and the iris; it has more blackness than the former and participates in some yellow. ¶ **Indigo** or **blackish** <note>original: "Indicus vl̄ nigellus"</note> is similar to the color of moderately dark-skinned people; it is sky-blue without yellow, with greater blackness and obscurity. ¶ **Leek-green** <note>original: "Pozralis"</note> is similar to the juice of leek leaves, which tends toward a certain blackness. ¶ **Lead-colored** <note>original: "Plūbeus"</note> is similar to the appearance of a drawing made on paper by the rubbing of lead. ¶ The colors pertaining to **blackness** are these: **Inops** <note>a dull, "destitute" black</note>, **sylcus**, and

<column-break/>

**true black**. These three colors do not differ except in degrees of intensity and faintness; they take their names from the very substances with which they are mixed, receiving their tint from that mixture. ¶ To understand this, it must be noted that although bile <note>original: "colera"</note> is citrine, when it is abundant and mixed, it causes darkness, as is seen in jaundice <note>original: "ycteritja"</note>. ¶ From which it follows that black urine can be made from citrine if much bile is mixed with it; it even produces the first of the black colors, called **inops**. ¶ The second color, namely **dark-brown** <note>original: "fuscus"</note>, is made from the admixture of black bile <note>original: "melācolie"; melancholy</note> itself; if there is much of it, it will cause not only brown but also blackness. ¶ The third of the colors—and this is the third degree—is caused by a great mixture of black bile through the process of coagulation; it properly causes a greenness mixed with blackness. ¶ Note, however, that what is said here of the black colors for their description applies even more to their significance <note>meaning their diagnostic value</note>, as will appear below in its proper place. ¶ The last genus of colors posited by Avicenna was the color **white**, of which 

<margin>White color can be taken in two ways.</margin>
many degrees were posited. But regarding this genus, it must be understood that the color white can be taken in two ways. ¶ First, as **translucency** with a lack of other colors; in this way, the air is said to be white. In the second way, as it is a **true color**: white, and the extreme among colors. ¶ **Mucilaginous white** urine is that which is similar in substance and heat to strained mucus or egg white. ¶ **Oily white**. ¶ **White like a pearl**, or like an "albula," which is a white spot that occurs in the eye. ¶ **Mushroom-colored** <note>original: "fungalis"</note>, or mushroom urine, is that which is similar to a mushroom, which is white with a certain redness or a ruddiness declining toward lividness, like a mushroom. ¶ **Red-white** declining toward livid, like paper upon which lead has been rubbed. ¶ **Spermatic white** is that whose color is similar to the color of semen. ¶ **Milky** is similar to whey, as above. ¶ **Lead-white** is so named for its likeness to the color of lead. ¶ **White after citrine** and **after red** can be described by the same reasoning, and so on for the others that follow.

### ¶ On the description of the contents, and their differences. Chapter II.

<note>An ornamental drop cap 'C' is decorated with floral and vine motifs, marking the start of a new section.</note>

**C**ontent <note>original: "Contentum"</note> is every body found in the urine besides its actual substance. Following the order of the verses of Gilles <note>Gilles de Corbeil</note>, we shall assign a description to each content—provided, however, that we first set down the definition of **hypostasis** <note>the heavy sediment at the bottom of a urine vial</note>. ¶ **Hypostasis** is the surplus of the second digestion exiting with the substance of the urine, signifying a curable condition. ¶ **Natural hypostasis** is a hypostasis that is uniform, smooth, and hanging at the bottom. ¶ **Neozima** is a hypostasis situated in the middle of the urine. ¶ **Nephilis** <note>from the Greek for "cloud"</note> is a hypostasis found in the upper part of the urine. ¶ **Sediment** <note>original: "Sedimen"</note> is hypostasis reaching the very bottom of the urine. ¶ The **Circle** <note>original: "Circulus"</note> is the watery substance found at the top of the urine, found in a circular fashion around the circumference. ¶ The **Ampulla** <note>original: "Ampula"; a bubble</note> is a small sphere or globule generated from a viscous part of the urine with trapped air or windiness. ¶ The **Grain** <note>original: "Granula"</note> is foam that is submerged and joined in the circle, and submerged through various parts, both superficial and deep. ¶ **Foam** <note>original: "Spuma"</note>, however, is a gathering of many various bubbles joined together, as Hali <note>Haly Abbas, the 10th-century Persian physician</note> says in his commentary on the [Aphorisms] "Of those strangled," etc. It is truly the middle point between the bubble and the grain in terms of scarcity and abundance, and in size and smallness, and in position and stickiness. For the protruding bubbles of the foam itself are smaller than in an *ampulla*, larger than in *granula*; more numerous than in an *ampulla*, fewer than in *granula*. It does not tower over like an *ampulla*, nor is it so submerged as *granula*; the granular parts are diminished more, and less than the bubble-like parts. And thus, in all conditions, foam seems to hold the middle ground between the *ampulla* and the *granula*. From which things Pierleone <note>original: "Petrus leo"; the author Pierleone da Spoleto</note> also collects [his observations] on urines.

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of urinary "contents"—the various particles and sediments found in a specimen—before transitioning to a new chapter on how a physician should interpret these findings to diagnose the patient's internal state.</meta>

...to be very small among these contents. Indeed, under the name of **foam**, the other two are understood; hence it is customary among physicians to speak simply of "foam," as well as "bubbly foam" and "granular foam," all of which fall under the name of **foam**, as was said above. ¶ **Granular foam** is a collection of tiny grains around the surface of the urine, and especially around the "circle" <note>the 'corona' or upper rim of the urine in the flask</note>. ¶ **Bubbly foam** is a collection of large bubbles and grains across all or most of the surface of the urine. Regarding this, Hippocrates <note>original: "Hypo."</note> says: "In whichever urines bubbles float on the surface, they signify kidney disease and a long illness." ¶ A **cloud** is nothing other than a smoky vapor rising from the urine and thickened within it. ¶ **Pus** or **ichor** <note>original: "sames"</note> is digested humoral rot, reduced to whiteness and thickness. ¶ **Fat** is the oily part found in urine. ¶ **Slime** <note>original: "limus"</note> is a humor found in urine, specifically a phlegmatic one. ¶ **Mucilage** is a phlegmatic substance that is viscous, fluid, and sticky. ¶ **Blood** is a sweet, red humor retained in the urine. ¶ **Sand** is a very small solid part, granular and hard, resisting the touch. ¶ A **hair** is a certain long, thin substance like a hair, generated in the urine through the process of resolution <note>the breaking down of tissues</note>. ¶ **Husks** <note>original: "peccala"</note> are small bodies similar to wheat husks, or very thin bodies. ¶ **Bran** <note>original: "furfur"</note> is a substance from the surface of the organs or "bark-like"; these "bran-like" particles are somewhat thicker bodies, yet still quite thin. ¶ **Grain-like particles** <note>original: "lrinoydes" (urinoides)</note> are thicker bodies, such that a grain of wheat ground in a mill is broken into thicker parts. ¶ A **scale**, moreover, is a "bark-like" part made in the likeness of fish scales, differing little from "bran" and "husks." ¶ An **atom** or "atomic part" is the smallest bodily part, distinguishable to the eye and round, yet not resisting the touch. ¶ **Sperm** is the waste of the final digestion, found in the urine as thread-like strands. ¶ **Earthy ash**, moreover, is thin and ash-colored, residing at the bottom of the urine. ¶ **Sediment** <note>original: "sedimētū"</note> is the **hypostasis** <term>hypostasis: the heavy sediment that settles at the bottom of a urine glass, used by medieval doctors to judge the "heat" of digestion</term>, the thick humoral part found in urine. ¶ A **stone** <note>original: "calculus"</note> is a stony substance found in urine.

### ¶ Concerning the universal things to be considered regarding the differences themselves, and their causes and certain rules. Chapter III.

<note>A large decorative woodcut initial letter "T" containing an illustration of a scholar seated at a desk with books and writing instruments, surrounded by floral motifs.</note>
It is time that we come to the final part of this second distinction: namely, to the **meanings of the differences**, in which nearly the entire right and utility of the work consists. We shall treat this in two parts: first, where we will explain the absolute meanings of the differences listed above, simply and separately, without joining one to another or to other differences. Thus, we will collect what each difference signifies by itself; after that, we will unravel the meanings of two or more differences when they are complex or combined—for example, what "thick and white" urine signifies, and so on for the rest. ¶ For the delivery of all these matters, it must first be stated that their judgment in the significance of urines is not equal, but they produce a certainty of judgment according to "more" or "less." Hence, the **sediment** <note>hypostasis</note> is preferred and comes before the others; then the **substance**; afterward the **color**. Fourth is **transparency**; fifth is **odor**; sixth is **flavor**; seventh is **quantity**; and finally, the **manner of urinating**. But this should be understood to be true in most cases, and especially in those conditions where health or sickness depends on the good or bad digestion, whether it happens in a harmful or helpful way. The reason for this is as follows: the more something depends on the goodness or badness and the quality of digestion, the more significant it is in the urine regarding the conditions of the body. Such things are the sediment, the substance, and the color; these three hold the primacy among the rest in the certainty of judgment.

<column-break/>

Among these three, an order is again established: for the sediment surpasses the substance, and the substance surpasses the color. Regarding the sediment, this will be demonstrated in its own chapter, where we deal with its significance. Regarding substance and color, it will become clear a little later in this chapter. However, in other conditions that do not depend on the strength of digestion—such as in **wasting diseases** <note>original: "etbica" (hectic fever/consumption)</note>, or **diabetes**, or **strangury** <note>difficulty urinating</note>, and other such things—it is not unfitting for another order of primacy to exist among them regarding significance. And thus, in these conditions and similar ones, one must think similarly: since they depend more on other causes for their existence than on the quality of digestion. For example, the difficulty of urinating depends on another cause, and therefore it is a more direct sign of that specific thing. However, regarding the particular significance of all these, over which each holds primacy, we will explain them in their proper places where needed. ¶ Secondly, it must not be overlooked that meanings can be gathered through general consideration if we know the **causes** of the differences found in the urine. Then, by referring those differences back to their causes, we will gather their proper meanings, since every effect is a sign of its cause. Therefore, having examined the individual differences in order as we did above, let the cause of the differences be found more universally so that the effect may be referred to it. And thus, it becomes an effective and proper sign of that cause. Where this is done, I do not see why this tradition of the significance of urines should not be considered a proven demonstration. ¶ Thirdly, it should be noted:
<margin>There are three principal things to which they can be referred.</margin>

that there are three principal things in this category (though there may be more, which we will mention in their places) which can be the principal causes of the differences in urine, or to which the differences themselves can be referred: namely, the **humors**, the **quality of digestion**, and the **complexional quality** of the natural organs, especially the **liver** <note>original: "epatis"</note> and the **veins**. To these three, the differences in urine can be referred, either as a sign (where the three things named above will have the role of the things signified) or as an effect (where those three will have the role of the cause). But digestion, among the rest, acts in a double way. The cause of urinary differences can be twofold according to digestion: one is "helpful" <note>healthy</note> and the other is "harmful" <note>morbid</note>. Therefore, not without reason, we will later report not only the meanings of simple differences that depend on healthy digestion, but also the meanings of harmful digestion, especially in acute fevers, following Galen <note>the 2nd-century Greek physician</note> in the first book of *On Crises*. Since fever is a sickness in the pulsing veins <note>arteries</note>, and the pulsing veins enter into the origin of the veins, like a wick in which it is ignited; you are taught to consider urine by this reasoning. <margin>Color is caused by one of three things.</margin>
It must be understood that colors receive this third significance based on their reasoning, according to which they are seen to be caused by these three: the humors, the quality of digestion, and the complexional quality of the natural organs. And thus, physicians are accustomed to saying that color is generated in urine in three ways: by **mixture**, by **digestion**, and by **simple alteration**. For from the humors—that is, through their mixture—the urine is tinted in various ways according to which humor dominates in the body and is mixed with the wateriness of the urine. For if **yellow bile** <note>original: "colera"</note> is mixed with the urine, there is no doubt that the urine will be tinted with a saffron color; if **phlegm**, it will be white; if **blood**, it will be red. Secondly, the urine is tinted differently according to the variety of digestion, and especially the **second digestion** which occurs in the liver. For there it takes on a transformation and color while it is digested along with the humors. Because of the digestion in the liver, something takes on its own color. By the best digestion, therefore, there is no doubt that the urine will be produced as "citrine" <note>gold-colored</note> or declining slightly from citrine, such as "reddish-citrine" and "reddish." From diminished digestion, however, because of coldness, the colors in the urine will become close to white, such as "pale blue" <note>original: "glaucus"</note>, "grey-eyed" <note>original: "karopos"</note>, and the like.

<margin><unclear>... to which ...</unclear></margin>
...and similar things. From diminished digestion, however, due to the hindrance of excessive heat, colors in the urine tending toward red or black will be caused. Thirdly, urine is colored in various ways according to the variety of complexional qualities <note>the unique balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness in an individual</note>; hence one color is caused by cold, another by heat, and yet another by tempered heat and cold. For all colors above the middle range—namely redness and blackness—are caused by heat; all those below the middle range—specifically pale-yellowish and white—are caused by cold. From tempered heat, however, the lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrinus"</note> color and those close to it are caused. This manner of causing complexional colors in the urine through qualities can be reduced to that which concerns the quality of digestion; yet, it does not treat complexional qualities as identical to the quality of digestion, for they are distinct from it, as can be gathered from the mind of Avicenna <note>a Persian physician and philosopher, 980–1037 AD</note> when he says: urine is not to be retained long in the body, as it becomes colored by its stay. Almost the same is expressed in the first part of the fourth book on signs, taken from the "renity" <note>the kidney-like quality</note> of urines. Therefore, when you find any sufficient color in the urine, trace it back to its cause: namely, to the humor, the quality of digestion, and the complexional quality of the organs; and judge the urine in such a way regarding its color. ¶ Fifthly, it must be understood: besides what has already been said about colors, the same must be understood in its own way regarding other things observed in urine—namely: substance <note>thickness or consistency</note>, quantity, color, taste, and the rest—so that they are referred back to their causes in the humors, such as digestion, complexional qualities, and other causes, if there be any, 
<margin>Active qualities change the color more, while passive qualities change the substance of the urine.</margin>
as we shall see in their proper places. ¶ But substance and color should be understood specifically: because although there are four complexional qualities—namely heat, cold, dryness, and moisture—only two of them, the active ones (heat and cold), are better and more clearly signified by color than by the others, since colors themselves depend more on active qualities than on passive ones. For it is the nature of heat to color, but of cold to discolor or to make white <note>original: "alchificare"</note>. The other two, the passive ones—namely dryness and moisture—are more appropriately signified through differences in substance, as the greatest change in the substance of urine occurs through them. Indeed, they change the substance of urine well: for dryness causes thinness <note>original: "subtilitatem"</note> in the urine, and moisture causes thickness <note>original: "grossitiem"</note>. It is the nature of dryness to thin, and of moisture to thicken. These are the changes the complexional qualities produce in the urine. From these, one may collect two universal rules for the judgment of urines, both useful and necessary. ¶ The first rule: Every coloration of urine is caused by heat, and every discoloration by cold. <margin><unclear>... urine ... cause ...</unclear></margin> Corollary: Every colored urine signifies heat, and every discolored urine signifies cold. ¶ The second rule: Every thickness of urine is caused by moisture, and its thinness by dryness. Corollary: Every thick urine signifies a dominance of moisture, and thin urine shows a dominance of dryness. ¶ From which it finally follows that a middle range in both—namely color and substance—signifies a tempered state. ¶ Another rule is added further: the principal and common agent in the production of both—that is, both color and substance—is natural heat. For urine receives its substance and color from the action of natural heat, especially in a natural state. 
<margin>Whether the color or the substance of urine is more significant in diagnosis, and how they are generated in time.</margin>
¶ From these things, moreover, if well understood, one may finally resolve the difficulty that arises concerning the primacy between color and substance in signifying, as well as the timing of their generation, which the Conciliator <note>the "Conciliator" refers to the famous physician Pietro d’Abano, 1257–1315 AD</note> raises in Difference 85. Leaving aside the objections on both sides, let the truth of both be expressed, which is not only consistent with what was said above, but also stands in the mind of Galen <note>an influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire, 129–216 AD</note>: since there are three causes—namely of color, substance, and also the sediment <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> of urine—touching upon the action of qualities and humors from the impression of natural heat.

<column-break/>

And so it is not inconsistent for the color itself to be generated first in the urine, and upon the simple watery base, before that wateriness is in any way altered by natural heat. In that case, the color itself better signifies the action of qualities and the humors involved. ¶ If, however, color and substance are both referred to the action of natural heat and its own natural "decoction" <note>the "cooking" or processing of nutrients in the body</note>, there is no doubt that the action of heat first produces the liquid—that is, the substance of the urine—and afterwards the color; in this case, the sign of digestion is to be attributed more to the substance than to the color. ¶ But it should be understood that it also pleased Galen that color precedes the digestion of substance made by natural heat and then follows it, as gathered in the first book on crises when he said: pale or somewhat black urine signifies digestion, at least for the sake of the color. But it is necessary that this thickness be separated into three parts from the watery part, if digestion is to occur. And afterwards, summarizing, he adds: when digestion is complete, it intensifies those things belonging to color and less so the substance, which he proves by example. For if you keep a man fasting for a longer time, you will see the color itself becoming more intense. Therefore, from this text it is clearly gathered that color in some way precedes substance, and in some way follows it.

### On the Meanings of the Substances of Urine and its Differences. Chapter IV.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'R' is enclosed within a rectangular border, featuring stylized vine and leaf patterns. Inside the upper bowl of the 'R', a small scene is visible, possibly depicting a seated figure or scholar at work.</note>
**W**ith these things presupposed as foundations, following the order noted above, let us show the meanings of all of them. And first, those taken from the substance according to its differences taken separately, as we have said. Its differences were thinness, thickness, and the middle range.
¶ Thinness in the substance of urine, or thin urine, signifies a cold and dry complexion, or that a dry humor abounds in the body, or a lack of digestion, or an obstruction <note>original: "opilationem"</note>, or weakness of the digestive power of the liver, or of the attractive power of the kidneys not attracting anything but the thin part; or perhaps a strong attractive power of the kidneys; or weakness of the expulsive power, unable to expel anything but what is thin; or the drinking of much water. ¶ All these things are proved thus: if we first observe that the first three signified meanings of such urine signify of themselves as an effect signifies its cause; the others, however, signify by accident, since they are not the efficient or material causes of such urine except by accident. Therefore, such urine signifies a cold and dry complexion, a dominant dry humor in the body, and a lack of digestion of itself; but obstruction and the rest follow by accident. The first part of this conclusion is proved thus: Thin urine signifies of itself that by which it is immediately caused. But it is caused by such a complexion, and by the mixing of such a humor, and by diminished digestion. Therefore, it signifies such a complexion, such moisture, and such digestion; the following parts are no greater, and the lesser part is clear from what was noted above. The second part is deduced thus: And first regarding obstruction. For if such urine is not caused by any of the aforementioned, but by the deprivation of them, then it is a sign of the non-mixing of the humors with such urine. And thus it must signify an obstruction or weakness of the digestive power, because when the digestive power is weak, the humors cannot be mixed with the urine. Thus the liquid remains pure, watery, and thin. Or, if the power is strong and the humors are mixed, yet because of the narrowness of the passages and veins of the "gibbous" <note>hollow or rounded</note> part of the liver, the thick parts cannot pass to the kidneys. And thus only the thin and watery parts pass through, and for this reason the urine remains thin. ¶ It is further proved that it could signify weaknesses of the retentive power of the liver and the attractive power of the kidneys: for when the retentive power is weak, the urinary wateriness is not retained long enough for the humors to be mixed with the urine; and even if they are mixed, if the attractive power of the kidneys is weak...

# On the Substance of Urine

...it could not be drawn through them. ¶ It signifies, in the penultimate case, a strong attraction by the kidneys <note>original: "renum"</note>, or the drinking of much water. For by a strong attraction of the kidneys, there is a sudden drawing of wateriness from the liver <note>original: "epate"</note>, and it is not permitted to reside in the liver long enough to be mixed with the humors; thus, being unmixed and subtle <note>meaning thin or watery</note>, it is drawn off. But because of this strong attraction, which happens most often due to the heat of the kidneys, it can be easily distinguished: for this thinness from cold is joined with a small quantity of urine, whereas when it is from heat, it is joined with a large amount. There is also another distinguishing sign in the color: when it comes from cold, it is white and mostly clear; however, it is tinted when it comes from heat. ¶ In the final case, it signifies drinking much water, when its quantity relaxes the containment of the members and by its quality diminishes their heat. And so it exits as it was held: it was drunk as something thin, and thus it remains thin. ¶ Note, however, that such things are more verified if they are joined with a thin substance: whiteness regarding color, and clarity regarding transparency; for Hippocrates <note>original: "Hypo."</note> spoke of such in his fourth aphorism: *To whomever the urine is clear...* <note>original: "Quibuscunque urina limpida"</note>

For it signifies a hot and moist complexion; a strong digestion; and that moist humors are mixed with it, namely phlegm or blood. This is proven by the same reasoning as above, but in the opposite way: just as the opposite is in the opposite, so the proposed is in the proposed <note>a logical rule: if A leads to B, the opposite of A leads to the opposite of B</note>.

<margin>The significations of thick urine.</margin>

¶ Urine that is medium in substance signifies a tempered complexion: perfect digestion, not diminished by cold nor destroyed by excessive heat; and a balance in the matter, and a moderate collection of humors in the body. These are proven as follows: Thin and thick do not signify anything by themselves except indigestion; but when thin urine becomes thick, or thick urine becomes thin, then it signifies digestion, because it is a balancing toward the middle, since those states are the extremes. But medium urine must be made from the thickening of the thin or the thinning of the thick; therefore, in all things, it signifies mediocrity <note>here meaning a healthy middle state or balance</note>. ¶ A corollary derived from this proof: Thin urine appearing after thick, or thick after thin, if it occurs with a feeling of relief, signifies a good sign. ¶ Corollary: Thick urine remaining thick, or thin remaining thin, signifies indigestion. This is proven as above. ¶ A corollary that follows from the main principle: The urine of children until the age of youth ought to be thick. And from youth until the end of life, by merit of age, it ought to be thin <note>original: "subtilis"</note>. Therefore, thin urine in children is bad, and thick urine in youths is bad. ¶ The first corollary and its consequence are proven thus: The bodies of children abound in moist humors, namely phlegm and blood; therefore the urine ought to be thick. And by the opposite of the other ages, it ought to be thin. ¶ It is proven by a second corollary: Children and adolescents require more moisture, and consequently they draw in more <note>nourishment</note> than the bodies of other ages because of the growth necessarily required in them; and consequently, they multiply more superfluities <note>waste products</note>. Therefore the urine is thicker. The contrary is true in other ages. The consequence derived from the corollary is proven because: the further the urine is removed from its natural disposition, the worse the sign. But in children, when it is thin, it is further removed from its natural disposition, since it ought to be thick. Therefore it is a worse sign. ¶ If

# On Urines

...signifies the dominance of the bodily strength <note>original: "virtutis"</note> over the matter. Nor will these be proven in the following chapter, where propositions regarding the turbulence of dryness will be placed.

### On the Meanings of Transparency. Chapter V.

<margin>
Natural and unnatural heat act upon the urine and leave the traces of both within it.
</margin>

**It follows** that we should show the meanings of all kinds of transparency <note>original: "dyaphanitatis"</note>: to which substance it is most closely related, so much so that some think there is no other kind of transparency than substance itself; the contrary of which we have well proven above. Its dominant qualities are clarity, turbulence, and the middle state. But it must be understood first for a general knowledge of transparency, and also of substance, that natural and unnatural heat <note>Natural heat is the body's healthy metabolic fire; "preternatural" or unnatural heat refers to the heat of a fever.</note> act within the urine of the sick—just as in all living things—which later carries outward the traces of both agents. According to the greater impression of one or the other, there follows in the urine one or another dominance of both substance and transparency. Urine, therefore, becomes turbid from the mixing of opaque humors, or vapors, or fumes within the urinary substance. It is made thick and dense through the mixing of coarse and viscous humors. Turbulence and thickness do not coincide, nor do thinness and clarity. This was expressed by Avicenna <note>A foundational Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe.</note> in the chapter on the meanings of the substance of urine, finding the difference between thick, turbid, thin, and translucent, saying: "Truly, however, there exists a difference between the thick, the translucent, and the thin over-translucent; for the thick translucent urine flows with a surging motion, and its surging parts do not become very small; rather, they occur more within it." From this, its movements are slow; when it foams, its foam consists of many bubbles, and those bubbles do not burst quickly. It follows from this that if natural heat overcomes unnatural heat, it gradually becomes clearer. If, however, it is the opposite, the contrary happens, for it becomes continuously more turbid. Translucent white urine, especially if it is thick, signifies "gross phlegm" or "glassy phlegm" <note>original: "flegma vitreum"; a cold, thick humor associated with sluggishness and neurological issues</note> generated in the body, and the illnesses coming from it, as happens in cases of epilepsy. If it is tinted, it signifies vitelline bile <note>original: "coleram vitellinam"; bile the color of egg yolk, considered a sign of severe digestive imbalance</note>. The first part is proven because it signifies a mixture of white and thick humor, which is phlegm. The second is proven because it cannot be anything but the same humor tinted, which is nothing other than intestinal bile, etc.

<margin>
Translucent urine, whether thick or thin, always signifies indigestion.
</margin>

Transparent or translucent urine always signifies indigestion, whether it be thin or thick. In the case of thick urine, it was proven above because it signifies glassy phlegm if it is white, or vitelline bile if it is tinted, and both these humors signify a failure of digestion. Likewise, it is proven in thin urine: whether it is white or tinted, a thin substance always signifies indigestion, since digestion is more closely observed in the substance than in the color. For proper digestion is the due mixing of the moist with the dry, but in such qualities, a difference occurs in the substance. Therefore, the substance has more to say regarding digestion. Thin urine, therefore, signifies indigestion. Thus, the proposition is rendered true: that translucency signifies indigestion regardless of whether it is joined with thinness or thickness, or whether it is tinted or untinted. Transparent urine with a diversity of colors signifies "combustion" and "burning" <note>original: "adustionem et incendium"; terms used to describe humors being "overcooked" by excessive feverish heat</note>. This is proven because tinting does not occur except from heat, and the variety of tinting argues for a multiplicity of heat; but such heat causes burning. Therefore, such urine signifies burning. Transparent urine with "furfur" <note>original: "furfuribus"; literally "bran," referring to small flaky sediments resembling skin or scales</note>, if the illness is not in the urinary vessels themselves, signifies the liquefaction and burning of phlegm. This will be proven elsewhere. Turbid urine signifies a multitude of humors, especially opaque ones, which are being expelled by nature. It also signifies the labor of nature in separating and balancing the humors. This is clear because such turbulence only comes from the mixing of such humors, or vapors and fumes, as was said above. Therefore, it signifies the expulsion of such humors. Turbid urine in

<column-break/>

neutral or healthy people signifies a headache. This is proven just as was said above concerning thick substance in those same bodies. Turbid urine in acute fevers signifies the boiling of humors or their liquefaction. This is proven because it signifies the mixing of opaque and thick parts with the urinary wateriness, and the elevation of vapors mixed together. Therefore, where there are no opaque humors, it is necessary for another thick moisture to be mixed in, which is capable of making the urine turbid; this is nothing other than the nutritional moisture of the members. Therefore, one is discerned from the other by this reasoning: that which is through liquefaction suddenly congeals and thickens. That which is through boiling does not do so as quickly, nor does it congeal as much. Urine that is passed turbid and remains turbid while the patient's strength remains firm signifies a long illness and imperfect digestion. And if the same continues with a weakening of strength, it signifies death. The first is proven thus: such urine only argues for much thick and gross matter which nature has not yet freely overcome. Nature labors much, however, from which many fumes are raised, even while strength appears firm; but such matter combined with the labor of strength makes for a long illness. The preceding is clear because turbulence is caused by nothing other than such humors, and its permanence is caused by nothing other than their multitude. The second is proven thus: because it comes from nothing but a multitude of gross humors, much labor, and many fumes, which the strength cannot overcome since it is weak. Therefore, the disease will overcome and the patient will succumb, and thus death can be judged from such a sign.

<margin>
Transparent urine remaining transparent or clear.
</margin>

Transparent or clear urine that remains transparent and watery signifies a total lack of digestion. This is proven because transparency signifies indigestion, as proven above; therefore, if the transparency continues, the indigestion consequently continues. Urine that is first passed clear and afterwards becomes turbid, or after being passed turbid quickly becomes clear, signifies that nature is beginning to overcome the disease and process the matter; but it is not perfectly passed with the matter. The operation and impression of natural heat and the active strength do not yet reside in it; and as long as such operation of the agent stands, it stays clear. But when the operation of the natural agent (that is, the natural heat) no longer remains in it, it is then left to the action of the heat of the air and the environment, or to the cold. Therefore, it is made turbid by the action of the external heat of the environment. Thus, if this happens alongside an alleviation of symptoms, it signifies what was said. Urine that is passed turbid and afterwards becomes clear—especially if there is a separation of thick parts that reside at the bottom—signifies a greater digestion, showing nature's mastery over the disease more than when it is passed clear and then becomes turbid. This is clear because it is not made turbid except by the action of the environment. Therefore, if it is passed turbid and clears up, the impression of nature in it is strong, such that the environment cannot disturb it. This is expressly the opinion of Master Haly <note>Haly Abbas (930–994 AD), a famous Persian physician whose work preceded Avicenna.</note> in the third chapter on crises. These signs establish a concord between Haly and Avicenna in the chapter on the signs of urines, who seemed to agree with Haly. But this opinion, being well-proven, is suited to both, as is clearly evident to one who understands.

<margin>
Urine neither transparent nor turbid, but in the middle.
</margin>

Urine, therefore, which is not transparent like clear water, nor turbid like that of beasts of burden <note>original: "subiugalium"; literally animals under the yoke, such as oxen or horses</note>, but consisting in the middle, portends health. And through these things said here, you will more clearly understand what was said above in the first part of the chapter on distinguishing the urines of humans from other liquids or the urines of other animals.

### On the Meaning of Quantity in Urine and its Differences. Chapter VI.

**Another** kind of thing to be considered regarding urine was quantity, the meanings of whose differences we shall now show. Its differences were continuous and discrete, concerning which...
