# On Urines

<margin>Urine is called much or little in two ways.</margin>
We must speak in order. However, it must first be understood regarding the quantity itself, both absolute—meaning continuous—and discrete: for urine can be called "much" or "little" in two ways, whether continuously or discretely. In the first way, it is called so **absolutely**; in the second, **relatively**. We assert that the continuous or discrete quantity of some urine is absolutely little or much if it would be so in comparison to a healthy body. And whatever is compared to a healthy body in this way is called the "absolute" mode, because it refers to a body that is absolutely and simply healthy. In the **relative** sense, or the second mode, a certain amount of urine is called much or little in comparison to those things which are eaten and drunk; this should be understood both in terms of the quantity and the quality of the things consumed. That is to say, the quantity of urine should correspond proportionately to the quantity and quality of the food and drink; for example, melons and their seeds, and all diuretics—especially asparagus—increase the urine by their quality. The same should be said in its own way regarding the frequency or rarity of urination <note>original: "mictus"</note> in discrete quantity, just as was said regarding littleness and abundance.

<margin>Little urine in continuous quantity in comparison to a healthy body.</margin>
Let us therefore speak of continuous quantity, the differences of which are "much" and "little." Urine that is little in continuous quantity—and absolutely little, that is, in comparison to a healthy body—signifies a weakness of the faculties, both the **attractive** faculty of the kidneys and the **expulsive** faculty of the other organs. For when the attractive faculty of the urinary organs is strong, they suck up much watery fluid, which they do not suck up when that faculty is weak. Similarly, when the expulsive faculty of the liver and other organs is strong, they transmit a great quantity of humors, purging themselves along with the urinary water. Therefore, when both faculties are weak, a small quantity of urine results, which signifies exactly that: namely, that both faculties are weak.

<margin>Little urine in continuous quantity in comparison to things consumed.</margin>
Urine that is little in continuous quantity in comparison to the quantity and quality of things consumed <note>original: "assumptorum"</note> signifies one of four things: either great dissipation <note>original: "resolutionem"</note>, or a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, or excessive sweating, or a future dropsy <note>original: "hydropisiz"; a condition of swelling/edema</note>. All of these are proven thus: It is certain that the watery fluid generated from the quantity or quality of food, or from the power of anything else taken internally, is not being transmitted through the urinary passages, since the quantity of urine is less than what is generated from those things consumed—as it is said to be "little" in comparison to the intake. Therefore, it necessarily follows that it is either being transmitted through other paths or is being retained in the body. If it is transmitted through other paths, it is either sensibly or insensibly. If sensibly, it is either through sweat or through stool, according to the opinion of the Aphorisms <note>original: "asso."; likely referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates</note>. Much urine passed at night signifies little bowel movement, and vice versa; thus, it signifies either a flux of the belly or of sweat. If it is transmitted insensibly, it signifies dissipation <note>through the pores of the skin or breath</note>. Furthermore, if it is retained in the body so that it is neither sensibly nor insensibly dissipated or expelled, it is then collected and stored in some organ, and thus it is a cause of dropsy. This happens either because its quality hinders the digestion of the liver, or because the retained fluid returns through the mesenteric veins and is thrust into the cavity between the *siphac* and the *mirach* <note><term>siphac</term> and <term>mirach</term> are medieval anatomical terms derived from Arabic, referring to the peritoneum and the abdominal wall/muscles.</note>.

<margin>Much urine, both absolutely and in comparison to things consumed.</margin>
A large quantity of urine, both absolutely and in comparison to things consumed, signifies a "liquefaction" of the body <note>the medieval idea that the body's fats or humors are "melting" due to fever</note> or an evacuation of superfluities that have been liquefied in the body. This is proven as follows: A greater quantity of urine than a healthy state requires, or more than the quantity of things consumed, cannot be produced or generated unless humors are being liquefied. In such cases, they are not expelled by the force of nature expelling waste matter through the veins—as happens in cases of "crises"—but rather they are expelled after they have been liquefied, either by the movement of the body or the mind, or by febrile heat while the retentive faculty is weak. By the way of "aggravation" <note>the weight or pressure of the excess fluid</note>, they exit with the urine, and thus they signify liquefaction. If it occurs in the first way, it signifies evacuation, and this was hinted at by Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical text of the era.</note> in the chapter 

<column-break/>

on the quantity of urine, saying: "And we can know the differences of these according to the disposition of the faculty."

<margin>Much urine in acute fevers.</margin>
An abundance of urine in acute fevers signifies either the resolution of the fever, or a conversion into a hectic fever <note>original: "ethicam"; a wasting fever associated with consumption</note>, or a spasm from depletion <note>original: "inanitione"</note>. This is proven: for either such abundance occurs with a feeling of relief, and thus comes from the strength of the expulsive faculty (signifying the end of the fever); or it occurs because of the intensity of the heat and with a weakness of the faculty, and thus, as such a cause persists, it will dry out the body greatly. This will lead it into a hectic fever, or a spasm from depletion, or both.

<margin>Urine in a proportioned quantity.</margin>
Therefore, urine in a proportioned quantity signifies health: health of nature and health in relation to the quantity of things consumed. This is proven by the statements above.

The certain significance of the differences in **discrete quantity** <note>frequency</note> cannot be understood unless it is first presupposed that "discrete" comes from the division of the "continuous." Therefore, a certain continuous quantity must be presupposed, to be noted by the separation of the discrete quantity itself. From this it follows that the meanings must be distinguished from one another; therefore, the total sum of urine passed in a day must be calculated, whether it is passed in many or few sessions. Judgments must be made on that total sum according to the rules set above. Then it must be observed whether it is passed in few or many sessions, and a judgment is made based on these kinds of differences.

<margin>Frequently passed urine.</margin>
It is said, therefore, that frequently passed urine—setting aside the judgments of continuous quantity—signifies a weakness of the **retentive faculty**, or an acridity <note>sharpness/irritation</note> of the urine, or an injury to the bladder. This is proven: for when the retentive faculty is strong and not stimulated by the quality of the urine or by an illness of the bladder, it keeps the urine for the proper number of times, to be expelled at the right time and in a proportionate interval. Therefore, if it is expelled more frequently than is proper, it comes from one of these; therefore, it signifies one of them. The distinctions that signify which one of these it is can be easily obtained.

Urine passed less often than the nature of a healthy man or the quality of things consumed requires signifies the strength of the retentive faculty, or an insensibility of the bladder, or a distraction and diversion of the mind. This is proven: that which causes one to retain urine beyond what is proper is what is signified by the actual urination, since rare urination only occurs from such retention. But insensibility of the organ or a diversion of the mind causes this kind of thing. Therefore, rare urination signifies one of these. This is well known; the major and minor premises are proven because when the faculty does not feel a contrary or burdensome object, it retains the urine beyond what is proper, and is more rarely stirred to its expulsion. But when the faculty of the organ is dulled, or the internal sensory faculty is distracted, the contrary or burdensome object is not felt. Therefore, insensibility of the organ and diversion of the mind is the cause of rare urination.

### On the Meanings of the Manner of Urinating and Its Differences. Chapter VII.

<margin>Easily passed urine.</margin>
<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a large Gothic letter 'A' entwined with foliate patterns.</note>
We now add the meanings taken from the manner of urinating, since they have a great agreement with the meanings taken from discrete quantity. Let us speak of them in this place for the sake of good instruction. Urine that is passed easily and with force, without labor, portends health. For that urine shows health—as far as the manner of urinating is concerned—which preserves the conditions of a healthy person. But such is this kind. Therefore, etc. For a healthy person emits it with ease, with force, and without any labor at appropriate times. Urine passed drop by drop <note>original: "guttatim"</note> with a distressing sensation portends a burning of the urine, and consequently **strangury** or **dysuria** <note><term>strangury</term> is a painful, frequent urge to urinate; <term>dysuria</term> is general difficulty or pain during urination.</note>. It is proven thus: for such a distressing sensation either proceeds...

# On Urines

<margin>Urine passed drop by drop in acute and non-acute illnesses.</margin>
This either arises from the sharpness of the urine and high sensitivity of the bladder, or from a lesion in the bladder, such as occurs in excoriation or an ulcer. Whichever of these modes is responsible, it signifies a burning sensation. Therefore: ¶ The same urine passed involuntarily in acute illnesses, without preceding signs of digestion <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" or "coction" referred to the process by which the body's heat processed raw humors into a healthy state.</note>, signifies delirium <note>original: "desipientiam"</note> and a corruption of the mind. ¶ This is proven as follows: such urine only occurs because the mind tends toward the higher parts—that is, toward the brain and nerves. Due to this, the nerves are damaged along with the brain, and thus the sensory power of the bladder is numbed and impaired. Therefore, the urine is not felt in the bladder; but this cannot happen without a corruption of the operations of the internal senses, since its organ is damaged. ¶ Such urine appearing in fevers that are not very acute, and with preceding signs of digestion, foretells a future flow of blood from the nostrils. It is proven thus: the involuntary emission of urine argues for harm to the muscles serving the retentive power, which signifies harm to the brain and superior parts, as has been said. Since such harm occurs alongside signs of digestion, as is presupposed, an expulsion will take place through the parts where there is stimulation. But stimulation occurs in the upper parts, and among them, there is no more convenient place for expulsion than the nostrils; thus it occurs through the exit of blood from the nose. It would be otherwise if the faculty did not send it: then signs of digestion would not have appeared, and it would signify delirium, as stated above. Such urine passed drop by drop is usually white.

<margin>Urine passed weakly.</margin>
¶ Urine that is passed weakly, and over a long duration or lacking force, accompanied by a distressing sensation—especially if it cannot be held for long—signifies a weakness of the expulsive faculty and a relaxation of the bladder, particularly its neck. ¶ This is evident for this reason: if the retentive faculty were strong, it would expel with force and suddenly; and if the organ were not relaxed, it would reserve the urine until a proper time. There is no bad quality in the urine itself, nor any other lesion in the organ, since there is no distressing sensation. It arises solely from a weak faculty and relaxation of the bladder, which this condition alone signifies. ¶ Urine passed drop by drop without pain, and in a non-acute illness, signifies a thickness of the urine or an obstruction <note>original: "opilationem"</note> of the bladder neck caused by a stone <note>original: "lapide"</note>, or a callus, or a buildup of mucus; this is sufficiently clear from the signs.

# ¶ On the Significance of the Different Odors of Urine.
## ¶ Chapter VIII.

<margin>The urine of a sick person can, in three cases, be similar to the urine of a healthy person in odor and color.</margin>
It is time for us to come to the significations of the different odors of urine. ¶ First, it must be understood that it is not out of place for the urine of a sick person to sometimes be similar to that of a healthy person in odor. This happens in three cases: either when the illness is immaterial; or, if it is material, the matter tends toward other pathways than the urinary ones—whether this arises from an obstruction of the urinary paths or because nature directs itself toward expelling through other paths; or because a person of a naturally choleric <note>The "choleric" temperament was associated with yellow bile, heat, and dryness.</note> temperament has shifted toward a cold state through a change in regimen. Then, if they are overheated internally by a preternatural heat—to the extent that their natural complexion was golden—it is certain that the urine will have the same odor as it had before; yet they were healthy before and are now sick. Thus the urine of the sick is similar to the healthy in odor; the same can be said of its color in its own way.

<margin>When the urine of a healthy person is similar to the urine of the sick.</margin>
¶ It must also be understood that the reverse is not out of place: namely, that the urine of a healthy person may become like the urine of the sick. This happens in those who have eaten asparagus, in whom the urine is made very foul-smelling, and yet there is no illness in the urine.

<margin>Urine lacking odor.</margin>
¶ Urine lacking odor signifies a rawness <note>original: "cruditatem"</note> of the humors and a coldness of the complexion. It is proven: Odor is a quality founded in smoky evaporation, as was said above regarding definitions; at the very least, it does not exist without such smoky evaporation. Where there is no odor, there is no smoky evaporation; thus there is supreme coldness, since

<column-break/>

smoky evaporation is caused by heat. Therefore, urine lacking odor indicates rawness. ¶ If the same urine appears in acute illnesses, and especially in fevers, it signifies death—unless a change and diversion has been made to other pathways. For such an acute fever is, for the most part, from hot matter. Therefore, by virtue of both the fever and the matter, that smoking out <note>original: "effumatio"</note> ought to occur. If it does not occur elsewhere, it can only happen because of the mortification of the natural heat through the way of resolution and suffocation; and in whatever way the natural heat is consumed, it announces death. Therefore.

<margin>Stinking urine</margin>
¶ Stinking urine with signs of digestion or maturation signifies scabies <note>In this context, "scabies" refers to internal skin-like eruptions or roughness, not necessarily the modern mite-borne disease.</note> or ulcers in the urinary paths. The distinction between these is known through scales or pus <note>original: "saniem"</note>. For scales signify scabies, while pus signifies an ulcer. ¶ Each part of the proposition is proven, starting with the first: signs of digestion argue for a good cooking of the humors and the health of other members, excluding the bladder and kidneys. Therefore, no stench is caused in the urine by those humors or by the qualities of the other members. It remains that it is caused only by some harm in the urinary paths; but this harm causing the stench can be nothing other than scabies or an ulcer, because other harms would not cause a stench. Therefore. ¶ The same urine without signs of digestion signifies either an abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note> in the urinary paths or a blackness dispersed in other members. These are easily deduced from the above. ¶ Stinking urine in acute fevers, while the urinary paths are healthy, threatens danger. For what arises except from a bad putrefaction brings danger. Such a stench is of this kind. Therefore. For where there is great putrefaction, it is digested with difficulty and over time; but the disease is short, and being acute, it offers no truce. Therefore, etc.

<margin>Urine of a sharp odor.</margin>
¶ Urine of a sharp <note>original: "acris," meaning sour or vinegary</note> odor signifies the putrefaction of cold humors. It is proven: A vinegary odor in urine does not occur except from the presence of a vinegary humor through evaporation; but a vinegary humor is cold. Therefore, it signifies a cold humor; but that it is putrid is proven by the fact that that stinking evaporation smokes out from it. This is the odor that most often appears in phlegmatic fevers. ¶ The same in acute illnesses signifies death. This is proven because in such cases sharpness does not arise by virtue of the matter, since it is hot, nor by virtue of the febrile heat. Therefore, it only arises from the extraction of natural heat and the dominance of the preternatural; but this signifies death. Therefore.

<margin>Stinking urine</margin>
¶ Stinking urine of a sweet odor signifies the dominance of blood that is not putrefied. It is proven: since such an odor is not made except by the admixture of something sweet, but in the body nothing is sweeter than blood. Therefore. ¶ Stinking urine with the bitterness of choler signifies its dominance; it is proven like the other. ¶ Stinking urine that is more sharp in healthy people signifies the dominance of melancholy. ¶ This is added to the above: because it is said to be "more stinking." It is indeed more stinking due to combustion <note>original: "adustionem," the "burning" of humors</note>; but by "more stinking" we understand it as having a more foreign odor—that is, more piercing in its stench. While absolutely sanguine urines are more stinking, that stench is not so horrific according to the mind of Galen in his *Therapeutics*. ¶ Stinking urine persisting in the healthy signifies either a future fever or the expulsion and conquest by nature, which is recognized by an ensuing relief. Both are proven: for stench is not released without putrefaction. Therefore, it signifies a present putrid matter which, if not expelled, will breed a putrid fever. Therefore.

<margin>Rule</margin>
¶ If the stench is suddenly removed from stinking urine in acute illnesses without a praiseworthy crisis <note>A "crisis" in medieval medicine was a turning point in a disease where nature either expelled the illness or succumbed to it.</note>, it signifies death. It is proven: because since stench arises from putrefaction, it is not gathered from the urine.

...unless the decay <note>original: "putredo"</note> is separated from the urine. But decay cannot be separated from the urine unless it is either expelled outward or diverted from the path of the urine. However, what is retained within is not expelled by chance, but only because of the weakness of the vital power; and the decay itself does not cease to stimulate, until the power succumbs, and consequently death follows. It would be otherwise if it were expelled outward, so that assistance and alleviation would follow; this would signify that the vital power had prevailed, and consequently it would be a sign of health.

### On the Significance of the Taste of Urines. Chapter VII.

It was intended earlier that I should treat the significance of the taste of urines. But since such a speculation is beautiful in itself and offers many notable considerations serving many medicinal matters—and among others, it serves most greatly in the knowledge of the complexion <note>The "complexion" is the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within an individual.</note>—and in this present matter, it provides help toward a full knowledge of the urine; nevertheless, because it is not to be brought into practice and experience <note>The author suggests that while tasting urine is theoretically interesting for diagnosis, it is not recommended in clinical practice.</note>, as far as this treatise is concerned, we shall therefore reserve it for a more convenient place where that matter will be treated fully and exquisitely. Here, however, let it suffice to have enumerated its differences, just as we did above. For anyone will be able to easily judge for themselves through them concerning the significance of the odor of those urines, since the differences and meanings are nearly the same, or differ very little according to the physician’s consideration.

### On the Significance of the Colors of Urines. Chapter VIII.

<margin>What color signifies primarily, what the substance of urine signifies, and what the sediment signifies.</margin>
We must now approach the significance of colors. It must first be understood, however, that it is not our intention to show the meanings of the colors of urines according to that threefold assignment of the multiplicity of colors. For that would be trifling and useless, since it is enough to understand the number of colors and the reason for their multiplication, as well as the method and agreement in assigning various colors in their diversity, as was clearly shown above in the division of colors. Now, however, it will suffice to show the meanings of all the colors collected from that third division, since in it all the differences of colors noted in others appear. Nor is there a color for which a reason is not held there; and thus the remaining ways of assigning colors are implicitly and explicitly included in it. Therefore, without repeating the others, we shall follow the order of the third assignment. If, however, we first recall to memory what we said generally above regarding the significations of all things—and particularly regarding colors—whose significance we asserted depends on three things, just as they are caused by three things and are said to depend on them in the urine: namely, the quality of digestion <note>In medieval medicine, "digestion" or "coction" refers to the body's internal processing and refining of humors.</note>, the abundance of humors, and the quality of the complexion. And although any of these three can be signified by the color itself, it signifies most primarily the quality of the complexion. Secondarily, it signifies the abundance of humors which dominate in the body; and thirdly, it represents the quality of digestion. For the colors in urine primarily depend on the action of the qualities of the complexion within the wateriness of the urine itself. Secondarily, they are caused by the mixture of staining humors, or by humors mixed with the wateriness; thus color signifies in the second place the humors. And thirdly, they are less primarily caused by digestion, and therefore they signify less primarily the quality of digestion. As for the substance <note>The "substance" refers to the density or thickness of the urine.</note>, although it has the same three significations as color, it signifies most primarily the nature and dominance of the humors, since the substance of the urine itself is generated immediately and primarily from the nature of the humors and their own substance. Secondarily, it signifies the quality of digestion, as that which would be caused in the second place. Thirdly, it signifies the digestion. Finally and least primarily, it signifies the complexional qualities, as those things on which it least primarily depends. The sediment <note>original: "Hypostasis"; the solid matter that settles at the bottom of a urine glass.</note>, however, primarily signifies digestion, and secondarily the abundance and quality of humors...

<column-break/>

</margin>
...thirdly, [the sediment signifies] the complexional qualities of the limbs, as we shall say in its proper place. Keep this in mind, for it is of great value in confirming the judgments of urines. ¶ Now, the assignment of the third division of color was as follows: some are simple, others are composite. We must treat the simple colors first, since for the most part, knowledge of the composite depends on knowledge of the simple; for as a thing is in its being, so it is in its being known. Composite colors are for the most part caused by simple ones. Simple colors were divided by this reasoning: for every color is either extreme or intermediate, and each was subdivided: for it is either truly intermediate or intermediate by approximation. And similarly, an extreme is either truly extreme or extreme by approximation to the true extreme itself; and the further assignments that follow we have already explained sufficiently above.

<margin>Rule: what intermediate and black colors signify.</margin>
¶ Coming therefore to the significations, we say first in general: that the color which is truly intermediate is truly a sign of health and temperament <note>A "temperament" is a balanced state of the humors and qualities.</note> in the qualities, humors, and digestion. An extreme color, however, signifies illnesses and distemperament in the same, according to the nature of that extreme. For the color white, which is truly one of the extremes, signifies cold illnesses, a cold complexion, cold moistures, and the absence of digestion. Black, however, which is the other extreme, signifies illnesses of combustion <note>original: "adustio"; the "burning" or scorching of humors, often associated with melancholy or intense fevers.</note>, intense heat, sharp and burnt humors, and corrupted digestion. ¶ Likewise, black color can also signify illnesses of mortification <note>Death or decay of tissue.</note> when it occurs by way of congealing. As for colors that are such by approximation—whether intermediate or extreme—they coincide in meaning with those they approach, according to more or less. Those which approach whiteness concur with the color white in meaning; those which approach blackness with black; and those which approach the intermediate with the intermediate color itself, though more or less according to a greater or lesser approximation, as has been said.

<margin>White urine and what those close to it signify.</margin>
¶ Descending more specifically, however, we say that the color white and all those that approach it—which according to that third reasoning of the division of colors are: crystalline, mucilaginous, oily, like egg-white, milky, bluish-gray <note>original: "glaucus"</note>, and karopos <note>A technical term for a pale yellow or "camel-colored" urine.</note>. All these colors, therefore, signify a weakness of digestion, an abundance of raw humors, and the dominance of cold, especially in the natural members. This is proven by reason, since such colors cannot be caused by anything else unless there is an obstruction, or a diversion to other paths, or the drinking of much water, or whatever inappropriate thing from the non-naturals <note>The "six non-naturals" (diet, environment, exercise, etc.) were the external factors that medieval doctors believed controlled health.</note> occurs to the body that is capable of producing that color in the urine. ¶ And note well: that what I now say about white colors is to be understood similarly in others in their own way: that is, provided no external thing occurs to the body capable of otherwise changing the urine, as was clearly expressed above in the additions to be observed in the judgments of urine. ¶ And from these things it is clear: that urine may be white, and yet the person may be hot in proportion and hot humors may dominate in the body; and conversely, urine may be red, and yet the person may be cold in proportion and cold humors may dominate—as is evident in colic. The same is also evident where phlegm <note>original: "flegma"</note> becomes putrid in the urinary path, so that the urine would be stained because of the decay.

<margin>White crystalline urine.</margin>
¶ White crystalline urine signifies the coldest state of all things and a weakness of digestion proceeding from that same coldness. The reason for this is: because where there is the greatest transparency, there is the greatest indigestion and no mixture of humors; for digestion and the mixture of humors have the power to impede transparency through the mixture of earthy parts with the diaphanous <note>A transparent medium.</note>. But in such crystalline whiteness and similar transparency—since it is called crystalline—[the transparency remains] etc.

<margin>Urine</margin>
¶ White mucilaginous urine signifies a mixture of raw phlegm. This is clear because such urine is caused by the admixture of such phlegm. Therefore, etc.

¶ White oily or pearl-like urine signifies that a liquefaction of phlegm is taking place, for the same reason as above.

# On Urines

<margin>Spongy White</margin>
Spongy urine <note>original: "Sfungalis urina"</note> signifies one of three things: pus <note>original: "sanie"</note>; or a crude, phlegmatic matter mixed into the urine; or a stone. The reason for this is that for it to be such, it cannot occur except through the mixture of some solid body. That body is either pus or phlegmatic matter—and such matter is that from which a stone is generated.

The distinguishing signs between these are as follows: pus resides at the bottom and produces a stench. Phlegmatic matter resides at the bottom but does not produce a stench. In the case of a stone <note>original: "calculosa"</note>, certain particles of stone appear at the bottom. Note, however, that pus could sometimes be mixed with the entire substance of the urine, especially when the pus comes from the whole body or from very distant members; for then it mixes, which does not happen when it comes from the kidneys or the bladder.

<margin>Milky Urine</margin>
Milky urine, which truly resembles milk, signifies death or phthisis <note>A term for wasting diseases, most commonly tuberculosis.</note>, as it signifies the extinction of natural heat. Note, however, that milky urine—whether resembling milk or barley water—can arise from a weakness in the digestion of the liver <note>original: "epis/hepar"</note>. I have sometimes seen this in the elderly as a manifest sign of the weakness of natural heat; when the liver is strengthened, the urine becomes thinner and more colored.

<margin>Leaden Urine</margin>
Leaden urine signifies the beginning of the mortification of heat <note>The "death" or failure of the body's internal metabolic fire.</note> proceeding from coldness, or from the drinking of poison. This is proven because, insofar as it is white, it denotes a lack of heat. But insofar as it is dark <note>original: "fuscedinis"</note>, which expresses the leaden quality, it signifies not only weakness but even extinction and mortification. It follows that we should relate the whiteness of urine to other conditions, just as we dealt with substance and transparency above, as well as the rest, so that we may finally explain all its significations.

<margin>White or milky urine in acute fevers.</margin>
Let us say, therefore, that white urine in acute fevers, or milky urine appearing after it had been tinted, signifies that the choleric matter <note>Yellow bile, one of the four humors.</note> has diverted to other places away from the paths of the urine. Thus, it is either carried to the intestines, where it will cause a flux <note>Diarrhea.</note>; or to the head, where it will cause frenzy <note>original: "frenesim"; a state of delirium or inflammation of the brain.</note>; or to some other member, where it will cause an aposteme <note>An abscess or swelling.</note>. Consequently, such urine will necessarily signify one of these. For an acute illness—and especially a fever—does not depend on anything except hot humors, or at least from strong heat. Therefore, by the merit of its current state, the urine ought to be tinted, yet it is not. Thus, that hot matter is tending elsewhere, far from the urinary paths. White urine continued in fevers without flux, frenzy, or any other aposteme, signifies a change into a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every third day, associated with "melancholy" or black bile.</note>. This can be gathered from the reason assigned above. Likewise, it can be proven because such a change does not occur except through the subtle resolution of the matter and the multiplication of thick and melancholic matter, especially if it is thin in substance.

<margin>White urine in jaundice.</margin>
White urine appearing in jaundice <note>original: "yctericia"</note> signifies a weakness of the heat of the liver, and also of its expulsive power; consequently, it threatens dropsy <note>original: "hydropisim"; the accumulation of fluid in the body.</note>. This is clear because it happens that the choleric matter which causes jaundice is retained in the liver.

White urine persisting in health signifies the beginning of digestion, especially if other differences are joined to it. This is proven because the heat is weak.

White urine persisting in health, if it is copious and luminous and with thick sediment, signifies that cold, viscous humors and phlegm are multiplying in the body.

White urine persisting in health that is thin and clear indicates that melancholic humors are multiplying in the body. Anyone will easily be able to prove all these propositions for themselves from the things said above; therefore, I pass over their proof.

Copious and dark white urine signifies the hiding of choler.

White urine at the beginning of fevers that afterwards turns black signifies the expulsion of humors through the paths of the urine, as in a continuous fever.

<margin>Milky Urine</margin>
Milky urine similar to whey <note>original: "sero"</note>, from which butter has been extracted, then signifies death or phthisis. This is clear because it signifies the extinction of heat.

<margin>What the middle colors signify, etc.</margin>
All colors that approach the middle from the side of whiteness (after those which have been named), and also those which approach the same middle from the side of redness, signify the action of heat and

<column-break/>

the strengthening of digestion, and the presence of hot humors. They signify this in a different way, however; for all those that are after citrine <note>A lemon-yellow color, considered the standard for healthy urine.</note> signify heat more expressly, because its trace appears in them more clearly. Thus, "pale" <note>original: "palearis"; straw-colored.</note> and citrine, as such, do not signify heat in comparison to others, yet in another comparison they do signify it well. The reason is commonly said to be that "pale" signifies coldness and citrine signifies a temperate state, for this reason: in "pale" there is no trace of the dominance of heat over cold, as appears in citrine. And therefore citrine is said to signify heat, although Haly Abbas <note>A famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note> (in the first book of *On Crises*, chapter 13) says the best color is citrine mixed with redness; and the same in the commentary on the second book of *Prognostics*; and also Theophilus <note>A 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note>. The best color of urine is citrine, and it is also a sign of the best health. This is because he wants the urine of a healthy person to incline from citrine toward red rather than toward pale. This clearly appears in his words saying that it inclines toward tinted citrine and bright red. But yet it sometimes happens so, though one does not take judgment absolutely concerning the intention of greater heat; because the last degree of citrinity (namely, red) signifies greater heat than the other two degrees of citrinity immediately preceding it. For those red colors signify less heat (as has been declared) because the colors of citrinity are above yellow, and also because the color is bright red. As Haly Abbas pleased in the same chapter 13 of the first book of *On Crises*, it is thus a middle between the natural color of blood and the natural color of choler. Wherefore it is inferred that such a color signifies more intense heat than the color red absolutely, and less than pure choleric color. This reason is supported because that color is made by the admixture of pure blood, while the other is made by the admixture of pure choler and blood; by their mixture, it produces a bright red. Choler, however, produces citrine.

It should be understood, moreover, that although all colors related to citrinity signify temperament and moderation, they do not always portend an essential and intrinsic moderation, but sometimes an extrinsic and accidental one. For these colors are produced not only from temperate natural heat, but also from heat increased by fasting and abstinence, as well as from strong movement of the body and mind, and similarly from pain. Therefore, before a certain judgment is made, one must always examine whether they have labored with work of the mind or body, whether they have fasted, or whether they have suffered pain; and afterward, judgment should be rendered.

<margin>Pale Urine</margin>
Therefore, pale urine <note>original: "palearis"</note> in color signifies the beginning of the action of heat and diminished digestion.

Yellow-citrine signifies somewhat more increased digestion.

Urine of intense citrinity, or citrine-orange <note>original: "citriangularis"</note>, denotes almost perfect and complete action of natural heat and digestion.

Golden urine signifies a true balance of digestion and equality of humors, and a balanced temperament by merit of its color; all these propositions are apparent from what was said above.

Urine similar to saffron in color signifies the dominance of red choler.

Fiery urine, or that similar to fiery saffron, signifies inflammation and acute fever, especially if the substance is thin.

Citrine urine at the beginning of an illness, if it proceeds by intensifying all the way to the limit of fieriness, is a sign that the heat of the fever is continually and incessantly increasing; and in this, the limit of citrinity stands.

<margin>What the red colors signify.</margin>
Truly the colors which are near to citrine on the other side, and proceeding away from it toward black, are the red colors. All these, according to their degrees, signify the dominance of blood in the whole body, except in these cases: namely, weakness of the liver, dropsy, and the rupture of a vein, or in the dilation of the vessels <note>original: "colatozy"</note>; in which red urine can appear even while there is a scarcity of blood in the whole. For it may be argued thus: colors are made either by the admixture of humors, or by the dominance of heat, or by the strength...

<margin>Red urine in acute illnesses</margin>
...of digestion: but the red color as such is not due to the dominance of heat, as was proved above, nor from strong digestion. Therefore, it is a mixture of red humor, which is nothing other than blood. Thus, it signifies an abundance of blood in and of itself, as I have said. ¶ However, a red urine that is like blood <note>original: "quasi sanguinea"</note> is safer than a choleric red <note>Urine colored by yellow bile, or choler.</note>, because the latter signifies a greater "burning" <note>original: "incendium"</note>, as was proved above. ¶ Specifically, let us discuss the individual degrees of redness: we say that red urine resembling blood without the opening of a vein <note>i.e., not caused by a physical wound or hemorrhage</note> in acute illnesses signifies a superfluous repletion, particularly of blood. ¶ If the aforementioned red urine in the same case is emitted slowly, drop by drop, and with a foul odor, it signifies the rush or course of malignant, evil humors to the vital organs <note>original: "loca suffocantia," referring to organs like the heart or lungs where humors might cause "suffocation."</note>; this is especially true if the urine is thin. It is proved by this: because it is thin, it signifies lack of digestion, and consequently, it cannot occur from a natural "crisis" <note>The turning point of a disease.</note> but rather from the force of a symptom, by which those evil humors retreat from the external parts to the internal members, such as the veins. I noted specifically that it cannot occur from a natural crisis, because where the urine is plentiful and thick, and occurring on a critical day with preceding signs of digestion, it would be a sign of the illness’s termination, as is clear to those who understand. ¶ If the aforementioned urine in the same case is emitted in large, thick amounts at the beginning, but then suddenly becomes thin, it is never a good crisis; such a crisis indicates imperfection and consequently a relapse, for the reasons noted above. ¶ Red urine that has become jaundiced <note>original: "ycteritia"</note>, yet with little redness, while the jaundice remains in its disposition, signifies a weakness of the heat of the liver and its suffocation; consequently, it threatens dropsy <note>original: "hydropisim"; a condition of swelling and fluid retention.</note>. ¶ It is possible for very red urine in healthy bodies to signify that a long fast has preceded, especially in a warm body, since heat is sharpened by hunger and thus inflames the urine. 
<margin>
Red urine with heaviness of the kidneys. Red urine in headaches. Red urine in acute cases.
</margin>
¶ Red urine in illnesses of the kidneys—that is, with a heaviness in them—signifies a hot abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note> in the kidneys. ¶ Red urine during headaches signifies delirium <note>original: "desipientia"</note>, because it indicates a mixing of humors and spirits. ¶ Red urine in acute cases that begins to redden and remains so without forming a sediment <note>original: "epar," likely a contraction or Greek-derived term for sediment/liver-like deposit.</note> signifies a difficult or malignant abscess of the kidneys. ¶ If this same urine is turbid <note>cloudy</note> along with the factors mentioned, it signifies the same thing, or else a weakness of the liver. ¶ What has been said about the significations of the red colors appears partly proved by what was said, and partly can be proved by the fact that all heat in the urine comes either by way of digestion, or the primary qualities, or a mixture of humors. Regarding digestion, it is certain that a red color comes from digestion hindered by excessive heat. ¶ Regarding the action of the primary qualities, there is no doubt that all red colors depend on heat; among them, dark red comes from the "boiling" of the blood, and a "powdery" red comes from the putrefaction of the blood, because incinerated parts are mixed with the urine. ¶ Regarding the mixture of humors, it is certain that either choler or blood is mixed. If choler is mixed, it becomes a fiery red, which signifies greater heat than other reds, as we said above, since it is made by the mixture of choler, which is the hottest of humors. If blood is mixed—since blood is of two types, arterial and venous—a pure red is made by the mixture of venous blood, while a rosy red is made by the mixture of arterial blood.
<margin>What green colors signify.</margin>
¶ Green colors similarly signify an extreme state, since they depend on it, especially if the substance is thin. If it has a thick substance, it does not generally signify coldness. Because verdigris-green <note>original: "eruginosus"</note> and leek-green <note>original: "porralis"</note> signify a great deal of "adustion" <note>A term for humors that have been "burnt" by excessive heat, making them toxic.</note>; however, leek-green does not signify adustion as vehemently as verdigris-green. In short, all green urines are bad, especially if they appear without a sediment <note>original: "hypostasi"</note>; there is no need to describe more green colors specifically, as these seem sufficient

<column-break/>

for general and specific knowledge. We might add, however, that this color sometimes signifies the drinking of poison. Furthermore, if it occurs with a sediment, it portends that nature will eventually conquer the matter.
<margin>What black colors signify.</margin>
¶ All black colors signify a great "burning" <note>incendium</note>, or a great mortification of the innate heat, or a positive congealing of the same. They also signify the mixture of burnt choler or burnt melancholy, and thus the dominance of another liquid in the body; or thirdly, they signify a future or present crisis, as will be seen more specifically. These can be proved from the general significations mentioned above: for such colors depend either on the action of qualities, or a mixture of black humors, or nature's purging after digestion. Therefore, such urines signify one of these, or two, or all three together. 
<margin>Black urine</margin>
¶ Black urine proceeding by way of a "corvinus" <note>raven-like</note> color, as in jaundice, signifies the thickness of the choler, or the beginning of its burning, which eventually portends jaundice. ¶ Black urine proceeding from dark brown signifies the dominance of black choler. ¶ Black urine proceeding from green or indigo signifies black and burnt choler in the body. ¶ Black urine preceded by green or livid color with little sediment signifies the dominance of positive coldness and that nature is succumbing, especially if it lacks an odor. ¶ Black urine preceded by red or lemon-yellow, accompanied by a loss of strength, signifies the mortification of the innate heat and privative coldness <note>The absence of vital heat.</note>. ¶ Black urine at the beginning of fevers, if there are no signs of a good crisis, signifies that the disease is overcoming nature, and a malignancy or failure of natural heat. ¶ Black or dark red urine in acute fevers, if emitted thin and slowly over a long time, with a sharp odor, and occurring around the time of a crisis, signifies the evaporation of matter to the head. Consequently, it signifies either a ringing in the ears and delirium of the senses, or a future crisis through a nosebleed. ¶ Black urine at the end of melancholic illnesses, which was preceded by thick and watery urine and followed by relief—especially if the quantity is large or occurs on a critical day—signifies that nature is performing a crisis through vomiting and signifies the termination of those illnesses, such as quartan fever <note>A form of malaria.</note>, dizziness, splenic illness, or uterine pain following the retention of hemorrhoids or menses. ¶ Black urine in acute fevers that is not in any of the aforementioned cases, where no critical signs preceded, and especially if it is scant and thick, signifies a total dominance of adustion, that the disease overcomes nature, and the consumption of the "radical moisture" <note>The essential fluid believed to sustain life.</note>. ¶ Black or dark red urine sometimes signifies the heavy drinking of dark wine, especially when drunk with a relaxation of the urinary passages, because the urine has done nothing to the wine and thus has not removed its colors. ¶ Black urine sometimes also signifies heat in the kidneys or thick humors stuck in them. ¶ Black urine in the elderly, and similarly in women, signifies the corruption of the innate heat. Not all things are easily shown by reason if the above are not properly applied to particular cases; let these words on simple colors suffice.

...of substantial moisture: or a critical expulsion <note>The "crisis" was the turning point in a disease where the patient either began to recover or declined toward death.</note>: the distinguishing sign of which is the progression of signs of digestion and the subsequent relief of symptoms. ¶ Oily urine <note>original: "urina oleaginea"</note> whose oiliness is foul-smelling—and especially if only a little is passed—signifies internal consumption and the "liquefaction" <note>The historical belief that the body's fat or substance was literally melting away due to fever.</note> of the body. ¶ Oily urine mixed like the washings of meat signifies consumption and the liquefaction of the liver and its substance, and most especially signifies dropsy <note>edema or fluid retention</note>, phthisis <note>wasting disease, usually tuberculosis</note>, or a bodily suffering of the parents <note>suggesting a hereditary condition</note>. ¶ Oily urine that was preceded by black urine, if relief follows, signifies the cleansing of "burnt" humors <note>humors that have become toxic through excessive heat</note>. ¶ If oily urine appears on the fourth day in very acute illnesses, it signifies the victory of febrile heat; however, on the seventh day, it confirms preparation for death. ¶ Simple oily urine marks the beginning of consumption and the onset of phthisis. ¶ Oily urine, in both color and substance, briefly signifies the complete liquefaction of matter, or advanced phthisis and its final state. ¶ Urine of a "canine" color <note>Likely referring to a pale, yellowish-white color similar to dog bile or certain coats</note> signifies the burning of both humors simultaneously. ¶ Red urine in which a composite blackness occurs signifies fevers or the thickness of putrefied humors. ¶ Black and red urine, if the blackness is extreme, signifies an abscess of the side <note>likely pleurisy or a lung infection</note>. ¶ It is common to almost all composite colors to signify consumption and the liquefaction of the substantial moisture of the body. But they differ among themselves: for that which resembles the color of the liver signifies its consumption and liquefaction; that which resembles the color of the kidneys signifies the same for them; and that which resembles the lungs likewise signifies it in its own way.

<margin>The color of the urine will resemble the color of whichever member is being consumed.</margin>
And briefly, whichever member's color the urine resembles, it signifies the consumption of that member and the liquefaction of its substantial moisture. Let these things said about the meanings of the differences in colors suffice.

# On the meanings of the contents, where sediment <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> is treated first, and its various distinctions. Chapter IX.

## Concerning the meanings of the contents, let us first explain the meanings of "laudable" <note>healthy or favorable</note> and "unlaudable" sediment, and then discuss the remaining contents.

<margin>Sediment is the primary factor in the judgment of urine.</margin>
Regarding the sediment <term>hypostasis; the solid matter that settles at the bottom of a urine sample</term>, it holds the primary place among the other things that occur in the judgment of urine. Therefore, let us investigate its meanings more exquisitely. This is best done if we recall to memory what we said generally at the beginning of this distinction and apply those things specifically to the sediment. We noted three things above: those that the differences in urines primarily signify because they depend on them as their own causes: namely, the qualities of the temperament <note>the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, the humors that dominate in the body, and the quality of digestion. To these we can now add a fourth: the "term" or stage of the illness. But this fourth indicates things by way of prognosis, while the other three indicate by way of demonstration. Among those three, the quality of digestion is to be examined most, since its good or bad disposition is most proportional to the disposition of our body, and the certainty had regarding digestion excels all others. Among other things, the knowledge of the sediment achieves this, because colors relate more to the action of qualities, and the liquid or substance relates to the dominance of humors, while sediment alone is equated to digestion—and especially the "third digestion," which occurs in the members <note>The final stage of nutrition where the body's organs assimilate food into their own substance</note>. For although, as we said above, these three (qualities, humors, and digestion) can be signified, one of them is more proportional to the other. Therefore, since the sediment is more proportional to digestion, although it can signify the rest, it provides greater

<column-break/>

certainty regarding the dispositions of our body. Therefore, let its meaning be intended more diligently, and we shall examine it more carefully than the rest. ¶ It is also added, secondly: because, according to common opinion, the matter of the sediment is a portion of the humors or blood digested in the third digestion and already fit to nourish the members. The body rejects it as superfluous, for it transmits it with the liquid of the urine to the liver, as if by reflux, and from there through the bladder and kidneys to the outside of the body. From this it can be gathered that although color and substance signify the quality of digestion in some way, they signify more the quality of the "second digestion" <note>digestion occurring in the liver</note>, while the sediment shows more the quality of the "third digestion." ¶ Let us speak, therefore, first of the sediment, then of the remaining contents: and first of the "laudable" and natural sediment. A natural sediment is characterized by its conditions: namely, in color it is white; in substance and quantity it is moderate; in the mixture of its parts it is equal and smooth; in position, its parts are continuous, appearing quickly and lasting long, residing or descending to the bottom; in position, it is round; or in form, it is "pineal" <note>shaped like a pine cone</note>. Such a sediment, therefore, signifies a digestion that is occurring in the whole body, and especially that the third digestion is complete and perfect. This can easily be deduced from what was presupposed, as is clear to the observer. Furthermore, the meaning of natural sediment will become more manifest if we show the necessity of its conditions; for from its conditions, complete digestion in the whole body is argued. This is because such a sediment is caused by the victory of natural heat over matter resisting conversion; therefore it is white, equal, etc. The consequence is clear: since natural heat, regulating and disposing matter, introduces every mode of preparation by which it can convert that matter into the substance of the members. If it cannot entirely convert it into nourishment, it at least disposes it to be similar to the proper nourishment of the "radical" members <note>the fundamental, solid parts of the body</note>, which are white, equal, and pineal in form; for it is the nature of heat to ascend in the figure of moisture. This first point is known of itself, for otherwise the sediment would not be natural and natural heat would not conquer the resisting matter. This necessity also appears from a certain similarity which Galen notes in the first book of *On Crises* and which Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, a famous 10th-century physician</note> repeats: namely, that sediment behaves in the humors and blood no differently than semen behaves in natural dispositions for procreation, and milk for the nourishment of infants, or in unnatural dispositions like the pus <note>original: "sanies"</note> of a white abscess behaves toward the blood and humors. But semen, milk, and pus are made by nature to be white, smooth, equal in their parts, and round in form—even if the pyramid shape does not appear, there is still a globularity and roundness descending to the lower parts and the like. These things are proved by reason. And first, it is proved why it is white: for when nature dominates in its "decoction" <note>the "cooking" or processing of humors by body heat</note>, the well-cooked moisture is made white in color, good in odor, and moderate in other factors. If it fails in decoction, this can only be by the privation or diminution of natural heat, or the dominance of unnatural heat; thus it renders the moisture either raw and undigested, or "burnt." And so it becomes horrible in odor, deformed in its parts, and in color either white and "mucilaginous" <note>slimy</note> or pale. One should not worry if the sediment achieves whiteness through its own "laudable" color while the urine itself is white and signifies rawness. But it must be said, following Isaac: because the sediment is a superfluous, useless part which nature rejected from the nourishment of the final digestion, it must have taken on the color and form of the members. Likewise, even the blood is "twice-cooked," which loses its redness after completion. And since no color is more similar to the members, or more fit to receive the colors of the members than whiteness, therefore whiteness is attributed to it, just like to pus, semen, and milk. Other things indeed...

# Of

...or fluid: since it only receives the first or second action of heat; nevertheless, it is deprived of the color of wateriness, and thereafter a faint color begins to appear in it from the action of heat. Therefore, from the beginning, when no color appears, digestion is said to be lacking, especially the first or second stages. It tends toward the lower part since it is the more corporeal among the parts of the urine; yet it remains suspended and does not descend totally because, preserving the impression of natural heat, it is made lighter, even though its part may be the coarsest of the whole urine. ¶ It should also be pine-shaped <note>original: "pinealis"; cone-shaped like a pine nut.</note> and round, because this form is very natural <margin>Sediment <term>Hypostasis; the solid matter that settles at the bottom of a urine sample.</term> in a form similar to the heart, although the opposite might seem persuasive.</margin> and those things which naturally move upward, like fire, take this shape for themselves, as it is a form indicating refinement and lightness. Of this sort also is the shape of the heart, where the seat of natural heat resides. Therefore, where its action is free, it will not only imprint other qualities but will do so according to a form that seems similar to others; for the base of the heart appears in the upper part and the pyramid <note>the apex or point</note> in the lower. In the sediment, however, the opposite occurs: since the base appears lower and the pyramid higher. But this difficulty is easily removed if we understand man to be an inverted tree <note>A common medieval medical concept where the "roots" of the human are the brain/head and the branches are the limbs.</note>. ¶ It should also be equal and uniform, so that it appears the humors are equally obedient and nature is equally disposed to its actions. ¶ And lastly, it is light and easily moved to the upper and lower parts, so as to be obedient to nature, and nature regulates it without mixing it with the substance of the urine. From all of which it is easily concluded: that where all these things are found in the sediment, they argue for complete and perfect digestion, especially the third stage <note>Medieval medicine divided digestion into four stages: in the stomach, the liver, the blood vessels, and the individual tissues.</note>. If, however, all are lacking, it signifies the most imperfect digestion. If some are present in greater or lesser degrees, the sediment becomes unnatural and therefore indicative of indigestion.
<margin>Unpraiseworthy sediment.</margin>
¶ We must now speak of unpraiseworthy <note>original: "illaudabili"; clinically unfavorable or "bad" signs.</note> sediment: that which is unpraiseworthy is that which lacks one or more of these conditions, and it will be worse for each person the more conditions it lacks. Let us say universally, first, that all unpraiseworthy sediment signifies a lessening of the action of natural heat, especially regarding the actions of the third digestion. ¶ Discussing the particulars individually, let us say in the first place that the quantity and colors of the sediment take on those twenty differences enumerated above; however, it will be enough for us to explain the six principal significations, since the others will become manifest from these. These six are: black, red, citron, white, and green. And first, establishing a graduation among them: white is less bad than the others. Then red, after that citron, after that green, and lastly black. The reason for all these can be deduced from the order of nature's defect in scorching heat, or in coldness, and the approach or proximity to moderation. ¶ Sediment is not white in the way we spoke of natural sediment above, but white, mucilaginous <note>slimy or thick</note>, and foamy signifies crudity <note>undigested matter</note> or a vehement mixing of oiliness. ¶ Black sediment signifies nearly the same as black urine, except that black sediment without blackness of the urine is better than the reverse. ¶ Green sediment, being on the way to blackness, signifies the same, but not as strongly. ¶ Citron sediment signifies the most burning heat. ¶ Red sediment signifies an abundance of blood and a feeling of loathing <note>original: "fastidium"; possibly nausea or physical aversion.</note>. ¶ The significations of the differences in the substance of unpraiseworthy sediment are the same as the significations of the substance of the urine itself. ¶ The judgments of the quantity of the sediment are similar to the judgments of the quantity of the urine. ¶ Judgments of deformity argue for matter that is heterogeneous and heat that is not uniformly applied. But it must be understood that in unpraiseworthy sediment, deformity is less bad than uniformity. ¶ Similar is the judgment

<column-break/>

concerning the continuity and discontinuity of the parts: for although continuity is appropriate for natural sediment, in unpraiseworthy sediment, the more continuity there is, the worse it is. ¶ The time of the sediment's appearance argues for the slowness or brevity of digestion. For the later it appears, the weaker it signifies nature to be and the more disobedient the matter, and vice versa in its own way. ¶ The signification of the site <note>the position in the vessel</note> of the sediment is held to be thus: when it is floating at the top and is called a "cloud" <note>original: "nubes"</note>, it signifies the beginning of digestion, if it concurs with the other conditions of good urine. And therefore, it falls short of the goodness of digestion as far as that site is from the bottom. Hanging in the middle, however, it signifies an increase in digestion. When it has descended to the bottom, it signifies the completion of digestion. ¶ On the contrary, one must understand these three sites in the opposite way if they coincide with bad conditions of the urine: for when it is floating and is called <term>nephilis; a high-floating, misty cloud in the urine</term>, it signifies the first dominion of the disease; when it is in the middle, called <term>neozima; sediment suspended in the mid-section of the urine</term>, it signifies an increase [of the disease]. When it is settled completely at the bottom, then it signifies a defect of nature and the victory of the disease. These propositions are proven because nature, in cooking the humors and making the sediment, first dissolves the humors into a certain coarse windiness, which, when it moves upward, it raises as if to its proper place, so that when it has ascended, it renders the liquor of the urine turbid and thickens it; carrying with it the coarse parts and fecal humors, by the power of its motion, it creates something like a mist. When nature progresses further in the work of decoction <note>the "cooking" or ripening of humors by internal heat</note>, it further refines the windiness; once refined, the earthy part cannot be carried so high, and thus remains in the middle, where it is condensed into sediment. When the action and decoction are further completed, the airy and windy part, being entirely resolved, flies away; the coarse and earthy part remains at the bottom, where it forms the sediment while the remaining substance of the urine stays clear. In the opposite way, it happens when the malice of the disease overcomes nature. Therefore, it was said to the doctor that such sites signify good only if there is a concurrence of other good signs. For the location of the sediment, whether as a place or as such a place, does not have the power to signify good or evil by itself. Therefore, although floating sediment signifies the beginning of digestion with the concurrence of other good signs, nevertheless it sometimes signifies the beginning of the victory of the disease; and residing in the middle, its increase; and residing at the bottom, the final dominion of the disease, if it concurs with other bad signs.

### On the significations of the remaining contents, Chapter X.

After we have explained the significations of sediment, both laudable and unpraiseworthy, it is time to proceed to the remaining contents, among which first occurs the ring <note>original: "circulus"; the rim or topmost layer of the urine against the glass.</note>, then the bubble <note>original: "ampulla"</note>, and so on. <margin>Concerning the ring.</margin> ¶ Let us say of the ring at present that it has a signification over the dispositions of the brain, as was proven clearly enough in the first distinction. ¶ A ring that appears entirely foamy—that is, when the entire substance of the ring is foamy—signifies a disturbance of the internal senses, because such foaminess argues for viscosity and windiness in the ventricles <note>the cavities</note> of the brain, by which the operations of the brain are dulled, such as the internal sense and all others. ¶ A leaden-colored ring signifies epilepsy; this is evident because it signifies melancholy or phlegm in the passages of the brain, blocking its paths and coarsening the senses. ¶ A green ring also signifies melancholy, because it argues for the brain's heat being mortified <note>deadened or extinguished</note> according to those things...

# Of Urines

...according to what was said above regarding the green color. ¶ A red ring signifies a flow of blood from the nostrils, especially if other signs occur. It indicates that blood holds dominion in the parts of the head. ¶ A trembling ring signifies paralysis and spasm caused by repletion <note>original: "ex repletione"; a state of being over-full or congested with humors.</note>, because it shows that a very fluid phlegm is found in the brain.

<margin>On foam.</margin>
¶ The meanings of foam according to all its differences must now be collected. First, the color of the foam: Foam whose color is black, lemon-yellow, or reddish, besides what it signifies [in itself], indicates black, splenetic, lemon-colored, or green matter.

<margin>Similar foam.</margin>
¶ Foam found in urine always signifies windiness <note>internal gas or "vapors"</note> combined with viscosity. For its obstruction, two things are required from the "mother-matter": namely, moist or viscous matter, and trapped vapor or windiness. This occurs when the moving heat acts as the agent. This motion agitates the moist and viscous parts and traps the airy windiness beneath the watery or viscous moisture. Heat also thins the moist parts, turning them into vapor and producing foam; sometimes both motion and heat concur at once, as appears in running horses foaming at the mouth.

<margin>Bubbling foam.</margin>
¶ Bubbling foam that remains for a long time signifies obstructions, especially when the bubbles are large. It also shows viscous matters in the body and proves that windiness is found in the urine. This is because obstruction <term>opilatio; a medieval term for a blockage in the vessels or organs</term> prevents the venting of natural heat; when it is not vented, windiness is generated if it finds matter that can be turned into gas. Such windiness, when transmitted with the urine, creates bubbles. ¶ Bubbling foam, according to the opinion of Hippocrates, signifies <term>nephresis; kidney disease</term>. The reason is that it argues for a multitude of raw matter along with its viscosity; since the natural heat in the body is weak compared to so much matter, although it is not strong enough to digest or resolve the whole mass, it will nevertheless lift some part of it into windiness. This windiness, trapped in that viscous and not easily expanded matter, will create large bubbles. When these appear, they argue that the raw matters are located very close to the urinary paths. For if this windiness came from distant parts, it would be divided into tiny bits and thus would not make large bubbles, but rather granular ones. Therefore, large bubbles lasting a long time signify raw matter existing in the paths of the urine, and thus portend nephresis.

<margin>Granular foam.</margin>
¶ Granular foam generally signifies catarrh, but it signifies that the catarrh tends toward different members in different ways, depending on which part or region of the urine it appears in. For if it remains on the surface, it denotes catarrhal matter that does not descend to the lower members. If it is in the airy part of the urine (the second region), it points to the respiratory <note>original: "spiritualia"; the lungs and heart</note> members. If it descends further, to the nutritive members. If it goes to the bottom, to the joints. The reason for these can easily be gathered from what was said in the first distinction, and also from what will be said in the third. But it must be understood that if granules are found in any part of the urine and are black or red, they denote acute catarrh and signify a burning <note>original: "adustione"; a scorched or overheated state of the humors</note> in the members corresponding to that region.

<margin>Foam between those.</margin>
¶ Foam that is properly between the bubbling and granular types signifies either strong heat or a weakness of color. This is proven because its cause is either strong heat causing evaporation, thinning and rarefying the moisture and converting it into vapor which, when trapped in viscous matter, makes foam; or, conversely, windiness is raised by weak heat and trapped in viscous matter to create foam. But the distinguishing signs between these two causes are taken from the color of the foam. For if the foam tends toward lemon-yellow, it argues it was produced by strong heat. If toward white, by coldness and weakness of heat. ¶ Cortical <note>original: "corticalis"; like bark or husks</note> urine

<column-break/>

with large white petals <note>flakes</note>, although it most often signifies an ulcer, is nevertheless a good sign of the same. The reason is that it signifies its cleansing <note>original: "mundationez"; the clearing of an infection</note>, as is clear regarding the one who took cantharides <note>Spanish fly, a toxic beetle used as a diuretic or irritant</note>, as Altabas said in the 7th book of his *Practice*.

<margin>White petals of urine.</margin>
¶ Scaly urine, whose scales are red, signifies a disease of the kidneys, since it is a sign that parts are falling away from a fleshy member.

<margin>Red scales.</margin>
¶ Scaly urine, whose scales are white, signifies a disease of the bladder, since all things bear witness to their origins. ¶ Scaly urine, whose scales are dark or of an obscure color, or similar to fish scales, is a bad sign. The reason is that it signifies the ultimate dissolution in the body and the radical <note>fundamental or vital</note> members, or even in the veins and arteries.

<margin>Vetch-like sediment.</margin>
¶ Urine whose sediment <term>hypostasis; the solid matter that settles at the bottom</term> is vetch-like <note>original: "orobina"; resembling the seeds of the bitter vetch</note>, which does not break apart, being red or declining toward lemon-yellow, or pressed down, or dark, signifies burnings of the upper members.

<margin>Bran-like sediment.</margin>
¶ Urine whose sediment is bran-like <note>original: "furfurea"; resembling wheat bran</note>, with itching of the head of the penis, stench, and an admixture of pus or oiliness from the upper members, along with health or strength [of the body], signifies scabies <note>an itchy skin or internal irritation</note> in the bladder. ¶ Urine whose sediment is bran-like without stench or burning, but with weakness of the virtue of the upper members and difficulty urinating, with inflammation and oiliness and a dark bran color, signifies a melting <note>liquefaction</note> of the upper members as stated above.

<margin>Fine-flour sediment.</margin>
¶ Urine whose sediment is fine-flour-like <note>original: "simulaginea"; like fine wheat meal</note>, like fine-ground grain divided into thick parts: if it draws toward redness, it signifies burning in the blood; if toward blackness, burning in the spleen; if toward whiteness, burning in the bladder. ¶ Corollary: All urines in which scales, or dissolutions, or bran appear—if they are not from causes in the bladder, kidneys, or urinary channels—signify evil in acute diseases. This is proven because they cannot happen except from the burning of blood or of the fleshy members.

<margin>Fleshy sediment.</margin>
¶ Fleshy sediment is most often from the kidneys and sometimes from the liver.

<margin>Fatty and oily urine.</margin>
¶ Fatty and oily urine with floating droplets in great quantity signifies a melting of the kidney fat. If that oiliness is lemon-yellow, it is worse, because it signifies the dissolution of old fat (which is yellow) and not just new fat. If it is in small quantity and much mixed with the liquid of the flesh's substance, it signifies a dissolution of the kidneys.

<margin>Purulent sediment.</margin>
¶ Purulent <note>original: "saniosa"; containing sanies, a mixture of blood and pus</note> sediment, or urine in which pus appears, signifies the opening of an ulcer. However, if they occur with good substance of the urine, and the urine itself is of good quality, it signifies that the ulcer is in the urinary paths. Briefly, wherever pain precedes the arrival of pus, it signifies a rupture there. ¶ Little bits <note>original: "frustula"</note> signify a weakness of the digestive power of the stomach and mesaraic veins. This is proven because, due to such weakness, some parts remain chunky and are easily dissolved, especially in the digestion of milk and lime.

<margin>Sandy sediment.</margin>
¶ Sandy sediment residing at the bottom signifies that stones are being generated or dissolved in the kidneys or bladder. If it does not reside at the bottom but is mixed with the watery part of the urine, it signifies burning in the liver if it declines to red, or in the spleen if it declines to lemon-yellow. This is proven as above regarding the fine-flour sediment.

<margin>Mucilaginous sediment.</margin>
¶ Mucilaginous sediment signifies an abundance of raw humors, or a crisis of sciatica, or of the joints, or phlegmatic diseases, or a coldness of the complexion. But there is a difference between purulent and mucilaginous sediment: the purulent stinks, while the other does not at all. Signs of disease precede the purulent; they do not precede the other. Mucilaginous parts are not easily separated or joined; it is turbid and thick. Purulent sediment, however, joins and separates easily.

<margin>Hair-like sediment.</margin>
¶ Hair-like sediment, or urine in which hairs appear, signifies the consolidation of a hidden vice <note>disease or defect</note> by the action of heat.
