### On the significations of combined urines. Chapter XI.

<note>A decorative drop cap 'U' featuring foliate designs inside a square border.</note>
The significations of urines having been demonstrated according to simple differences, those that occur from combinations must now be declared. However, we should first understand that although the significations of combined signs can for the most part be gathered from the simple signs, it often happens that they must be judged otherwise. For first of all: although an extreme sign of one category might seem to have a combined meaning with a moderate sign of another category, it is nonetheless not so; for either the simple meaning of the extreme remains, or its meaning is refracted <note>altered or diminished by the presence of the other sign</note>. Examples of both should be added. Urine that is thin in substance (which is an extreme of one category) with a free manner of urinating (which is a moderate sign of another) retains its simple meaning for itself, not refracted, nor making a third meaning with the other. The same thin urine with a lemon-yellow color does not retain its simple meaning, but takes on a combined meaning with the other, or a refracted meaning from it. Hence it signifies a somewhat diminished digestion, and thus has a refracted meaning; or it denotes an over-heating of the liver and kidneys along with raw humors. Although it may be that it is sometimes altered and sometimes combined, it more often happens that its simple meaning remains. Therefore, when we show the significations of combined differences, we shall often (not without reason) pass over the combination of an extreme of one category with a moderate sign of another. ¶ Secondly, it must be understood that no sign of one category is combinable with another sign of its own category, except in sediment <note>original: "hypostasi"</note>; for the differences of sediment are combinable among themselves, and therefore we shall make a special chapter for it. ¶ Thirdly, it should again be noted that although some of these combinations—those which are paired, so to speak—have complete significations, it is impossible for all of them to have a complete signification unless a third or fourth difference is added; and sometimes more are joined, and the judgment is then so much more perfect and certain. Thus, the discussion that takes place here concerning the significations of two differences apart from the observation of others is not because one should always proceed this way in judging, but to show the fullness and completion of the art: so that if at any time, among the other things observed in the signs of urine, two or more "noble" <note>prominent or significant</note> differences appear, it may be known what those parts signify together. For just as we showed the significations of simple differences separately for the completion of the art, it was so that when one sign occurs that is particularly notable among the others, it may be known that it alone signifies [the condition], and that it should be weighed above the others in

<column-break/>

judging, and the "palm of victory" for the meaning of that urine should be granted to it. It may be more or less according to whether the others agree or disagree; the same must be understood regarding combinations: that judgment is perfect and complete which is drawn from a consideration of all the differences found in the urine. Other judgments are more or less certain and skillful according to how many of the aforesaid differences are observed, and especially those which are more powerful in signifying according to the doctrine handed down above. For since it is always necessary in urine for there to be a difference of substance, quantity, color, transparency, smell, manner of urinating, and contents, one must therefore always inspect what kind of substance, what kind of quantity, what color, what manner of urinating, and what contents are present. Finally, one must see the signification of each by itself, then of two together, then of three, four, and five, and finally all eight. For eight differences are always found in any urine. ¶ Lastly, it must be understood that while this is the most skillful and complete method of judging, the authors did not always follow it; because if they noted only four of the principal differences—namely substance, color, sediment, and quantity—the judgment is sufficiently perfect, as the significations of the other differences are overshadowed by these, and one should rely on them. And although these four—quantity, color, substance, and sediment—are absolutely the most principal, yet in many dispositions the manner of urinating takes precedence (as in diseases of the bladder), in some transparency, and in others color, according as the condition has more quality in one category than another, and thus claims the primary role in signifying for itself. In such cases, one must rely principally on that sign.
<margin>The principal differences upon which we must rely in the judgment of urine.</margin>
¶ Let us therefore pursue the significations of the combined differences, and speak according to the order of the first part of this distinction.
<margin>White, thick urine.</margin>
¶ Urine whose substance is white and thick most often signifies that crude <note>undigested</note>, thick, or viscous humors abound in the body <note>original: "vase"; literally 'vessel', referring to the body as the container of humors.</note>, and consequently suggests a future stone in the bladder. ¶ Thick white urine on a "critical day" <note>a day when a disease reaches a turning point</note>, and especially on the fourth day, signifies liberation from joint pain and from an abscess behind the ears. ¶ If the same appears after a crisis, it demonstrates a return of the illness. ¶ In acute cases, the same signifies distress and trembling. ¶ The same, appearing like pus <note>original: "sanies"</note> in "phrensy" <note>delirium or brain inflammation</note> or in burning fevers, signifies death. The proof of this is as follows: because urine of this kind argues a diversion of the heated matters from the pathways of the ducts and their seizure toward the head. Also, because this kind of urine is disproportionate to very burning fevers, it signifies either the eruption of an abscess or the hiding of the fever-matter. <margin>Thick, milky urine.</margin> ¶ Thick, milky urine signifies a stone of the bladder. ¶ The same, appearing in the beginning of an illness, is deadly within eight days. ¶ The same is deadly when accompanied by greenish <note>original: "eruginoso"; like copper rust</note> vomiting and dryness of the tongue. <margin>Thick, pale-gray urine.</margin> ¶ Thick, pale-gray <note>original: "charopos"; a bluish-gray or "sea-colored" hue.</note> and clear urine signifies many bad humors. But if it is turbid, it signifies a present or future headache. The same in acute cases signifies that there are disturbances, and if a multitude of thin urine follows it, it signifies the end of the fever. <margin>Thick, reddish urine.</margin> ¶ Thick and reddish <note>original: "subrubia"</note> urine signifies long but safe illnesses. ¶ Thick red urine signifies the dominion of blood. ¶ The same, if passed bit by bit in acute cases, signifies danger. ¶ The same, if it is turbid and passed bit by bit with a headache and jaundice of the midriff <note>original: "hypocondrioz"</note>, signifies a crisis on the seventh day. <margin>Thick, black urine.</margin> ¶ Thick black urine, if it occurs with relief, signifies the purging of the melancholic humor and the resolution of melancholic illnesses (which we named above). The reason is that the melancholic humor is black and thick; when expelled through the urinary passages, the nature is unburdened by it, and consequently it signifies the resolution of illnesses—unless it occurs with a fever. For if it is fierce without a defect of the bladder, it signifies "adustion" <note>over-heating or scorching of the humors</note>, putrefaction, and likewise the danger of death.

<margin>Thick urine with a thick circle and a lead-colored circle.</margin>

### On the urines of natural things. Chapter I.

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial E contains a seated figure, likely a scholar or physician, working at a desk with books and decorative foliage surrounding him.</note>
**H**aving dispatched these things concerning the simple and composite significations of urines without relation to any specific disposition, but absolutely, as each difference taken by itself or complicated with another might signify regarding the dispositions of the body, it is now time that we come, in the final place, to noting the urines of determined dispositions: namely natural, non-natural, and against nature <note>The "three things" of Galenic medicine: physiology (natural), lifestyle/environment (non-natural), and pathology (against nature)</note>. Beginning first with the natural ones, since they are divided according to the divisions of the natural things themselves, following their order, one should begin with the elements. But since the elements properly have no signification except themselves—which is of the complexions, humors, and also the virtues and operations specified by the urine—through these, the urines of the elements will also be noted. All these are noted from the same differences: from the colors we accept significations mostly concerning complexions; from the liquids or substance, mostly concerning humors and elements; and from both, concerning the virtues or operations, as will appear quite clearly. If, however, we first describe the urine of healthy bodies, it is because we choose it as the form by which all other resulting urines are judged, since the "straight is the judge of itself and of the crooked" <note>A common medieval philosophical maxim meaning one must know the healthy standard to recognize the deviation.</note>.

<margin>Urine is of the body.</margin>
¶ The urine of the healthy, therefore—as pleases Galen in the first book *On Crises* and in the commentary on the first *Prognostics*—is that which is moderate in substance between thin (like water) and thick (like the urine of a donkey); and in color, it is "citrine" <note>a yellowish-gold</note> declining toward the tint or clarity of red <note>original: "charam"</note>; and it has a sediment sitting at the bottom that is white, light, equal, pine-cone shaped, and lasting. It is similar in quantity to the sediment of rose water, moderate between much and little in proportion to the things consumed; the odor and stench are not entirely absent, but somewhat sharp, having a clarity that is not excessive and lacking froth. ¶ This, therefore, is the urine which simply pronounces the best healthy bodies and the better of forms. Those which afterwards vary from this, signify the various dispositions of bodies in their natural lapses or errors, according to sex and other factors, as we shall demonstrate shortly. ¶ These conditions of the urine of healthy bodies can be deduced in order. And first regarding substance: which is said to be moderate because it follows the goodness of the digestion of blood in the liver and veins, and a competent and proportional mixing of the humors. Just as blood is most tempered in us when it is best purified from chyle and dregs, it is necessary in this case that the urine which is strained from it be, in its own way, better than the urines of other animals, and consequently hold more to moderation in substance and also in clarity. But as a temperate man stands in relation to other men, just as a man stands to other species of animals, it is necessary that his urine relate in its own way to the urine of other men, just as the urine of a man relates to the urine of other animals. Since that urine, as has been said, holds a moderation between them, therefore the urine of a healthy person holds a moderation in substance among the urines of other men, and also in other conditions, especially regarding its transparency. ¶ The color, indeed, is said to be such as has been described because this kind of color absolutely attests to the temperament of the blood, since it is sequestered from the blood and deservedly receives a tint from it that is proportionate to the impression of the blood. ¶ The quantity, indeed, is moderate because, when digestion is complete, the remaining superfluity expelled from it is proportionate to the things consumed; and things consumed are supposed to be in a moderate quantity when they are taken by healthy bodies, which take no more than is convenient. ¶ The odor also ought to be such as was said, because if it lacked all stench, that would happen through the extinction of heat or mortification. If, indeed, it were too fetid from putrefaction, then only moderation is rendered convenient for it. ¶ It is clear, indeed, for that reason...

It is: because the separation of the urine from the humors must occur, and a perfect mixing within the substance of the urine. Therefore, it is clear: so that it might determine the best sight. ¶ It is placed without foam: when the blood, from which it falls, is without viscosity and windiness <note>original: "ventositate"; referring to "gas" or "vapors" in the bodily fluids</note>, from which foam is created, as was sufficiently proven above. ¶ The <term>hypostasis</term> <note>The sediment that settles at the bottom of a urine sample</note> is placed as white, even, hanging at the bottom, and pine-cone shaped: because all these show the completion of digestion, just as was demonstrated above where the significance of sediment was treated specifically in all its parts. When all are removed, the third digestion is entirely taken away from the members. Therefore, Hippocrates was not without merit when, wishing to describe good urine—having set aside the conditions of substance, color, quantity, and the rest—added only the conditions of good sediment enumerated above. ¶ Nor is it an obstacle what Galen said regarding bodies in the best of health: which are of a temperate complexion and perfect in their powers, since they take no more food than their nature digests. Consequently, no sediment is formed because of the strength of the members, which resolve the superfluities of their nourishment through the pores; consequently, the superfluity of the third digestion is not returned from the members to the liver itself, to go out in the kidneys with the straining of the blood. And consequently, no sediment appears. This is understood to be true in healthy bodies and robust members, perfect in the third digestion and expulsion: either no sediment appears, or if it appears, it is of those dispositions which were mentioned above.

## On the urines of complexions and humors. Chapter II.

<margin>Urines of simple complexions.</margin>
After the description of the urine of those who are simply healthy, it is now time to demonstrate the urines of the remaining bodies. First regarding the complexions. Then regarding the humors, and so forth: of which the urines of simple complexions are shown first, and finally the composite ones. ¶ The urine of a simple **hot complexion** must have a "tinge" or deep color. ¶ The urine of a simple **cold complexion** is white, or lacking color. ¶ The urine of a simple **dry complexion** must be thin in substance. ¶ The urine of a simple **moist complexion** is thick in substance. ¶ The reasoning for these four descriptions is proven from the alteration or action of the impression of the primary qualities; the rest are proven from the admixture of humors. From these are drawn the urines of composite complexions
<margin>Urines of composite complexions.</margin>
in this order. ¶ The urine of a **hot and moist complexion** is tinged or colored, and thick in substance: colored because it is hot, and thick because it is moist. ¶ The urine of a **hot and dry complexion** is colored and thin: colored because it is hot, and thin because it is dry. ¶ The urine of a **cold and moist complexion** is white and thick: white because it is cold, and thick because it is moist. ¶ The urine of a **cold and dry complexion** is white and thin: white because it is cold—this is what comes from coldness—and thin because it is dry. And this is because

it proceeds from a dry humor. Therefore, the urine of a composite complexion and its proportioned humor will be the same: namely, the urine of a hot and moist complexion will be the same as the **urine of blood**. Hot and dry with the **urine of choler** <note>Yellow bile</note>. Cold and moist with the **urine of phlegm**. ## On the urines of the powers and operations. Chapter III.

The urines of the powers and operations are noted by almost the same differences by which the urines of the elements, complexions, and humors were noted above. Among these, although color testifies more to the complexions, substance testifies more to the humors. However, color and substance taken together and added to the sediment testify more to the **power**, and also to the **operations**. Among these, only that which pertains to this part—namely, the **natural power** and its operation, which is **digestion**—must be discussed. The dispositions of the remaining powers and operations can be discerned little or not at all through the urines, but rather through signs more proportioned to them: for example, the **vital power** and its operations through the pulse and breath; the **animal power** and its operations through sense and motion. Therefore, no mention of their urines will be made in any way. ¶ However, so that there may be certain knowledge of the urines of the natural power and its operation, which is digestion, it must be understood: that because the digestive power uses **natural heat** as its own proper instrument, the strength or weakness of the digestive power must be measured—as well as the perfection, imperfection, completion, and diminution of digestion—according to the strength or weakness of the natural heat. Since digestion...

Urinis

<meta>This page transitions from the general qualities of sediment to how digestion—driven by "natural heat"—is reflected in the urine of different demographic groups, including children, the elderly, and pregnant women.</meta>

Digestion does not occur except by the action of natural heat upon nourishment. Therefore, our entire reasoning regarding the consideration of urines in terms of their power must be referred to this heat. <margin>Urine of complete digestion.</margin> Natural heat can be weakened in two ways: either by cold, which diminishes it, or by a preternatural <note>original: "praeternaturali"; heat that is outside the normal state, such as a fever</note> heat that dissolves it. From this, it is gathered that a weakness of the digestive power, or imperfect digestion, can happen for one of two reasons: one is an overcoming coldness, and the other is a strong, preternatural heat. That which is in the middle of these is temperate and natural heat, which perfects digestion. Let us, therefore, set down the urines that signify indigestion coming from cold, and also those signifying indigestion coming from heat. But since "the straight is the judge of itself and the crooked," <note>An Aristotelian principle: one must understand the healthy/perfect state to recognize the deviations.</note> one must first understand the urine of complete digestion, because other urines are understood by their lapse from this standard, whether by being more or less than the ideal. <margin>Urines signifying indigestion.</margin> The urine of complete digestion, therefore, is simply the urine of healthy people, which we described above. This signifies that digestion and the natural power are strong, and that the natural heat is robust.

However, urine that is white like the purest water—known as <term>glauca</term> <note>A bluish-grey or watery-white color</note>—or milky like goat’s whey with substance, or very thick without sediment, or with a great deal of phlegmatic sediment, signifies great indigestion. Camel-colored urine <note>original: "karopos"</note>, like the skin of a camel; or sub-pale, like new straw; or straw-colored; or pale like the water from half-cooked meat; with a white or red sediment swimming on the surface and a substance tending toward the middle-ground, signifies the beginning of digestion. Wine-colored urine <note>original: "inopos"</note>, like dark wine; or livid like lead; or green; or black; and <term>cyanos</term> <note>A dark blue or blackish-blue</note> in substance, whether very thin or thick and murky in transparency without sediment, signifies the "mortification" <note>the dying out or extinguishing</note> of natural heat. <term>Cyanos</term> urine, like the darkest wine; or black as coal, whether thin or thick in small quantity, with a sediment sinking to the bottom, signifies "adustion" <note>over-cooking or burning of humors</note>, a defect of indigestion, and corruption from an overabundance of preternatural heat. The spirits of the urine have no other differences from those predicted, which is why it is not necessary to describe their urines.

On the urines related to natural things, namely ages and sexes. Chapter III.

## <note>A decorative initial letter U contains a portrait of a man's face wearing a cap or cowl inside the bowl of the letter, representing a physician or scholar.</note> In the final place, after the urines of natural things, we shall begin to describe the urines of those things attached to them, namely ages and also sexes. First of ages, and then of sexes. <margin>Urines of children.</margin> The urine of children tends toward white in color; that is, it is straw-colored or camel-colored in a substance of fatty richness and in great quantity. It tends toward whiteness because of the imperfection of digestion and "cooking" <note>original: "coctio"; the metabolic transformation of food</note> occurring from an abundance of moisture, and not from a lack of natural heat, since natural heat is strong in them. It is thick in substance because of the mixture of many superfluities within the urine, or because of the dominance of phlegm or blood in their bodies. It is high in quantity because of their greediness and the large amount of food and drink they consume, and especially because there is very little resolution of moisture through other paths, as they lack exercise and their heat <margin>Urines of young men.</margin> is not sharp. The urine of young men is more tinted in color, thinner in substance, and low in quantity for the opposite reasons; especially because of the sharpness of their heat and their multiple exercises, which tint the urine, thin it, and decrease its volume by dissolving part of it. <margin>Urines of the elderly.</margin> The urine of the elderly is very thin, faint in color (tending toward white), and low in quantity. The causes are readily apparent. It is thin due to the dominance of the melancholic humor. It is faint in color due to the weakness of natural heat, and low in quantity due to their abstinence from food and drink.

<column-break/>

The urine of women is white, thick, clear, and bubbly <margin>Urines of women.</margin> compared to the urine of men. It is white because of an abundance of coldness and a failure of the "cooking" process. It is thick because of the width of their passages. It is bubbly because of the viscosity of their humors. It is clear because of the "perfection" or compactness of the mixture of humors in the substance of women's urine more than in that of men. Thus, the best sign to distinguish between the two urines is that if women's urine is shaken or moved, it becomes little or not at all turbid; however, men's urine becomes turbid when shaken, especially in the upper part, because of its heat. <margin>Differences between the urines of young and old women.</margin> Men's urines are opposite to all these in every difference for the opposite reasons. However, there is a difference not to be overlooked between young women and old women: the urines of young women are more beautiful and brighter. Those of the elderly are not only "cruder" <note>undigested</note>, but also thicker and more livid. The reason for both is that, being female, both have a defect of heat; however, the elderly have much more of a defect, as they are closer to the extinction of their heat due to the course of age. Thus, their urine is less digested, less bright, and more livid, the opposite of which is true in young girls.

The urine of virgins is clear, very bright, and thin, because there has been no "ebullition" <note>boiling or agitation</note> in the blood through sexual intercourse, nor an enlarging of the orifices, nor thirdly, a lack of menses and their mixing with the substance of the urine. The urine of those who have had intercourse is thicker in substance and murky in transparency, and often "threads of the body" <note>original: "somatis fila"; likely referring to mucus threads or cast-like structures</note> appear in it. The urine of menstruating women is almost bloody in color and substance, and murky in transparency; the reason is quite obvious, as it occurs from the mixing of menstrual blood with the substance of the urine. The urines of pregnant women in the first, second, and <margin>Urines signifying the first months [of pregnancy].</margin> third month are mostly white, thin, and clear, with a certain cloud <note>original: "nebula"</note> of a thin color similar to an iris or a rainbow; and it is the color of a rainbow. There is also in it something like carded wool <note>original: "corum carminatum"</note> or a divided sediment in which there are grains that ascend and descend. This last sign is the best.

The reason for these things can be gathered as follows. First, regarding the heat and clarity: at the beginning of pregnancy, the natural heat is much withdrawn and united at the cavity of the womb to achieve generation. The superfluities that used to be mixed with the urine and expelled are therefore retained; because of the lack of these superfluities, the urine remains clear and thin. Due to the withdrawal of heat to the womb and its separation from the pathways of the urine, the urine remains white. But note that this is true as long as there is no commotion in the menses. The closer the beginning of the pregnancy, the more distinctly such signs will appear. Secondly, regarding the "cloud," it is proven thus: because heat acts on the thin part of the superfluities mixed with the urine, and since there is little of it and it lacks thickness, that action lifts it to the upper part of the urine, condensing it into a cloud, while leaving the rest of the urine like pure water. Thirdly, concerning the "rainbow," it must be understood that different colors do not appear all at once in the manner of a rainbow—so that green and red appear at the same time as the urine color—for that would be entirely false. Rather, according to the varying action of heat on the "matter" from which the fetus is nourished during the process of pregnancy, the color of that arc varies; beginning from the first month and proceeding toward green until it reaches red, which is near the time of birth. Fourthly and finally, it was said that there is something like carded wool or a divided sediment in which grains appear moving up and down. The reason for this is that while in the time they are not pregnant, due to the mixture of many superfluities and the weakness of heat (which is unable to separate the thick from the thin), sediment usually does not appear in them in this way.

When women are indeed pregnant, due to the retention of those superfluities: when the coarse parts are very few, the natural heat is able to sequester the subtle from the coarse, and to collect and gather them into one. Once gathered together, they form a "windy" <note>original: "carminatum"; likely referring to the presence of bubbles or gas indicating the action of heat on moisture</note> substance that is said to appear in them. ### Chapter V.

->On the urines regarding non-natural things.<-

<note>A large ornamental drop cap letter P contains a seated figure, likely a scholar or physician, within a rectangular frame.</note>

**F**or a clearer understanding of what the signs of urines signify regarding "non-natural" <note>In Galenic medicine, "non-naturals" are external factors that affect health but are not part of the body's innate nature, such as food, drink, sleep, exercise, and emotions.</note> things: it must first be understood that non-natural things are signified by urines in a proportionate way, just as a cause is signified by its effect. For non-natural things—occurring differently in quantity, quality, and timing—are the causes of changes in the substance, quantity, and quality, and even the sediment <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> of the urine. We shall arrive at an understanding of these causes through the urines as their effects; and first, concerning food and drink. Regarding these, it must be understood that what ought to be known through the urine about food and drink is quantity and quality. Therefore, the differences in the quantity of urine must be set down. The differences in quantity are: much, little, and moderate. In quality, regarding the primary qualities, food is: hot, cold, dry, and moist.

<margin>
Urine color and drink in quantity.
</margin>
¶ Therefore, urine that is great in quantity, thick in substance, turbid, declining toward white, and crude <note>original: "cruda"; meaning undigested</note> indicates a great intake of food. ¶ Urine that is little in quantity, subtle in substance, and tinted in color indicates a small use of food. ¶ Moderate urine signifies moderation. ¶ The first proposition is proven: A multitude of food and drink multiplies all moisture in the body, and consequently the urinary moisture. Similarly, phlegm is multiplied. Indeed, the superfluity of phlegmatic blood is for the most part thick. Third, it is crude, because by the multitude of food and drink the natural heat is weighed down and hindered in digesting due to the disproportion of the matter. Indeed, when food is not perfectly digested, the blood is not perfectly "cooked." From this, a defect in the tint of the urine necessarily follows. This is the urine of gluttons and drunkards. And this is what Galen said: "Urine is diversified according to quantity." What if the liquid of the urine grows much? It is diminished <note>in quality</note>. Hippocrates says: "The tint of the urine is lessened, and it approaches whiteness most closely." ¶ The second proposition is proven by the opposite: It diminishes moisture, and consequently the heat is sharpened, which tints the urine and diminishes the quantity. Similarly, yellow bile <note>original: "colera"</note> is multiplied, and the superfluity becomes subtle and clear. Thirdly, the heat not only prevails over its object but is inflamed, from which it follows that it colors the urine beyond the tint of "citrine" <note>a yellowish-orange color</note>. This is the urine of those who fast. Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a famous Persian physician</note> says: "If there is little liquid, it makes little urine, much sediment, and a greater tint." ¶ The third proposition can be proven in its own way.

<margin>
Urine of food and drink in quality.
</margin>
¶ How urine that signifies the quality of food is recognized: ¶ Tinted and red urine signifies the use

<column-break/>

of hot things, such as spices and pungent foods. ¶ This is proven: foods of this kind heat the liver; when it is heated, the blood is tinted, and the blood becomes red. And the urine becomes red along with it. ¶ Discolored and crude urine signifies the use of cold foods, because such things, by the opposite, extinguish heat. ¶ Urine that is much, turbid, and thick with whiteness designates the use of moist foods. This is proven: because such foods increase and multiply moisture, suffocate the heat, and take away its ability to refine and separate waste. Therefore it will be turbid, unless it is otherwise disposed by an obstruction <note>original: "opilatione"</note>. ¶ Urine that is subtle, clear, and little signifies the use of dry foods. This is proven: because dryness dries things out and removes turbulence; it will be colored or discolored according to whether heat or cold is joined with that dryness. ¶ Take note, however: although besides the primary qualities, foods have secondary and tertiary ones which can also vary the urines, let it be seen that a doctrine could be made of them; however, because this is not the place for it, let it be omitted for now. For such foods mostly lead the body into sickness. Therefore, the urines of those foods and the sicknesses produced by them will be the same. For example: if they are foods that cause obstructions, the urine of these foods will be the urine of obstruction; if they are "opening" <note>original: "aperitiui"; laxative or diuretic</note> foods, they will similarly have the same urine as diseases caused by excessive opening. However, some foods also imprint an odor on the urines, especially the "opening" ones, such as asparagus; which not only open the passages and make much urine by opening them, but also make it thick and foul-smelling. And so it can be understood in its own way regarding the rest, such as poisonous foods: which, if joined with coldness, produce the urine of those killed by cold; if with heat, they produce the urine of those consumed and inflamed. ¶ Urine that is little in quantity, subtle in substance, and tinted in color, passed after a struggle or laborious exercise, signifies such labor—unless the motion was immediately after food. For labor and bodily motion heat the liver, the heart, and the whole body, and it clears out superfluities by resolving them insensibly <note>through invisible perspiration</note>; whereby the urinary moisture is diminished, becomes clear and subtle, and is tinted with color. I said secondly "unless the motion was immediately after food," because such motion hinders digestion, and thus causes crude urinary moisture to pass through; so that it is crude, turbid, and of greater quantity. Or clear, white, and watery, as in those having wide passages and a hot liver and kidneys. ¶ Much, thick urine signifies idleness. This is proven by the opposite, as above. ¶ Moderate urine in these differences portends moderation in exercise and rest. ¶ The same as above is proven regarding emptiness <note>original: "inanitione"; fasting or depletion</note>, fullness, and similar proofs.

<margin>
Urine of motion and the types of bitterness, also regarding depletion.
</margin>
¶ Urine that is much in quantity, moderate in substance, and clear and colored signifies joy. This is proven: for a temperate heat perfects digestion and does not dry out the moisture. Therefore, the heat, substance, and transparency will be praiseworthy, and the quantity greater, because the heat does not dry out the moisture. ¶ Intense and subtle urine signifies anger, anxiety, sadness, and fears. This is proven: because through anger the blood is inflamed; through worry the humors are moved and the heart is heated, and thus the urine is tinted. The same happens from anxiety, but they differ because the heat in anxiety is less sharp and punishing, as it comes suddenly to the heart and recedes suddenly before its complexion <note>the body's balance of humors</note> changes. Heat from sadness is much sharper, because it lingers in the heart until its cause is removed. By which its complexion grows hot.

<margin>
Urines of the accidents of the soul.
</margin>
¶ Urine that is little in quantity, tinted in color, subtle in substance, and crude signifies much wakefulness <note>insomnia</note>. This is proven because...

<margin>
Urines of sleep and wakefulness.
</margin>

...since wakefulness heats the animate spirit <note>original: "spiritum animatum"; the subtle substance believed to carry life and sensation through the nerves</note> and inflames the whole body. It also diverts natural heat away from digestion, thereby hindering it. Conversely, the opposite should be said regarding excessive sleep.

<margin>
Urine of regions and seasons of the year.
</margin>
Urine that is sharp, or from a hot season or a hot region, is tinted, sparse, and thin. This is proven because heat resolves moisture through the pores—either as vapor or sweat—and thus dries the body, inflames the blood, and makes the urine more colored but lesser in quantity. ¶ However, raw, white, and plentiful urine signifies cold air, or a cold season or region. This is proven because intense cold penetrating the interior of weak bodies extinguishes the natural heat and, through its constriction, prevents the heat from acting. Yet, a mild cold that closes the pores multiplies internal moisture and blunts the heat itself. ¶ Note, however, that the opposite can often happen "by accident" <note>meaning due to specific circumstances rather than the general rule</note>. For in summer, the innate heat is dissolved by the intensity of the air's heat and seeks the exterior parts of the body, leaving the interior cold and diminishing its operations—especially the digestion of chyle and chyme <note>The stages of digested food in the stomach and intestines</note> from which urine is produced. ¶ It also happens by accident that cold humors multiply in summer because of the use of many cold things <note>such as cold drinks or foods</note>. ¶ Conversely, in winter, there is a multiplication of hot humors because of the use of hot foods; and because of the fortification of internal heat <note>heat being trapped inside by the cold outside</note>, it happens by accident that urine is sometimes plentiful, thick, and colored. Therefore, in judging, one must always be mindful of what occurs by accident, lest the judgment be corrupted. ¶ The same reasoning should be applied to different regions in their own way.

¶ Urine of moderate color is a sign of spring and autumn. The first part is proven because in these seasons, heat and cold are tempered; therefore, their action is also tempered. The cooking and tinting of the urine's moisture will likewise be tempered. Thus, by virtue of the goodness of the seasons' heat, the urine is moderate in color. The second part is proven: in autumn, dryness flourishes, and in spring, moisture. In autumn, this lessens the substance of the urine, while in spring, it thickens and increases it, as has been proven elsewhere in this same treatise.

<margin>
Urine related to non-natural things such as craftsmen, etc.
</margin>
¶ A similar judgment can be made regarding the urines of other non-natural things that are not primary, such as crafts, games, sexual intercourse, baths, and massages. ¶ Hence, the urines of blacksmiths are similar to the urines of bodies that exercise much; and the urines of bench-workers <note>original: "banchaziozum"; likely craftsmen or laborers who work seated at benches</note> are like those of fishermen and those who exert themselves near water. ¶ The urines of those who have had intercourse are similar to those in a state of depletion, except that a "hairy" spermatic substance usually appears in the contents. ¶ But take note: there is a great difference among the urines of those who have intercourse. He who has recently engaged in it will produce more tinted urine, and that tint is due to the shaking and inflammation of the spirits, with excess matter mixed into the urine. ¶ But the urine of those who engage in intercourse frequently, or who have not done so recently, will be thin, clear, and sparse because of the dissipation of natural heat and the consumption of moisture. ¶ The urines of those using baths vary according to the variety of the baths. For those who bathe in cold water, their urine is virtually discolored and thickened in many ways. If they bathe in sulfurous waters, it becomes sparse and thin. ¶ The urines of those serving in steam rooms <note>original: "stuffis"; heated rooms or dry baths</note> are sparse and raw because the heat is diverted to the exterior, leading to imperfect digestion and the consumption of moisture. ¶ It must be understood, however, that whatever is said about the urines of these non-natural things is verified only insofar as that specific factor is concerned; there should be no excess or defect in the other factors. The same must be felt in other clinical signs, as was said in the first part, so that no error occurs. In these matters, if several factors coincide, they should be weighed against each other and a judgment made by comparison.

<column-break/>

### On the urines regarding things against nature. Chapter VI.

Things "against nature" are said to be three: disease, the cause of disease, and the "accident" <note>symptom or complication</note> of disease. These are the primary things, to which is added one related thing: the timing of the disease. Among the primary things, the urines of the diseases themselves must be categorized. Regarding the causes of disease—since they are nothing other than the efficient causes of health being improperly applied, or they are other diseases that cause a secondary one, or they are "dispositional" causes which are simply natural things—there is no need to describe their urines separately, as we have already explained urines regarding natural and non-natural things in their proper places. Therefore, among all primary things against nature, it will suffice for us to describe only the urines of diseases. Nor is it necessary to conduct a separate investigation into the "accidents" (symptoms), because accidents are either diseases themselves—and thus will be sufficiently covered where we place the urines of diseases—or they are pure accidents which, since they depend on the diseases, can be signified by the same urines that signify the diseases. For that which is a sign of a cause can also be said to be a sign of the effect. We shall add, moreover, the timing of the disease through the urines, so that there may be a fuller knowledge of illnesses, not only as to their essence but also their progression. Let us speak, then, beginning from the head.

<margin>
Urine of the phrenetic.
</margin>
¶ The urine of a phrenetic <note>someone suffering from "phrenitis," an acute fever with delirium</note> is white in color, thin in substance, clear in transparency, and sparse in quantity. This appears especially in acute fevers after the urine was previously highly tinted, thick, and not so clear, and has thus changed imperceptibly without any relief for the patient. The reason for this can be that since it was previously plentiful, tinted, and thick, it showed that many sharp humors were present in the body; and since they were not expelled externally by a "crisis," they must have moved elsewhere. Because such humors are hot and light, it can easily be conjectured that they sought the upper parts and, collecting in the regions of the brain, caused an abscess <note>original: "apoſtema"</note>.

<margin>
Urine of the lethargic.
</margin>
¶ The urine of the lethargic is white or reddish in color, thick throughout the substance, but livid <note>bluish-gray</note> from the middle region upward, having a thick ring. It is usually passed imperceptibly or with great effort.

¶ The urine of the epileptic is thin, with much substance, white in color, dark in transparency, and has a thick, leaden-colored ring.

¶ The urine of the pleuritic <note>suffering from pleurisy, inflammation of the chest</note> is thin, with much red or reddish substance, thick throughout, but livid or dark around the middle region.

¶ The urine of the peripneumonic <note>suffering from pneumonia</note> is tawny or sub-tawny in color, thick in substance, and distinctly livid in the middle region.

<margin>
Urine of any respiratory ailment.
</margin>
¶ For any poor condition of the respiratory organs <note>original: "spūalium membꝛoꝛ"; the "spiritual" members, i.e., the heart and lungs</note>, the urine is generally tawny, sub-tawny, citrine, sub-citrine, pale, sub-pale, greenish-gray, milky, or white; it is thin or moderate in substance, turning livid from the middle upward or around the middle, especially if it is without granules.

¶ In an abscess of the liver, the urine is red or wine-colored <note>original: "inopos"</note> from the middle downward; but above, it is green, livid, black, or near-black, and thick throughout its substance.

<margin>
Urine of the jaundiced.
</margin>
¶ The urine of the jaundiced is black when it results from a vehement "burning" <note>intense heat/inflammation</note> and the patient suffers from great heat. This was preceded by citrine or red urine, and its sediment is fragmented, unequal, and disconnected. It is not an intense black, but rather tends toward citrine and saffron, and is dark in transparency.

¶ Urine that is tawny or sub-tawny in color, moderately thick in substance, and has a saffron-colored foam on top signifies a "saffron" jaundice <note>yellow jaundice</note>.

¶ Red, sub-red, or wine-colored urine with a thick substance and green foam signifies "green" jaundice.

¶ Wine-colored urine with a thick substance and black foam signifies "black" jaundice.

¶ The urine of those with liver or spleen issues is citrine or sub-citrine...

# Concerning [the Signs of Urines]

...citrine <note>a yellow-gold color resembling citrus fruit</note> in color and thin in substance—indeed, very thin—and lasting a long time, like a long small rod. ¶ The urine of an obstruction of the liver or spleen proceeding from a cold cause: white or inclining toward white in color, thin, clear throughout, rod-like, and lasting for a long time.

<margin>
The urine of dropsy and hyposarca.
</margin>
¶ The urine of hyposarca <note>original: "hyposarce"; a type of dropsy characterized by generalized swelling under the skin</note>: pale or sub-pale in color, greyish-blue <note>original: "karopos"</note>, sea-green <note>original: "glauca"</note>, milky, or white. It is thick in substance throughout, sparse in quantity, and lasts a long time in this state, especially in autumn, winter, or the beginning of spring. ¶ The urine of ascites <note>dropsy characterized by fluid accumulation in the abdomen</note>: reddish or sub-reddish in color, moderately thick or thick in substance, sparse in quantity, appearing shaded and leaden <note>original: "liuens"; a bluish-grey color associated with poor circulation or deathly humors</note> on the top, and appearing so for a long time. ¶ The urine of tympanites <note>dropsy where the abdomen is distended by gas, sounding like a drum</note>: reddish in color, thin or moderately thick in substance, lasting a long time, particularly in autumn, winter, and the start of spring.

<margin>
The urine of a diabetic or a wasted body.
</margin>
¶ The urine of a diabetic <term>diabetes: then understood as a "wasting" disease where the body melts into urine</term> or a wasted body: white or sub-pale, thin and plentiful, passed frequently, accompanied by wasting and thirst, and persisting for a long duration.

¶ The urine of a stone is said to be twofold, according to the two differences of the stone: both regarding the place where it is generated and regarding its state. Concerning the place: some are generated in the bladder and some in the kidneys. Concerning its state: some are in the process of forming and being confirmed; some are already fully formed and confirmed; and some are briefly in the process of dissolving. Therefore, keeping all these in mind, the urine must be noted. First, regarding a stone in the kidneys according to all three differences—forming, formed, and dissolving—and then regarding a stone in the bladder according to its differences.

¶ The urine of a stone forming in the kidneys: thin in substance, with an increase in heaviness and pain around the kidney regions, and a decrease in red sand granules <note>original: "arenularum rubearum"</note>. ¶ The urine of a stone already formed and confirmed: the aforementioned urine but discolored and thin without sand granules; with pain, heaviness, and difficulty urinating, especially if it appears after a previous abundance of sand. ¶ The urine of a stone dissolving, or one that is being diminished and broken down: discolored, coarse, plentiful, and turbid, with the appearance of many red sand granules, and the relief of pain and heaviness around the kidney regions, along with the removal of difficulty in urinating; especially if it appears after a period of being thin and clear without sand, but with heaviness and difficulty.

¶ The urine of a stone in the bladder, according to all differences—forming, formed, and dissolving—is the same as above, except for the red sand and the heaviness in the kidneys; for in the case of a bladder stone, the sand granules are white, the heaviness appears in the bladder alone, and the difficulty in urinating is greater.

<margin>
Nephritic urine.
</margin>
¶ Nephritic <note>relating to kidney disease or inflammation</note> urine is white and thick, with much white, mucilaginous sediment, passed in small quantities and frequently. ¶ The urine of strangury <note>painful, drop-by-drop urination</note> is exactly the same as the one mentioned above. ¶ The urine of an excoriation <note>a "scraping" or raw ulceration</note> of the bladder or kidneys is scaly, with pain in the kidneys or bladder. If the scales are white, they signify excoriation of the bladder; if red, they signify the kidneys. ¶ Furthermore, the urines of the kidneys and bladder with pus <note>original: "sanie"</note> and difficulty urinating: if the pus is red and plentiful, it signifies an ulcer of the kidney; if it is white and sparse, an ulcer of the bladder.

<margin>
The urine of arthritis and gout.
</margin>
¶ The urine of gout <note>original: "podagre"</note> or arthritis: reddish or sub-reddish, citrine or sub-citrine, pale or sub-pale, thin in substance, especially in its lower parts. If red granules appear, it signifies arthritis or gout from hot humors. ¶ White, pale, or sea-green urine that is thin with white granules signifies arthritis proceeding from cold matter.

¶ The urine of the first type of hectic fever <term>hectic fever: a chronic, wasting fever, often associated with consumption or tuberculosis</term>: reddish or sub-reddish, citrine or sub-citrine in color, moderate in substance, with leaf-like <note>original: "petaloicis"</note> residues <note>small flakes like dried leaves</note>, unless they are caused by a defect of the bladder; and this is if it follows another fever, especially a humoral one.

<column-break/>

If, however, it follows an ephemeral fever <note>a fever lasting only a day</note> or starts on its own at its beginning, it is not unusual for it to be similar to natural urine in color and substance. But it differs in its content, for it is necessary for many leaf-like residues to appear in it. And on the surface of the urine, there is a certain oiliness, as if oil had been placed upon it.

¶ The urine of the third type of hectic fever: reddish or citrine in color, somewhat thick in substance, and oily throughout; it has a film floating on the surface, and if the urine is tilted slightly to one side, the film will stick to the opposite side. This urine also contains hair-like <note>original: "crynoidales"</note> residues.

¶ From these, it is easy to understand the urine of the second type, as it is intermediate between the others. Thus its urine behaves proportionally in its own way, having bran-like <note>original: "furfures"</note> flakes as content where the others have leaf-like or hair-like residues.

<margin>
The urine of choleric fever.
</margin>
¶ The urine of a simple choleric fever: reddish in color, thick in substance, plentiful in quantity, and somewhat dark in transparency. ¶ The urine of a continuous tertian fever <note>a fever recurring every third day, or roughly every 48 hours</note>: reddish or sub-reddish in color, thin in substance. ¶ Urine citrine in color and moderately thin in substance signifies a tertian fever from citrine <note>yellow</note> bile.

<margin>
The urine of phlegmatic fever.
</margin>
¶ Green or black urine in acute fevers signifies the generation of bile that is rusted <note>original: "passue"</note> or verdigris-colored <note>original: "eruginose"</note>. ¶ The urine of a quotidian <note>daily</note> fever from natural phlegm: sub-pale, citrine, or sub-citrine in color, and equally thick throughout without any leaden <note>livid</note> tint. ¶ Urine sub-citrine in color or close to paleness, of moderate substance, signifies a quotidian fever from acid phlegm. ¶ Urine reddish or sub-reddish in color, thick throughout without any leaden tint, signifies a quotidian fever from sweet phlegm. ¶ Urine reddish or sub-reddish in color, moderately thin in substance, signifies a quotidian fever from salt phlegm.

<margin>
The urine of quartan fever.
</margin>
¶ The urine of a quartan fever <note>a fever recurring every fourth day, or roughly every 72 hours</note>: citrine in color and thin in substance on the day following the paroxysm <note>the "fit" or peak of the fever</note>; on other days it appears pale or sub-pale in color, unless it is at its end. For at the end of a quartan fever, if the urine appears plentiful, black, and thick, it signifies the termination of the fever, because it indicates that the thick and black melancholic humor is being expelled and purged through the urinary paths.

¶ Urine that is intense sub-citrine in color and thick throughout signifies a double quotidian fever. ¶ Urine that is red or sub-red in color, moderately thin in substance, and shaded on the top, in a young person of choleric temperament, signifies a double tertian fever. It would be otherwise in an old person or a melancholic one; or in a phlegmatic woman, where only reddish or sub-reddish urine signifies a double tertian.

¶ Urine that is deep red or sub-deep red in the lower part, wine-colored <note>original: "inopos"</note> on top, thick throughout, and somewhat leaden/livid on the very top, signifies a localized <note>original: "domotenuz"; perhaps referring to a localized or internal infection</note> fever. ¶ Urine that is first deep red or sub-deep red, and afterward wine-colored, thick throughout, and manifestly leaden on top—or appearing so when a hand is placed [behind the vessel]—signifies the "increase" stage <note>of the disease</note>. ¶ Urine red in color like watery blood, or sub-red, or deep red like oriental saffron, thick throughout and unequal, without leadenness but with a certain clot of blood, signifies an "inflated" <note>congested or gassy</note> stomach.

¶ Urine that is intense citrine or sub-citrine in color, thick throughout, without manifest leadenness, but appearing leaden when a hand is placed behind it, signifies a continuous quotidian fever. ¶ Urine red or sub-red in color, moderately thin (tending more toward thinness), without manifest leadenness, but leaden when the hand is placed behind it, and with a certain foam, signifies a continuous tertian fever.

Urine often signifies various simple fevers, and sometimes one composite fever. However, it is necessary for the physician to note the difference of bodies and the state of other symptoms that appear around 
<margin>Urine of burning fevers.</margin> 
the illnesses; and according to their variety, one may judge differently concerning the significance of one and the same urine. ¶ Urine that is intense or flaming in color, like fire, moderately thin in substance—though declining more toward thinness—without

For through those things which have been written about these, the rest can be easily understood, since all depend on causes that are primitive, antecedent, or conjoined. ¶ The urines of primitive causes are the same as the urines of "non-natural" things <note>the 'six non-naturals' in medieval medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions</note>. The urines of antecedent causes are the same as the urines of preternatural humors; however, those of conjoined causes differ somewhat from these. And since enough has been said about these above, we will not repeat them further. Let these things, therefore, be sufficient for the urines of causes, and also for the remaining diseases depending on them. From what has been said, all things can be easily proven regarding the designation of simple differences accommodated to those things which are said here. It remains, therefore, as pertains to this fourth part, that we describe the urines of the times of disease and its process—provided, however, we first add a chapter in which the doctrine of knowing the location of the illness is handed down.

### On the knowledge of the location of the disease through urine. Chapter VII.

<margin>In every urine there is a vestige of the members.</margin>
To gain foreknowledge of the location of the disease through urines, certain things must first be presupposed which have been proven in general regarding universal signs: namely, that in every urine there is a vestige <note>a trace or physical sign</note> of the body's members. 
As we have said above, every member sends the surplus of its nourishment back to the liver—or at least the wateriness returns to it, which was carried with the blood to the members— and it is sent out through the kidneys and bladder. This surplus of nutrition, or the urine itself, carries with it the impression and vestige of the members from which it returns. ¶ Secondly, it must also be presupposed that different parts in the urine correspond to the different members of our body; these are called "regions" by physicians. There are also members—as we have said—of four kinds: animal, spiritual, natural, and 
<margin>Knowledge of matter in the head.</margin>
generative. Four regions are proportioned to these: the "circle" <note>the top ring of the urine</note> to the head; the airy or uppermost part of the urine to the spiritual members <note>the heart and lungs</note>; the middle to the natural members <note>the liver and digestive organs</note>; and the lowest part to the generative members. ¶ These things being presupposed, let us say that the "circle," according to its various differences of color, thickness, or size, and its properties—namely of foam or granules—shows various passions of the head or brain. ¶ The dispositions of the spiritual virtues are known in the uppermost airy part of the urine; if lividity or darkness appears there, it argues that humoral matter is contained there. For where humoral matter is contained, a multitude of fumes or vapors is generated. For those fumes elevated from the humors and transmitted with the urine occupy that part of the urine which is proportional to the place of the humors from which they are created. Therefore, urine appearing [altered] in the region proportioned to the spiritual organs 

<column-break/>

announces that humors or illness are in the spiritual members. ¶ But it should be noted that these humors which are contained in the spiritual members are there either by way of catarrh <note>the downward flow of excess fluid</note>, or from their own repletion, or from "compassion" <note>sympathetic suffering where one organ affects another</note> with other parts; these are distinguished by specific signs. For if there is lividity or darkness in the aforementioned part along with foam or granules in the "circle," it is a certain sign of catarrh toward the chest. But if that same lividity remains in that part without granules, and with a heaviness around those parts, it portends that it proceeds from repletion <note>an overfilling of the vessels</note>. If, however, the same urine appears without granules and heaviness, but with "compassion" of the stomach or diaphragm, it announces that the illness occurs in these members through sympathy. ¶ The dispositions of the 
<margin>Knowledge of the dispositions of the natural members.</margin>
natural members are known in the middle part of the urine. For if there is lividity in that place, it argues for repletion, or a light obstruction, or weakness of the liver. This is proven by the appearance of humors by the same reasoning as above, and especially when it happens from repletion. If it appears from obstruction, at first glance it seems contrary, since from obstruction the urine should become clear and thin. That is true if the obstruction is total. If it is slight, it prevents the exhalation of smokiness, and thus they are reserved in these members; likewise, such lividity appears from weakness. For a weak liver is sufficient to elevate vapors, but not to 
<margin>Knowledge of the dispositions of the generative members.</margin>
resolve them. ¶ The dispositions of the genital and lower members—namely the intestines, the womb, the kidneys, and the bladder—are known from the lividity appearing in the bottom of the urine and from its contents. For lividity or darkness in the bottom of the urine is caused by smokiness elevated in the womb from menstrual humors, or from menstrual blood flowing or retained, communicated to the urine itself. Similarly in the intestines, from smokiness elevated from humors, as in fluxes <note>diarrhea or dysentery</note>, or matter found in them, or from the virtues, or from a flux of hemorrhoids. By the same reasoning, smokiness is elevated in the kidneys or bladder from humors or ulcers found in them. But in dispositions of the kidneys and bladder, they are more certainly diagnosed from the contents <note>sediment</note>, as has been sufficiently shown. ¶ It must be understood that lividity is sometimes universal and not determined to one region of the urine, but is found indifferently through the whole substance of the urine. Even with this, it may happen that while lividity appears universally throughout, it is more intense in one region than another. Therefore, let us demonstrate the signs of these diversities. For universal lividity signifies an arthritic passion, or a diversity of humors through their perturbation. It appears internally [to signify] combustion, the wasting of members, and finally the mortification of natural heat. These are the distinguishing signs: Universal lividity with granules signifies arthritis. Universal lividity with pain of the internal members signifies [disease of] those members in whose region the darkness appears most distinctly. Universal lividity with "resolutions" <note>breakdown of tissue</note> or hair-like filaments signifies combustion. Universal lividity without these other signs announces a perturbation of the humors or their diversity. These things are sufficient for now; if they are joined to the things above, many of the statements made will become clearer.

### On the urines of the different times of disease. Chapter VIII.

<margin>Urine of a perfectly healthy person.</margin>
The times <note>stages</note> of urines are especially [judged] by the matter; and though they can be distinguished by the diversity of symptoms, the distinction is essentially according to the diversity of the digestion of the matter, which the urine shows through its appearance. Therefore, wishing to describe the urines of the [disease] stages, we wish to signify the stages according to the diversity of digestion through them. ¶ It must first be presupposed, however, what the urine of a perfectly healthy person is like; for by the departure from it, the measures of digestion or indigestion are judged, as we said above regarding natural lapses. It being presupposed, therefore, that the urine of a perfectly healthy person is that which is moderate in quantity, substance, and transparency, of a citrine or clear red color. It should contain "clouds," "substances," and "sediments" <note>three types of healthy contents: nubecula, sublime, and sedimentum</note> resting at the bottom. From this it follows: that which departs from these in color, substance, quantity, and contents will be indicative of indigestion, according to the greater or lesser departure of these properties from moderation. Such urine will be thinner or thicker, whiter or redder, darker or more lipid-like...

...of the standing urine being of another color, place, or shape will be a sign of indigestion <note>original: "indigestionis"; in medieval medicine, this refers to the body's failure to "cook" or process the humors properly</note>. ¶ Let us proceed further by showing the stages of all times <note>The four stages of a disease: beginning, increase, peak, and decline.</note>. ¶ **The Beginning.** Urine is either thin or thick and remains turbid; it is reddish or ruddy, or white or pale, lacking a sediment <note>original: "stentis" / "hypostasis"</note> or having it in the upper part of the urine. ¶ **The Increase.** Urine begins to approach a moderate state in substance, color, and clarity; or, if it was turbid and thick, it suddenly becomes clear and begins to show a visible sediment. ¶ **The Peak.** Urine is moderate in all respects, having a white, light sediment along with the other required conditions. ¶ **The Decline.** The urine remains the same, except that it is more perfect in its conditions, especially in the quantity of the sediment; for there is either no sediment left <note>meaning the "matter" has been cleared</note> or it is of a much smaller quantity. I believe all these things can easily be deduced from what was said above; they were most skillfully collected by Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the foundational authority for medieval medicine</note> in his work *On Crises*, so we do not labor to prove them further. ¶ Note, however, that the progression of digestion in bodily illnesses without putrefaction can be gathered from what is said here, and also from what was said in the chapter on the strengths of the virtues. If you return to that chapter and join it to this completion, you will have the full doctrine.

### Chapter IX.

Every piece of knowledge that can be gained from the urine regarding the dispositions of the human body is highly useful and necessary; yet among these, that which shows the termination of the illness toward good or evil is to be esteemed most of all. For even if other signs serve for the knowledge of the illness and the regulation of its treatment, they similarly certify the state and consistency of the illness, especially at the time they occur. Truly, this more than anything else makes the physician in some way divine, more secure in his work, and worthy of the highest praise and honor. Therefore, even if the other things we noted above have been sufficiently discussed, these things which are delivered here concerning the "good way" <note>the path to recovery</note> must be written after more diligent examination. Let this chapter be kept in memory as a singular treasure. And let it not be a burden if you find many things here that were delivered above in various places; for when things of great honor are repeated ten times, they shall still please. ¶ Urine without strong signs of digestion is not necessarily fatal, for the sick person may be liberated through the long duration and resolution of the humors, if their strength can tolerate it or if a future crisis is expected—specifically when the humor is not of a vehement malice—or perhaps they will be liberated by evacuation through medicine, by which the malignant matter is expelled along with the benign. ¶ Urine that remains entirely "good" in the color of healthy urine, in substance and clarity, and with a laudable sediment, is actually pernicious and fatal in an acute illness. For it signifies that the patient is tending toward death, and Nature, as if despairing, has abandoned the fight. ¶ Urine that is "bad" in color, substance, transparency, and sediment, but is plentiful on critical days <note>specific days of a disease, like the 7th or 14th, when a "crisis" or change was expected</note>, signifies liberation if signs of digestion preceded it.

### ¶ Signs from Quantity.
**Urine** that is sometimes passed in small amounts and sometimes in large amounts, or is sometimes retained in acute fevers, is a bad sign. It signifies either a vehement struggle between the illness and Nature (where sometimes one prevails and sometimes the other), or a laboring of the innate heat and Nature, or a thickness of the matter that makes it difficult for digestion to take place. If this occurs in fevers that are not acute, it indicates a long duration of the illness due to the thickness of the humors.

### ¶ Signs from Substance, Transparency, and Odor.
**Urine** of thin substance sometimes passes as it does in diabetes; if there is also constant thirst, frequency of urinating, and ease of passage, it signifies a very bad sign. But if it occurs because of rawness <note>undigested matter</note>, it would not be as bad. If, however, it is because of an obstruction preventing the exit of thick matter, it is bad. Or if it is from a weakness of the transformative power <note>the body's ability to process fluids</note> and does not pass easily, it is of less malice than in diabetes. ¶ Thin urine persisting for many days

In these cases, however, one must also attend to the color joined with the substance, for from these two, the significance is more plentiful and certain. ¶ Thin urine that turns into thick urine in continuous acute fevers with good signs signifies a crisis through sweat. ¶ This same urine, if joined with bad signs, is very bad, for it signifies a burning in the heart or liver. ¶ Turbid urine that clears up before a crisis does not signify a good thing; it argues for the retention of the matter and a failure of Nature in expelling it. ¶ Thick, turbid urine that does not settle when it clears signifies an evil thing; it argues for a boiling of the humors from a vehement external heat or a weakness of the innate heat. ¶ Thick urine, especially that which is not associated with a nosebleed, signifies an evil thing. ¶ White urine in acute illnesses is bad, for it signifies that the matter is being dispersed through the vapors of the urine; wherever these vapors rush, an illness can be caused unless signs of digestion preceded, in which case they signify a crisis through vomiting or withdrawal. ¶ Thin white urine in acute fevers, which is followed by turbulence and thickness along with its whiteness, signifies a spasm and death. ¶ Black urine in acute illnesses is a bad sign, though not absolutely fatal; for if bad signs are associated with it, but the patient's strength is strong, it can produce various evacuations of every kind; if relief follows these, it is a sign of health. ¶ The less black urine there is, the worse it signifies. For it signifies the consumption of the body's humidity, especially if it becomes thicker. ¶ Black urine declining toward thinness with a large sediment and a sharp odor in acute fevers signifies headache and confusion of the senses. It can also signify a nosebleed or sweat, especially if signs of digestion preceded; however, the crisis will be imperfect in both cases, because the thick part will be retained while the thin part is expelled. ¶ Black urine associated with a "hanging" sediment <note>sediment suspended in the middle of the glass</note> that looks like a black, round, aggregated thing, accompanied by a foul odor, tension in the sides, swellings in the upper abdomen <note>hypochondria</note>, and sweat, signifies death; for the tension portends a spasm and the sweat signifies weakness. ¶ Thin, watery urine reaching toward blackness signifies a long duration due to its thinness and the malice of burning due to its blackness. ¶ Thin black urine passed in acute illnesses when the patient craves hot foods signifies death. ¶ Thin black urine that turns thick and yellow or whitish, if no relief follows, signifies a disease in the liver, specifically jaundice. For if relief were to follow, it would signify a lessening of heat and the start of digestion. If there is only a pause in symptoms, it is because the obstruction has increased and an abscess <note>aposteme</note> is forming in the liver. ¶ Thin black urine passed in acute fevers little by little over a long time, joined with pain in the head and neck, signifies a gradual obstruction of the reason; in women, however, this is not as bad. ¶ Red and thin urine with good signs signifies a swift crisis. The same with opposite signs signifies a swift death, because it proceeds from vehement inflammation. ¶ Thin red urine in acute illnesses signifies headache and confusion. ¶ Thick red urine in acute illnesses, which comes out little by little and frequently and with a stench, signifies vehement heat, restlessness, and a defect of nature; therefore it is to be feared. If, however, its passage were abundant with much sediment, it signifies proper preparation or separation of the humors, and thus is a good sign. ¶ Pure blood, when passed in acute illnesses, signifies a vehement over-fullness <note>repletion</note> of blood with the sharpness of boiling; one must fear "suffocation" <note>an internal overwhelming of the organs</note> which occurs from the over-filling of the ventricles...
