...of the ventricles of the heart: if it moves toward the heart, it signifies death; or apoplexies <note>original: "apoplexias"; a sudden loss of consciousness, often a stroke in medieval terminology</note> if it moves toward the brain, which is a fatal sign. ¶ **Very red urine**: if it appears in fevers caused by exhaustion and turns thick, and then a great deal of sediment appears that does not sink, and there is a headache, it signifies a long-lasting illness. If the same urine appears with good sediment, it signifies a crisis <note>original: "crisim"; the turning point of a disease</note> through sweating, because the matter is moving toward the veins. But the cause of the long duration is that the matter is stubborn and therefore does not thicken nor sink quickly, provided the strength <note>original: "virtus"; the patient's vital life force</note> is still powerful. ¶ Note, however, that such urine is similar to the urine of those with jaundice, except that it does not stain the vessel. ¶ **Red urine**, thin in substance and in its sediment, signifies rawness <note>original: "cruditatē"; the state of humors that have not yet been "cooked" or processed by the body's internal heat</note> and a long duration, especially if the redness is not intense and tends toward turbulence. ¶ **Yellow or whitish urine** in acute fevers, when it turns to whiteness or blackness, signifies an evil outcome, because it indicates vapors rising to the upper parts, and the blackness shows the sharpness <note>the toxicity or intensity</note> of the quality of the illness.

<margin>Signs from the sediment.</margin>

### Sediment 

**Sediment** that is varied in substance and color is bad; for it signifies a multitude of different humors. Likewise, if it consists of tiny parts, it is worse, because it signifies that nature cannot expel it except after the parts are broken down. ¶ Smooth sediment is sometimes better than white. ¶ Red sediment, if it is smooth, is good, because nature is acting upon it. ¶ If the sediment tends toward whiteness and is divided in substance with thick parts, it is fatal; for smoothness of substance obeys expulsion more strongly than the quality of the color. Therefore, where the sediment is smooth, nature has acted upon it; where it is white, not as much. ¶ Foamy sediment and foam whose whiteness comes from air mixing with it is very bad; for much is departing from nature <note>meaning the body's vital force is being leaked out</note>. ¶ Raw and non-sharp sediment is bad. ¶ Sediment whose upper parts are round and move is better than sediment whose upper surface is clotted; for it signifies a swift resolution in acute cases. ¶ Red sediment that was not preceded by thinness and a small amount of urine found at the beginning signifies a multitude of humors and not the digestion of humors; it argues for a large and thick matter. ¶ However, red sediment after the onset of digestion, and after thin urine and a small amount of deposit <note>original: "hypostasis"</note>, is good. ¶ Intense staining of the urine without much sediment—that is, with much or none—and when it is not as it should be, does not signify good; sometimes it signifies recovery and maturation, sometimes it occurs because of intense heat, and sometimes because of hunger—for hunger both stains the urine and increases the sediment. ¶ Red sediment signifies a multitude of blood and a delay in digestion. But if the illness extends to 40 days, a crisis is perhaps not to be hoped for until the 60th. ¶ Floating red sediment that stays near the top with thin urine in acute cases signifies a disturbance of reason <note>delirium or mental confusion</note>. If it persists, destruction <note>death</note> is approaching. ¶ Red sediment, when the substance of the urine begins to thicken and the floating sediment begins to sink and turn white, signifies health. ¶ Sediment in the form of a piece of flesh in acute fevers without signs of digestion signifies that it comes from the wasting away of the limbs and not from the kidneys. However, this sediment of "flesh," when there is no digestion or fever, signifies what you know to be from the kidneys <note>likely referring to kidney stones or tissue sloughing</note>. ¶ Sediment with scales like pitch without signs of digestion in acute fevers comes from the scraping of the nerves, bones, veins, and the bladder. ¶ Bran-like sediment signifies something similar, and that the fever is beginning to scrape from the depths. The distinguishing sign

<column-break/>

when it is from the bladder is found in the signs of harm to the bladder, signs of digestion, and thickness. ¶ Oily urine in itself is bad, but if it is accompanied by other good signs, it is not entirely bad. ¶ Oily sediment is bad unless it occurs after black urine, for then it is good; but it is worse if it appears at the beginning of the disease. ¶ Oily sediment on the fourth or seventh day signifies death. ¶ A sudden change of urine to bad signs in acute cases signifies death, because it argues for a collapse of strength, either from toxicity or from the apparent "health" of the symptoms. ¶ Oily urine can occur because of dehydration and signifies a disturbance of reason. ¶ Urine in which there are pieces of clotted blood in acute fevers with a dry tongue is bad; and if the tongue is black, it is worse. For blood does not appear in the urine unless either because of intense sharpness breaking the vessels, or because it clots due to intense heat. ¶ Thin white urine with foam and a bright yellow cloud is extremely frightening, as the urine signifies an exacerbation and intense sharpness of the matter. ¶ **Thin, yellow, whitish urine** at the start of acute illnesses, when it turns to thickness and whiteness, then remains dreggy and turbid like the urine of a donkey, begins to pass involuntarily, and is accompanied by wakefulness and restlessness, signifies a spasm of both sides, followed by death. For yellow urine does not become thin except because of the dominance of the choleric humor, and it does not thicken or become dense except through the worsening of the illness and a commotion in the state of the matter. ¶ A small amount of urine with the color of blood, especially when the patient has sciatica <note>original: "passio sciatica"; hip or nerve pain</note>, is bad. ¶ The inability to urinate except for a little, and with pain without an injury or abscess in the urinary organs in acute fevers, accompanied by a frequent and weak pulse, is bad. ¶ Retention of urine in a continuous fever with intense headache and much sweating signifies a spasm. ¶ Urine that drips drop by drop in a quiet fever signifies a nosebleed. If it is in an acute fever, it signifies an approaching evil in the brain; in a quiet fever, it signifies at least fullness and the weakness of nature in expelling. ¶ Involuntary urine in acute illnesses with a weakness of strength argues for damage in the brain, because the sharp, hot matter rises to the brain, which communicates with the muscular parts <note>original: "membra lacertosa"</note>. ¶ Watery urine following thick, foul-smelling, black, or even thick urine is bad. ¶ Urine in which something rises from the bottom to the top like smoke is completely fatal and death is near. ¶ "Pignus" urine <note>A technical term for a specific cloudy or "pledge" appearance</note>, the color of which is like the color of meat-water <note>the liquid resulting from washing raw meat</note> with a foul smell, is fatal. ¶ Although many of the things contained in this chapter are found in several places in this treatise, they were not put in order for the purpose of recognizing an illness as they are here. In other places, they were positioned for the absolute knowledge of the differences in urines; but here, they are placed so that through them we might recognize the end of an illness, whether for good or for evil. And let these things said about urines suffice. In which, as we said from the start, not only should the things said be attended to—which certainly will not be thought of as very well digested <note>A play on words: "digested" means both the body's processing of humors and the author's organization of the text</note>—but we think the method of proceeding should be considered more, which has been specifically drawn out in the example of urines. And let these things suffice for the treatise on urine.

->The End.<-

Here end the golden and most unique treatises on urines and pulses, composed in verse, with the commentaries of the same most profound physician, Master Gilles. <note>Gilles de Corbeil (c. 1140–1224) was a famous French physician whose poems became standard medical textbooks.</note> Together with the distinguished treatise on urines by the most excellent doctor of arts and medicine, Master Pierleone of Spoleto, <note>Pierleone da Spoleto (d. 1492) was the personal physician to Lorenzo de' Medici.</note> now published for the first time; expertly reviewed and corrected of all errors. Added is an elegant table which demonstrates all the principal questions in a marvelous order. Printed by the order and at the expense of the heirs of the noble man, Master Octavianus Scotus, citizen of Monza, and his associates, with the greatest diligence in Venice by Giorgio Arrivabene. In the year of our Lord 1494, on the 22nd day of November.
